## [Smithsonian Office of the Under Secretary for Education arrow-right](https://www.si.edu/education/office-under-secretary)

The Smithsonian has set an ambitious goal to reach every classroom across the U.S. with relevant, engaging, and free education resources. To realize this vision, the Office of the Under Secretary for Education is developing a robust network of partnerships with state education agencies, school districts, educators, and community organizations nationwide to engage teachers and students in the classroom and during out-of-school time.

![Image 5: An intern is instructed about gardening techniques. ](https://www.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/grid/public/screen_shot_2023-10-11_at_9.42.58_am.png.webp?h=eb3ff6ff&itok=J7YRqvRB)

## [Smithsonian Office of Academic Appointments and Internships arrow-right](https://www.si.edu/ofi)

The Smithsonian’s Office of Academic Appointments and Internships has the central management and administrative responsibility for the Institution's internships, fellowships, and other academic appointments. Hundreds of graduate students, scientists and scholars come to the Smithsonian to do independent research under the guidance of a member of our world-class research staff. Fellows conduct research and study utilizing the Smithsonian collections, facilities, and experts in their fields and beyond. In addition, more than 1,800 students pursue internships supporting learning experiences across the Institution.

![Image 6: A young student explores a fossil on the Learning Lab platform.](https://www.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/grid/public/screen_shot_2023-10-11_at_9.46.44_am.png.webp?h=f0dbee23&itok=qANEZx49)

## [Smithsonian Office of Educational Technology arrow-right](https://learninglab.si.edu/)

The Smithsonian Office of Educational Technology (OET) puts the Smithsonian at your fingertips, serving as the gateway to the Institution’s digital educational resources. OET produces and maintains the Smithsonian Learning Lab, an award-winning interactive platform that provides digital tools and resources to help educators and families access Smithsonian resources, customize learning experiences, and create meaningful connections to our museum artifacts from anywhere in the world. It offers free digital access to millions of Smithsonian artworks, artifacts, specimens, recordings, learning activities, and teaching materials for the PK-12 classroom from across the Smithsonian’s 21 museums, education and research centers, and the National Zoo. OET collaborates through partnerships with educational organizations, libraries, school districts, and universities to engage various audiences in using the Lab.

![Image 7: Photograph of the Smithsonian Castle with a blue sky.](https://www.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/grid/public/screen_shot_2023-10-11_at_9.48.51_am.png.webp?h=bf4f5e64&itok=Qp24VScl)

## [Smithsonian Associates arrow-right](https://smithsonianassociates.org/ticketing/)

Smithsonian Associates offers unparalleled access to the Smithsonian's world of knowledge through innovative, engaging learning experiences for people of all ages. The largest museum-based educational program in the world, Smithsonian Associates annually offers more than 1,000 livestreamed and in-person lectures, seminars, performances, studio art classes, study tours, and children’s programs. Performances at Discovery Theater, Smithsonian Nighttime Adventures and Sleepovers, and more than 80 educationally focused summer camps are among the programs that foster the joys of learning for young people and their families.

![Image 8: A group of students wearing masks smiles at the camera. One is holding a shark jaw.](https://www.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/grid/public/nmnh-interns-2_1.jpg.webp?h=0530bff3&itok=zCb0hBxD)

## [Smithsonian Affiliations arrow-right](https://affiliations.si.edu/)

Smithsonian Affiliations share the Institution’s resources with Americans in their own communities by developing collaborative relationships with museums, cultural, and educational organizations. Together, we bring the Smithsonian, in all of its breadth and scope, to local communities and create lasting experiences that broaden perspectives on science, history, world cultures, and the arts. There are more than 200 Smithsonian Affiliates in nearly every state, Puerto Rico, and Panama. Affiliations is a program of Smithsonian Institution Traveling Exhibition Service | Smithsonian Affiliations.

![Image 9: A woman interacts with a screen in an exhibition.](https://www.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/grid/public/sites_education_060a0752.jpg.webp?h=57788987&itok=D3PVkgNj)

## [Smithsonian Institution Traveling Exhibition Service arrow-right](http://sites.si.edu/)

The Smithsonian Institution Traveling Exhibition Service (SITES) serves as the Institution’s ambassador and emissary through traveling and virtual exhibits that bring knowledge, discovery, and experiences to people across America and beyond. Wherever SITES goes, it stimulates conversations: between the national and local, between the expected and unexpected. SITES’ presence changes lives, institutions, and communities. SITES is a program of Smithsonian Institution Traveling Exhibition Service | Smithsonian Affiliations. (Image: courtesy the Heinz History Center)

![Image 10: A community leader tells stories on a porch while a filming crew captures the moment.](https://www.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/grid/public/moms.png.webp?h=77f54421&itok=VHZTyvBp)

## [Museum on Main Street arrow-right](https://museumonmainstreet.org/)

Museum on Main Street is a Smithsonian outreach program that engages small town audiences and brings revitalized attention to underserved rural communities. We partner with state humanities councils to bring traveling exhibitions, educational resources, story collection projects, and programming to small towns across America through their own local museums, historical societies, and other cultural venues. Museum on Main Street is a program of Smithsonian Institution Traveling Exhibition Service | Smithsonian Affiliations. (Image: courtesy St. Joseph Museum and Cultural Center)

![Image 11: A group of 4H members pose in a museum courtyard.](https://www.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/grid/public/rural.png.webp?h=ef835768&itok=7yTYN8MS)

## [Smithsonian Rural Initiative arrow-right](https://www.si.edu/education/rural-communities)

The Smithsonian Rural Initiative, founded in 2021, provides space for dialogue, prioritizes diversity, and leads our collaborations with networks of local organizations serving rural communities. Working with local leaders to identify specific needs, the Smithsonian commits to expanding programming and resources in regions where needs are greatest. As much as we seek to share, we aim to learn even more from communities across the country.

![Image 12: Two young students investigate a museum object.](https://www.si.edu/sites/default/files/styles/grid/public/ssec_inside_image_2_0.jpg.webp?h=604fe604&itok=PiSbv4hk)

## [Smithsonian Science Education Center arrow-right](https://ssec.si.edu/)

The Smithsonian Science Education Center is transforming K–12 Education through Science in collaboration with communities across the globe. This unique organization promotes inquiry-based STEM teaching and learning; ensures diversity, equity, accessibility, and inclusion in K–12 STEM education; advances STEM education for sustainable development; and translates the research and collections of the Smithsonian into meaningful tools and convenings for K–12 students, teachers and administrators through its STEM curriculum, digital assets, professional development, and leadership development.

This webpage describes the Smithsonian Institution's Education Centers and the organization's educational mission. The Smithsonian is described as "a laboratory for learning and innovation" that shares its collections and research with learners of all ages and educators everywhere. Key facts include: more than 300 educators and 200 Affiliate organizations bring Smithsonian knowledge to more than 8 million learners across the globe each year. The institution encompasses 21 museums, 14 education and research centers, and the National Zoo, all committed to reaching diverse audiences including under-resourced communities and underserved individuals.

The page profiles several key education-focused offices and programs:

1. **Smithsonian Office of the Under Secretary for Education** – Working to reach every classroom in the U.S. with relevant, engaging, and free education resources through partnerships with state education agencies, school districts, educators, and community organizations.

2. **Smithsonian Office of Academic Appointments and Internships** – Manages internships, fellowships, and academic appointments. Hundreds of graduate students, scientists, and scholars conduct independent research under Smithsonian research staff, with more than 1,800 students pursuing internships annually.

3. **Smithsonian Office of Educational Technology (OET)** – Produces and maintains the Smithsonian Learning Lab, an award-winning interactive platform offering free digital access to millions of Smithsonian artworks, artifacts, specimens, recordings, learning activities, and teaching materials for PK-12 classrooms.

4. **Smithsonian Associates** – The largest museum-based educational program in the world, offering more than 1,000 livestreamed and in-person lectures, seminars, performances, studio art classes, study tours, and children's programs annually, plus Discovery Theater performances and over 80 educationally focused summer camps.

5. **Smithsonian Affiliations** – Shares the Institution's resources with Americans in their own communities through more than 200 Affiliates in nearly every state, Puerto Rico, and Panama.

6. **Smithsonian Institution Traveling Exhibition Service (SITES)** – Serves as the Institution's ambassador through traveling and virtual exhibits across America.

7. **Museum on Main Street** – An outreach program engaging small-town audiences and underserved rural communities through partnerships with state humanities councils.

8. **Smithsonian Rural Initiative** – Founded in 2021, collaborates with networks of local organizations serving rural communities.

9. **Smithsonian Science Education Center** – Transforms K-12 education through science, promoting inquiry-based STEM teaching, diversity and inclusion in STEM, and translating Smithsonian research into tools for students, teachers, and administrators.

The page also promotes the National Education Summit 2026 (July 14-16, 2026) for PreK-12 educators, librarians, media specialists, and policymakers, and encourages tax-deductible gifts to support education reaching every classroom and community in the nation.

**The Smithsonian offers many resources and programs to support educators, caregivers, and students in the classroom, at home, and at our museums, research centers, and zoo.**

These offerings encompass an extensive collection of online lesson plans, interactive activities, and multimedia materials, all tailored to various grade levels and subjects. Educators can access primary source documents, museum exhibits, and expert-curated content, allowing them to enhance their classroom instruction and engage students in rich, real-world learning experiences. The Smithsonian also hosts professional development opportunities, workshops, and webinars for teachers, fostering continuous growth and innovation in the field of education. Additionally, the Institution's museums, galleries, and research facilities serve as invaluable teaching spaces, where educators can bring their students to explore and interact with the vast and diverse world of knowledge and culture that the Smithsonian preserves and showcases.

This is the homepage of the Smithsonian Science Education Center (SSEC), which describes its mission as transforming K-12 education through science by connecting classrooms worldwide with the science, history, research, and culture of the Smithsonian. The organization provides hands-on STEM curriculum, resources, and professional development programs to inspire curiosity, empower educators, and ensure every learner has access to high-quality science education.

Key areas of focus include three main goals: Innovation (K-12 STEM teaching and learning), Inclusion (DEAI in STEM), and Sustainability (sustainable development). The center offers a wide range of curriculum resources including Smithsonian Science for the Classroom, Smithsonian Science for Global Goals, Smithsonian Science Stories, STCMS, Explore Smithsonian, Smithsonian Science for Makerspaces, and Smithsonian Science for Computational Thinking. Professional development offerings include academies for teachers, Good Thinking!, and programs for English Learners in STEM. Leadership development programs include Zero Barriers in STEM, NESST, STEAM Schools of Distinction, and the Strategic Planning Institute.

Founded in 1985, the center's Director is Dr. Carol O'Donnell, who holds the newly established Douglas M. Lapp and Anne B. Keiser Endowed Directorship. Featured content highlights include the "Stories of Women in STEAM Innovation: Celebrating America's 250th" eBook, "Zero Barriers!" curriculum guide, "Innovation! How can we create new solutions for the changing climate?" (developed with IAP), educational games such as Global Health Connect, Pick Your Plate, and Whale Protection Corps, sustainability lesson sets, the "Yuck! That Tastes Terrible" genetics resource, and reports on Educating for Sustainable Development. The center also has a 2021-2026 Strategic Plan.

# Learning Programmes

Opportunities for people to create, play, and learn with art

![Image of mangrove steel pan band playing to an audience in the Duveens at Tate Britain](https://media.tate.org.uk/aztate-prd-ew-dg-wgtail-st1-ctr-data/images/Screenshot_2025-06-26_at_16.42.06.width-420.png)

* [Early Years and Families](#early-years-and-families)
* [Schools and Teachers](#schools-and-teachers)
* [Young People's Programmes](#young-peoples-programmes)
* [Public Programmes](#public-programmes)
* [Learning Research](#learning-research)

## Who we are

We are Learning and we invite visitors to create, play, question with and learn from art. We draw inspiration from Tate’s collection and exhibitions, as well as issues that interest artists past and present and the role art, artists, and museums can play in society.

## What we do

We create activities and resources for people of all ages to engage with art, in our London galleries and online. Our programme includes large-scale events and festivals, workshops, talks, tours, film screenings, and paper and digital resources – things to see, make, read, do, play with, and learn from.

Our programme is free and often requires no ticket. We do not presume any art knowledge or experience – all are welcome!

## Who we programme with

We work with artists throughout our programme. We also partner with organisations – across youth, cultural, education, community sectors, and beyond – to share knowledge and resources and to create new opportunities for people to enjoy art and take up space in our galleries.

## Early Years and Families

![Image of two children playing in the studio in bright colours](https://media.tate.org.uk/aztate-prd-ew-dg-wgtail-st1-ctr-data/images/Screenshot_2025-06-26_at_16.44.24.width-420.png)  

UNIQLO Tate Play, Joy of Feeling, Tate Modern, 2024

Taking inspiration from the art on display, our activities, events, and resources offer families new ways to get creative and explore art together.

We have dedicated spaces in gallery where families can make, play, read, imagine, and spend time together. Our resources and creative materials are on offer during term time and there are exciting things to see and do every day in the school holidays.

Everyone is welcome – whether it’s your first visit or have come with your family many times before.

[See our early years and families offer](https://www.tate.org.uk/visit/families-at-tate)

## Schools and Teachers

![](https://media.tate.org.uk/aztate-prd-ew-dg-wgtail-st1-ctr-data/images/Paint_Rooms_-_Schools_Week_Tate_Britain_2024_1.width-420_PfO1N9B.jpg)  

Paint Room. 2025. Schools Week © Tate (Larina Fernandes)

Our Schools and Teachers programme supports young people and teachers to learn about themselves and others through being with art.

We offer options at our galleries and online that invite school students and teachers to try out new ideas and processes, and introduce ways to extend and develop these back in the classroom. We have activities suitable for students of all ages and backgrounds including students with special educational needs or disabilities.

[See our schools and teachers offer](https://www.tate.org.uk/visit/school-visits-to-tate)

## Young People's Programmes

![](https://media.tate.org.uk/aztate-prd-ew-dg-wgtail-st1-ctr-data/images/TateLatebyLittleSimz-4897-use.width-420.jpg)  

© Karolina Wielocha

We create space for young people from all backgrounds to explore the world around them through art, culture, and ideas. We champion the creativity of diverse young Londoners while offering global perspectives on artists and artistic practices.

Our programme is a mix of large-scale events and small, regular opportunities for young people to connect with artists, their peers, and Tate’s collection and spaces.

We collaborate with young people, artists, and partners to create our programme. [Tate Collective Producers](https://www.tate.org.uk/tate-collective/producers) are a group of 15–25-year-olds who work with us to create events, activities, and resources for their peers, while also building their own creative skills.

[See what's on for young people](/whats-on?event_group=all&gallery_group=all&daterange=fromnow&audience_type=young_people)

## Public Programmes

![](https://media.tate.org.uk/aztate-prd-ew-dg-wgtail-st1-ctr-data/images/Tate_Modern_An_Evening_of_South_African_Musicl.width-420.jpg)  

An Evening of South African Music. 2024

We create opportunities where adults can engage with art, artists, and ideas as well as broader social and cultural issues.

Our programme is a mix of large-scale events and smaller workshops, talks, film screenings, live music, and other gatherings. We support life-long creative learning and enjoyment of art, championing the different ways this can take place in our galleries and online.

[See our public programme](/whats-on?event_group=all&gallery_group=all&daterange=fromnow&audience_type=adult_learners)

## Learning Research

Research and evaluation inform all of our programming. We also undertake specific research projects which look at topics across creative learning, arts education, and the cultural sector more broadly.

[Read more about our research](/research/research-centres/tate-research-centre-learning)

# How British Museum artefacts are coming out of the cabinets and into the classroom

## An ongoing initiative aims to inspire youngsters around England

[Gareth Harris](/authors/gareth-harris)

16 October 2025

Share

![A session of the British Museum’s International Training Programme focuses on how institutions around the world can engage with primary schools © The Trustees of the British Museum](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/cxgd3urn/production/faaa531b8352a9544059febd0036ccc04af6b279-2447x1572.jpg?w=1200&h=771&q=85&fit=crop&auto=format)

A session of the British Museum’s International Training Programme focuses on how institutions around the world can engage with primary schools © The Trustees of the British Museum

Objects owned by the British Museum are hitting the road. In recent years, the London museum has quietly taken awe-inspiring artefacts into classrooms across England, giving students in primary schools the chance to view ancient treasures normally kept behind glass.

British Museum in your Classroom, part of the National Programmes partner organisation programme, is an ongoing project that involves taking museum items to schools. In one example, in late 2022, Billingham South Community Primary, Stockton, and St Joseph’s Catholic Primary in Middlesbrough came together to select an object from the British Museum to study and savour. They chose a 3,500-year-old canopic jar, which became the centrepiece of exhibitions hosted by both schools and a focus of their history topic work.

“The children were bouncing off the walls; we had children coming up to read the hieroglyphs,” says Loretta Kilroe, the British Museum’s curator for Sudan and Nubia. The initiative, developed with Tees Valley Museums, was linked to the show *Ancient Egyptians: secrets of the afterlife* at the Dorman Museum in Middlesbrough.

The project sparked debate about how museum educators continue to engage with the public. But what makes up a museum learning department? At the British Museum, it encompasses around 20 staff who are supported by a team of 70 artists, educators and museum teachers; this is supported further by around 500 volunteers. In relation to schools, Shani Crawford, the museum’s head of learning and programmes, says that “most of our offer is geared towards Key Stage Two (KS2) students”, primary school children aged between seven and 11.

On-site activities are varied, from “tablet tours”—technology bringing galleries to life through augmented reality—to interactive presentations in the museum lecture theatre for multiple classes, which can be a “child’s first introduction to a lecture”, Crawford says. Other KS2 activities include smaller workshops for around 35 students. On the topic of ancient Greece, students find out in a workshop what it means to be an Athenian citizen in the fifth century BC.

The museum’s virtual visits

Digital learning platforms are highly important, with schools encouraged to take part in Virtual Visits, live interactive workshops linking classrooms to an expert in one of the museum’s learning rooms. The “peek into prehistory” programme, for instance, for KS2 students, aligns with the UK national curriculum for history, helping children “discover how archaeologists uncover and interpret the timelines of the Neolithic, Bronze and Iron Ages in Britain”.

Linking to the UK history curriculum is crucial. “We are always keeping our ear to the ground and making sure that we’re aware of changes possibly coming up in the history curriculum,” Crawford says. Curators also feed into learning resources to ensure material is accurate, and check the language used.

“We have many digital resources. I think a lot about digital and how many of our national schools don’t have the opportunity to come to the museum,” Crawford says. “We’re currently doing a lot of work upgrading those resources. With virtual visits, we’re considering how we’re delivering those experiences to one class or sometimes multiple classes.” Schools can keep up to date by signing up to the museum’s monthly schools newsletter. The department is also trialling livestreamed lessons where the museum expert cannot see the students. Course materials state that the students “might be asked to discuss an idea with a partner for a minute. They might be asked to point towards the screen to indicate an option from a list of possible multiple-choice answers”.

An anonymous teacher at a south London primary school says: “I have been a few times to the British Museum with KS2 [students] to look at certain things. They have some very good material online that you can download. I’ve never done their workshops as I like to keep trips free but the price seems fair if you have a class of 30.” Another teacher says that she has to constantly monitor budgets in relation to museum visits so is mindful generally of costs when planning trips.

Students with additional learning needs are also catered for at the museum. Crawford stresses that the department offers provision to children who are neurodiverse: “We do a lot of facilitated activity, but schools can also just make plans to come here without our input.” The museum has posted online two whiteboard presentations for use in classrooms to help students with additional learning needs and their teachers prepare for visits.

The department does not shy away from looking at sensitive topics either. “We have used interesting schools resources, designed by two artists and educators of African Caribbean heritage, who invited young people to think around a lot of issues linked to empire and slavery,” Crawford says.

Adult learning activities can take a number of forms, from short courses and gallery talks to lectures and festivals. The key is diversity, Crawford says. “The biggest shift since the pandemic has been towards online events. We’re also asking: Are we focusing on younger people, people under 35, or people who may not be experts in the subject matter?”

> It sounds trite but the British Museum is for everyone
>
> Shani Crawford, head of learning and programmes, British Museum

The BM’s initiatives for younger audiences have flown under the radar to a degree, though. The project Where We Are...is a national programme for young people, specifically underserved groups aged 16 to 24. With the support of the British Museum, local partner institutions manage the recruitment of 15 young people and the co-production of a youth-led arts or cultural project. From 2023 to 2024, partners have included Wakefield Museums and Castles in West Yorkshire. Hanouf Al-Alawi, the museum’s national outreach manager, told *UK Museums Journal* that the group of young people in Wakefield had not set foot in a museum before: “By the end of the sessions they had created the Youth Forum [a group of ten 16- to 25-year-olds that meets monthly to explore a different topic or area of the museum service]. I can say with a lot of confidence that the programme has made a huge difference to young people.

She continued: “It’s not about teaching young people how to engage with museums; the onus of that disengagement is on the museums themselves.”

Where next for the learning department? Changes are afoot as the museum embarks on its masterplan, a cultural redevelopment project that will be “the biggest transformation of any museum in the world”, says the director, Nicholas Cullinan, in a statement.

“The museum’s masterplan presents a really great opportunity for us to review our learning programme and to look at how it works in the new version of the British Museum,” says Crawford, who adds that this development has sparked new discussions around “object-based learning”.

“With things coming off display, we see this as a great opportunity,” she says. “Part of that puzzle—and being able to continue to reach the volume of schools that we’re reaching—is how do we then add to that experience of being able to get close up and perhaps even touch objects as well?”

So, what are Crawford’s priorities? “With the masterplan, changing and adapting our learning programme will be guided by and inclusive of what our schools want, as well as being curriculum led. That’s a huge priority.” She is also looking at how the museum ensures it is reaching those schools that are not coming to the museum. “With our adult programmes, we have talked about diversity in the programming. I think everything is audience-led in terms of understanding; it sounds trite but the British Museum is for everyone.”

This feature article from The Art Newspaper (published 16 October 2025, written by Gareth Harris) examines how the British Museum is taking artefacts out of its cabinets and into classrooms across England through an ongoing initiative called "British Museum in your Classroom," part of the National Programmes partner organisation programme. The project brings museum objects to primary schools, giving students access to ancient treasures normally kept behind glass. In late 2022, Billingham South Community Primary (Stockton) and St Joseph's Catholic Primary (Middlesbrough) collaborated to select a 3,500-year-old canopic jar, which became the centrepiece of exhibitions at both schools and was linked to the show "Ancient Egyptians: secrets of the afterlife" at the Dorman Museum in Middlesbrough.

The British Museum's learning department comprises approximately 20 staff supported by a team of 70 artists, educators and museum teachers, plus around 500 volunteers. Head of learning and programmes Shani Crawford notes that most of the museum's school offer targets Key Stage Two (KS2) students (ages 7-11). On-site activities include "tablet tours" using augmented reality, interactive presentations in the museum lecture theatre, and smaller workshops for around 35 students (e.g., exploring what it meant to be an Athenian citizen in fifth-century BC Greece).

Digital learning is highly important, with Virtual Visits (live interactive workshops linking classrooms to museum experts), a "peek into prehistory" programme aligned with the UK national history curriculum, and trials of livestreamed lessons where experts cannot see students. The department also offers provision for neurodiverse students and students with additional learning needs, including whiteboard presentations posted online to help prepare for visits. The museum has also used schools resources designed by artists and educators of African Caribbean heritage to address issues linked to empire and slavery.

For young people, the "Where We Are..." national programme targets underserved groups aged 16 to 24, with partners such as Wakefield Museums and Castles (2023-2024). National outreach manager Hanouf Al-Alawi told UK Museums Journal that the programme helped create a Youth Forum in Wakefield and made a huge difference to young people, noting "the onus of that disengagement is on the museums themselves."

Looking ahead, the museum's masterplan (described by director Nicholas Cullinan as "the biggest transformation of any museum in the world") presents an opportunity to review the learning programme, with new discussions around "object-based learning" and the possibility of getting closer to—and even touching—objects as they come off display. Crawford's priorities include making the learning programme curriculum-led and inclusive of what schools want, reaching schools that don't come to the museum, and ensuring diversity in adult programmes, stating: "It sounds trite but the British Museum is for everyone."
args.key_excerpts: "The children were bouncing off the walls; we had children coming up to read the hieroglyphs," says Loretta Kilroe, the British Museum's curator for Sudan and Nubia., "It sounds trite but the British Museum is for everyone" — Shani Crawford, head of learning and programmes, British Museum., "It's not about teaching young people how to engage with museums; the onus of that disengagement is on the museums themselves." — Hanouf Al-Alawi, the museum's national outreach manager., "With the masterplan, changing and adapting our learning programme will be guided by and inclusive of what our schools want, as well as being curriculum led. That's a huge priority." — Shani Crawford., "The museum's masterplan presents a really great opportunity for us to review our learning programme and to look at how it works in the new version of the British Museum" — Shani Crawford.

The page categorizes cookies into five main types:

1. **Necessary cookies** (no consent required by law) - Used for basic website functionality including session state preservation, user consent state storage, security (bot detection, WAF protection), shopping cart functionality, and load balancing. Providers include Adobe, Cookiebot, Blackbaud, Cloudflare, Google, and the museum itself.

2. **Preference cookies** - Remember user settings such as language preference and country/region. Providers include Sketchfab and WordPress.

3. **Statistics cookies** - Collect anonymous data on visitor behavior for analytics and reporting. Providers include Microsoft, Google Analytics, Quantcast, Hotjar, TikTok, and others. These track page views, visit duration, heatmaps, and user navigation patterns.

4. **Marketing cookies** - Track visitors across websites to display relevant, targeted advertisements. Providers include Google, Microsoft, Meta (Facebook), TikTok, LinkedIn, YouTube, StackAdapt, Soundcloud, PayPal, and others. These enable ad tracking, conversion measurement, and cross-site user profiling.

5. **Unclassified cookies** - Currently being classified with providers including Blackbaud, New Relic, Twitter, and others.

The page also lists the 13 processing "purposes" under GDPR/consent framework:
- Store/access information on a device (794 vendors)
- Use limited data to select advertising (750 vendors, legitimate interest)
- Create profiles for personalised advertising (612 vendors)

## You are in the Schools section

*   [Learn](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn)

## On this page

 On this page 

*   [Home Education Days](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/home-educators#home-education-days)
*   [Ages 7–11 (KS2)](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/home-educators#ages-711-ks2)
*   [Ages 9–14 (KS2 and KS3)](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/home-educators#ages-914-ks2-and-ks3)

*   [Family activities](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/home-educators#family-activities)

## Key information

The next[Home Education Day](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/home-educators#home-education-day)for ages 7–11 (KS2) will be Thursday 1 October 2026.

[Sign up to our Schools and Families newsletters (Opens in new window)](https://emails.britishmuseum.org/k/British-Museum/sign_up_form_from_website_box?)to receive the latest news and booking information.

The British Museum welcomes UK Home Educators.

Spanning ancient Egypt, ancient Greece, ancient Britain, ancient Rome, the Americas, Africa and Asia, the unparalleled collection at the Museum provides inspiration across a number of curriculum areas.

When visiting the Museum, UK Home Educators can enjoy [family activities](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/home-educators#family-activities), with trails free to download and to use on your personal device. UK Home Educators can also book free tickets for most paid [exhibitions](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/home-educators#museum-exhibitions).

Please note that all Home Educator sessions must be booked in advance by calling the Box Office team on +44 (0)20 7323 8181.

## Home Educator's offer update

We have some exciting changes happening that support our path to net zero as part of the [Museum's Masterplan](https://www.britishmuseum.org/about-us/masterplan "The Masterplan"). This will mean some reductions in public programmes, including facilitated school programmes, in-person school group visits and lunch and locker capacity at the Museum whilst key infrastructure work is carried out. The Museum recognises that this reduction in capacity may lead to some disappointment for home educators and students, however, the Museum's learning team are working hard to bring new programming opportunities.

The following programmes will be going ahead in the 2026/27 academic year:

*   Ages 7–11 (KS2): [presentations](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/home-educators#ages-711-ks2)delivered in the BP Lecture Theatre
*   Ages 7–11 (KS2): [taught workshops](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/home-educators#ks2-taught-workshops)delivered in the Clore Centre for Education
*   Ages 9–14 (KS2 and KS3): creative workshops in the Clore Centre for Education and Museum galleries
*   Ages 11–14 (KS3): [presentations](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/home-educators#ages-1114-ks3) delivered in the BP Lecture Theatre
*   Ages 14–16 (KS4): [gallery-based talks](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/home-educators#ages-1416-ks4)

If you're looking for inspiration at home, the Museum provides a range of free learning resources on a host of topics.

Please [sign up to our schools e-newsletter (Opens in new window)](https://emails.britishmuseum.org/k/British-Museum/sign_up_form_from_website_box?_gl=1*ube6j6*_gcl_au*MTIyOTcwNzAxLjE3NDM1MTg5NjI.*_ga*MTYxNjU0NTkyOC4xNzQzNTE4OTYy*_ga_08TLB9R8X1*MTc0MzUxODk2MC4xLjEuMTc0MzUxOTMzMy4yMC4wLjA.) for the latest news on our schools offer and check our school web pages regularly.

![Image 3: Graphic rendition of the British Museum site showing three new buildings outlined in blue which form the Energy Centre.](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/uncropped_huge/public/2024-08/Bloomsbury_Energy_Centre_1920x1080.jpg?itok=kGEfTSyV)

 Graphic showing an aerial view of the Museum's Camden site. The Energy Centre Programme includes three new buildings (outlined in blue) that only build on 1.8% of the Museum site's footprint: the South West Energy Centre (bottom right), the East Road Building (top) and the Incoming Substation (middle right). Photo © Wright & Wright Architects. 

## Home Education Days

**(Clore Centre for Education and Museum galleries)**

Home Education Days are an opportunity for UK Home Educators to join us with their children to enjoy a day of activities and workshops.

**Ages 7–11 (KS2)**

**Thursday 1 October 2026, 10.00–15.30**

Aimed at young learners aged 7–11 (Key Stage 2), these days are a chance to take part in elements of the taught school offer and also experience more informal, drop-in learning activities. This day will focus on the [_Korea_](https://www.britishmuseum.org/exhibitions/korea)exhibition in the morning with taught workshops in the afternoon. [View the programme](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/2026-08/Home_Education_Day_programme_October_2026.docx) for more information about the activities available.

Each child in this age group attending the day will need to pre-book a ticket costing £9.00 per child (accompanying adults free) which is payable at the time of booking. All booked children should be accompanied by an adult.

To book, please call the Box Office on +44 (0)20 7323 8181.

![Image 4: Mosaic double-headed serpent](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/uncropped_huge/public/2020-04/Double-headed-serpent.jpg?itok=6UsKhkWf)

[Mosaic of a double-headed serpent](https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/E_Am1894-634),Mexico, 15th–16th century. 

## Ages 7–11 (KS2) presentations

**(BP Lecture Theatre, Clore Centre for Education)**

UK Home Educators are able to book spaces for their own children on all Key Stage 2 presentations.

Home Educators spaces are available at both the 10.30 and 12.00 sessions on any date when presentations are programmed to run. Book tickets by phoning the Box Office on +44 (0)20 7323 8181. There is a charge of £2.50 per attending child (accompanying adults free) which is payable at the time of booking. Bookings for a Home Education space on any Key Stage 2 presentation need to be made at least 48 hours in advance. See [terms and conditions](https://www.britishmuseum.org/terms-use/school-bookings) on school bookings.

Full details for each presentation, including support notes and dates, can be found on the presentation pages below.

![Image 5: Stone relief showing a Harpy in profile with large feathered wings outstretched behind her.](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/uncropped_huge/public/2026-01/Harpy-tomb-1000x500.jpg?itok=OWF7fhMI)

[Relief panel from the Harpy Tomb](https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/G_1848-1020-1-3?selectedImageId=32808001), found in Xanthus, modern day Turkey and dated 470–460 BC. 

## School Sessions

*   ![Image 6: Students in a lecture hall ](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_media_small/public/2019-10/SCHOOLS_Lecture_5.jpg?h=f2082b41&itok=t3u9iGjb)  ### [School presentation: Daily life in ancient Egypt](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/ages-7-11/ancient-egypt/school-presentation-daily-life-ancient-egypt)

 For ages 7–11 (KS2) with curriculum links to History, explore the famous tomb-painting of Nebamun in this interactive presentation.      
*   ![Image 8: Students in a lecture hall ](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_media_small/public/2019-10/SCHOOLS_Lecture_1.jpg?h=673e19d8&itok=cWAGrKQE)  ### [School presentation: Egyptian mummies](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/ages-7-11/ancient-egypt/school-presentation-egyptian-mummies)

 For ages 7–11 (KS2) with curriculum links to history, dispel popular misconceptions about mummies in this interactive presentation.      
*   ![Image 10: Students in lecture hall](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_media_small/public/2019-10/SCHOOLS_Lecture_6_0.jpg?h=8ef0dd84&itok=a9FtgAh_)  ### [School presentation: Greek myths](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/ages-7-11/ancient-greece/school-presentation-greek-myths)

 For ages 7–11 (KS2), with curriculum links to History, this interactive presentation focuses on Greek myths through Greek pots.      
*   ![Image 12: Students in a lecture hall ](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_media_small/public/2019-10/SCHOOLS_Lecture_2.jpg?h=8236a2d8&itok=HdZO8VLs)  ### [School presentation: How Roman was Roman Britain?](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/ages-7-11/ancient-rome/school-presentation-how-roman-was-roman-britain)

 For ages 7–11 (KS2) with curriculum links to history, explore objects about Romanisation in this interactive presentation.      

## Ages 7–11 (KS2) taught workshops

**(Clore Centre for Education)**

Taught workshops are available for UK Home Educators and their children aged 7–11 (KS2).

Book tickets by phoning the Box Office on +44 (0)20 7323 8181. There is a charge of £3.00 per attending child aged 7–11 years old (accompanying adults free) which is payable at the time of booking. All booked children should be accompanied by an adult. These sessions are designed for children aged 7–11 (KS2). Spaces are not available on these sessions for younger or older siblings outside the 7–11 age range. See [terms and conditions](https://www.britishmuseum.org/terms-use/school-bookings) on school bookings.

Taught workshops take place in the seminar rooms in the Clore Centre for Education, where you will work alongside other Home Educators. Each workshop lasts 60 minutes. Please see the available workshops and dates below.

![Image 14: An illustrated scene of eight figures in preparation for death.](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/uncropped_huge/public/2019-10/book-dead-hunefer-egypt-mummies-british-museum-1000x500.jpg?itok=VBh_JDPO)

[The Book of the Dead of Hunefer](https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/Y_EA9901-3).The scene shows episodes in Hunefer's judgement. Egypt, 19th Dynasty. 

## Available workshops

### Prehistory

**(Digital Discovery Centre, Clore Centre for Education)**

Discover the range of natural materials used by people in prehistoric Britain to help provide food, shelter and safety for their communities. Handle a range of materials and develop your critical thinking skills as you explore different aspects of prehistoric life.

*   Friday 27 November 2026 at 14.00

### A question for the people

**(Rooms A and B, Clore Centre for Education)**

Use a range of resources to find out what it meant to be an Athenian citizen in the 5th century BC. Then gather as the Athenian Assembly and put their values into practice using role play and decision making.

### Excavation in Egypt

**(Rooms A and B, Clore Centre for Education)**

Explore the history of ancient Egypt using a timeline linking Egypt's past and present. Handle replica objects and discover the fascinating contents of an Egyptian tomb and how archaeologists work.

### How to find out about Greek life

**(Rooms A and B, Clore Centre for Education)**

Develop your enquiry skills by studying images of ancient Greek pots then handle replica Greek objects and use them to find out about different aspects of life in ancient Greece.

## Ages 9–14 (upper KS2 and KS3) creative workshops

**(Clore Centre for Education and Museum galleries)**

Home Education creative workshops offer an opportunity to work with an artist to create a personal response to objects in the Museum collection. These workshops include opportunities for individual and collaborative work with plenty of hands-on activity, creativity and fun. All materials are provided by the Museum and all outcomes can be taken home to add to your own art collection.

These workshops use age-appropriate objects, images, tools and materials. They are suitable for learners aged 9–14 to support art and design skills equivalent to upper Key Stage 2 and Key Stage 3.

Book tickets by phoning the Box Office on +44 (0)20 7323 8181. There is a charge of £5.00 per attending child aged 9–14 years old (accompanying adults free) which is payable at the time of booking. All booked children should be accompanied by an adult. Spaces are not available on these sessions for younger or older siblings outside the 9–14 age range. See [terms and conditions](https://www.britishmuseum.org/terms-use/school-bookings "School bookings") on school bookings.

Japanese book binding took place on 23 April 2026 at 11.00. There are no future sessions available to book at the moment.

![Image 15: Mosaic double-headed serpent](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/uncropped_huge/public/2020-04/Double-headed-serpent.jpg?itok=6UsKhkWf)

[Mosaic of a double-headed serpent](https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/E_Am1894-634),Mexico, 15th–16th century. 

## Ages 11–14 (KS3) presentations

**(BP Lecture Theatre, Clore Centre for Education)**

UK Home Educators are able to book spaces for their own children on the age 11–14 (KS3) presentations in the Museum lecture theatres.

Spaces are available at all sessions on any date when these presentations and talks are programmed to run. Book tickets by phoning the Box Office on +44 (0)20 7323 8181. There is a charge of £2.50 per attending child (accompanying adults free) which is payable at the time of booking. See [terms and conditions](https://www.britishmuseum.org/terms-use/school-bookings) on school bookings. Full details for each session, including content and dates, can be found on the pages below.

* KS3 presentations will only run if 20 paid spaces or more have been booked. If bookings are below this number two weeks before the session is due to take place it will be cancelled, and a refund issued.

![Image 16: The Great dish from the Mildenhall Treasure, a large concave silver platter with beaded rim (135 beads in total) on a circular vertical foot-ring positioned exactly one-third in from the rim. ](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/uncropped_huge/public/2023-11/Mildenhall_Treasure_1000x500.jpg?itok=B__XhW6_)

[The Mildenhall Bacchic platter](https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/H_1946-1007-1), England, 4th century.

## KS3 presentations

*   ![Image 17: Limestone woman's head with a furrowed expression.](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_media_small/public/2022-11/sonte-female-head-1920.jpg?h=d1cb525d&itok=5QWpKUDi)  ### [School presentation: an introduction to Roman Britain](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/ages-11-14/school-presentation-introduction-roman-britain)

 In this presentation explore the evidence that objects provide about key aspects of life in Roman Britain. For ages 11–14 (KS3).      
*   ![Image 19: Marble relief depicting men riding on horses.](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_media_small/public/2022-11/parthenon-north-frieze-1920.jpg?h=d1cb525d&itok=xYlBN1OH)  ### [School presentation: an introduction to the Parthenon sculptures](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/ages-11-14/school-presentation-introduction-parthenon-sculptures)

 Students will be introduced to the ancient Greek cultural, social and historic context for the sculptures. For ages 11–14 (KS3).      
*   ![Image 21: Helmet with grille of linked circles to protect the face, and a broad brim.](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_media_small/public/2022-11/bronze-gladiator-helmet-1000.jpg?h=5dabf909&itok=KeI6T8uj)  ### [School presentation: an introduction to ancient Rome and Roman city life](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/ages-11-14/school-presentation-introduction-ancient-rome-and-roman-city-life)

 In this presentation explore the evidence objects provide about key aspects of life in ancient Rome. For ages 11–14 (KS3).      

## Ages 14–16 (KS4) gallery-based talks

**(Museum galleries)**

Gallery-based talks are available for UK Home Educators and their children aged 14–16 (KS4).

Book tickets for each session by phoning the Box Office on +44 (0)20 7323 8181. There is a charge of £3.00 per attending child (accompanying adults free) which is payable at the time of booking. All booked children should be accompanied by an adult. These sessions are designed for children aged 14–16. Spaces are not available on these sessions for younger or older siblings outside the 14–16 age range. See [terms and conditions](https://www.britishmuseum.org/terms-use/school-bookings) on school bookings.

All gallery-based talks begin at the Roman rider statue in the Great Court and use relevant public galleries in the Museum, where you will work alongside other UK Home Educators. Each talk lasts 50 minutes. Please see the available workshop and dates below.

![Image 23: Students in the Enlightenment Gallery ](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/uncropped_huge/public/2019-10/SCHOOLS_KS4_Galleryart_2.jpg?itok=2XLSSrfV)

 A group of students in the Enlightenment Gallery taking part in a gallery session. 

## Ages 14–16 (KS4)

### Parthenon

**(Rooms 17 and 18)**

Focusing on the prescribed material source, the Parthenon sculptures, this gallery-based talk is designed to support the Classical Civilisations GCSE component Myth and Religion (J199/11). Students will investigate, analyse and interpret material evidence to explore the ancient Greek social, cultural and historic context in which they were created.

*   Thursday 12 November 2026 at 13.00

## Resources

The Museum provides a wide range of free activity sheets and resources aimed at schools that are available to download. All resources are available in Word and can be edited to suit your specific needs.

Resources can be found on the following pages:

## resources

*   ![Image 24: Students with their artwork for printmaking](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_media_small/public/2019-10/KS1_Landingpage.jpg?h=3e72537f&itok=JU6P4NB2)  ### [Ages 3–7](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/ages-3-7)

 Take a look at our ages 3–7 (EYFS/KS1) schools programme.      
*   ![Image 26: Students using tablets in G18 for a self-led ](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_media_small/public/2019-10/KS2_Landing_2.jpg?h=2d732997&itok=j0pIYuai)  ### [Ages 7–11](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/ages-7-11)

 Take a look at our ages 7–11 (KS2) schools programme.      
*   ![Image 28: Students in the gallery ](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_media_small/public/2019-10/SCHOOLS_KS3_Landingpage.jpg?h=b801dc38&itok=CfYqaYJO)  ### [Ages 11–14](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/ages-11-14)

 Explore our ages 11–14 (KS3) schools programme.      
*   ![Image 30: Students in the enlightenment gallery ](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/16_9_media_small/public/2019-10/SCHOOLS_KS4_Galleryart_3.jpg?h=63dd80ae&itok=o6yTsHzm)  ### [Ages 14–16](https://www.britishmuseum.org/learn/schools/ages-14-16)

 Explore our ages 14–16 (KS4) schools programme.      

## Museum exhibitions

UK Home Educators can book free tickets for themselves and their own children for most paying exhibitions as part of the education offer. Spaces can be booked on school exclusive mornings or alongside the general public.Home Educator tickets should be booked via the Box Office by phoning: +44 (0)20 7323 8181.

Please find more information about our current [exhibitions and events](https://www.britishmuseum.org/exhibitions-events "Exhibitions and events").

![Image 32: A section of Sun, Moon and Five Peaks, a painting in vivid blues, greens and reds of mountains, trees and the sun on a folding screen.](https://www.britishmuseum.org/sites/default/files/styles/uncropped_huge/public/2026-06/Korea_main_image_teaser_0.jpg?itok=2a1hP8Fq)

[_Korea_](https://www.britishmuseum.org/exhibitions/korea "Korea") will explore the story of Korean visual and material culture from 300 BC to today. Photo © National Museum of Korea. 

## Activities

There are a number of family activities that can be used to provide learning experiences at the British Museum and from home.Delve into our Museum explorer trails or Museum Missions for families that offer a structured context for visits or home exploration to engage children with the collection.Discover our YouTube playlist of short videos about historical periods in school curriculums. The museum welcomes UK Home Educators, whose collection spans ancient Egypt, Greece, Britain, Rome, the Americas, Africa, and Asia, providing curriculum inspiration across multiple subjects.

KEY OFFER AND CHANGES: The museum is undergoing infrastructure changes as part of its Masterplan (net zero initiative), which will reduce some public programmes. Programmes continuing in the 2026/27 academic year include KS2 presentations (BP Lecture Theatre), KS2 taught workshops (Clore Centre for Education), creative workshops for ages 9–14, KS3 presentations, and KS4 gallery-based talks. All Home Educator sessions must be booked in advance by calling the Box Office on +44 (0)20 7323 8181.

SPECIFIC PROGRAMMES AND PRICING:
• HOME EDUCATION DAYS: Next event for ages 7–11 (KS2) on Thursday 1 October 2026, 10.00–15.30, focusing on the Korea exhibition in the morning with taught workshops in the afternoon. Cost: £9.00 per child (accompanying adults free).
• AGES 7–11 (KS2) PRESENTATIONS: Available at 10.30 and 12.00 sessions; £2.50 per child, adults free. Bookings must be made at least 48 hours in advance. Topics include Daily life in ancient Egypt, Egyptian mummies, Greek myths, and How Roman was Roman Britain?
• AGES 7–11 (KS2) TAUGHT WORKSHOPS: £3.00 per child, 60-minute sessions in the Clore Centre for Education. Available topics: Prehistory (Friday 27 November 2026), A question for the people, Excavation in Egypt, and How to find out about Greek life.
• AGES 9–14 CREATIVE WORKSHOPS: £5.00 per child; artist-led workshops with all materials provided. Japanese book binding took place on 23 April 2026; no future sessions currently available.
• AGES 11–14 (KS3) PRESENTATIONS: £2.50 per child. Topics include an introduction to Roman Britain, the Parthenon sculptures, and ancient Rome/Roman city life. KS3 presentations only run if 20+ paid spaces are booked; otherwise cancelled with refunds two weeks prior.
• AGES 14–16 (KS4) GALLERY-BASED TALKS: £3.00 per child, 50-minute talks beginning at the Roman rider statue in the Great Court. The Parthenon talk (Rooms 17 and 18) supports the Classical Civilisations GCSE component Myth and Religion (J199/11), scheduled for Thursday 12 November 2026 at 13.00.

RESOURCES: Free downloadable activity sheets and resources are available in Word format, organized by age group: Ages 3–7 (EYFS/KS1), Ages 7–11 (KS2), Ages 11–14 (KS3), and Ages 14–16 (KS4).

EXHIBITIONS AND FAMILY ACTIVITIES: UK Home Educators can book free tickets for most paying exhibitions (via Box Office). Family activities include Museum Explorer Trails (free downloadable trails), Museum Missions (free phone/tablet-based activities), YouTube videos for young learners, and the Young Friends membership programme.

CONTACT/MUSEUM DETAILS: Great Russell Street, London WC1B 3DG. Opening hours: Daily 10.00–17.00 (Fridays until 20.30), last entry 16.45 (Fridays 20.15). Newsletter sign-up available for Schools and Families news.

### [Museum Learning](https://www.museumnext.com/article/category/learning/)

# Designing for the Classroom: How Tate Schools Is Rethinking Digital Learning with Art

May 23 2026

![Manuel Charr](https://www.museumnext.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/manuel-1.jpg)

**By Manuel Charr**

What happens when a national museum stops asking “how do we make our collection available online?” and starts asking “what do teachers actually need?” The answer, as Tate’s Effie Coe explained at the Museum Digital Summit 2026, looks quite different from most museum digital education platforms.

When Tate set out to build a new digital learning platform for schools, the team began with a deliberately uncomfortable question: why would teachers want to engage with art through digital spaces at all? It was an honest starting point — and it set the tone for everything that followed.

The result is Tate Schools, a platform developed between 2023 and 2025 through a major digital infrastructure project and close collaboration between Tate’s Learning and Digital teams. Effie Coe, Curator of Digital Content in the schools and teachers team, presented the project at the [Museum Digital Summit 2026](https://www.museumnext.com/events/museum-digital-summit/), walking delegates through the design thinking, the teacher partnerships, and the SEND-first approach that shaped the platform from the ground up.

SEND — Special Educational Needs and Disabilities — is the term used in the UK education system to describe the range of learning differences, disabilities, and additional needs that may require specialist support in the classroom. It encompasses everything from sensory and physical disabilities to conditions such as autism, ADHD, and profound and multiple learning disabilities (PMLD). In a museum learning context, designing for SEND learners means thinking carefully about sensory experience, cognitive load, clear structure, and flexible delivery.

**Want more insights like this?** Explore our upcoming virtual conferences [here](https://www.museumnext.com/events/)

## **Starting from Classroom Reality**

The founding insight behind [Tate Schools](https://www.tate.org.uk/schools) was straightforward but easy to overlook: simply making content available is not enough. Digital learning resources are most powerful when they are shaped by classroom context and real teaching practice.

Rather than working outward from the collection and asking what could be adapted for schools, the team worked inward from the classroom — asking teachers what they needed, where current resources fell short, and what would make them confident enough to bring art into their lessons on a regular basis.

To do this systematically, Tate established a teacher friends group drawing on educators from across the UK — from the Shetland Islands and Newcastle to Birmingham, London, St. Ives, and Margate. Recruited through local networks and regional contacts, the group was designed to bring genuinely diverse expertise and classroom contexts into the process. Members meet regularly, with structured sessions complemented by surveys and follow-up discussions covering everything from sensitive content and curriculum development to usability, accessibility, and practical classroom application.

Crucially, teachers are not simply consulted at the end of the process — they help identify gaps and priorities in resource provision from the start, ensuring the platform reflects what teachers will actually use rather than what institutions assume they need.

A separate strand of the platform, Teacher Spotlight resources, takes this one step further. Each resource is co-created with an expert teacher and shares a real-world example of how they have used specific artworks in their teaching — giving other educators both permission and practical inspiration to try similar approaches.

## **An SEND-First Approach**

One of the most distinctive aspects of Tate Schools is its commitment to an SEND-first design philosophy. Rather than building for a mainstream audience and adapting content for learners with additional needs, the team set out to create resources that are immediately relevant, engaging, and exciting for students with profound and multiple learning disabilities — without any adaptation required.

The logic behind this approach is compelling: resources designed to work for the most complex and diverse learners tend to work better for everyone.

The process began with one-to-one conversations with six SEND practitioners to understand how art-based digital resources are used in sensory classrooms and where the real barriers lie. From these conversations, a clear set of principles emerged: resources need to be intuitive, multisensory, structured in clear steps, and flexible enough to support different learners and contexts.

Two commissions illustrate what this looks like in practice. Lightbox, developed in collaboration with creative digital studio The Workers, is an interactive digital resource designed to support sensory and SEND learners through creative exploration with light, colour, and movement, connecting directly to artworks in Tate’s collection. It was shaped through iterative classroom testing, with teachers and students directly informing how it functions.

**Put these ideas into practice!** Our virtual conferences are designed to help museum professionals do exactly that.  [Find out what’s on](https://www.museumnext.com/events/)

All The Feelings is the first commission in a new Immersion series — a video artwork created by artist India Harvey in collaboration with students and teachers in a special school setting. It invites learners into a playful, immersive experience using movement, sound, and sensory interaction to engage with emotion and creative expression. The Immersion series is designed to evolve, with a new artist commission introduced every two years to ensure fresh perspectives continue to shape how art is experienced in the classroom.

## **Transforming the Collection**

At scale, Tate Schools now offers over 80 resources spanning key stages one to five, featuring more than 300 collection artists. Seventy-five percent of content foregrounds underrepresented artists in UK classrooms — including global majority artists, disabled artists, LGBTQ+ artists, working class artists, and women artists — and over 40% of resource series have been co-produced with artists, teachers, students, or sector peers.

This focus on representation is a direct response to evidence from the field. The Visual Eyes Report, a major study into race and inclusion in art education, found that teachers want to diversify their curriculum but need better resources to support them in doing so. Tate Schools is a practical answer to that need.

The platform organises resources across several core formats. Discover Art transforms collection works into a versatile series that refreshes and diversifies classroom references. Art Makes invites students into hands-on, curiosity-led art making inspired by Tate artworks, with step-by-step activities that encourage experimentation and personal creative choices. Artist Stories brings artists into the classroom in their own words through video and discussion prompts, while Meet The Artist goes further still — students encounter contemporary artists, learn about their journeys, and explore workshop-style questions alongside them.

Teachers can search resources by key stage, art form, or SEND accessibility, and use them flexibly as a full lesson, a short activity, or a source of creative inspiration.

## **A Collaborative Model**

Building Tate Schools required genuine cross-team collaboration throughout — not just at launch, but across every stage of design, testing, and refinement. Curators, digital designers, learning specialists, and accessibility advisors all contributed, with communication and shared goals embedded into the process from the start.

Coe was frank about what this kind of collaboration demands: aligning creative vision, digital functionality, and classroom usability requires sustained effort, not a single kick-off meeting. External experts in the digital and education sectors were also brought in to advise on accessibility, usability, and pedagogical design.

The measure of success, as Coe put it, is ultimately the classroom itself. Teachers report that Tate Schools resources are helping them introduce contemporary art, stimulate discussion, and spark creative making. Students respond positively to interactive and sensory-rich activities, and teachers highlight the flexibility and accessibility of the resources as key to their value.

## **What Comes Next**

Tate Schools is described as just beginning. Future plans include extending the Immersion series into the gallery space, introducing new digital tools to celebrate and share classroom creativity, and deepening the SEND-first approach through ongoing research and feedback.

The platform offers a model that will be of interest to any institution working at the intersection of digital learning and cultural collections — one that puts teacher insight, accessibility, and genuine classroom utility at the centre of the design process, rather than treating them as afterthoughts.

As Coe observed in closing: what happens when digital learning resources are designed collaboratively, with accessibility and classroom relevance at the forefront, is something meaningfully different from what most institutions currently produce. Tate Schools is an attempt to show what that difference looks like in practice.

**Our virtual conferences are one of the most affordable ways to stay at the forefront of museum practice.** Explore our upcoming events [here](https://www.museumnext.com/events/)

Effie Coe presented at the Museum Digital Summit 2026. Tate Schools is available to explore at [tate.org.uk/schools.](https://www.tate.org.uk/schools)

This article from MuseumNext (published May 23, 2026, by Manuel Charr) covers a presentation by Effie Coe, Curator of Digital Content in the schools and teachers team at Tate, delivered at the Museum Digital Summit 2026. The article details the development of Tate Schools, a digital learning platform for schools built between 2023 and 2025 through collaboration between Tate's Learning and Digital teams.

Key elements of the project include:
- A teacher friends group drawn from educators across the UK (from the Shetland Islands, Newcastle, Birmingham, London, St. Ives, and Margate) who help identify gaps and priorities in resource provision from the start, rather than being consulted at the end of the process.
- An SEND-first design philosophy (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities), meaning resources are designed to work for the most complex and diverse learners first, based on the principle that this approach tends to work better for everyone. This was developed through one-to-one conversations with six SEND practitioners.
- Two notable commissions: Lightbox, an interactive digital resource for sensory and SEND learners developed with creative studio The Workers, and All The Feelings, the first commission in a new Immersion series — a video artwork by artist India Harvey created with students in a special school setting. The Immersion series will feature a new artist commission every two years.
- Tate Schools now offers over 80 resources spanning key stages one to five, featuring more than 300 collection artists. Seventy-five percent of content foregrounds underrepresented artists (global majority, disabled, LGBTQ+, working class, and women artists), and over 40% of resource series were co-produced with artists, teachers, students, or sector peers.
- The platform includes formats such as Discover Art, Art Makes, Artist Stories, and Meet The Artist, searchable by key stage, art form, or SEND accessibility.

The article notes the representation focus responds to the Visual Eyes Report, which found teachers want to diversify their curriculum but need better resources. Future plans include extending the Immersion series into gallery spaces, introducing new digital tools to share classroom creativity, and deepening the SEND-first approach. The article frames Tate Schools as a model for any institution working at the intersection of digital learning and cultural collections.
args.key_excerpts: "When Tate set out to build a new digital learning platform for schools, the team began with a deliberately uncomfortable question: why would teachers want to engage with art through digital spaces at all?", "resources designed to work for the most complex and diverse learners tend to work better for everyone", "simply making content available is not enough. Digital learning resources are most powerful when they are shaped by classroom context and real teaching practice.", "The measure of success, as Coe put it, is ultimately the classroom itself.", "what happens when digital learning resources are designed collaboratively, with accessibility and classroom relevance at the forefront, is something meaningfully different from what most institutions currently produce. Tate Schools is an attempt to show what that difference looks like in practice."

<webpage_content>
# Regional action

Reaching out to all audiences

The creation of Centre Pompidou in 1977 marked the starting point of a movement to open museums up to new audiences. True to its original mission, Centre Pompidou continually seeks to make art and creation accessible to as many people as possible, and to develop initiatives capable of reaching audiences who do not have immediate access to culture.

Beyond its walls, it develops numerous projects in forms adapted to each context: loans of works and exhibitions; the co-creation of venues and scientific and cultural projects; mediation and training initiatives; and cultural programmes that reflect its fundamental multidisciplinary character: live performance, cinema, symposiums and more.

## Regional outreach

The roll-out of actions in Ile-de-France is accompanied by an equally important national presence. Centre Pompidou is constantly exploring new forms of hybrid, innovative and durable partnerships with local authorities in search of new channels for dissemination and collaboration.   
 Find out more about some of our flagship projects below.

![Centre Pompidou-Metz by night](/fileadmin/_processed_/e/7/csm_RH1896-0228_95e776b0a8.jpg)  

Centre Pompidou-Metz © Shigeru Ban Architects Europe and Jean de Gastines Architectes, with Philip Gumuchdjian for the design of the competition winning project/ Metz Métropole / Centre Pompidou-Metz © Roland Halbe

## Centre Pompidou-Metz

As the most visited modern & contemporary art centre in France, outside of the Paris region, Centre Pompidou-Metz is an outstanding example of this regional foothold.

An opening to all audiences and the intersection of fields are at the heart of Centre Pompidou-Metz, with projects designed for school-goers and more remote audiences, collaborations with activist organisations, with Metz hospital, or actions in rural areas of the region, in a blend of live performance and exhibitions.

[Centre Pompidou-Metz website](https://www.centrepompidou-metz.fr/en/welcome)

---

## Centre Pompidou Francilien – fabrique de l’art

![](/fileadmin/_processed_/a/7/csm_action-territoriale_massy_pca-stream-00_medium_fe5ea09e0f.jpg)  

Centre Pompidou Francilien © PCA-STREAM

Centre Pompidou is building a new conservation and creation centre in the Ile-de-France region.

With 30,000m² of space and designed as a model for innovative arts institutions, it will be:

* a centre of excellence for the conservation and restoration of the works in its collection;
* a venue for cultural dissemination and creation strongly anchored in its territory.

The new venue will open in the spring of 2027 in Massy.

In anticipation of its opening, and in collaboration with local stakeholders—cultural, academic, educational, and community-based—Centre Pompidou has, since 2019, developed a programme that reaches across the Île-de-France region. This initiative presents works from the collection, circulates educational tools, encourages engagement with new artistic practices, and forges research and training partnerships with the academic world.

[More information on the project](/en/centre-pompidou/regional-action/centre-pompidou-francilien-fabrique-de-lart)

---

## Expertise and Consultancy

Driven by its commitment to initiating, supporting, encouraging, and facilitating projects, Centre Pompidou develops consulting and cultural advisory services for partners seeking to benefit from its experience and expertise.

### Co-designing new cultural spaces:

![](/fileadmin/_processed_/9/0/csm_atelier-jeux_mille-forme_clermont-ferrand_b44e5265df.jpg)  

Des enfants jouent à mille formes © Direction de la communication, ville de Clermont-Ferrand

### mille formes A network of art initiation centres for children aged 0–6

The mille formes centres are multidisciplinary spaces of artistic exploration designed for early childhood and their accompanying adults. These venues encourage art discovery through play, manipulation, sensory experience, and hands-on creation. Visitors can engage with interactive exhibitions, take part in workshops, and attend dance or music events, among others. The programming spans a wide range of artistic disciplines and is developed by and with contemporary artists from fields such as visual arts, performing arts, graphic design, music, and culinary design.

These centres also serve as resource hubs for issues relating to art and early childhood, and are open to professionals from all backgrounds.

#### mille formes Clermont-Ferrand

Inaugurated in 2019, the first centre has already welcomed over 35,000 visitors and hosted 150 artistic offerings.

Its gallery, studio, agora with a small stage, mini-museum, 0–2-year-old area, first-time sessions, and café/kitchen were all designed by Laure Jaffuel in collaboration with architect Sharmily Guyot.

[Watch the opening day video report](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nXsVFOTOy1s) (2 min)

[Website](https://www.milleformes.fr/)

#### mille formes Montpellier

A new 1,000 m² space, inaugurated on 6 February 2026, was designed by artist and architect Sarah de.Gouy and is located in the heart of the city.

Spanning two levels connected by a slide-staircase, it includes: two exhibition galleries (for 0–2 and 2–6 age groups), a studio, a room for performing arts, a room for reading, a parenting support area.

[Inaugural programme](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/fr/programme/agenda?no_cache=1&lieux%5B%5D=Montpellier&sousCategories1%5B%5D=Jeune+public&dateType=)

---

## Professional Training

As a leading institution in the field of cultural mediation, Centre Pompidou supports local authorities by sharing its expertise and know-how.  
 Its professional training programmes are tailored to the specific contexts of each beneficiary. They aim to strengthen the skills of all professionals involved—from decision-makers to their teams—in support of each community’s cultural policy development.

[Training offers for local authorities](/en/lecole-du-centre-pompidou/formations-pour-les-collectivites-territoriales)

---

## Loans and deposits of works

Centre Pompidou’s territorial outreach is exemplified by its active policy of promoting [public collections](/en/collection) under its care by presenting them beyond the walls of the Musée National d’Art Moderne / Centre de Création Industrielle (Mnam/Cci). This ambition has made Centre Pompidou the world’s leading lender of artworks.

In 2023, just over 2,200 works were loaned within France, and approximately 5,350 works are currently on deposit in various institutions in Paris and across the regions.

[View the map of loans in France and worldwide](https://collection.centrepompidou.fr/movements/map)

---

## Travelling Museums

![](/fileadmin/_processed_/b/d/csm_action-territoriale_centre-pompidou-mobile_patrick-bouchain_2011-2013_0a974381aa.jpg)  

Le Centre Pompidou mobile à Chaumont, 2011 © Centre Pompidou, MNAM-CCI/Philippe Migeat

![](/fileadmin/_processed_/5/d/csm_action-territoriale_le-mumo_52ad9d86f6.jpg)  

Le MUMO © Fanny Trichet 2020

Centre Pompidou has developed travelling museum projects to reach new audiences and territories.

From 2011 to 2013, the [Centre Pompidou mobile](/fr/ressources/media/3YzH8jm)—a large demountable pavilion designed by architect Patrick Bouchain—brought masterpieces of modern and contemporary art to regions with limited access to cultural offerings (Aubagne, Boulogne-sur-Mer, Cambrai, Chaumont, Libourne) and, in particular, to audiences furthest removed from cultural life.

In 2022, the [MuMo](https://centre-pompidou.musee-mobile.fr/) (Mobile Museum, founded in 2011 by Ingrid Brochard) partnered with Centre Pompidou, with the support of the Art Explora Foundation and the French Ministry of Culture, to present thematic exhibitions based on Centre’s collection in a new travelling museum truck. The initiative has been touring various regions of France for 40 weeks per year, and is now in its third consecutive year.

---

## Mediation for young audiences

Centre Pompidou places great importance on young audiences and encourages their awareness of modern and contemporary creation through three specially dedicated spaces: the Children’s Workshop, the Galerie des Enfants and Studio 13/16. A [dedicated programme](/en/program/youth-audience) designed to capture and hold the attention of young audiences transmits key concepts and forges a relationship with art and creation from the earliest age.   
    
 Centre Pompidou exports this know-how by proposing travelling exhibitions and workshops that can be set up in a variety of environments. Whatever the domain explored, each proposal is based on everyday experience and a sensory approach in order to develop children's awareness and facilitate encounters with today's creations.

![](/fileadmin/_processed_/b/8/csm_offres-pros_itinerances-jeune-public_dans-la-foret_marion-barraud_6947e32a52.jpg)
