# Our Favorite Museums to Introduce Children to Culture

Inspiration

![Frédéric Lovino / Musée Louvre-Lens](https://asset-prod.france.fr/optimized_01_4_6405e64c5b.jpg)

© Frédéric Lovino / Musée Louvre-Lens

Reading time: 0 minPublished on 11 May 2024

Culture is not inherited, it is conquered," said André Malraux. So why not start early, even very early! Customized guided tours, creative workshops, activity booklets—across France, the most prestigious museums adapt to children aged 2 to 12 so that each one can discover art at their own pace and, who knows, develop a taste for science and knowledge... Here are a few ideas for cultural and playful outings in the museums of France.

## An Impressionist Awakening at the Musée d'Orsay in Paris.

Musée d'Orsay, Paris, France

![Sophie Crépy](https://asset-prod.france.fr/atelier_enfants_sur_le_mouvement_c_Sophie_Cr_py_2e3916307e.jpg)

© Sophie Crépy

There's no age limit to appreciating a [Monet](https://www.france.fr/en/article/fondation-monet-giverny/) or a [Cézanne](https://www.france.fr/en/article/aix-en-provence-cezannes-footsteps/)! Alongside its permanent collections and temporary exhibitions, the Musée d'Orsay offers workshops to introduce young audiences to the creations of the Impressionist movement. After a guided tour, comes the hands-on part, where children aged 6 to 8 or 8 to 12 take up the brush themselves and play, draw, and create, sometimes in the style of Van Gogh, Renoir, or Pissarro...

[Visiting the Musée d'Orsay](https://www.musee-orsay.fr/en/families)

## And Wonder at the Louvre Museum

Louvre Museum, Paris, France

![© Florence Brochoire / Musée du Louvre - Atelier jeune public au musée du Louvre, à Paris.](https://asset-prod.france.fr/OK_atelier_au_mus_e_du_Louvre_2010_mus_e_du_Louvre_Florence_Brochoire_785d0a99f0.jpg)

© © Florence Brochoire / Musée du Louvre - Atelier jeune public au musée du Louvre, à Paris.

We nurture our little budding artists in the majestic Louvre, where children are welcome! Workshops, storytelling tours, shows, and youth films related to the current programming. Every effort is made to ensure families have a good time. To extend your visit, head to the Petit Louvre, the museum's digital extension specially designed for the youngest. There is video content, comics, coloring pages, and for the more adventurous, puzzles to solve in Greece, Egypt, or in search of the Mona Lisa!

[Visit the Louvre Museum](https://www.louvre.fr/en/visit/visit-as-a-family)

## Introduction to contemporary art at the Centre Pompidou-Metz, in the Grand Est region.

![Pierre Defontaine / Lorraine Tourisme](https://asset-prod.france.fr/optimized_Centre_Pompidou_Metz_3_56d8c98a58.jpg)

© Pierre Defontaine / Lorraine Tourisme

In unique spaces of the Centre Pompidou-Metz, children as young as 5 can become acquainted with contemporary art by combining creative activities with encounters with artists. On the agenda: creating phonograph records out of chocolate, or drawing record players, as well as screen printing on pancakes. Young Picassos are exposed to all forms of contemporary production, accompanied by a team of youth docents.

[Visit the Centre Pompidou-Metz](https://www.centrepompidou-metz.fr/en/programme)

## An Interactive History Lesson at the Caen Memorial

![A fun tour of the Caen Memorial, designed for young visitors with period objects, in Normandy.  ](https://asset-prod.france.fr/optimized_visite_famille11_web_a1d168eab5.jpg)

© Caen Memorial - A fun tour of the Caen Memorial, designed for young visitors with period objects, in Normandy.

Numerous school groups visit Caen to honor and learn about the events of World War II. And for good reason! The museum-memorial of the Second World War allows to understand the major stakes of the Normandy Landings in June 1944 and the Battle of Normandy. The visit is adapted to children start at 8 years old, an age when they start studying the history of the 20th century at school. During school holidays, visits specially dedicated to families are organized in the by entertaining guides equipped with a curious suitcase filled with archival documents and period objects for children to explore. Enough to captivate the attention of dreamy or disruptive children from the start to finish of the presentation.

[Visit the Caen Memorial](umerous school groups visit Caen to honor and learn about the events of World War II. And for good reason! The museum-memorial of the Second World War allows to understand the major stakes of the Normandy Landings in June 1944 and the Battle of Normandy. The visit is adapted to the public from 8 years old, an age when we start studying the history of the 20th century at school. During school holidays, visits specially dedicated to families are organized in the presence of guides equipped with a curious suitcase filled with archival documents and period objects to manipulate. Enough to captivate the attention of dreamy or disruptive children from beginning to end)

## A Treasure Trove of Children's Activities at the Louvre-Lens, in Northern France egion.

![© Frédéric Lovino / Musée du Louvre-Lens - Atelier dessin au musée du Louvre-Lens, dans les Hauts-de-France.](https://asset-prod.france.fr/optimized_01_20_0114fe54ed.jpg)

© © Frédéric Lovino / Musée du Louvre-Lens - Atelier dessin au musée du Louvre-Lens, dans les Hauts-de-France.

From sensory experiences for the little ones to 'squat the museum' afternoons for generations Y and Z, there's something for all ages at the Louvre-Lens. With the charter 'The 10 Rights of the Little Visitor at the Louvre Lens', the Lens museum gives full (or almost full) power to your budding geniuses. The right to have a favorite artwork, to share impressions, to only look at the details of a painting, to sit down, to close your eyes, and even the right to dream... Mini-tours, painting, engraving, or drawing, the museum is bursting with creative activities to unleash the inventiveness of young minds who, for a moment, feel like queens and emperors of the Gallery of Time.

[Visit the Louvre-Lens Museum](https://www.louvrelens.fr/en/)

## The Palais Fesch in Corsica: Tracing the Footsteps of Napoleon

![OTI Pays d'Ajaccio](https://asset-prod.france.fr/DJI_0087_867a6643e4.jpg)

© OTI Pays d'Ajaccio

There's no age limit for admiring a work of art, especially on the Isle of Beauty. In the heart of Ajaccio, in Corsica, just steps from the ferry terminal, stands the  impressive Palais Fesch, built by [Napoleon's](https://www.france.fr/en/article/ajaccio-napoleon-footsteps/) uncle. It houses the imperial chapel and the second largest collection of Italian paintings in France after the Louvre.  From the age of 6, children engage in culture by creating their own plastic works. Meanwhile, older kids (from 11 years old) explore behind the scenes of the fine arts museum, learning to design exhibitions, which might even inspire some to pursue careers in the field! The museum also offers theatrical tours.

[Visit the Palais Fesch.](https://www.musee-fesch.com/visites-numeriques)

## Layover in the Mediterranean at the Mucem in Marseille, Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur

![Julie Cohen / Mucem](https://asset-prod.france.fr/optimized_1_Minute_fabrique_exposition_salammbo_Julie_Cohen_Mucem_7eb774494e.jpg)

© Julie Cohen / Mucem

The Museum of European and Mediterranean Civilisations (Mucem) in Marseille is an architectural marvel situated by the sea, offering stunning 360-degree views of the Fort Saint-Jean and the Mediterranean. With its bold design and captivating exhibitions, it stands as a cultural beacon, renowned internationally as an emblem of architectural and artistic innovation.In addition, the Mucem offers children's groups a rich program of encounters focusing on Mediterranean peoples and artworks. Explore our offerings, choose your activity, and prepare for your visit to the museum.

## The Journey to Nantes continues at the Museum of Arts in Pays de la Loire.

![C.Clos / musée des Arts de Nantes](https://asset-prod.france.fr/optimized_4_Un_t_en_famille_au_mus_e_Mus_e_d_arts_de_Nantes_C_Clos_53c9dd461b.jpg)

© C.Clos / musée des Arts de Nantes

The island of Nantes captivates both young and old with its [gigantic mechanical and fantastical animals](https://www.lesmachines-nantes.fr/en/), starting with the unbeatable elephant always ready to welcome you on its back or the giant spider. To extend the experience, cross the royal river towards the Chamber of Dragons at the Museum of the History of the City, located in the heart of the Castle of the Dukes of Brittany, much to the delight of your little monsters. Illustrations, tactile and even sound terminals, will tell you everything about these strange creatures very present in medieval culture.

A few steps away, the Museum of Arts in Nantes offers several sensory awakening workshops. Accompanied by an adult, the youngest ones explore the museum's collections of ancient art in search of the aptly named Pascal lamb, and its flock lost in the halls...

[Visit the Museum of Arts](https://museedartsdenantes.nantesmetropole.fr/en/home.html) and  the [Museum of History of Nantes](https://www.chateaunantes.fr/en/)

## A Splash of Culture and Grape Juice at the Cité du Vin in Bordeaux, Nouvelle-Aquitaine

![AV/ Cité du Vin / Casson Mann](https://asset-prod.france.fr/optimized_PP_Terrasse_CDV_15_08_21_AV_55_a7791f302d.jpg)

© AV/ Cité du Vin / Casson Mann

No need to leave the children at home to visit the Cité du Vin (City of  Wine)  7 year may not drink alcohol, but they have a thirst for knowledge. Through a customized tour, children soar over [vineyards](https://www.france.fr/en/article/wandering-heart-bordeaux-vineyard/) from all corners of the earth, learn about grape cultivation, travel back to Roman and medieval times, and put their knowledge to the test. This playful immersion culminates at the belvedere on the 8th floor of the building, offering a panoramic view of [Bordeaux](https://www.france.fr/en/article/culture-for-everyone-in-bordeaux/) and the Garonne, punctuating the sensory journey with a tasting experience Via Sensoria. For the younger audience, the glass of wine made from grapes from around the world offered to adults is replaced by a tasting of organic and local grape juice...

[Visit the Cité du Vin](https://www.laciteduvin.com/en)

## Shoot for the Stars at Gazing up at the stars at the Cité de l'Espace in Toulouse, Occitanie

![Cité Espace ](https://asset-prod.france.fr/5_F5_A9546_8bf19679b3.jpg)

© Cité Espace

What child hasn't dreamed of becoming an astronaut one day? At the Cité de l'Espace, our favorite young scientists embark on a journey through the universe, taking on various challenges. They climb aboard the MIR space station, get up close to robots exploring the planet Mars, experience the vacuum of space, and dive into the world of asteroids with the IMAX 3D film "Asteroid Hunters."

The exploration begins almost from birth. At the Little Astronauts' City, children as young as 4 learn to prepare rockets and organize missions. French astronaut Thomas Pasquet should be worried. Sooner or later, our budding astronauts will spread their wings and fly on their own...

[Visit the Cité de l'Espace.](https://en.cite-espace.com/)

## Pencil sketching at the Musée des Beaux-Arts in Dijon, Burgundy

![musée des Beaux-Arts de Dijon](https://asset-prod.france.fr/optimized_IMG_5184_6a163033e5.JPG)

© musée des Beaux-Arts de Dijon

It's well known that children have boundless imagination... Located in the east wing of the former Palace of the Dukes of Burgundy, the [Musée des Beaux-Arts in Dijon](https://www.france.fr/en/article/5-top-reasons-museum-art-dijon/) is a fantastic source of inspiration for budding artists! Triangles, trapezoids, rhombuses – the rich collections of paintings and sculptures offer a multitude of geometric shapes perfect for coloring practice. Several workshops are available to cultivate creative minds. From drawing portraits of dukes and duchesses with colored pencils to collaborative works on paper with elaborate oriental motifs, or sketchbooks for drawing in front of the canvases. For those with a flair for the dramatic, acting out theater scenes inspired by medieval altarpieces is a favorite.

[Visit the Musée des Beaux-Arts  in Dijon](https://musees.dijon.fr/)

## You Sank My Battle Ship at National Maritime Museum of Brest, in Brittany

![© Sen / Adobe Stock - Sous-marin de poche exposé au musée national de la Marine, à Brest, en Bretagne.](https://asset-prod.france.fr/optimized_Adobe_Stock_327387030_ccb94cc472.jpeg)

© © Sen / Adobe Stock - Sous-marin de poche exposé au musée national de la Marine, à Brest, en Bretagne.

At the heart of the Brest Castle, overlooking one of the world's largest roadsteads, the National Maritime Museum offers a journey through France's maritime history. Warships, famous three-masters, submarines—the exhibition halls recount the great naval battles. Young sailors better hold onto the helm tight. The adventure promises to be tempestuous whether they opt for guided tours or workshops. Sailing around the world, tracking underwater sounds like golden-eared experts, modeling figureheads, making holed biscuits to feed the crew—not to mention pirate-style treasure hunts for ages 4-6. If they accompany their parents, the young sailors can rely on the indispensable logbook to be obtained at the reception for a fun and enjoyable visit. All aboard!

[Visit the National Maritime Museum of Brest](https://www.musee-marine.fr/en.html)

## The Genius of Leonardo at the at Clos Lucé, in the Centre-Val de Loire

![© David Darrault / Parc Leonardo da Vinci - Découverte des inventions de Léonard de Vinci dans le Parc Leonardo da Vinci au chteau du Clos Lucé, à Amboise, en Val de Loire.](https://asset-prod.france.fr/optimized_Ch_teau_du_Clos_Luc_Parc_Leonardo_da_Vinci_David_Darrault_c0d1db725f.jpg)

© © David Darrault / Parc Leonardo da Vinci - Découverte des inventions de Léonard de Vinci dans le Parc Leonardo da Vinci au chteau du Clos Lucé, à Amboise, en Val de Loire.

Engineer, mathematician, architect, painter, and even anatomist, Leonardo da Vinci truly deserves his nickname as the genius of the Renaissance. The [Parc du Clos Lucé](https://www.france.fr/en/article/the-astounding-inventions-of-leonardo-da-vinci-at-clos-luc%C3%A9/), his last residence located in Amboise, at the heart of the Loire Valley, is an open-air museum where both young and old discover machines inspired by the artist's models, including the tank, greatly appreciated by children who don't hesitate to spin the flying propeller...

To make the experience as lively as it is interesting, families can join a theatrical tour during holiday periods with Mathurine, Leonardo's cook, in the lead role, sharing amusing anecdotes along the way. Young geniuses can also create their own machine provided they follow Leonardo's advice carefully as outlined in the Inventor's Notebook.

[Visit the Leonardo da Vinci Park at the Chteau du Clos Lucé](https://vinci-closluce.com/en)

## Journey to the Center of the Earth at the Confluences Museum in Lyon, Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes

![ © Studio Picabel / musée des Confleunces - Atelier coloriage au musée des Confluences, à Lyon.](https://asset-prod.france.fr/optimized_HD_Musee_Confluence_Digital_ete_2018_16_credit_Studio_PICABEL_a42769abf2.jpg)

© © Studio Picabel / musée des Confleunces - Atelier coloriage au musée des Confluences, à Lyon.

Let's explore the depths of the Earth! In connection with the temporary exhibition 'Secrets of the Earth' (until December 31, 2024), the Musée des Confluences in Lyon offers children the opportunity to discover the precious stones and minerals essential to human activities. A sensory workshop where budding adventurers can not only observe but also touch some of the natural resources (with their various colors and shapes) presented. A perfect way to raise awareness among children about the scarcity of resources and the challenges of climate change.

Visit the Confluences Museum.

Additional information:

* [Trips to France that Your Children will Love](https://www.france.fr/en/article/france-holidays-family-children/)

By Colombe Freynet et Kevin Bonnaud

This webpage from the official France tourism board (france.fr) is a guide titled "Our Favorite Museums to Introduce Children to Culture," published on 11 May 2024. It highlights 14 museums across France that offer family-friendly, educational, and creative activities for children aged 2 to 12. The article quotes André Malraux: "Culture is not inherited, it is conquered," as its thematic inspiration.

Key museums featured include:
1. Musée d'Orsay (Paris) – Impressionist workshops where children aged 6-8 and 8-12 paint in the style of Van Gogh, Renoir, or Pissarro.
2. Louvre Museum (Paris) – Workshops, storytelling tours, shows, youth films, and the "Petit Louvre" digital extension with videos, comics, coloring pages, and puzzles.
3. Centre Pompidou-Metz (Grand Est) – Contemporary art introduction for children as young as 5, including chocolate phonograph records and screen printing on pancakes.
4. Caen Memorial (Normandy) – WWII museum with visits adapted for children from age 8; family tours with guides carrying archival documents and period objects.
5. Louvre-Lens (Hauts-de-France) – "The 10 Rights of the Little Visitor" charter; sensory experiences, mini-tours, painting, engraving, and drawing activities.
6. Palais Fesch (Ajaccio, Corsica) – Napoleon's uncle's palace with the second largest collection of Italian paintings in France; children from age 6 create plastic works; older kids (11+) design exhibitions; theatrical tours offered.
7. Mucem (Marseille) – Museum of European and Mediterranean Civilisations with children's programs on Mediterranean peoples and artworks.
8. Museum of Arts (Nantes, Pays de la Loire) – Sensory awakening workshops; children explore ancient art collections including the "Pascal lamb"; nearby Chamber of Dragons at the Castle of the Dukes of Brittany.
9. Cité du Vin (Bordeaux, Nouvelle-Aquitaine) – Customized wine-themed tour for children (7+) with grape juice tasting replacing wine; panoramic belvedere view on the 8th floor.
10. Cité de l'Espace (Toulouse, Occitanie) – Space museum with MIR space station, Mars robots, IMAX 3D film "Asteroid Hunters," and the "Little Astronauts' City" for children as young as 4.
11. Musée des Beaux-Arts (Dijon, Burgundy) – Drawing and coloring workshops focused on geometric shapes, portraits of dukes and duchesses, and theatrical scenes from medieval altarpieces.
12. National Maritime Museum (Brest, Brittany) – Maritime history with warships, three-masters, submarines; workshops on sailing, underwater sounds, figureheads, treasure hunts for ages 4-6, and family logbooks.
13. Clos Lucé (Amboise, Centre-Val de Loire) – Leonardo da Vinci's last residence; open-air park with his machine inventions (including a tank); theatrical tours with "Mathurine, Leonardo's cook"; Inventor's Notebook activity.
14. Musée des Confluences (Lyon, Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes) – "Secrets of the Earth" exhibition (until December 31, 2024) with sensory workshops on precious stones and minerals, raising awareness about resource scarcity and climate change.

The article was written by Colombe Freynet and Kevin Bonnaud. It also links to related articles about family travel in France, including tips for making children love cities, Loire Valley castles, and family-friendly trips.
args.key_excerpts: "Culture is not inherited, it is conquered," said André Malraux, inspiring the article's theme of introducing children to culture early. "There's no age limit to appreciating a Monet or a Cézanne!" — regarding the Musée d'Orsay's Impressionist workshops. "No need to leave the children at home to visit the Cité du Vin... they have a thirst for knowledge" — on the Bordeaux wine museum's child-friendly tour. "What child hasn't dreamed of becoming an astronaut one day?" — introducing the Cité de l'Espace in Toulouse. "Engineer, mathematician, architect, painter, and even anatomist, Leonardo da Vinci truly deserves his nickname as the genius of the Renaissance" — on the Clos Lucé park.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
# Children have their say

## "Il était une ville"

### An exhibition-workshop by Sara de.Gouy with and for children

Galerie des enfants, 13 February – 30 June 2025

![Exhibition-workshop ](/fileadmin/_processed_/b/7/csm_prog_jeune-public_sara-de-gouy_audio_affiche-2_c1f02584d5.jpg)  

© Sara de.Gouy, 2025

#### "Il était une ville", an exhibition-workshop by space designer, architect, and visual artist Sara de.Gouy, invites visitors to imagine and experiment with a city that is more joyful, poetic, and sustainable—one designed with children in mind.

#### The artist developed this project in collaboration with two second-grade classes from a Parisian elementary school in the spring of 2024. Through a series of workshops, the students observed their surroundings, reimagined objects and urban spaces, and worked alongside the artist to envision the city of their dreams.

Here, discover some of their ideas for reinventing the city.

[artist Sara de.Gouy]

I am Sara de.Gouy, architect, designer and artist. I like to think about my projects in collaboration with those they are destined for. I imagined this workshop-exhibition for Centre Pompidou with students from a primary school in Paris. Here are some of their ideas for a city that would be more joyful, more poetic, more sustainable, more adapted to children. What would your ideal city be like?

[children having participated to the project]

If I were an architect, I would have made a multicoloured helter skelter around the Eiffel Tower.  
 If I were an architect, I would want to change the city… I would make the cars prettier and less polluting and to go to school I would make slides or ziplines. Yes, the city would be more adapted to children.  
 What I don’t like is the noise, I don’t like it!  
 That the cars are too noisy… I’d like to have more space for pedestrians.  
 What I don’t like about the city is the dog poo, because you can walk in it and then you have poo on your foot, it’s gross. We should have dog loos.  
 A city where the only transport would be bicycles and some imaginary buildings. Skyscrapers and buildings with strange, coloured shapes.  
 And for example, in the rue Ménilmontant I’d like to make a zipline to go down, that way it’s more fun because it’s on a hill. It would be more fun for the children… it would be useful for old people that way, especially if they’re disabled, that way they wouldn’t have to, for example, with their crutches, walk with crutches, that way they’d just hop on the zipline and Zoom!

#### The Play Crossing

A more fun city would have more colours, and more colours on zebra crossings.  
 Yes, I like to play in the street.  
 Some children invent games with zebra crossings. For example, you can’t step on the cracks on the ground. On the little squares, you have to avoid the lines.  
 I invented a game where you have to avoid the colours to cross the street.  
 It’s a maze zebra crossing. The goal is to get to the manhole cover. All the lines are walls or passages. You have to do the sequence: turn, jump, slide; turn, jump, slide. Then there’s a little bridge to get to the manhole cover.  
 There’s one way to cross over on this side and another on the other side.

#### Buildings in Colour

I’d like the buildings to be more colourful.  
 I’d like there to be more colours because buildings are often black or white. They would be all the colours.  
 I coloured in the balconies and the windows, I think it’s prettier like that.  
 I made this building into a work of art. I used colours because it was a bit sad and so this made it happier. I used yellow, orange, blue… Loads of different colours. Then I started to make imaginary shapes, big ones, small ones… funny ones.  
 It would be a very funny, very colourful city.

#### The Bench – Children Have their Say

I’d like more swings, slides and benches.  
 I’d like a bench where you could sit standing up. A bench where you could lie down and read, and with something to rest on. And a last bench, where you could lie like this and have a little nap while you wait for the bus. And when the bus comes, some music would start so that if someone’s asleep they could wake up and catch the bus.  
 A bench to meet people.

#### The Apple Tree of Possibilities

I’d like there to be more fruit trees in the city.  
 A tree covered in fruit. You could just eat it in the street.  
 I’d like to have a tree that would show you lots of games. And another tree next to it that would show you vegetables. And another tree to show you crisps, sweets. And a clothes tree.  
 There’s a little system inside the tree that throws down everything you want. On this robot-tree… figs, apples, pears, cherries and some vegetables too. That would be great, it would replace all the shops full of crates.  
 It’s a guessing tree.  
 It’s a question tree. If you get the right answer, you get loads and loads of cherries.  
 You hide wishes in the fruit. Yes, they always come true.  
 A wishing tree. Actually, you write a wish on a letter. If you don’t know how to write, an animal comes. There are three types of animals who can come and write. There can be a squirrel, an owl or a fox. Five years later, the wish will come true.  
 It would be like future poetry, for what could exist.

#### The Extraordinary Garden

Generally, parks are a bit small. I’d rather they were… a bit bigger.  
 I’d like there to be bees in the park. They could gather pollen on the flowers here. And I could take some of their honey because it’s really delicious. And something I’d like but that’s sort of impossible, would for there to be chocolate fountains.  
 I’d put strawberry or apricot perfume on the bins so that they smell nice. It would be a sort of nice-smelling city. To smell the nice smell of flowers, of the bakeries.  
 I imagined a hut where you can rest, read books and play. It’s in a tree.  
 It’s a secret passage, you can sit down and sleep. It’s a passage built with clovers and sticks. It’s made with branches, tree trunks.  
 My hut is underwater. It’s round and there’s nothing in it. And there are loads of little fish.  
 My dream hut is called Flying Griffon. It has pillars everywhere. It has a zipline.  
 It was a flower hut. The hut is a rose. In my hut you go up and up, and once you’re up there you rest and you can bring books. To go up, you use the roses’ thorns.

#### Rain is Life!

And then we have a water butt, with different things. One for big plants, so logically it will be bigger, and another for the small plants, that could have pipes, for example a reservoir but with pipes everywhere.  
 It’s a water butt, that way you can get water for the plants when the rain falls.  
 It’s rain water that goes into a butt.  
 To not use the tap water, to pollute less too.

#### Wind over the Roofs

Wind turbines work from the wind’s energy. The wind makes them turn, then it produces energy. They could be on the roofs.   
 On the roof because there’s much more wind up high than down low.  
 I’d like to walk around on the roofs. I’ve always wanted to see Paris from above. That’s why I’d also like to go up one day, on the roofs.  
 At night I go out and then I climb up buildings and then I start to go further and further. And that’s how I walk around on all the roofs. I’d like to lie down on a roof and maybe have fun counting the stars and finding the Plough.

This webpage presents "Il était une ville" (Once Upon a Time, a City), an exhibition-workshop by space designer, architect, and visual artist Sara de.Gouy, held at the Galerie des enfants at Centre Pompidou, Paris, from 13 February to 30 June 2025. The exhibition invites visitors to imagine and experiment with a more joyful, poetic, and sustainable city designed with children in mind.

The project was developed in collaboration with two second-grade classes from a Parisian elementary school in spring 2024. Through workshops, students observed their surroundings, reimagined objects and urban spaces, and worked alongside the artist to envision their dream city. The webpage presents their ideas across several themed sections:

- **The Play Crossing**: Children propose more colorful zebra crossings and invent games to make street crossing fun (e.g., a "maze zebra crossing" with sequences of turn, jump, slide).
- **Buildings in Colour**: Children want more colorful buildings rather than the typical black or white, treating buildings as works of art with imaginary shapes.
- **The Bench**: Ideas for benches where you can sit standing up, lie down and read, nap while waiting for the bus (with music to wake sleepers), and meet people.
- **The Apple Tree of Possibilities**: Dreams of fruit trees, "wishing trees" (wishes written on letters come true after five years, with help from squirrel, owl, or fox), and trees that dispense games, vegetables, clothes, or treats.
- **The Extraordinary Garden**: Requests for bigger parks, bees and honey, chocolate fountains, perfumed bins, and dream huts (in trees, underwater, flower-shaped, or with ziplines).
- **Rain is Life!**: Water butts to collect rainwater for plants and reduce tap water use and pollution.
- **Wind over the Roofs**: Wind turbines on rooftops (where wind is stronger) and children's desire to walk on roofs to see Paris from above and count stars.

The page includes audio excerpts of children's voices and the artist's introduction. Credits list interviews by Alice Maxia and Laura Samoilovich, recording/editing/mixing by Bastien Pigeon, production by Fanny Cerizier, and the voices of 22 participating children plus Sara de.Gouy.

# Visiting the Pompidou Kids Studio

* Flora
* Oct 8, 2022
* 6 min read

Updated: Mar 18, 2023

Visiting Paris is an exciting time for art lovers. This city hosts the Louvre, the Orsay, along with countless other world-class art museums. But what if you are bringing young children? Many families will simply forego visits to these historic places, thinking their kids won’t connect to the art on display.

But not so fast!

A lot of the best art museums have plenty to entertain and educate your little ones — [you just need a tour guide](https://www.tours-in-paris.com/biography) who knows how to make it fun and engaging!

When you have the right approach, these places are as wonderful for children as they are for adults. And that’s important to know, because far too many families end up excluding art from their itinerary, when really everyone could get so much out of it.

One of the best places in Paris to open the world of art to children is the Centre Pompidou, Europe’s largest modern art museum. Like many institutions in the city, they’ve created kid-specific programming. And their ability to awaken the wonder and awe of art for kids is commendable.

On your next trip to Paris, don’t be afraid to take your children to art museums. It turns out they can have a great time, learn a lot about the world around them, and discover the world of art. So let’s look at some of the lessons I’ve learned on how to turn museum tours into fun experiences for kids, and then, let’s look at how the [Centre Pompidou](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/) in particular does it.

## 1 - My Experience with teaching Art to children

Over more than a decade, I’ve honed my skills as a professional tour guide, and I’ve always made a point of learning how to keep these tours as exciting for children as they are for adults.

We all remember being kids, when our parents would drag us to do something they found entertaining but we didn’t. It breaks my heart to think that a child finds themselves in [a place like the Louvre](https://www.tours-in-paris.com/post/american-history-of-france), and there is no one there to make it interesting for them!

I was lucky. My mother was an art museum tour guide herself. She started teaching me both English and art history from a very young age. And when she could not find a babysitter, she would even take me along on tours. I was extremely lucky, having a mother who knew how to ignite an interest and love of art in a young child.

I think the results are pretty clear. I ended up loving art museums so much [I became a tour guide myself](https://www.tours-in-paris.com/biography)!

I know first hand that children can become fascinated with art museums! So I’ve always made that a large part of my continuing professional development. A large part of that work is to find the people who are running arts education programs for kids the right way and learn from them.

For instance, the Musée en Herbe is a Paris art museum dedicated entirely to children. They’ve been running since the mid-70s, so they’ve had almost 50 years to hone their collection and programming to fit kids of all ages. It’s an inspiration to visit, and it also reminds you that art really is at its best when it's *fun*, no matter what age you are.

I’ve also explored the Cité des Enfants at the City of Science and Industry in Paris. This area is made to teach children concepts from science and engineering. The enthusiasm of their presenters and the cleverness of their exhibit designs really impresses me every time I see it.

By reading, attending kid-friendly tour and learning from the Musée en Herbe and the Cité des Enfants, I developed several approaches of my own that I practiced during the last 10 years.

One of my favorites is the [Treasure Hunt in the Louvre](https://louvreguide.com/treasure-hunt-for-kids). This is a fun way for children to really lose themselves in the beautiful art all around them. Rather than reiterating to kids that this art is “important” and “very serious” — the treasure hunt gets them to think about what they are looking at. After all, these paintings should be thrilling!

On top of that, I stay on top of children’s art education by reading many magazines and journals on the subject. This allows my kid-focused tours to stay up on the latest insights.

Helping children get the most out of art museums has proven to be one of the most rewarding parts of my career, especially when you consider all [the benefits of children’s art education](https://www.tours-in-paris.com/post/a-tour-of-the-louvre-for-kids).

## 2 - What is the Centre Pompidou ?

The Centre Pompidou is a leading art institution in Europe. Not only does it contain France’s National Museum of Modern Art (the Musée National d'Art Moderne), it also has an enormous public library, and even a music and acoustic research center focused on avant-garde sound art.

To bring it all together, the center is housed in a breathtaking high-tech architectural style. It looks kind of like a ship, or maybe a building turned inside out — making it a work of art in its own right.

And the Pompidou does something very few museums in the world do. [They create special programming around their touring exhibits](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/programme/for-kids-and-teens) that basically “translates” the shows for children. That allows the entire family to enjoy a new exhibit in a way that fits everyone’s age.

Plus, they have a variety of exhibits that are made entirely for teens and children. This gives young ones a feeling of having something for themselves, which can be important for them to feel ownership over their visit.

Still other places are set aside to allow children to experiment with making art. [The Kids Studio](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/visit/children-and-families) (or the[*Atelier des enfants*](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/fr/ressources/media/iBt4I9U)) allows art making to happen, and that’s where the fun really starts! There is even an entire room where you can draw on the wall. It’s paradise for budding artists.

**If you are bringing teenagers** (who aren’t going to be interested in programming for little children) the Pompidou has Studio 13/16, which has programming tailor-made for older kids.

Recently, I took my daughter to see how the children’s tour had developed and what they offer right now. I was pleasantly surprised!

### **The Pompidou Guided Tour for Children**

The children’s tour of the Pompidou gets so much right. It aims to teach children not only about art but how to draw your own conclusions about art. To help this along, they keep things calm and orderly while still allowing the kids to express their excitement, joy, and insights.

The pace is kept slow, meaning your 3 or 4 year old isn’t going to be left behind or tire out. And the entire thing takes about an hour.

It all begins with some basic yoga stretches. This gets all the kids to chill out, and it reminds them to listen to the voice of the instructor. To encourage focus, this is followed by a meditation, which includes having the kids close their eyes and imagine colors and lines. The tour has only just begun, and the children are already thinking like artists!

After these visualization and focusing exercises are complete, it’s time to enter the gallery. And how do they do this? With a fun activity where they have to walk carefully on a black line drawn across the ground.

You remember the kid’s game where the floor is lava? It’s kind of like that, only this time it teaches children to be quiet and respectful in a museum setting, as well as staying back from the artwork.

On their way up to see masterpieces by the likes of Marc Chagall and Henri Matisse, they get a spectacular view of Paris that includes Notre Dame and the Sacre-Coeur.

Once in front of these paintings, a lot of basic concepts are discussed. Children are encouraged to look at the colors, the use of lines. Nothing is “dumbed down” — instead, it’s all taught in a way that’s relevant to children.

Painters like [Piet Mondrian](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/ressources/oeuvre/c5pRBL) are perfect for this. The New York City artist ([Paris loves everything New York, as these are two deeply connected cities](https://www.tours-in-paris.com/post/american-history-of-france)) presents simple lines and colors in striking and interesting ways. Children really light up when they see his work!

Other works, like [Joan Miro’s](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/ressources/oeuvre/HZBRjXX) [*Blue I*](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/ressources/oeuvre/HZBRjXX) [(1961)](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/ressources/oeuvre/HZBRjXX) is the perfect chance to get children to see an abstract painting in many different ways, showing them how their own imagination is a big part of looking at art.

There’s a special talk on how sculpture and painting differs, as well as a chance to walk through a [Yaacov Agam](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/fr/magazine/article/agam-la-seule-langue-que-je-parle-cest-le-visuel) installation, where your position in the room changes the piece dramatically.

In a short amount of time, children begin to appreciate how wide the field of fine art is and how much fun it can be to learn and think about. What’s more, they are encouraged to talk about what they think about the things they see, which builds confidence.

### **English-Speaking Kid-Friendly tour guide in Paris**

While the Pompidou Kids Studio and related programming are only in French, I can translate these for your children. But if that doesn’t seem like enough, don’t worry. [There are plenty of other children’s art tours](https://louvreguide.com/treasure-hunt-for-kids) I can give your family directly in English!

## 3 - My thoughts on Kids visiting Art Museums

Art is messy, expressive, creative, and playful — so why shouldn’t children of all ages be able to enjoy it?

The truth is, they do! Just as long as you have the right approach. Rather than lecture about art history, engage them directly with the art itself. And it’s also important to keep it a bit short. That way they leave the museum excited, not tired or bored.

If you do it right, your kids will come to see art museums as awesome places to be!

Let's schedule a kids tour of an art museum in Paris with a kid-friendly tour guide - This is one of my best recommendations for your family.

[Contact Flora](mailto:flora@tours-in-paris.com)

## Recent Posts

# International offers

[Translate to English:] Version originale en anglais, sous-titrée en français

40 years of expertise and innovation

As France’s national modern and contemporary art center, home to one of the world’s two largest collections in modern & contemporary art, Centre Pompidou develops partnerships with museums, art centers, public administrations and private companies.

With decades of experience in travelling exhibitions, co-creating dedicated spaces for art and culture in Metz in 2010, [Málaga](/en/centre-pompidou/international/centre-pompidou-malaga) in 2015, Louvre Abu Dhabi in 2017, [Brussels](/en/centre-pompidou/international/kanal-centre-pompidou) in 2018, [Shanghai](/en/centre-pompidou/international/centre-pompidou-x-west-bund-museum-project-shanghai) in 2019 as well as designing innovative and local mediation projects, spaces and programmes for public or private partners, Centre Pompidou has acquired a vast array of experiences in all fields of cultural expertise.

Centre Pompidou-Málaga welcomed more than 500,000 visitors during two and a half years, in a city of 600,000 inhabitants. Kanal-Centre Pompidou welcomed more than 60,000 visitors during its first month.

## Travelling exhibitions and events

One of the world's two leading collections of modern and contemporary art

The collection of over 120,000 works from all the founding movements in the history of modern and contemporary art includes works by some of the period’s masters such as Vassily Kandinsky, Henri Matisse, André Derain, Sonia Delaunay, Pablo Picasso, Marcel Duchamp, Yves Klein… and covers all fields of creation: the visual arts, drawing, photography, architecture, design, the new media, experimental film and the moving image.

Exhibitions based on Centre Pompidou's collection, covering every field of creation for its international partners

Centre Pompidou proposes ambitious monographic or thematic exhibitions to its partners, covering all areas of 20th and 21st century art and creation.

These exhibitions have met with great success in the past:  
 •  “Elles: Women Artists in the Collection of Centre Pompidou” at the CCBB, Rio de Janeiro: 250,000 visitors  
 •  “Vassily Kandinsky : a Retrospective” at the Palazzo Reale, Milan: 215,000 visitors  
 •  “Masterpieces from Centre Pompidou” at the Metropolitan Art Museum, Tokyo: 200,000 visitors

![Centre Pompidou Málaga - vue de nuit](/fileadmin/_processed_/1/0/csm_malaga_a322815525.png)  

Centre Pompidou Málaga © DR

![Vue de l’exposition « Kandinsky. A Retrospective » au Milwaukee Art Museum](/fileadmin/_processed_/c/b/csm_Texte-Des-expositions-itinerantes-concues-a-partir-des-oeuvres-de-la-collection_textsection_be8cdeed50.jpg)  

Vue de l’exposition « Kandinsky. A Retrospective » au Milwaukee Art Museum © John R. Glembin 2014

## Expertise integrated at all levels

Centre Pompidou is a reference partner in all fields of art and creation : the definition of a cultural and scientific project, assistance in an acquisition strategy, building management and security, the definition of a visitor strategy, exhibition design, conservation and more.  
 The variety of services also includes publishing, expertise in communication and in the digital ecosystem.

# Top 10 VR Trends of 2026: Future of Virtual Reality

12 min read   [Augmented and Virtual Reality](https://hqsoftwarelab.com/blog/augmented-and-virtual-reality/)

**In 2026, Virtual Reality has become more mainstream than ever before, with a significant increase in adoption rates across various industries. The global pandemic of 2020-2021 accelerated the demand for VR technology as people sought alternative ways to work, learn, and socialize remotely. Numerous news stories have highlighted the ways that renowned brands and corporations are venturing into the industry. Given how eventful the past year has been, 2026 is poised to be even more so.**

**As an expert with more than 10 years in [AR/VR development](/solutions/ar-vr-development/), in this article I’ll delve into the major Virtual Reality trends anticipated for the upcoming year, offer insights into potential developments, and underscore why the current moment presents an opportune time for businesses to seek out a VR development company for a potential partnership.**

## What VR Trends Were Dominant in Recent Years?

In the past few years, I’ve observed several emerging VR trends that have gained popularity, paving the way for the future of [Virtual Reality](/solutions/virtual-reality-development/). Some of these include:

* **Wireless VR.** One of the most prominent trends is the widespread adoption of wireless VR headsets that offer freedom of movement. These advanced devices ensure a highly realistic experience without the hassle of cables.
* **Haptic feedback and eye-tracking.** Eye-tracking lets you navigate more naturally, reduces motion sickness, and makes you feel more present in virtual worlds. Haptic feedback adds realistic touch and texture to virtual objects, making your interactions feel more real.
* **Artificial Intelligence (AI).** [AI algorithms](/solutions/data-analytics/artificial-intelligence/) create more realistic non-playable characters in gaming, facilitating personalized learning experiences in education and enhancing [virtual training simulations](/portfolio/vr-aviation-training-platform/).
* **VR in education and training**. VR has been increasingly adopted in educational and [professional training settings](/portfolio/vr-trainings-proof-of-concept-for-manufacturing-3-week-prototyping/), allowing for realistic hands-on learning experiences without real-world risks.
* **Social VR.** The rise of social VR platforms, such as VRChat and AltspaceVR, has enabled users to connect in shared virtual spaces, fostering a sense of presence.
* **VR in healthcare.** Virtual Reality offers new possibilities for patient care and well-being in [pain management](/blog/virtual-reality-pain-management/), physical therapy, and mental health treatment.

These dominant trends have shaped the VR landscape, setting the stage for the exciting developments and innovations we can expect down the road.

> ![Untitled design 5 round - Top 10 VR Trends of 2026: Future of Virtual Reality]( "Top 10 VR Trends of 2026: Future of Virtual Reality")

## VR Popularity and Adoption in 2026

The global VR market was valued at around $67.66 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow significantly through the decade. This growth can be attributed to several factors, including the increasing affordability of VR hardware, the development of more user-friendly and intuitive interfaces, and the growing library of engaging VR content. In the picture below you can find some Virtual Reality future predictions up to 2030.

The gaming industry remains one of the primary drivers of VR adoption, with an estimated 70% of VR users engaging with gaming content regularly. However, VR has also made significant inroads in other sectors, such as education, healthcare, and professional training. 

In 2026 in particular, it’s estimated that about half of universities and colleges worldwide will offer VR-based courses, while 69% of healthcare decision-makers are planning to invest in VR for patient treatment and staff training. The enterprise sector has also embraced VR technology, with businesses leveraging it for remote collaboration, product design, and customer engagement. A recent survey revealed that over 75% of Fortune 500 companies have implemented VR in their operations, citing improved productivity, reduced costs, and enhanced innovation as key benefits.

So, with ongoing advancements in hardware, software, and content creation, the popularity and adoption of VR are poised for even greater growth in the years to come.

## What Are the Key Virtual Reality Trends of 2026?

As Virtual Reality becomes more accessible and integrated with other emerging technologies such as AI, AR, and blockchain, the possibilities for immersive experiences are boundless. Whether it’s through more realistic avatars, enterprise applications, or haptic feedback, VR is impacting how we interact with digital worlds. After a thorough analysis of over 50 VR projects, I’ve identified the key Virtual Reality trends that have emerged in 2026.

### **1. Affordable VR hardware for the masses**

With competitive pricing and subscription models, the future of VR headsets and content is such that they’re now within reach of a broader audience. One of the most significant shifts in VR hardware is the rise of standalone headsets. Devices such as Meta Quest 3 and Pico 5 have eliminated the need for external PCs or consoles, offering all-in-one solutions that deliver high-performance VR experiences. 

These wireless, portable devices are making VR more accessible and convenient for both casual users and enterprise applications, without compromising on quality. This trend is crucial for mainstream adoption and will drive further innovation and investment.

### **2.Multi-sensory technology on VR devices**

2026 is seeing a continued focus on haptic feedback and other sensory technologies that enhance immersion in VR experiences. Haptic gloves, suits, and even full-body rigs are becoming more affordable, allowing users to feel touch, pressure, and movement within virtual environments. This new Virtual Reality technology is particularly valuable in industries like gaming, healthcare, and training, where the sense of touch can add a critical layer of realism and engagement.

### **3. Ultra-realistic graphics and immersive worlds**

Driven by VR advancements in graphics processing, virtual environments are becoming more detailed and lifelike. These visual leaps are allowing for more immersive experiences, where users can explore virtual worlds with photorealistic textures, lighting, and high frame rates. Combining all this with full-body tracking, users can now fully embody their avatars, enhancing the overall immersion.

For instance, at HQSoftware we’ve developed [BodyScope](/portfolio/vr-medical-app-for-visualizing-ct-and-mri-scans/), a VR tool designed to improve medical learning by using highly realistic visualization. The VR app allows users to create 3D models from their CT, MRI, or PET/CT scans and manipulate them. In particular, you can view and rotate 3D models, scale them, apply image filters, create custom slices, and use measurement tools for detailed analysis, all enhanced with adjustable lighting.

### **4. Growth of VR in entertainment and media**

In entertainment, VR is used to create immersive experiences in gaming, movies, museum tours, and live events. For example, in the film industry VR creates virtual movie experiences, such as virtual tours of sets and behind-the-scenes footage. In the media industry, in VR  you can provide virtual news broadcasts and educational programs. 

One example is a [VR museum journey](/portfolio/vr-museum-journey/) that we’ve engineered by HQSoftware, transporting museum visitors into an immersive environment that accurately recreates the historical period and setting of the gallery exhibits. Through this innovative solution, you can fully engage visitors in the culture and daily life of the featured cultural group.

### **5. VR fitness and wellness boom**

Immersive workouts are transforming how we approach fitness, blurring the lines between gaming and exercise. Platforms such as Supernatural, FitXR, and Holofit are altering workouts into immersive, gamified experiences. Users can now box in virtual arenas, cycle through futuristic landscapes, or meditate in serene, otherworldly environments. 

These VR fitness applications offer personalized coaching and progress tracking, enhancing motivation and consistency. As more people look for engaging ways to stay active, VR fitness is becoming a popular alternative to traditional exercise routines.

### **6. Advanced therapy applications**

Healthcare professionals use VR exposure therapy to treat various phobias, pain management, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD),  depression, and anxiety disorders, allowing patients to confront their fears in a controlled environment, potentially decreasing the need for pain medication. For cognitive rehabilitation, VR applications help patients recovering from strokes or brain injuries to relearn daily tasks in a safe setting. 

VR training for providing [effective dementia care](/portfolio/dementia-vr-training/) has been created by the HQSoftware team. The VR training teaches professionals and families how to provide compassionate dementia care, demonstrating best practices and preventing common mistakes that cause emotional distress. This immersive VR dementia care simulation covers daily living challenges, behavior management, dining, and effective communication strategies, highlighting potential pitfalls.

### **7. AI integration in VR**

The use of Artificial Intelligence in VR content creation is expanding dramatically in 2026. In 2023, the global [AI in VR and AR market](/blog/ai-and-ar-vr/) was valued at $39.2 billion. However, with [over 10.8 million Virtual Reality devices sold](https://academyofanimatedart.com/virtual-reality-statistics/), this figure could reach significant growth. 

AI is being used to generate procedural environments, create intelligent non-player characters, and even design entire worlds autonomously. This trend is allowing for more dynamic and personalized VR experiences, where virtual worlds can evolve based on user behavior. In gaming, tourism, and virtual retail, AI is enabling experiences that feel more organic and responsive, pushing the limits of what’s possible in VR storytelling and design.

### **8. Emergence of VR in education and learning**

The use of Virtual Reality in education is a major trend in 2026, with schools and universities adopting the latest VR technology to create immersive learning environments. Whether it’s a virtual simulation of a historical event or a virtual exploration of anatomical structures, VR is enhancing the way students learn. Medical schools, for example, are using VR for diagnosis training, allowing students to practice procedures with a virtual patient or separate organs. 

[VR medical training](/portfolio/vr-medical-app-for-education/) developed by HQSoftware offers various virtual environments, including lobbies and classrooms, for collaborative learning. Students can interact in dedicated virtual rooms, sharing 3D models, videos, and presentations, and collaboratively exploring anatomy, medical procedures, and theoretical concepts through interactive VR simulations and live lectures. Using the app, students increased their knowledge retention by up to 63%, and user engagement improved by up to 72%.

### **9. Expansion of Virtual Reality in the workplace**

VR is increasingly being adopted by businesses for more than just entertainment. The new Virtual Reality technology helps improve employee training outcomes, offers remote collaboration possibilities, and assists users in acquiring new specialized skills. VR creates immersive training simulations and virtual walkthroughs, enabling global real-time collaboration for complex industrial sectors such as manufacturing, automotive, and aviation.

One brilliant example is a [VR training program to master hard skills](/portfolio/vr-training-simulations/) in engineering, mechanics, and [aviation](/blog/virtual-reality-aircraft-maintenance-engineering/). This occupational training software helps employees acquire new job skills, such as performing propeller inspections, engine repairs, brake replacements, etc., allowing for repeated practice without real-world risks. The results show an 84% engagement rate and 67% knowledge retention during VR training, proving its effectiveness and enabling global reach.

### **10. Integration of Augmented Reality**

2026 has seen a convergence of AR and VR technologies, creating Mixed Reality experiences. While VR creates fully immersive virtual worlds, AR overlays digital information onto the real world. AR integration, via smart glasses, heads-up displays, and mobile apps, expands VR’s potential, fueled by VR advancements in spatial computing. This allows for real-time interaction with the physical environment, creating transformative applications across various sectors and blurring the lines between reality and virtuality.

Overall, these trends shaping VR in 2026 highlight not just the technology’s potential, but its growing influence across industries.

The possibilities are limitless, and at HQSoftware we’re excited to be at the forefront of this promising technology.”*

## Which Industries Are Using Virtual Reality in 2026?

Based on HQSoftware’s extensive [AR/VR development experience](/industry/augmented-virtual-reality/), we can highlight the key sectors currently utilizing VR. This include:

* healthcare;
* education and training;
* gaming and entertainment;
* retail and e-commerce;
* architecture and real estate;
* military and defense;
* manufacturing and logistics;
* travel and tourism.

### **Healthcare**

Virtual Reality impacts healthcare through applications in:

* **Surgical training.** VR provides a safe environment for medical students to hone their skills, reducing errors and improving patient outcomes.
* **Pain management.** VR therapy reduces chronic pain, anxiety, and PTSD symptoms. Studies have shown that VR can reduce pain levels by up to 50% and decrease anxiety by up to 40%.
* **Patient engagement.** VR improves patient understanding and treatment adherence through interactive education.

### **Education and training**

VR improves education with immersive, interactive learning that boosts student engagement and knowledge retention. Key areas include:

* **Virtual labs.** Students can conduct experiments and simulations in a safe and controlled environment as many times as they need, from anywhere.
* **Language learning.** VR simulates real-life conversations and scenarios.
* **Soft skills training.** VR helps in improving soft skills such as communication, teamwork, and leadership without fear of offending anyone.

### **Gaming and entertainment**

The gaming industry spearheads VR innovation, constantly pushing boundaries with increasingly realistic graphics, advanced haptic feedback systems, and more intuitive controls.

* **Immersive gaming** offers players an interactive experience that simulates real-life environments.
* **E-sports** allow players to compete in virtual tournaments and leagues.
* **VR arcades** provide a social experience for gamers.

### **Architecture and real estate**

VR can enhance the way we design, build, and sell properties. For instance, this can encompass:

* **Virtual property tours.** Homebuyers can take virtual tours of properties, reducing the need for physical viewings and improving the buying experience.
* **Design and planning.** Architects and designers can use VR to create immersive and interactive models of buildings and spaces, improving collaboration and communication with clients.
* **Interior design.** VR is being used to design and visualize interior spaces, allowing homeowners to see how furniture and decor will look in their homes.

### **Retail and eCommerce**

VR can help cut returns and boost sales by letting customers experience products virtually before buying. Here are some ways it’s being used:

* **Virtual try-on**. Consumers can try on virtual clothing and makeup, reducing the need for physical returns and improving the shopping experience.
* **Product demonstrations.** Retailers can use VR to demonstrate products, reducing the need for physical product displays.
* **Virtual shopping experiences.** By creating interactive shopping experiences, retailers allow customers to explore products in a virtual environment.

### **Travel and tourism**

[Travel companies are using VR](/solutions/ar-vr-in-tourism/) to create immersive experiences, allowing customers to explore destinations before booking. They can provide, for example:

* **Virtual tours.** Travelers can take virtual tours of destinations or landmarks, improving the planning process.
* **Destination marketing.** Destinations are using VR to market themselves, offering immersive and interactive experiences that showcase local culture and attractions.
* **Cultural preservation.** VR brings history to life, letting visitors experience cultural heritage sites and artifacts virtually.

### **Manufacturing and logistics**

Manufacturers leverage VR to enhance production and logistics by implementing:

* **Design and prototyping.** Automakers can use VR to design and prototype vehicles, improving collaboration and reducing development time.
* **Assembly and production.** In VR, workers can master assembly and production processes, improving efficiency and reducing errors.
* **Employee training.** VR is being used to train drivers, help workers acquire new hard skills, or to improve safety protocols.

To conclude, as Virtual Reality continues to advance in 2026, its integration across industries shows no signs of slowing down. With innovations in immersive experiences, training, and collaboration, VR is poised to become an essential tool for both businesses and consumers, driving the future of digital interaction.

### What Are the Top VR Trends to Watch in 2026?

In 2026, VR is moving beyond gaming into health, education, and remote work. Expect lighter headsets, realistic haptic feedback, and AI-driven experiences. Social VR spaces will expand, and mixed reality blending digital and real worlds will become mainstream, transforming how we connect, learn, and collaborate.

No, VR isn’t declining, it’s evolving. While early hype slowed, adoption is growing steadily across industries. Advances in hardware, more affordable devices, and practical uses in training, therapy, and design keep VR relevant. Rather than fading, it’s becoming a powerful everyday tool beyond entertainment.

### What Is the Future of Virtual Reality?

The future of VR is about immersion and accessibility. Devices will be smaller, more affordable, and more comfortable. VR will integrate seamlessly into daily life, supporting remote work, healthcare, education, and entertainment. Virtual Reality will shift from novelty to necessity in both personal and professional spaces.

### How Does Generative AI Change VR Content Creation?

Generative AI makes VR content faster and more personalized. Instead of long development cycles, creators can instantly generate environments, characters, and interactions. This lowers costs and opens creativity to more people. The result is endless, dynamic worlds where experiences adapt to individual preferences in real time.

The global **virtual museums market** was valued at **$3.8 billion** in 2025 and is projected to reach **$12.6 billion** by 2034, expanding at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of **14.2%** during the forecast period from 2026 to 2034. Virtual museums have transitioned from static digital repositories to fully immersive, interactive platforms that leverage virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), mixed reality (MR), and advanced 3D visualization to recreate and enhance physical museum experiences. The COVID-19 pandemic served as a pivotal inflection point for the industry, compelling institutions worldwide to accelerate their digital transformation roadmaps and invest in sophisticated online visitor engagement tools. By 2026, more than 92% of the world's top 100 museums by attendance have established some form of permanent virtual exhibition infrastructure, a figure that was below 60% as recently as 2021. Investments in cloud-based delivery architectures have made high-fidelity virtual tours accessible on consumer-grade devices, removing traditional hardware barriers and expanding the total addressable audience by hundreds of millions of users globally. Educational institutions represent one of the fastest-growing demand verticals, with school systems across North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific integrating virtual museum access into approved digital curricula, generating consistent subscription revenue for platform providers. Government-backed digitization programs in the European Union, South Korea, Japan, and India are further catalyzing market growth by funding large-scale 3D scanning and photogrammetry projects that feed content to virtual platforms. The convergence of generative AI with virtual museum platforms is enabling hyper-personalized visitor journeys, where AI guides adapt narrative depth, language, and pacing to individual user profiles, dramatically improving dwell time and return visit rates. The global immersive simulator market is a closely adjacent space that increasingly shares technology stacks with virtual museum platforms, creating cross-industry synergies in rendering engines, haptic feedback systems, and real-time streaming infrastructure. As 5G network densification accelerates across all major regions, latency constraints that previously hampered mobile VR experiences are rapidly dissolving, opening a new frontier for on-the-go cultural engagement. The competitive landscape is intensifying as technology giants, specialist EdTech firms, and traditional museum institutions all vie for audience share, creating a rich ecosystem of partnerships, licensing deals, and co-development arrangements that are collectively driving innovation at an unprecedented pace.

## Virtual Museums Market Regional Outlook 2025-2034

**North America** commanded the leading position in the global virtual museums market in 2025, accounting for **38.4%** of total revenue, equivalent to approximately **$1.46 billion**. The region's dominance is underpinned by the presence of world-renowned institutions such as the Smithsonian Institution, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Art Institute of Chicago, and the National Gallery of Art, all of which have made substantial multi-year investments in digital infrastructure. The United States federal government has allocated significant grants through the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) to support digitization and virtual access initiatives, particularly targeting underserved communities that lack geographic proximity to major cultural centers. Canada has similarly prioritized virtual cultural access through programs administered by the Canada Council for the Arts and provincial heritage ministries. The North American market benefits from extremely high household broadband penetration rates, a mature consumer VR device ecosystem anchored by platforms such as Meta Quest and Apple Vision Pro, and a well-developed ecosystem of EdTech companies that bundle virtual museum access into educational subscriptions. Corporate sponsorships from major technology companies headquartered in the region have also injected substantial non-traditional funding into virtual museum development, enabling ambitious multi-year digitization projects at scale. North America is forecast to maintain its regional leadership through 2034, driven by continued institutional investment, curriculum integration mandates, and the rollout of next-generation spatial computing platforms.

**Europe** represented the second-largest regional market in 2025, holding a share of approximately **29.1%** of global revenues, and is forecast to grow at a CAGR of **13.8%** through 2034. Europe's cultural wealth, home to institutions such as the Louvre, the British Museum, the Uffizi Gallery, the State Hermitage Museum, and the Rijksmuseum, provides an exceptionally rich content base for virtual museum platform development. The European Union's Horizon Europe research program has designated digital cultural heritage as a priority funding area, channeling hundreds of millions of euros into 3D documentation, semantic metadata enrichment, and open-access platform development. The Europeana digital platform, which aggregates content from more than 3,000 European cultural institutions, continues to expand its virtual experience offering, providing a federated infrastructure that smaller institutions can leverage to reach global audiences. National digitization programs in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom have produced some of the highest-fidelity 3D museum collections in the world, with scanning resolutions capable of capturing sub-millimeter surface detail on fragile artifacts. The GDPR framework has prompted European virtual museum operators to develop privacy-first [visitor analytics](/report/visitor-analytics-market) platforms, creating a differentiated regional approach to audience intelligence that is increasingly being adopted by operators in other jurisdictions.

**Asia Pacific** is the fastest-growing regional market, projected to expand at a CAGR of **16.9%** from 2026 to 2034, driven by massive government-backed digitization programs, a vast and digitally engaged youth demographic, and accelerating smartphone and 5G penetration. China's National Cultural Big Data Strategy, launched with multi-billion RMB funding, is enabling large-scale virtual access to collections at the National Museum of China, the Palace Museum, and hundreds of provincial heritage sites. South Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism has invested heavily in AR-enhanced museum experiences, supporting the National Museum of Korea's acclaimed virtual exhibition program. Japan's Society 5.0 framework explicitly identifies digital cultural access as a social infrastructure priority, resulting in substantial public funding for virtual museum development. India's DigiYatra and Digital India initiatives are creating new pathways for rural and semi-urban populations to access cultural content that was previously geographically inaccessible. **Latin America** and **Middle East and Africa** collectively accounted for the remaining market share in 2025, with Latin America growing at a CAGR of approximately **12.4%** and the Middle East and Africa expanding at **11.8%**, supported by tourism-oriented virtual experience investments in the Gulf Cooperation Council countries and UNESCO-backed digitization efforts across sub-Saharan Africa.
