Plan promotes cultural digitalization

Updated: June 23, 2022 09:10 China Daily [![](/static/2023GW/images/Artical_Print.jpg)](javascript:window.print())

The digital revolution has fundamentally altered the way in which culture and cultural services are produced, distributed and accessed.

With its wealth of cultural resources, China is set to embrace this revolution with a grand plan: the digitization of culture.

According to a new guideline published on May 22 by the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China and the State Council, China's Cabinet, the country aims to digitalize and connect its cultural resources.

Digitization is the conversion of data, documents and processes from analog to digital form, while digitalization is the transformation of business processes via digital technologies.

According to the guideline, a big data system focused on culture will be developed by 2035 to allow digitized cultural products to be shared by all people.

It also outlined eight key tasks, including: setting up a Chinese cultural database and building a national cultural network using existing cable TV network facilities and 5G mobile networks; speeding up the digitization of the cultural industry; creating companies engaged in the fields of cultural data collection, processing, trade, distribution and presentation; and supporting initial public offerings of eligible digital culture enterprises in the science and technology sectors.

More efforts are needed to formulate policies to support the digitalization of the culture industry, step up financial support, and establish national scientific and technological innovation centers and key laboratories to support cultural digitization, it added.

During this year's two sessions－the annual meetings of the National People's Congress, China's top legislature, and the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, its top political advisory body－national digitalization efforts, especially the digitization of cultural heritage and the development of digital infrastructure, were highlighted.

The digitization of museums, archives and libraries is one of China's most important undertakings in the digital era.

Bai Gengsheng, a member of the Standing Committee of the National Committee of the CPPCC, said that with the country making great progress in the study of cultural artifacts, more digital technologies should be used to preserve cultural heritage and make information available to the public.

"New methods could be used to bring ancient Chinese culture alive, especially methods that appeal to the young generation, like video games, online music, videos and literature," said Bai, who is also vice-president of the China Writers Association.

Shang Jin, director of the China Information Development Research Institute, said, "The latest move to promote the digitalization and high-quality development of the cultural industry is expected to help create new forms of online and offline consumption and inject fresh ideas into the traditional cultural industry."

"A digitized cultural database can drive research and innovation, which requires efforts from a variety of different entities, including art institutions and technology companies," Shang added.

The in-depth integration of the cultural industry and digital technology has spawned a variety of emerging businesses, such as online video streaming services, livestreaming, online gaming and music platforms, and virtual exhibitions and tourism.

On June 11, National Cultural and Natural Heritage Day, a virtual tour of the Great Wall was launched by the China Foundation For Cultural Heritage Conservation and the Tencent Foundation.

For the first time, the Great Wall has been digitized in the form of a video game. Players are not only able to enjoy an interactive virtual tour but can also restore the Wall, repairing the cracks virtually.

"Digital technology offers the public countless opportunities to visit cultural sites online and has promoted collaboration between cultural and technology companies. With the help of technology, one can visit a place miles and miles away and learn about it much more easily," said Li Zhe, a researcher at Tianjin University's School of Architecture. The university is a participant in the Great Wall project.

Museums have hastened digitization efforts as a result of the COVID-19 epidemic, so those who are housebound can enjoy exhibitions online.  
According to a report by China Central Television on May 18, this year's International Museum Day, Beijing's Palace Museum has organized about 90 online exhibitions to date. Some 700,000 of its relics have been digitized, with 70,000 to 80,000 pieces being added annually.

The China Record Group, one of the country's largest and oldest record companies, launched an online music library in December comprised of some 100,000 recordings and about 200,000 songs dating back to the early 20th century. Some of the records were made before 1949, and include traditional Chinese operas and folk music. Earlier this year, the company announced a collaboration with popular short-video app Douyin to help make old records accessible to young people.

According to Fan Guobin, general manager of the record group, the company has been repairing and digitizing old records since 2011. In total, about 200,000 songs, 450,000 traditional instrumental compositions and 500,000 traditional Chinese operas have been digitized and shared online, including the materials in the online music library.

On April 23, the Music Research Institute of the Chinese National Academy of Arts also launched the Chinese Traditional Music Sound Archives, which comprises 7,000 hours of digital musical recordings collected by several generations of musicians.

The collection, which includes recordings from all over the country, some of which date back to 1950, is displayed under 12 categories, including Chinese folk songs, opera, dance music and quyi, a collection of storytelling, crosstalk and other spoken art forms.

Among the most important repositories are six works by Hua Yanjun (1893-1950), also known as Abing, a blind musician who specialized in playing the erhu and pipa. His compositions－including The Moon Reflected on the Erquan Spring, one of his most famous－were collected and recorded by musicologists Yang Yinliu and Cao An during the 1950s.

"This is the most comprehensive collection of Chinese traditional music, and we want to share it with a wider audience. Those who sang and played have mostly died, and even most of the musicologists who made the recordings are no longer with us. This is why we have a deep sense of responsibility to preserve these audio materials," said Han Ziyong, head of the academy, adding that audio recordings are vital as much of China's musical history was passed down orally.

# Network ICOM Annual Report 2025 is now online!

![]()

## The International Council of Museums (ICOM) is pleased to share the activities, achievements, and initiatives carried out across the global museum network during 2025.

The 2025 Annual Report highlights the collective efforts of ICOM members, National and International Committees, Regional Alliances, Working Groups, and partners in advancing museums as spaces for dialogue, innovation, education, and sustainable development. As ICOM approaches its 80th anniversary in 2026, this report reflects on a year marked by collaboration, resilience, and a shared commitment to shaping the future of museums.

Throughout 2025, ICOM continued to strengthen its international presence and advocacy efforts, reinforcing the role of museums in addressing contemporary global challenges. Through engagement with international institutions, strategic partnerships, and participation in major global forums, ICOM championed culture and heritage as essential drivers of sustainable development, social cohesion, and peace.

Highlights of the year include the continued implementation of the ICOM Strategic Plan 2022–2028, the celebration of the 27th ICOM General Conference in Dubai, the first edition of the ICOM Award for Sustainable Development Practice in Museums, the Annual Meetings, International Museum Day 2025, and the advancement of key initiatives supporting museum professionals worldwide. The report also showcases the ongoing work of ICOM’s committees and members in strengthening professional standards, fostering international cooperation, and promoting ethical museum practice.

The 2025 Annual Report demonstrates the strength and diversity of our global community and its capacity to respond to change while remaining committed to the values that unite us.

We thank ICOM members, partners, and supporters for their continued engagement and dedication throughout the year.

To view the Annual Report in full screen, please click the blue button below. You may also browse the embedded version at your convenience.

# UNESCO in action: Education highlights in 2025

In 2025, as UNESCO marked 80 years since its founding, education stood at the centre of some of the world’s most pressing challenges. Climate change, rapid technological disruption, demographic shifts and resurgent conflict are reshaping societies and redefining how and where learning takes place.

![UNESCO in action: Education highlights in 2025](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/article/2025-12/endyear2025_610px.jpg.webp?itok=URrXgYPs "UNESCO in action: Education highlights in 2025")

© UNICEF/UNI582947/Elfatih; CatherineLProd/Shutterstock.com; © Bosque Escuela Tena/Ecuador; © UNESCO/ Weiwei Kang; © UNESCO/ Olivier Marie

18 December 2025

Last update:22 December 2025

With the stakes higher than ever, UNESCO continued throughout the year to protect learning, support teachers and learners, and ensure that education remains high on the global political agenda. From financing and teachers to artificial intelligence, emergencies, peace and climate action, here are some highlights of UNESCO’s work in education in 2025.

## Financing education: an urgent political imperative

In 2025, concerns over declining investment in education sharpened. [New analysis](https://www.unesco.org/gem-report/en/2025aidtoeducation) from UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report warned that international aid to education could fall by more than a quarter between 2023 and 2027, with a 12% decline already observed in 2024. [New figures from UNESCO](https://world-education-blog.org/2025/06/09/the-out-of-school-population-is-higher-than-previously-thought-and-rising/) also showed that disengagement by aid providers is growing at a time when 272 million children and young people are out of school, half of them in Africa. UNESCO called on donors to renew their commitment to education.

![PR FfD4 Sevilla Conference ](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/article/2025-07/Image%20%288%29.jpeg.webp?itok=kPmfcrR9 "PR 2025 FfD4 Sevilla Conference ")

© UNESCO

Against this backdrop, in 2025, UNESCO led a renewed global push to prioritize education financing. At the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Sustainable Development, held in Sevilla, Spain, [UNESCO called on donors](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/financing-development-matter-urgency-education-culture-and-sciences) to renew their commitment to these key areas of development. Education was rightly featured as central to the global financing conversation. The Organization emphasized the need to go beyond short-term solutions toward structural approaches that link education investment to debt sustainability, innovative financing mechanisms, and efficient public financial management.

## Teachers: recognizing and rewarding the key agents of change

As the world faces a massive shortage of qualified teachers, UNESCO intensified its focus on strengthening and revalorizing the teaching profession. At the first [World Summit on Teachers](https://www.unesco.org/en/teachers/2025-world-summit), co-organized with Chile in August, global leaders committed to reinventing the teaching profession and supporting teachers as a cornerstone of education systems. The adoption of the [Santiago Consensus](https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000395718) provided a concrete framework of guiding principles and priority actions to strengthen teacher policies and ensure their sustainable financing.

[Thumbnail

![Teachers cannot be coded](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_full_mobile/article/oembed_thumbnails/awiakZCOoEro86wY53ObHggwNW11k3Ut2ZdkEUVYpAc.jpg.webp?itok=-jNsWj3r)

*play\_arrow*](/en/unesco-media/4308670/lightbox)

©UNESCO

UNESCO also led the ‘Teachers cannot be coded’ campaign, highlighting the irreplaceable role of teachers in an era of rapid technological change. In Chile, UNESCO worked with the Ministry of Education and partners to [strengthen teachers’ digital competencies](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/strengthening-teachers-digital-competencies-chile) through an inclusive, participatory approach aimed at supporting professional development and national policy reform.

## Artificial intelligence and the future of learning

Artificial intelligence continued to be at the centre of global education debates throughout the year, introducing both transformative opportunities and complex challenges. UNESCO used its convening power and normative role to help countries navigate this evolving landscape, ensuring that technology in education supports inclusion, equity and human agency.

![Digital Learning Week 2025](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/article/2025-12/DLW-web-visual-610px.jpg.webp?itok=4FZ3MMfp "Digital Learning Week 2025")

© UNESCO/ Weiwei Kang; © UNESCO/ Olivier Marie

[Digital Learning Week](https://www.unesco.org/en/weeks/digital-learning?hub=84636), in September, explored how artificial intelligence is reshaping education and what it means for learners, educators, and education systems worldwide. On this occasion, UNESCO released two publications: [*AI and the future of education: disruptions, dilemmas and directions*](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-and-future-education-disruptions-dilemmas-and-directions?hub=83250), featuring perspectives from global thinkers, and [*AI and education: protecting the rights of learners*](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/ai-and-education-protecting-rights-new-digital-reality?hub=83250), which underscored that the use of AI in education must be firmly anchored in the right to education and safeguarded by human rights principles.

AI is creating disruptions in education. This raises human and policy dilemmas and forces us to reflect on the directions we should take. The future of education will be shaped by the policy choices that we make about education investment, about pedagogy, about governance and about the ethical principles we uphold. For this, strong, decisive leadership is critical.

![Stefania Giannini](/sites/default/files/styles/square_64/article/medias/image/people/2024/12/stefania_giannini-c-unesco-square.jpg.webp?itok=MS8wa3e0)

Stefania GianniniAssistant Director-General for Education

With 739 million young people and adults still lacking basic literacy skills, UNESCO warned that digital transformation risks deepening inequalities, and highlighted literacy as essential to making digital change inclusive, relevant and meaningful for all.

## Education in emergencies: protecting the continuity of learning

In crisis and conflict situations, education remains both a lifeline and a source of hope, resilience, and recovery. On [International Day to Protect Education from Attack](https://www.unesco.org/en/days/protect-education-attack) in September, UNESCO underlined its deep concern about the [44% increase in attacks on educational facilities](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-warns-dramatic-increase-attacks-against-schools-2024?hub=67607) in 2024.

![children participating ](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/article/2025-07/Ajyal%20%2864%29.jpeg.webp?itok=EcgQLgSo)

Ajyal for Creativity and Development

In Gaza, where prolonged conflict has severely disrupted education, UNESCO provided [Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS)](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/mental-health-and-psychosocial-support-displaced-children-and-families-gaza?hub=67607) to 1,200 displaced children and adolescents and supported 20,000 higher education students through the Gaza Virtual Campus.

In Sudan, UNESCO, the Global Partnership for Education and national partners launched the Transitional Education Plan (TEP) 2025–2027 – a roadmap to protect the right to education amid one of the world’s most complex humanitarian crises.

UNESCO also continued to alert the international community to the ongoing ban on education for girls in Afghanistan, where [2.2 million girls are still banned from school](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/afghanistan-four-years-22-million-girls-still-banned-school?hub=67607). A [new UNESCO report](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/new-report-warns-afghanistans-education-crisis-threatens-future-entire-generation) released in October warned of deepening impacts on literacy, skills development and gender equality. In December, UNESCO launched new EU-supported programmes to strengthen education for crisis-affected communities in Haiti and Afghanistan.

## Education for peace and human rights

In a world marked by rising polarization and conflict, UNESCO reinforced its work on education for peace and human rights.

Recognizing education as both a universal right and one of the most powerful tools to fight the root causes of hatred, UNESCO launched a new publication on ["Addressing violent pasts through education: a policy guide"](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/what-you-need-know-about-unescos-policy-guide-addressing-violent-pasts-through-education) and [two new publications](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-launches-two-new-publications-how-teach-about-and-against-antisemitism) on how to teach about and against antisemitism: a guide for teachers and lesson activities for secondary education.

[Thumbnail

![Interview with UNESCO Specialist on Hate Speech and Genocide Prevention Karel Fracapane](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_full_mobile/article/oembed_thumbnails/2NfmOj3gtX-6PW01izMpIc15LnQRqgFD5OF4nNLSOLo.jpg.webp?itok=lWPywT3k)

*play\_arrow*](/en/unesco-media/4079382/lightbox)

© UNESCO

In December, the [first UNESCO Global Citizenship Education Prize](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/projects-ecuador-and-united-republic-tanzania-win-first-edition-unesco-global-citizenship-education?hub=343), funded by the Republic of Korea, recognized a school project in the Amazon rainforest in Ecuador and a youth-led organization in the United Republic of Tanzania for their efforts to promote empathy, civic engagement and peace.

## Greening education

As climate change continues to disrupt lives and livelihoods, UNESCO stepped up efforts to green education systems worldwide. Ahead of COP30, new UNESCO data showed that 96,000 schools in 93 countries have adopted green practices recommended by the Organization. These findings were presented at a COP30 Ministerial Roundtable on greening education, where [UNESCO called on governments](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/cop30-unesco-calls-urgent-action-accelerate-green-schools) to continue their efforts to integrate environmental issues into all school curricula, with the goal of greening 50% of schools in every country by 2030.

![ESD Prize 2025 laureates](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/article/2025-11/ESD-Prize-2025-laureates.jpg.webp?itok=5dB1N1Yd)

© La culture au coeur du développement, © Instituto Akatu, © Fundación Pro Eco Azuero

Also in November, [three projects from Benin, Brazil and Panama](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-awards-outstanding-education-sustainable-development-projects-benin-brazil-and-panama) were awarded the 2025 UNESCO–Japan Prize on Education for Sustainable Development, recognizing innovative and inclusive approaches to preparing learners for climate action.

## Mainstreaming the General History of Africa into education systems

Sixty years after embarking on the ambition of restoring, documenting and chronicling the history of the African continent from Prehistory to the present day, UNESCO announces the completion of the last three volumes of the [General History of Africa](https://www.unesco.org/en/general-history-africa/education) in October.

![Mainstreaming the General History of Africa into education systems](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/article/2025-12/GHA-PUB.jpg.webp?itok=Z-ya6tRJ "Mainstreaming the General History of Africa into education systems")

© UNESCO

On this occasion, UNESCO also unveiled the [General History of Africa Curriculum Pathway Tool](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/mainstreaming-general-history-africa-education-systems-curriculum-pathway?hub=74448) proposing guiding principles and approaches for designing and implementing the General History of Africa into the curriculum. It puts forth curriculum outlines for basic and secondary education to offer renewed and broader perspectives on the history of Africa and its diasporas, and their contributions to humanity. The aim is to convey a history free of prejudice and to empower younger generations to understand the diversity and richness of African heritage.

*Looking ahead to 2026, UNESCO will strengthen SDG 4 global coordination and leadership as the international community begins to shape the education agenda beyond 2030. UNESCO’s work on teachers will remain central to advancing the global education agenda and supporting national transformation efforts. Engagement in countries affected by crisis will be scaled up, including planning to strengthen education systems. As digital transformation continues to reshape learning, UNESCO will step up support to human-centered digital transformation that strengthens education systems and supports countries to shape the future of learning.*

This is a UNESCO news article (published 18 December 2025) summarizing UNESCO's key education achievements and initiatives throughout 2025, marking the organization's 80th anniversary. The article covers several major themes:

1. **Financing Education**: UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report warned that international aid to education could fall by more than a quarter between 2023 and 2027, with a 12% decline already observed in 2024. There are 272 million children and young people out of school, half of them in Africa. At the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Sustainable Development in Sevilla, Spain, UNESCO called on donors to renew commitments and pursue structural approaches linking education investment to debt sustainability.

2. **Teachers**: UNESCO co-organized the first World Summit on Teachers with Chile in August, where the Santiago Consensus was adopted to strengthen teacher policies and sustainable financing. UNESCO also led the 'Teachers cannot be coded' campaign and worked with Chile to strengthen teachers' digital competencies.

3. **Artificial Intelligence**: Digital Learning Week in September produced two publications: "AI and the future of education: disruptions, dilemmas and directions" and "AI and education: protecting the rights of learners." UNESCO warned that 739 million young people and adults lack basic literacy skills, and that digital transformation risks deepening inequalities.

4. **Education in Emergencies**: UNESCO highlighted a 44% increase in attacks on educational facilities in 2024. In Gaza, UNESCO provided Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) to 1,200 displaced children and supported 20,000 higher education students via the Gaza Virtual Campus. In Sudan, UNESCO and partners launched the Transitional Education Plan (TEP) 2025-2027. UNESCO continued to alert the international community about 2.2 million girls banned from school in Afghanistan. New EU-supported programmes were launched for Haiti and Afghanistan in December.

5. **Education for Peace**: UNESCO launched a policy guide on "Addressing violent pasts through education" and two publications on teaching about and against antisemitism. The first UNESCO Global Citizenship Education Prize (funded by the Republic of Korea) was awarded to projects in Ecuador and Tanzania.

6. **Greening Education**: Ahead of COP30, UNESCO data showed 96,000 schools in 93 countries adopted green practices. UNESCO called on governments to green 50% of schools in every country by 2030. Three projects from Benin, Brazil and Panama won the 2025 UNESCO-Japan Prize on Education for Sustainable Development.

7. **General History of Africa**: UNESCO completed the last three volumes of the General History of Africa in October (60 years after starting the project) and unveiled the General History of Africa Curriculum Pathway Tool for integrating this history into basic and secondary education curricula.

Looking ahead to 2026, UNESCO plans to strengthen SDG 4 global coordination, keep teachers central to its agenda, scale up engagement in crisis-affected countries, and support human-centered digital transformation.

The article includes a quote from Stefania Giannini, UNESCO Assistant Director-General for Education: "AI is creating disruptions in education. This raises human and policy dilemmas and forces us to reflect on the directions we should take. The future of education will be shaped by the policy choices that we make about education investment, about pedagogy, about governance and about the ethical principles we uphold. For this, strong, decisive leadership is critical."

args.summary: The ICOM-CECA (Committee for Education and Cultural Action) Facebook post from September 22, 2025, announces the publication of "Best Practice 13" — the thirteenth edition of the ICOM-CECA Best Practice Book, a benchmark resource in the field of museum education. The publication is available online, open access, in English, French, and Spanish on the ICOM CECA website. Margarita Laraignée served as the Best Practice awards Publication Coordinator and editor. The 2025 edition received 29 proposals (higher than the previous year), submitted from 21 countries across five geographic regions: Asia (10), Europe (9), Africa (1), Latin America (6), and North America (3). The winners of the 2025 Best Practice Award are Alice de Lagarde, Eugenia Law, and Jeongmin Ryu, representing institutions including Musée Picasso Paris, Centre for Heritage Arts and Textile (Hong Kong), and Seoul Children's Museum.
args.key_excerpts: "With deep satisfaction and renewed enthusiasm, I am honored to present the thirteenth edition of the ICOM-CECA Best Practice Book, a work that has become a benchmark in the field of museum education." - Margarita Laraignée, Publication Coordinator/editor

 PhD Ricard Huerta. Artist and Full Professor of Art Education in the University of Valencia (Spain). Regular member at the Institute of Creativity and Educational Innovation, and member of InSEA and ICOM. Head of the Research Journal EARI Educación Artística Revista de Investigación. Director of Museari www.museari.com. Graduate in Fine Arts, in Music, and Communication. Head of the international Cemeteries project. Invited researcher in universities of France, Italy, Spain, United Kingdom, Cuba, Uruguay, Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, Argentina, Portugal, Paraguay, Costa Rica and Chile. He has coordinated several publications and activities inside the areas of Visual Arts, Education, ICT and Museums. Head of the project “Dechados Inclusive creativity in secondary school”. Member of the Seminar on Gender and Sexual Diversity of the Museums of Catalonia. He has published books and articles in specialized journals, having coordinated numerous publications within the fields of art, education, teacher education, heritage and museums. Letters and alphabets are a relevant aspect of his work both at an educational level and artistic creation. He has presented exhibitions with themes heavily impregnated by typography and calligraphy in different countries. He has directed international seminars on research in art education and seven international congress.

## Abstract

This study explores current and potential connections between museums, schools, and universities. It is based on 18 expert interviews with representatives from 19 institutions, conducted between 2015 and 2024, to assess feasibility and gather ideas for improving communication and collaboration between these educational institutions. Of the 19 participating institutions, 17 are Hispanic. The study is further enriched by interviews with two experts from Brazil and France, who collaborate within the Spanish university sector. This qualitative research uses interviews to analyze the key opinions of its participants, from both an analytical and propositional perspective. Five analytical categories are defined to extract and organize the final results: museum conceptualization, institutional relationships, collaboration strategies, pedagogical and methodological approaches, and transformation and development. The findings underscore the importance and feasibility of interinstitutional cooperation. The value of creating convergent narratives and developing collaborative and egalitarian projects is highlighted. The study suggests viewing museum as spaces with high educational potential, social function, and research capacity. The key lies in mediating cognitive/esthetic proposals; and educational approaches, fostering new perspectives and interconnections. This seeks to create a network of relationships that strengthens the bond between these three institutions, enhancing their joint educational impact.

## 1. Introduction

Rapid scientific and technological advances are transforming social contexts at a global scale, generating unprecedented challenges for formal and informal education systems. This evolution demands a redefinition of essential competences for 21st century citizens and an agile and effective adaptation of traditional educational models ([Castells, 2006](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B13-education-15-00543)). The current landscape demands professionals with skills that differ significantly from those required just a decade ago, particularly in terms of digital competency, critical thinking, creativity, and the ability for flexible and personalized learning ([World Economic Forum, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B69-education-15-00543); [UNESCO, 2024b](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B64-education-15-00543)). At the same time, the labor market is evolving rapidly, also requiring skills such as critical thinking, creativity, and interpersonal skills, forcing education systems and institutions to adapt their curricula to integrate these 21st century competences ([OECD, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B50-education-15-00543); [Hargreaves & Fullan, 2015](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B29-education-15-00543)). It is also crucial to provide continuous training and updating opportunities for educators, allowing them to keep up with the latest trends and adopt innovative pedagogical approaches ([Darling-Hammond et al., 2017](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B19-education-15-00543)).

In this context of constant change, it is crucial to foster a sense of identity that preserves cultural roots as an essential foundation of new societies, which has become an emerging challenge in the era of globalization ([UNESCO, 2024a](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B65-education-15-00543)). In this regard, the connectivist approach, which emphasizes the construction of learning networks and interaction between individuals, can facilitate the preservation and dissemination of cultural identity in an increasingly interconnected world ([Siemens, 2004](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B58-education-15-00543)).

## 2. Interinstitutional Collaboration: A Multidimensional Approach

It is crucial to explore new forms of integration between the school and university education system and its surrounding environment ([Huerta & Soto González, 2022](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B38-education-15-00543)), making it essential to create innovative collaborations and links with diverse organizations in order to enrich educational work ([OECD, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B51-education-15-00543)). In this context, museums emerge as fundamental allies, making it necessary to generate spaces for dialog where the voices of educational institutions, universities, and museums are heard ([Coca-Jiménez & Marín-Cepeda, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B17-education-15-00543)). The objective of these spaces would be to establish multidimensional connections with the environment at all levels of the educational system, making it more permeable and capable of interpreting and responding to the cultural, social, political, and economic signs of citizens in an environment of collaboration and consensus ([García-Canclini, 2001](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B25-education-15-00543)).

The links between museums, educational institutions, and universities have gained global relevance as strategies to promote pedagogical innovation, interdisciplinary research, and community development. The Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) in London stands out for its inclusive approach. In recent years, it has hired refugees as cultural guides, integrating diverse perspectives into its educational programs ([OECD & ICOM, 2019](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B52-education-15-00543)). This model not only fosters local employment, but also enriches the museum experience through intercultural narratives.

On the other hand, the report “Understanding the Value of Arts and Culture” ([Farrell, 2016](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B22-education-15-00543)), led by the Arts and Humanities Research Council, highlights the role of museums as catalysts for lifelong learning, especially through collaborations with universities. A concrete example is the alliance between the Tate Modern and University College London (UCL), which are researching techniques for the conservation of contemporary art using artificial intelligence and nanotechnologies ([Tate Modern, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B62-education-15-00543)).

According to the OECD in the ICOM Report (2019), “British museums are not mere repositories of objects, but social laboratories where education, technology, and civic participation converge” ([OECD & ICOM, 2019, p. 42](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B52-education-15-00543)).

Although available research emphasizes the internationalization of Canadian universities, such as the University of Alberta, and their links with economic sectors, museums also play a role in knowledge transfer. The Royal Ontario Museum (ROM) collaborates with the University of Toronto on archeological and anthropological projects, although these initiatives are not always thoroughly documented in public reports. Professional internship and artist residency programs, such as those at the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts, serve as bridges between academia and cultural management ([Government of Québec, 2022](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B28-education-15-00543)). The integration of museums into university networks allows for democratizing access to heritage and generating new pedagogical methodologies.

According to the American Alliance of Museums ([AAM, 2017](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B2-education-15-00543)), U.S. museums generate an annual economic impact of USD 50 billion and employ more than 726,000 people. Institutions such as the Smithsonian Institution have established strategic alliances with elite universities, including Harvard and MIT, to develop projects in digital heritage and STEAM education. A recent example is the “Art and Technology Lab” program at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York, carried out in collaboration with Columbia University, which explores intersections between art, artificial intelligence, and digital ethics ([MoMA, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B48-education-15-00543)). “Museums are economic engines, but also critical spaces for rethinking 21st-century education” ([AAM, 2017, p. 8](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B2-education-15-00543)).

### 2.1. The Transformative Role of Museums

Museums are faced with new demands from the formal education system and must adapt to these emerging demands ([Luna & Ibáñez-Etxeberria, 2020](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B45-education-15-00543)). In this new paradigm, the concept of heritage expands, encompassing not only the ancient and inherited, but also contemporary cultural manifestations ([Huerta & Rodríguez-López, 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B37-education-15-00543)). As [Arrieta Urtizberea](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B4-education-15-00543) ([2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B4-education-15-00543)) points out, “the notion of cultural heritage has expanded significantly, now including current cultural expressions and assets that reflect the identity and values of contemporary societies” (p. 45). This vision of cultural heritage, understood as a temporal continuum that integrates past and present, represents a paradigmatic shift in the way we understand and value our cultural heritage. Even heritage elements inherited from the past are now received, analyzed, interpreted, and transmitted from contemporary perspectives and contexts, creating a constant dialog between historical and contemporary aspects ([Fontal & Ibáñez-Etxeberria, 2017](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B23-education-15-00543); [AECID, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B1-education-15-00543); [Huerta, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B35-education-15-00543)).

### 2.2. Interconnected Educational Fabric

Museums, schools, and universities are not isolated entities; they form an interconnected educational network that encompasses diverse spaces and contexts ([Baig et al., 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B5-education-15-00543)). This interrelationship is fundamental for building realistic and relevant art education, adapted to the complexity of contemporary reality. It is crucial to reevaluate the complexities and connections between art and education, as they have historically been considered independent spheres. However, these divisions are currently unsustainable due to the expansion and interconnectedness of educational and cultural institutions. What were previously perceived as separate spheres have evolved into collaborative networks, where education becomes a central axis. Vicente Todolí, in an interview with [Manen](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B46-education-15-00543) ([2006](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B46-education-15-00543)), points out that interest in education is not only political, but also a strategic aspect for creating future audiences and addressing diversity.

In the 1970s and 1980s, Spanish museums began to integrate education as an essential resource, driven by political and institutional changes. The neoliberal economy required museums to fulfill dual functions: public service and cultural entertainment. This implies that museum education cannot be considered in isolation; it must be contextualized within its social and cultural environment. Collaboration with the urban and social environment is key to the development of effective educational policies ([Gil, 2019](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B26-education-15-00543)). According to [Szántó](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B61-education-15-00543) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B61-education-15-00543)), museums must become meeting spaces open for dialog, where education is a continuous and dynamic process.

While museum education has begun to attract children and young adults, university participation has historically been underestimated. However, new pedagogies are changing this perception, promoting mutual learning among visitors of diverse characteristics and abilities. As [Murillo et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B47-education-15-00543) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B47-education-15-00543)) point out, the inclusion of arts education in the university curriculum is essential for developing critical and creative citizens.

### 2.3. New Interdisciplinary Relationships

Currently, new relationships between museums and universities are emerging, becoming more interdisciplinary ([Nava & Pazos-López, 2020](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B49-education-15-00543)). This partnership is attractive, representing a shift toward a more accessible culture. In this regard, it becomes essential to examine the structures and policies of these institutions, as well as the accountability dynamics that govern them ([Vadillo Lobo, 2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B66-education-15-00543)). Mediation, therefore, becomes a process of institutional change that requires a reevaluation of the organizations and subjectivities involved ([Rodrigo-Montero & Collados-Alcaide, 2015](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B56-education-15-00543)).

[Calbó and Terradellas](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B11-education-15-00543) ([2005](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B11-education-15-00543)) argue that heritage education should be part of general education, as it contributes to human and cultural development. This perspective reinforces the need for innovative collaborative approaches between universities, museums, and educational centers. In this sense, [Cuenca López and Estepa Giménez](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B18-education-15-00543) ([2013](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B18-education-15-00543)) emphasize that collaboration between cultural and educational institutions is crucial for the development of projects that respond to contemporary needs.

### 2.4. Collaborative Research and Future Challenges

Research serves as a means to address new cultural and communicative challenges ([Delgado-Bardales, 2021](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B20-education-15-00543)). Therefore, universities should foster relevant contracts that unite professionals from different institutions, creating an environment conducive to collaborative research. In this regard, it is essential to design strategies that facilitate connections between schools, museums, and universities, thus addressing networked changes and collaborations. The creation of active research groups is crucial for coordinating projects involving diverse institutions. With this in mind, art education is presented as a driver of interaction, promoting spaces for collaboration and joint learning.

Collaboration between academia and museums plays a fundamental role in enriching contemporary art education. Creating this shared communication between educational institutions and museums requires a collaborative and innovative approach that recognizes student diversity and promotes active participation in the artistic experience. This process entails a constant reevaluation of educational practices and an openness to new forms of interaction between art, educators, and the public ([Hernández-Hernández, 2019](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B30-education-15-00543); [Huerta, 2010](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B34-education-15-00543)). In this context, digital strategies have emerged as catalysts for more fluid and efficient communication between institutions, as [Huerta and Navarro Espinach](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B36-education-15-00543) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B36-education-15-00543)) point out in their analysis of disruptive museums and new educational approaches.

### 2.5. Specialized Training and Cultural Mediation

The specialized training of educational staff is revealed as a key factor in transforming museum visits into truly meaningful experiences. [Fontal Merillas](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B24-education-15-00543) ([2013](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B24-education-15-00543)) emphasizes the need for universities and schools to forge collaborative networks that integrate pedagogical needs from early childhood education to postgraduate studies ([Castro-Calviño & López-Facal, 2019](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B14-education-15-00543)). In this scenario, educators assume a crucial role as cultural mediators, acting as what [Lewin](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B40-education-15-00543) ([1947](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B40-education-15-00543)) and [White](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B68-education-15-00543) ([1950](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B68-education-15-00543)) called “gatekeepers”, that is, information filters based on professional criteria and practical experience.

However, this cooperation between museums, universities, and schools is not without challenges. [Catibiela](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B15-education-15-00543) ([2017](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B15-education-15-00543)) and [Soto-González](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B60-education-15-00543) ([2015](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B60-education-15-00543)) identify significant obstacles, such as the scarcity of teaching tools adapted to museum contexts and insufficient initial training in visual culture skills. These challenges require the development of new collaborative action protocols that go beyond traditional institutional dynamics.

### 2.6. Pedagogical Innovation Strategies

To address these challenges, universities must implement pedagogical innovation strategies ([Pastor-Blázquez & Bernal-Bravo, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B55-education-15-00543)). [Xanthoudaki](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B70-education-15-00543) ([2016](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B70-education-15-00543)) and [Bevan and Xanthoudaki](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B7-education-15-00543) ([2008](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B7-education-15-00543)) propose the creation of ongoing training programs for museum educators, the development of interdisciplinary projects that use collections as teaching resources, and applied research on cultural mediation methodologies ([Triviño-Cabrera & Chaves-Guerrero, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B63-education-15-00543)). These initiatives should harness the potential of new technologies to create shared knowledge networks, also considering transmedia narratives and content outreach and dissemination efforts through social media ([Orozco Varela et al., 2022](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B53-education-15-00543); [Palencia-Triana, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B54-education-15-00543)).

Museums, for their part, are evolving toward a more active role as social laboratories for the construction of collective identities ([Carvalho, 1996](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B12-education-15-00543)). [Luelmo-Jareño](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B43-education-15-00543) ([2007](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B43-education-15-00543)) emphasizes that the educational role of museums transcends mere conservation, promoting critical readings of heritage through visual literacy strategies. This perspective requires rethinking models of collaboration between cultural and academic institutions ([Hooper-Greenhill, 2007](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B33-education-15-00543)).

### 2.7. Challenges in Contemporary Art Education

Awareness of the importance of arts education and heritage in museums was not consolidated until the 20th century. Although educational departments have been incorporated into museums in recent decades, they still face significant obstacles to effective educational action ([Arriaga, 2011](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B3-education-15-00543)). Despite the intense liaison between institutions, in many museums, educational work is not considered a priority, and educational teams often operate within rigid structures, adopting traditional discourses ([Calaf Masachs & Suárez, 2015](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B9-education-15-00543)).

Educational teams from contemporary art museums face particular challenges due to the complexity and, at times, lack of acceptance of the works on display. A lack of training in contemporary culture can lead to disinterest or rejection among school and university audiences ([Fontal & Ibáñez-Etxeberria, 2017](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B23-education-15-00543)). To address this issue, it is essential to share personal experiences that help reconstruct both individual and collective memories, facilitating new ways of interpreting and expressing memories based on the works on display.

### 2.8. Professional Development and Awareness

Faced with the accelerated obsolescence of knowledge, [González-Sanz and Feliu-Torruella](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B27-education-15-00543) ([2023](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B27-education-15-00543)) advocate for holistic training and continuous professional updating systems ([Sack & Thompson, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B57-education-15-00543)).

Similarly, raising awareness about art and education is essential to fully explore its esthetic, emotional, and social values ([Luna & Ibáñez-Etxeberria, 2020](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B45-education-15-00543)). This process requires a historical analysis that connects art with contemporary interests, ensuring its internal and external coherence ([Calbó et al., 2011](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B10-education-15-00543)). Raising awareness acts as a key turning point for achieving pedagogical objectives and promoting the symbolic appropriation of content, integrating it into individual’s own context and identity.

### 2.9. Experiential Learning and Cultural Identity

Learning must be based on previous experiences, given that memory stores what is meaningful and connected to personal reality. In this sense, teaching in schools, museums, and universities must be based on individual and collective experiences. As [Calbó et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B10-education-15-00543) ([2011](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B10-education-15-00543)) argue, “arts education emphasizes its cognitive consequences: working in art contributes to the development of complex and subtle ways of thinking” (p. 116). From an educational perspective, identity is a central value, given that learning is built from the interaction between individuals and their environment. Museums and heritage offer opportunities for the discovery and development of knowledge in multiple dimensions: conceptual, procedural, and attitudinal ([Lucas-Palacios & de Atalaya, 2025](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B42-education-15-00543)). Art becomes a mediator of identity, allowing students to relate to, understand, and identify with their cultural environment.

### 2.10. From Passive Observation to Active Reflection

The artistic innovations of the 20th century have rendered the passive attitude of mere observation of schoolchildren and university students ineffective. It is crucial to understand art as a reflective activity that can generate new situations or realities, which poses a significant challenge for most people ([Eisner, 2004](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B21-education-15-00543)). Museum educators play a fundamental role in revealing ways of approaching works, demystifying the idea that a special gift or exceptional wisdom is required to understand museum content ([López & Kivatinetz, 2006](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B41-education-15-00543)). Learning in museums is enriched when students adopt a reflective and active attitude, reinterpreting their prior experiences and knowledge. According to [Lois H. Silverman](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B59-education-15-00543) ([2009](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B59-education-15-00543)), memory plays a fundamental role in the construction of meaning by placing what is found within the context of personal experience.

Museums should prioritize experience over the work itself, consider sociocultural contexts, and avoid the museum’s authority as the sole source of knowledge ([Jara, 2016](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B39-education-15-00543)). This allows students to become the protagonists of their learning, fostering creativity and critical reflection ([Lull Sanz & Vallugera Fuster, 2024](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B44-education-15-00543)).

## 3. Materials and Methods

The research methodology employed in this study is based on qualitative techniques, specifically the use of interviews and the concept of triangulation. Triangulation, according to [Miguel S. Valles](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B67-education-15-00543) ([1996](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B67-education-15-00543)), involves the application of various methods and systems in the investigation of a single phenomenon.

### 3.1. Research Question

The research question guiding this study is: what connections currently exist, or could potentially develop, between universities, educational institutions, and museums within the Hispanic context?

### 3.2. Research Design

The design of this qualitative research used a research interview method with expert professionals in the fields of museums, schools, and universities. Arrangements for the interviews were made through email or phone to schedule the date and location, as visits needed to be planned. Out of the 18 interviews, only 2 took place via videoconference; the rest were held in person, involving visits to the participants’ workplace or various locations due to their involvement in conferences or events.

For the interview, four key questions were defined to delve deeper into the research question: what do schools need from museums in the Hispanic context? What can museums offer schools in the Hispanic context? What do universities need from museums and schools in the Hispanic context? What do museums and schools need from universities in the Hispanic context?

Transcriptions were made in verbatim format to provide the necessary documentation for data analysis and to compile the textual narrative of the discourse. The contributions were cross-referenced to identify shared inputs that informed the narrative text of the data analysis. This process involved making inferences, constructing bottom-up conclusions, and focusing on the main responses based on preference, as specified in processes of agreement or disagreement.

To complement the analysis, five categories were created to synthesize the content of the contributions made in the interviews. The categories are museum conceptualization, institutional relationships, collaboration strategies, pedagogical and methodological approaches, and transformation and development.

The appropriate responses were then identified as those questions that verified the research question and their contribution to the dimensions of analysis through their recurrence and assertiveness in relation to the research topic and its analysis format.

The triangulation included was carried out through an exploration and reflective discussion about schools, museums, and universities. The main contributions of the experts were included as a fundamental source for the reconstruction of knowledge, which reflects the findings of the fieldwork.

This qualitative methodology, based on the triangulation of diverse sources and perspectives, allowed for a deeper and more holistic understanding of the phenomenon studied, increasing the validity and consistency of the findings.

### 3.3. Data Analysis

The hermeneutic triangulation process was carried out once the information was completely gathered, which involved the gathering and dialectical crossing of all the information relevant to the object of study ([Benavides & Gómez-Restrepo, 2005](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B6-education-15-00543)). The practical procedure for triangulating the interviews followed the following steps: (a) compilation of the information obtained during the fieldwork; (b) triangulation of the information for each person or group; and (c) triangulation of the information between all the research questions.

Information was sorted based on criteria of relevance and consistency, considering only information directly related to the research topic and allowing for the identification of emerging issues specific to qualitative research ([Hernández-Sampieri, 2014](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B32-education-15-00543)). Four categories of analysis were created to synthesize the content: museum conceptualization, institutional relationships, collaboration strategies, pedagogical and methodological approaches, and transformation and development. The appropriate responses were used to identify those questions that met the objective of relevance, either due to their recurrence or their relevance to the research topic.

Triangulation of information by individual or group allowed us to understand the opinions of the different participants according to their institution of origin (museum, university, or school) ([Charres, 2018](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B16-education-15-00543)). This process was carried out through inference, drawing bottom-up conclusions and concentrating the main responses by preferences, specified in processes of coincidence or divergence.

The triangulation included throughout the text with the theoretical framework was carried out through a reflective exploration and discussion of specialized literature on education through art, schools, museums, and universities. This process was not limited to a mere theoretical framework, but was used as a fundamental source for the reconstruction of knowledge, sparking a new discussion between the existing literature and the findings of the fieldwork.

The correct formalization of the interpretation process was achieved thanks to the use of basic theoretical questions, which allowed for organic thinking and a systematic and sequenced arrangement of the synthesis and argumentation ([Valles, 1996](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#B67-education-15-00543)).

This qualitative methodology, based on the triangulation of diverse sources and perspectives, allowed for a deeper and more holistic understanding of the phenomenon studied, increasing the validity and consistency of the findings.

### 3.4. Participants/Context

The sample and data collection were based on 18 interviews conducted with national and international experts representing 18 institutions (see [Table 1](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/543#table_body_display_education-15-00543-t001)). Participants were selected based on their CVs, which guaranteed their expertise in the subject matter.

This is an open-access research article from the MDPI journal Education Sciences (Volume 15, Issue 5, 2025) titled "Educational Connections: Museums, Universities, and Schools as Places of Supplementary Learning" by Mᵃ Dolores Soto-González, Ricard Huerta, and Ramona Rodríguez-López, all from the Department of Didactics of Physical, Artistic and Music Education at the University of Valencia, Spain. The article (DOI: 10.3390/educsci15050543) was submitted 28 March 2025, revised 22 April 2025, accepted 24 April 2025, and published 28 April 2025.

The study explores current and potential connections between museums, schools, and universities, based on 18 expert interviews with representatives from 19 institutions (17 of which are Hispanic, plus two experts from Brazil and France) conducted between 2015 and 2024. The research uses qualitative methodology with interviews and triangulation. Five analytical categories structure the findings: museum conceptualization, institutional relationships, collaboration strategies, pedagogical and methodological approaches, and transformation and development.

Key findings highlight the importance and feasibility of interinstitutional cooperation, the value of convergent narratives and collaborative egalitarian projects, and the view of museums as spaces with high educational potential, social function, and research capacity. The research question asks what connections currently exist or could develop between universities, educational institutions, and museums within the Hispanic context. Four key interview questions address what schools need from museums, what museums can offer schools, what universities need from museums and schools, and what museums and schools need from universities.

The article's theoretical framework covers multiple themes: the transformative role of museums, museums/schools/universities as an interconnected educational fabric, new interdisciplinary relationships, collaborative research, specialized training and cultural mediation, pedagogical innovation strategies, challenges in contemporary art education, professional development, experiential learning and cultural identity, and moving from passive observation to active reflection. Notable international examples cited include the Victoria and Albert Museum's hiring of refugees as cultural guides, the Tate Modern's collaboration with University College London on AI-based art conservation, the Royal Ontario Museum's partnership with the University of Toronto, the Smithsonian Institution's alliances with Harvard and MIT, and MoMA's "Art and Technology Lab" with Columbia University. The article also cites that U.S. museums generate $50 billion in annual economic impact and employ over 726,000 people (AAM, 2017).

## What you need to know about UNESCO’s Futures of Education Programme

Our world is undergoing rapid and profound change. Geopolitical tensions, technological disruption, widening inequalities and accelerating climate crises are reshaping how we live, work and learn. Because education shapes the future, how we think about education today will influence the societies we build tomorrow.

UNESCO’s Futures of Education programme anticipates and imagines new possibilities for education. It looks beyond immediate policy cycles to consider the longer-term purposes, functions and processes of education – and how they can support more just, equitable and sustainable futures for humanity and the planet.

### What is the Futures of Education Programme?

UNESCO’s Futures of Education Programme was launched in 2019 in response to the UN Secretary-General’s call for UNESCO to lead the global debate on the future of education. It steers a global effort to rethink how knowledge, learning and education can shape more just, equitable, and sustainable futures for humanity and the planet. Guided by the vision outlined in the report of the International Commission on the Futures of Education ‘[Reimagining Our Futures Together: A new social contract for education](https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000379707)’, the Programme aims to inspire vision, foresight, research and dialogue that strengthen education’s transformative role. 

The Futures of Education Programme looks **beyond short-term responses** to crises and disruptions and considers the **long-term transformations needed in education**. It acknowledges the diversity of lived realities and the plurality of possible futures. In rethinking education, **UNESCO’s Futures of Education Programme strengthens education’s transformative role,** drawing on diverse perspectives and experiences from around the world.

### Why reimagine education?

Over the past several decades, millions of children, young people and adults have benefitted from expanded access to educational opportunities. Despite this, however, deep and persistent inequalities in education remain, while humanity and the planet face new increasingly complex and interconnected challenges. Rapid geopolitical, technological and economic shifts, deepening polarization, social exclusion, violent conflicts and environmental crises demand that we **reimagine our shared futures and the role of education.** We must change course if we are to repair past injustices while transforming the future.

Education is key to changing course, yet it cannot do so through the same models and systems that have too often reinforced competition, exclusion, excessive individualism, overconsumption and unsustainable ways of life. Renewed approaches are urgently needed to foster both individual and collective capacities for advancing social, economic, and environmental justice and wellbeing.

### What does new social contract for education mean?

Changing course requires renewing the social contract for education. This implies rethinking the purpose of education, the ways in which learning is organized, and the roles and responsibilities of all those involved. In the spirit of the [Reimagining Our Futures Together](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/reimagining-our-futures-together-new-social-contract-education) report, a new social contract for education should be grounded in **two foundational principles:** first, an expanded vision of **the right to education throughout life**, and second, **strengthening education as a public endeavour and a common good.** 

Renewing the social contract for education does not mean starting from scratch. We must, on one hand, protect and build on the strengths that we have nurtured over the years. On the other, we must critically acknowledge what in our practices is not working and why. Renewing the social contract is more than a mere course correction on a path already set. It implies more fundamental changes in our models and approaches. In doing so, it invites all to consider the following essential questions: 

https://www.unesco.org/en/futures-education/report

What should we continue doing?  
What should we abandon?  
What needs to be creatively reimagined?

### How can we transform education?

### What are current strands of work?

Looking beyond short-term responses, the Futures of Education Programme explores how education can be transformed to help societies change course and shape more just and sustainable futures. It does so by generating critical insights, undertaking innovative research, and by encouraging open and forward-looking dialogue. Current strands of research examine policy visions and narratives on the futures of education beyond 2030. [IdeasLAB](https://www.unesco.org/en/futures-education/ideas?hub=81942) think piece series, as well as the [ERF Working Papers](https://www.unesco.org/en/futures-education/research-and-knowledge-products) series offer fresh insights and provocations about the futures of education, while a range of [publications](https://www.unesco.org/en/futures-education/publications?hub=81942) chart pathways for education to foster more just, inclusive and sustainable futures. 

As a global convenor, UNESCO’s Futures of Education Programme also brings together multiple constituencies for dialogue and knowledge exchange about the futures of education. It explores emerging futures through monthly [Futures Dialogues](https://www.unesco.org/en/node/187407?hub=84637) webinars which mobilize the collective human intelligence and interdisciplinary expertise of UNESCO’s [global network of university chairs](https://www.unesco.org/en/unitwin). The programme also offers spaces for dialogue and peer learning through major annual convenings such as the flagship UN event [Digital Learning Week](https://www.unesco.org/en/weeks/digital-learning) and World Futures Day celebrations. 

### What was the International Commission the Futures of Education?

The [Futures of Education Initiative](https://www.unesco.org/en/futures-education/initiative) is a part a series of global [visioning exercises](https://www.unesco.org/en/futures-education/visions-education) that UNESCO has undertaken at critical junctures of rapid societal transformation. The reports produced have helped frame contemporary debates in education in policy, research, and practice. 

In 2019, the Director-General of UNESCO convened an independent International Commission of thought leaders from politics, academia, the arts, science, business and education, under the leadership of the President of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, HE President Sahle-Work Zewde, to develop a vision for the Futures of Education looking towards 2050. The mandate of the International Commission on the Futures of Education was to collectively reflect on how education might need to be rethought in a world of increasing complexity, uncertainty and precarity. The Commission was invited to challenge and re-evaluate the foundational principles laid out in previous UNESCO global reports about education. Through an extensive consultation process, over one million people from around the world contributed ideas and proposals through background papers, essays, artwork, surveys, and focus group discussions, which the Commission carefully considered. Looking towards the year 2050 and beyond, the Reimagining Our Futures Together report suggested visions and strategies for both education policy and education practice to adopt, taking into consideration the longstanding UNESCO commitment to a pluralistic, integrated and humanistic approach to education and knowledge as common goods. 

### What impact has the ‘Reimagining Our Futures Together’ report had?

Since its launch in November 2021, [Reimagining Our Futures Together](https://www.unesco.org/en/futures-education/report-resources) has had significant worldwide [impact](https://www.unesco.org/en/futures-education/impact). One of the most consulted UNESCO publications on-line, the report is now available in 17 languages including Amharic, Arabic, Bahasa Indonesia, Catalan, Chinese, English, French, Greek, Italian, Kiswahili, Korean, Latvian, Mongolian, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, and Spanish. It has generated thousands of citations in academic literature, is taught in university courses across numerous institutions and has informed teacher education programmes and research partnerships in a number of contexts.

The report has served as the key reference for the 2022 [**Transforming Education Summit**](https://www.un.org/en/transforming-education-summit) which brought together 65 world leaders, and it served to guide national consultations and statements of commitment in over 100 countries as part of the Summit process. It has also served as the main framing and anchor of other major global education policy forums, such as the [3rd World Higher Education Conference](https://www.unesco.org/en/higher-education/2022-world-conference) and [7th International Conference on Adult Learning and Education](https://www.uil.unesco.org/en/seventh-international-conference-adult-education) in 2022. More recently, it served as the foundation for the [**UNESCO International Forum on the Futures of Education**](https://www.unesco.org/en/renewing-education-transform-future)(Republic of Korea, December 2024) and its outcome document [Renewing the Social Contract for Education: Directions for change](https://www.unesco.org/en/renewing-education-transform-future).The report has also mobilized dozens of [national and regional events](https://www.unesco.org/en/futures-education/national-local-dialogues?hub=81942) for dialogue based on the Report.

Finally, Reimagining Our Futures Together has also informed major UNESCO instruments, including the 2023 UNESCO Recommendation on Education for Peace, Human Rights and Sustainable Development, and the 2024 Global Report on Teachers.

### Who are the partners?

The Futures of Education Programme, generously supported by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency, is engaged with numerous organizations and partners, whether as part of its Advisory Group, or beyond. These partners include the UNICEF Innocenti Office of Strategy and Evidence, the Center for Educational Innovation and Research (CERI) at the OECD, Education International, the Center for Engaged Foresight in the Philippines, the Center for Artificial Intelligence and Strategic Foresight at ICESCO, the Center for Sociodigital Futures at the University of Bristol, the Digital Educational Futures Initiative (DEFI) at the University of Cambridge, the Gyeonggido Office of Education in the Republic of Korea, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean (CAF), and others.

## Rebalancing relationships

The Futures of Education Programme examines the ways education can help societies and individuals alike rebalance their relationships with *each other*, *technology* and the *environment* – and, in doing so, lay foundations for more peaceful, just, humanistic and sustainable futures.

![Futures of Education - Observatory](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/public/2025-10/%C2%A9iStock-DNY59.jpg.webp?itok=6yc32xRx)

## Spotlighting change

While UNESCO’s Futures of Education Programme calls attention to emerging risks to education, it is equally attuned to positive change and innovation. It surfaces examples of how different education systems, whether at national or sub-national levels, are being renewed or transformed for the better.

![Futures of Education - Observatory](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/public/2025-10/iStock-TheaDesign.jpg.webp?itok=kBQeT50n)

## Multiple trajectories

UNESCO is sensitive to the diverse goals and objectives societies attach to education and its practice. Its Futures of Education Programme recognizes that just as there are different educational hopes and realities today, this will be true tomorrow and far into the future. We use the word ‘Futures’ in the plural form for a reason. There will be a multiplicity of educational futures – futures that reflect the distinct traditions, beliefs, aspirations and priorities of different cultures and societies.

![Futures of Education - Observatory](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/public/2025-10/%C2%A9iStock-Eoneren_0.jpg.webp?itok=mNiWWxQX)
![Futures of Education - Observatory](/sites/default/files/styles/banner_mobile/public/2025-11/AdobeStock_Christian-knssr-NeoLeo.jpg.webp?itok=zPAzR03v)

### Ultimately, no one can predict the future.

But the future is constantly being shaped in the debates, analyses, projections, actions and changes happening today. UNESCO uses its expertise and convening power to imagine and help build the future of education.

But the future is constantly being shaped in the debates, analyses, projections, actions and changes happening today. UNESCO uses its expertise and convening power to imagine and help build the future of education.

## Past events

## The Futures of Education

Our world is at a unique juncture in history, characterised by increasingly uncertain and complex trajectories shifting at an unprecedented speed. These sociological, ecological and technological trends are changing education systems, which need to adapt. Yet education has the most transformational potential to shape just and sustainable futures. UNESCO generates ideas, initiates public debate, and inspires research and action to renew education. This work aims to build a new social contract for education, grounded on principles of human rights, social justice, human dignity and cultural diversity. It unequivocally affirms education as a public endeavour and a common good.

![Future of education video](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_full_mobile/public/medias/image/video_thumbnail/2023/06/FoE%20video%20thumbnail.JPG?itok=ksckSQGy)

**No trend is destiny...Multiple alternative futures are possible... A new social contract for education needs to allow us to think differently about learning and the relationships between students, teachers, knowledge, and the world.**

Our work is grounded in the principles of the 2021 report “Reimagining Our Futures Together: A New Social Contract for Education” and in the report’s call for action to consolidate global solidarity and international cooperation in education, as well as strengthen the global research agenda to reinforce our capacities to anticipate future change.

The report invites us to rebalance our relationship with:

![Futures of Education Report](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/public/2021-11/51670883499_af47c284e5_o.jpg.webp?itok=lCnFkzDV)

## Summary of the Report

Interview with Stefania Giannini, Assistant Director-General for Education

## The International Commission

In 2019 UNESCO Director–General convened an independent International Commission to work under the leadership of the President of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia, H.E. President Sahle-Work Zewde, and develop a global report on the Futures of Education. The commission was charged with carefully considering inputs received through the different consultation processes and ensuring that this collective intelligence was reflected in the global report and other knowledge products connected with the initiative.

![UNESCO Futures of Education report explained by members of the International Commission](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_full_mobile/public/oembed_thumbnails/N3YzTjUZkx2SN11R58yEB9D39b0H_ySB5QGfRmWwMr4.jpg.webp?itok=eZrzwphj)

## Sustainable development challenges and the role of education

Our foresight work, looking towards 2050, envisions possible futures in which education shapes a better world. Our starting point is observation of the multiple, interlocking challenges the world currently faces and how to renew learning and knowledge to steer policies and practices along more sustainable pathways.The challenges are great. But there are reasons for optimism, no trend is destiny.

Our work responds to the call of the International Commission on the Futures of Education to guide a new research agenda for the futures of education. This research agenda is wide-ranging and multifaceted as a future-oriented, planet-wide learning process on our futures together. It draws from diverse forms of knowledge and perspectives, and from a conceptual framework that sees insights from diverse sources as complementary rather than exclusionary and adversarial.

![Reimagining cover white background](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/public/2023-06/Report%20Cover_WhiteBG.jpg.webp?itok=S95H-Cp1)

## The third in a series of major visioning exercises for education

[*Reimagining our future together: a new social contract for education*](https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000379707?posInSet=1&queryId=b21b4616-b65f-48ee-83ad-120dfa965d3c) is the third in a series of UNESCO-led once-a-generation foresight and visioning exercises, conducted at key moments of historical transition.

In 1972, the [*Learning to Be: the world of education today and tomorrow*](https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000223222?posInSet=3&queryId=720bd595-c359-4e47-b3a8-3f4304f62f24) report already warned of the risks of inequalities, and emphasized the need for the continued expansion of education, for education throughout life and for building a learning society.
