This webpage is UNESCO's official page for its Futures of Education Programme, which was launched in 2019 in response to the UN Secretary-General's call for UNESCO to lead the global debate on the future of education. The Programme anticipates and imagines new possibilities for education, looking beyond short-term policy cycles to consider the longer-term purposes, functions, and processes of education to support more just, equitable, and sustainable futures for humanity and the planet.

Key activities of the Programme include: imagining desirable futures and building consensus about new purposes and models for education; studying trends and forecasts to help countries anticipate possible futures; analysing what countries are saying about the future of education through reports and data; and convening debates through platforms for thinkers to share ideas.

The Programme is guided by the 2021 report "Reimagining Our Futures Together: A New Social Contract for Education," produced by the International Commission on the Futures of Education convened by UNESCO's Director-General in 2019 under the leadership of HE President Sahle-Work Zewde of Ethiopia. The report proposes a new social contract for education grounded in two foundational principles: an expanded vision of the right to education throughout life, and strengthening education as a public endeavour and a common good. It asks essential questions about what should be continued, abandoned, and creatively reimagined.

The report has had significant worldwide impact: it is available in 17 languages (including Amharic, Arabic, Bahasa Indonesia, Catalan, Chinese, English, French, Greek, Italian, Kiswahili, Korean, Latvian, Mongolian, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, and Spanish), generated thousands of academic citations, served as the key reference for the 2022 Transforming Education Summit (bringing together 65 world leaders and guiding consultations in over 100 countries), anchored the 3rd World Higher Education Conference and 7th International Conference on Adult Learning and Education (both 2022), and served as the foundation for the UNESCO International Forum on the Futures of Education (Republic of Korea, December 2024). It also informed the 2023 UNESCO Recommendation on Education for Peace, Human Rights and Sustainable Development and the 2024 Global Report on Teachers.

Current strands of work include the IdeasLAB think piece series, ERF Working Papers, monthly Futures Dialogues webinars with UNESCO's global network of university chairs, and annual events such as Digital Learning Week and World Futures Day. The Programme is supported by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency and partners include UNICEF Innocenti, OECD's CERI, Education International, and various universities and institutions.

The report is the third in a series of UNESCO-led once-a-generation visioning exercises, following the 1972 report "Learning to Be" and the 1996 report "Learning: The Treasure Within" (which proposed four pillars: learning to be, learning to know, learning to do, and learning to live together). The Programme examines how education can help rebalance relationships with each other, technology, and the environment, emphasizes multiple possible futures (hence the plural 'Futures'), and highlights positive change and innovation in education systems.

## Abstract

This study critically examines how digital technologies contribute to the sustainable conservation and revitalisation of urban–rural heritage in China, focusing on their empowering effects and inherent challenges. Through a qualitative multiple case analysis of 30 representative Chinese projects, it assesses technological applications in digital recording, information management, and public dissemination. The findings indicate a paradigm shift from static preservability to dynamic sustainability, driven by technologies such as high-precision scanning and Digital Twin, which enhance documentation accuracy and enable preventive conservation. Nevertheless, significant challenges remain, including gaps in technical standardisation, inherent governance paradoxes, algorithmic bias, data silos, and constrained community agency. These issues stem from a governance model that frequently prioritises technical rationality over humanistic values, such as cultural accuracy and narrative sovereignty. In conclusion, the study proposes an integrated rebalancing framework advocating for context-sensitive technical adaptation, a collaborative governance logic model for digital heritage, and the adoption of an ethics-aligned benchmarking matrix aligned with international charters. This approach aims to steer digital heritage practice towards more inclusive and sustainable outcomes.

## 1 Introduction

Urban historical heritage, as a vital carrier of human civilisation, faces dual challenges in the rapid global urbanisation process: erosion of physical spatial entities and fragmentation of cultural contexts. Within the Chinese context, historical urban areas are damaged by development, traditional memories fade through regeneration, and social networks risk disintegration, highlighting a fundamental contradiction between static, isolated restoration models and dynamic, complex urban development needs. Since the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (hereinafter UNESCO) launched the “Memory of the World Programme” in 1992, digital technology has offered an innovative approach to resolving the conflict between heritage conservation and development. Its virtual, open, accessible and visual characteristics enable preventive conservation and living transmission to achieve sustainability goals ①, sparking profound transformations in concepts, methodologies and governance.

In September 2025, the Cultural Heritage Digitalisation Forum at the World Internet Conference in Xi’an, China adopted the theme “Bridging History Through Digitalisation, Building Civilisation with Intelligence”, and released the World Internet Conference Cultural Heritage Digitalization Case Collection[2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR44 "World Internet Conference. (2025). World Internet Conference Cultural Heritage Digitalization Case Collection (2025). World Internet Conference. 
                  https://www.wicinternet.org/pdf/2025WorldInternetConferenceCulturalHeritageDigitalizationCaseCollection.pdf
                  
                ")), elevating digital heritage conservation to a level of global governance and policy dialogue ②. China has implemented multiple practices in this field, developing diverse local models. While demonstrating the effectiveness of technological applications, these initiatives also reveal underlying structural challenges. Digitalisation is not merely a recording tool but a mediator reshaping social networks and spatial justice. This study moves beyond the “how” of digitalisation to critically examine “for whom” it serves and how to safeguard authenticity in its wake.

## 2 Digital heritage: from static preservability to dynamic sustainability

### 2.1 Conceptual evolution and paradigm shift of digital heritage

The term “Digital Heritage”, or “Digitalisation of Heritage”, encompasses both born-digital heritage (resources created in digital form) and digitised heritage (physical heritage converted into digital format) (UNESCO, [2003](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR40 "UNESCO. (2003). Charter on the preservation of the digital heritage. 
                  https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000229034?posInSet=2&queryId=21d1708f-233b-42e5-a644-c89458543d53
                  
                "); Letellier et al.,[2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR17 "Letellier, R., Schmid, W., & LeBlanc, F. (2007). Recording, documentation, and information management for the conservation of heritage places: Guiding principles. Getty Conservation Institute. 
                  https://www.getty.edu/conservation/publications_resources/pdf_publications/pdf/guiding_principles.pdf
                  
                "); Bentkowska-Kafel et al.,[2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR3 "Bentkowska-Kafel, A., Denard, H., & Baker, D. (2012). The London Charter for the computer-based visualisation of cultural heritage (Version 2.1, February 2009). In A. Bentkowska-Kafel & H. Denard (Eds.), Paradata and transparency in virtual heritage (pp. 6). Routledge. 
                  https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315599366
                  
                ")). Its conceptual evolution has progressed through three distinct phases:

The first phase, the Digital Documentation Period (1960–2002), began with early digitisation attempts of documents and archives in Europe and America. Employing photography, videography, and two-dimensional (hereinafter 2D) scanning, the primary goal was the salvage recording and preservation of endangered heritage. Resulting databases were largely for internal institutional use, with digital technology serving as an auxiliary archival tool, not yet widely accessible to the public (Letellier et al.,[2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR17 "Letellier, R., Schmid, W., & LeBlanc, F. (2007). Recording, documentation, and information management for the conservation of heritage places: Guiding principles. Getty Conservation Institute. 
                  https://www.getty.edu/conservation/publications_resources/pdf_publications/pdf/guiding_principles.pdf
                  
                ")).

The second phase, the Digital Interpretation Period (2003–2018), was marked by the _Charter on the preservation of the digital heritage_ (UNESCO, [2003](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR40 "UNESCO. (2003). Charter on the preservation of the digital heritage. 
                  https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000229034?posInSet=2&queryId=21d1708f-233b-42e5-a644-c89458543d53
                  
                ")), which formally recognised both born-digital and digitised resources as heritage. Technologies like three-dimensional (hereinafter 3D) laser scanning, Virtual Reality (hereinafter VR), Augmented Reality (hereinafter AR), and Mixed Reality (hereinafter MR) were widely adopted for heritage restoration, scene reconstruction, and interactive display. The issuance of international guidelines such as the _London Charter_, _Ename Charter_, and the _Principles of Seville_ ③, alongside the emergence of online digital museums, signified a shift in objective from static preservation to dynamic interpretation and public dissemination (Bentkowska-Kafel et al.,[2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR3 "Bentkowska-Kafel, A., Denard, H., & Baker, D. (2012). The London Charter for the computer-based visualisation of cultural heritage (Version 2.1, February 2009). In A. Bentkowska-Kafel & H. Denard (Eds.), Paradata and transparency in virtual heritage (pp. 6). Routledge. 
                  https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315599366
                  
                ")).

The third phase, the Digital Reconstitution Period (2019–present), was accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, propelling digital heritage from a supplementary tool to a means of systemic reconstitution. Technologies like lightweight data capture, intelligent reconstruction, visual management, and remote collaboration not only enhanced the efficiency of data acquisition and processing but also profoundly participated in the reproduction and redefinition of heritage value. Practices such as Digital Twin (hereinafter DT) and immersive experiences are reshaping the ways heritage is perceived, disseminated, and engaged with, signalling a paradigm shift from a “technology-as-tool” perspective to “technology-as-enabler”. The digital dimension has become a core component of the heritage value system (Xiao et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR46 "Xiao, J., Bai, Z., & Mu, X. (2024). Heritage digitalization: Conceptual issues, research insights, and application practices. Urban Planning Forum, 6, 104–112. 
                  https://doi.org/10.16361/j.upf.202406014
                  
                . [in Chinese with English abstract].")).

This evolutionary trajectory demonstrates that digital technology has progressed from an auxiliary means to a core driver in heritage conservation, reflecting a profound conceptual shift from material preservation to value reconstitution. The focus of digital heritage has moved from static, defensive preservability towards fostering dynamic, creative sustainability. Consequently, any discourse on digital heritage must be situated within the broader framework of sustainable development, balancing conservation with development to ensure the perpetual continuity of cultural transmission and urban vitality.

### 2.2 Sustainable digital pathways for urban–rural heritage

Driven by sustainable development theory and digital practice, digital heritage has evolved into an integrated paradigm combining digital technology, heritage theory, and urban–rural sustainability. It aims to advance the Sustainable Development Goal 11 (hereinafter SDG 11) of “Make cities inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainable”(United Nations General Assembly, [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR42 "United Nations General Assembly. (2015). Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (A/RES/70/1). 
                  https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/post2015/transformingourworld
                  
                ")) through synergistic environmental, economic, and social pathways (Zheng et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR51 "Zheng, D., Lin, C., Wu, H., & Zhang, Y. (2023). Spatial research and framework of digital portrait technology for urban sustainable development. Urban Planning Forum, 6, 32–39. 
                  https://doi.org/10.16361/j.upf.202306006
                  
                . [in Chinese with English abstract].")).

The environmental sustainability pathway focuses on establishing a low-intervention, predictable preventive conservation system, grounded in the integration of Preventive Conservation and Resilient City theories (Masciotta et al., [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR24 "Masciotta, M. G., Morais, M. J., Ramos, L. F., Oliveira, D. V., Sánchez-Aparicio, L. J., & González-Aguilera, D. (2019). A digital-based integrated methodology for the preventive conservation of cultural heritage: The experience of HeritageCare Project. International Journal of Architectural Heritage, 15(6), 844–863. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/15583058.2019.1668985
                  
                "); UNESCO Office Bangkok and Regional Bureau for Education in Asia and the Pacific,[2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR27 "UNESCO Office Bangkok and Regional Bureau for Education in Asia and the Pacific. (2024). Building resilience: Disaster risk management for documentary heritage and digital archives; training toolkit. 
                  https://doi.org/10.58338/NNWI1226
                  
                ")). By creating virtual mappings of physical heritage, it enables full lifecycle management and reconfigures spatial–temporal workflows from macro to micro scales and instant monitoring to long-term forecasting, thereby reducing human intervention and ecological footprint.

The economic sustainability pathway, supported by Cultural Economy and the Diffusion of Innovation Theory (Jin, [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR16 "Jin, Q. (2025). Intergenerational transmission of digitized intangible cultural heritage: A study from the perspective of innovation diffusion theory. Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media, 106, 119–127. 
                  https://doi.org/10.54254/2753-7048/2025.CB25244
                  
                ")), centres on innovating value transformation models for heritage to lessen reliance on public funding. It enhances cultural consumption experiences through digital tourism, digital derivative products, and scene recreations, fostering a virtuous cycle between heritage conservation and economic development.

The social sustainability pathway aims to strengthen community cultural identity and agency, drawing on Empowerment Theory and Social Capital Theory (Rappaport, [1984](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR33 "Rappaport, J. (1984). Studies in empowerment: Introduction to the issue. Prevention in Human Services, 3(2–3), 1–7. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1300/J293v03n02_02
                  
                "); UNESCO, [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR41 "UNESCO. (2019). Culture | 2030 indicators. 
                  https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000371562
                  
                "); UNESCO World Heritage Committee, [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR39 "UNESCO World Heritage Committee. (2024). Progress report on the implementation of the Strategy for World Heritage in Africa (WHC/24/46.COM/5C). 
                  https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000390655

## 3 Digital technology in urban–rural heritage conservation: analysis of 30 Chinese cases

Digital heritage technology has evolved significantly: from initial 2D scanning for digital recording and documentation, to high-precision 3D modelling for conservation and information management, and now to artificial intelligence (hereinafter AI)-driven systems for education & dissemination (Xiao et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR46 "Xiao, J., Bai, Z., & Mu, X. (2024). Heritage digitalization: Conceptual issues, research insights, and application practices. Urban Planning Forum, 6, 104–112. 
                  https://doi.org/10.16361/j.upf.202406014
                  
                . [in Chinese with English abstract].")). This progression reflects not only technological advancement but also a paradigm shift in how cultural heritage is preserved, managed, and interpreted.

### 3.1 Data sources and case selection method

This study employs a multiple case study method, aiming to reveal the underlying mechanisms of digital technology in urban and rural heritage conservation across different contexts, ensuring the generalisability and relevance of its conclusions. Primary case selection screened 26 Chinese cases from the World Internet Conference Cultural Heritage Digitalization Case Collection[2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR44 "World Internet Conference. (2025). World Internet Conference Cultural Heritage Digitalization Case Collection (2025). World Internet Conference. 
                  https://www.wicinternet.org/pdf/2025WorldInternetConferenceCulturalHeritageDigitalizationCaseCollection.pdf
                  
                ")), excluding those where technology application remained conceptual, information was incomplete, or reporting was duplicated. 4 additional technically representative new projects from 2024–2025 were sourced from official websites of the Ministry of Housing and Urban–Rural Development (China) and the Ministry of Culture and Tourism (China), resulting in a total sample of 30 cases (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Fig2); see [Appendix](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Sec33) A: List of Research Cases). Case selection followed three principles: a) Technical Representativeness: covering full-chain technology application from data acquisition and management to dissemination; b) Diversity of Heritage Types: including ancient sites, historic buildings, cave temples, and intangible cultural heritage, with geographical distribution covering eastern, central, western, and ethnic regions of China; c) Difference in Governance Models: encompassing diverse models such as government-led, enterprise-partnered, and community-involved.

The analysis utilises thematic analysis. To maintain consistency with the original case collection, the initial 26 cases retain their original codes (e.g., “Protection 01”, “Exhibition 01”), while the 4 new cases are uniformly coded as “Other”. All 30 samples are categorised into three functional dimensions: “Digital Recording and Documentation”, “Digital Management and Conservation”, and “Digital Education and Dissemination”. Key observation indicators include: primary technological focus, data acquisition accuracy (mm/cm level), degree of interoperability (number of cross-departmental data shares), depth of community engagement (one-way notification/two-way interaction), and ethical compliance of technology application. Thematic analysis across these three dimensions revealed that digital technology significantly enhances efficacy at all stages. However, the depth and effectiveness of application varied markedly across stages and cases, with this imbalance itself suggesting deeper structural constraints.

### 3.2 From vague documentation to precise identification: digital recording and documentation in heritage data acquisition

#### 3.2.1 Technical framework and theoretical foundations

Heritage digitalisation aims to create a systematic recording framework with permanent preservation potential, ensuring the sustainable intergenerational transmission of cultural heritage information. In the event that the original heritage is damaged by natural erosion, disaster, or human activity, its identity and integrity can be preserved in digital form.

This process has evolved from early photogrammetry to the comprehensive acquisition and systematic documentation of heritage entities, associated records, and contextual data using knowledge graphs, machine learning methods, high-precision scanning, and AI recognition technologies. It establishes a heritage documentation system that combines reliability, sustainability, and structured management capability. Through standardised data acquisition, processing, storage, and presentation, digital documentation provides a solid foundation for conservation, restoration, development, academic research, and management decisions.

Digital recording and documentation are a crucial tool for scholars and the public to comprehend lost or fundamentally altered sites and a technical means to counter oblivion and decay, preventing cultural heritage from fading from collective memory and allowing future generations to perceive its value through high-fidelity, interactive digital surrogates (Guo et al., [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR12 "Guo, X., Yang, C., & Han, F. (2020). Research on digital record and innovative conservation of cultural landscape heritage. Chinese Landscape Architecture, 36(11), 84–89. 
                  https://doi.org/10.19775/j.cla.2020.11.0084
                  
                . [in Chinese with English abstract].")).

#### 3.2.2 Practical application and impact assessment

Heritage digital recording and documentation technology has achieved full-scale coverage from macro landscapes to microstructures. At the macro level, drones and laser scanning are mainstream. For example, the project “Digital Collection and Documentation of Buddhist Temple Ruins in Xinjiang” (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Fig2); see [Appendix](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Sec33) A: Protection 14) employed a drone swarm to conduct centimetre-level accuracy modelling of 82 sites, constructing a structured database exceeding 15 TB. Meanwhile, “Digital Scanning for the Protection of Shaoxing Ancient City Heritage” (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Fig2); see [Appendix](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Sec33) A: Protection 16) achieved millimetre-level accuracy reality modelling and dynamic documentation management for the entire ancient city through the integration of multi-source technologies.

At the micro level, technological innovation has addressed traditional challenges. The project “3D Modeling of Micro at Longmen Grottoes” (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Fig2); see [Appendix](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Sec33) A: Protection 4) utilised fine-scale photometric stereo technology to achieve sub-millimetre, non-contact modelling of carving traces shallower than 0.05 mm, enabling algorithmic auto-detection of early-stage weathering damage. “The Protection of Yungang Grottoes” (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Fig2); see [Appendix](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Sec33) A: Protection 8) further introduced muon imaging technology, performing “zero-intervention” internal “CT scans” of the rock mass to precisely locate hidden cavities and seepage channels.

#### 3.3.2 Practical application and impact assessment

Digital management and conservation technologies are reshaping heritage monitoring and decision-making models. “Risk Monitoring and Early Warning Platform for Grotto Temple Clusters” (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Fig2); see [Appendix](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Sec33) A: Protection 01) established a two-tier “region-heritage site” Internet of Things (hereinafter IoT) system, enabling a shift towards proactive prevention from real-time monitoring to closed-loop incident management. The DT system of “Liangzhu 5000 + ” (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Fig2); see [Appendix](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Sec33) A: Protection 06) integrates multi-departmental data. Utilising 55 sensor groups and AI video analytics, it achieves intelligent environmental risk perception and automated early warning with over 95% accuracy, forming a complete “perception-warning-response” operational cycle.

For value discovery, the project “Great Wall Heritage Value Mining” (Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Fig2); see [Appendix](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#Sec33) A: Protection 07) employs drone aerial surveying and AI image recognition. This approach not only quantifies spatial characteristics such as wall gradients but has also led to the new discovery of over 130 covert gate remains, deepening scholarly understanding.

### 3.4 From flat display to immersive experience: digital education and dissemination in public engagement

#### 3.4.1 Technical framework and theoretical foundations

Over the past three decades, heritage presentation has evolved from traditional, static formats into multi-dimensional, interactive, immersive systems. This shift is driven by the integration of technologies like AI, VR, AR, MR, high-precision 3D modelling, panoramic imaging, Near Field Communication (hereinafter NFC), and Bluetooth positioning.

These technologies not only change how heritage information is presented but also reshape public perception and experience through intelligent storytelling and cultural computing, offering new pathways for deep value extraction, cross-media narrative, and global sharing (Jarrier, [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR14 "Jarrier, É. ## 4 Structural challenges in digital technology for urban–rural heritage conservation

The application of digital technologies in recording, documentation, conservation, information management, and education & dissemination has undoubtedly brought revolutionary improvements in precision, efficiency, and participation to China’s urban heritage conservation, offering new organisational and operational paradigms (Dang et al., [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR9 "Dang, X., Hong, Q., Liu, W., & Wang, Y. (2025). China’s heritage governance blueprint: Revisiting evolutionary trajectories, reframing institutional priorities and mapping the national registry. Habitat International, 165, Article 103541. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.habitatint.2025.103541
                  
                ")). However, technology’s empowering effect is not automatic. When these advanced tools are embedded into China’s complex and unique urban–rural contexts, deep-seated structural dilemmas emerge, including inherent limitations of the technologies themselves, long-standing institutional deficiencies, and inherent contradictions between technological rationality and humanistic values. In this context, “humanistic values” refer not merely to the historical information of heritage, but more specifically to the “cultural accuracy”, the “narrative sovereignty” of communities over heritage interpretation, and the “interpretive agency” across generations. These values emphasise that technological application should not lead to the flattening of cultural meaning or deprive local communities of their right to cultural interpretation (Fenlon et al., [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR10 "Fenlon, K., Wise, N. M., & Sorensen, A. H. (2024). Community Partnerships in Digital Cultural Heritage: A Systematic Review. Proceedings of the Association for Information Science & Technology, 61(1), 908. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1002/pra2.1136
                  
                "); Hughes et al., [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR13 "Hughes, L., Alexander, M., Barker, H., Batista-Navarro, R., Hannaford, E. D., Nenandic, G., & Willcox, P. (2022). First report - Our heritage, our stories: Linking and searching community-generated digital content to develop the people’s national collection. Zenodo. 
                  https://doi.org/10.5281/ZENODO.7152510
                  
                ")).

### 4.1 Technical application bottlenecks: standardisation gaps and algorithmic bias

The application of digital technology in China’s heritage conservation is markedly uneven. The varying maturity of technological empowerment across different stages severely constrains the overall effectiveness of conservation, leading to a “technology gap” where digitised components are unbalanced or cannot be utilised effectively.

An underdeveloped digital standardisation system is the most prominent technical bottleneck. For instance, HBIM standards, primarily designed for modern or European traditional buildings, lack support for the specific structures and materials of Chinese traditional architecture, ethnic minority buildings, and vernacular architecture. This leads to frequent data loss and distortion during information transfer. The absence of standards results in a lack of uniform data standards and interface protocols between different systems, hindering data sharing and interoperability (Storeide et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR34 "Storeide, M. S. B., George, S., Sole, A., & Hardeberg, J. Y. (2023). Standardization of digitized heritage: A review of implementations of 3D in cultural heritage. Heritage Science, 11(1), Article 249. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1186/s40494-023-01079-z
                  
                ")). A nationally unified technical standard or specification system for the digital documentation of historical buildings remains to be established (Wei et al., [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR43 "Wei, L., Li, W., & Liu, J. (2016). Research on current situation and trend of digital culture heritage preservation standards in China and abroad. China Standardization, 6, 91–96. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3969/j.issn.1002-5944.2016.06.009
                  
                . [in Chinese with English abstract].")).

Another major issue is the lack of diversity and cultural sensitivity in algorithmic training datasets, leading to high misjudgement rates regarding the characteristics of ethnic minority architecture. For example, Lingnan ⑤ ethnic buildings in the Xiaoshui-Hezhou Ancient Road area of Guangxi are frequently misidentified by AI as derelict structures or roads (Cai et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR6 "Cai, J., Wen, R., Jiang, W., Yan, J., & Lu, L. (2023). Deeplabv3+ improved algorithm for national building recognition in traditional village aerial images. Bulletin of Surveying and Mapping, 4, 49–53. 
                  https://doi.org/10.13474/j.cnki.11-2246.2023.0103
                  
                . [in Chinese with English abstract].")), primarily due to insufficient samples of ethnic architecture in training datasets (Wu et al., [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44243-026-00079-4#ref-CR45 "Wu, Z., Guo, W., & Ai, X. (2016). Digital protection of minority architectural culture heritage. Guizhou Ethnic Studies, 37(4), 84–87. 
                  https://doi.org/10.13965/j.cnki.gzmzyj10026959.2016.04.018
                  
                . [in Chinese with English abstract].")), preventing accurate recognition of their structural features and cultural value. Similar issues exist in other ethnic regions, such as Diaojiaolou (Miao’s stilted dwelling) in Qiandongnan (Southeast Guizhou), mosque and Qubba-shrine in Northwest China, Zhulou (Dai’s bamboo dwelling) in Yunnan, and Diaolou (Tibetan Stone Tower House) in Kham and Ü-Tsang Regions, all facing value misjudgement risks due to algorithmic bias. This algorithmic systemic neglect, resulting from data gaps, constitutes a form of digital cultural exclusion. It directly contradicts the core objective – “encourage inclusiveness in the interpretation of cultural heritage sites”- advocated in the _Ename Charter_ adopted by the International Council on Monuments and Sites (hereinafter ICOMOS).

### 4.2 Lagging governance capacity: data silos and legal gaps

Although many regions in China have initiated the construction of heritage data platforms, departmental data silos represent the most significant institutional obstacle in digital heritage governance. For example, despite Guangdong provincial government unified mobile office platform “Yuezhengyi” linking 11 departments, the Cultural Heritage Bureau of Guangzhou Municipality’s data permissions are limited to 2 levels. 40% of Guangzhou’s cultural conservation data is not integrated with the urban construction platform, preventing access to real-time data ⑥. This data isolation phenomenon is widespread nationwide. While (Suzhou Municipality) Gusu District established a Digital Centre for Ancient City Protection to coordinate data permissions across planning, construction, and culture departments, operational hurdles persist ⑦. args.summary:
This is an open-access research article published on 01 April 2026 in the journal *Frontiers of Urban and Rural Planning* (Volume 4, article number 9), authored by Jianli Xiao and Zhicheng Bai. The study critically examines how digital technologies contribute to the sustainable conservation and revitalisation of urban–rural heritage in China.

**Methodology**: The study employs a qualitative multiple case analysis of 30 representative Chinese projects, drawing 26 cases from the World Internet Conference Cultural Heritage Digitalization Case Collection (2025) and adding 4 new technically representative projects from 2024–2025 sourced from the Ministry of Housing and Urban–Rural Development and the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. Case selection followed three principles: technical representativeness, diversity of heritage types, and difference in governance models. Cases were categorised into three functional dimensions: Digital Recording and Documentation, Digital Management and Conservation, and Digital Education and Dissemination.

**Key Findings**:
- There has been a paradigm shift from static preservability to dynamic sustainability, driven by technologies such as high-precision scanning and Digital Twin.
- Digital heritage has evolved through three phases: Digital Documentation Period (1960–2002), Digital Interpretation Period (2003–2018), and Digital Reconstitution Period (2019–present).
- Three sustainability pathways are identified: environmental (preventive conservation via virtual mapping), economic (value transformation via digital tourism and derivative products), and social (community cultural identity and agency).
- Notable case examples include: drone swarm modelling of 82 sites in Xinjiang (centimetre-level accuracy, 15+ TB database); sub-millimetre photometric stereo modelling at Longmen Grottoes (detecting carving traces shallower than 0.05 mm); muon imaging at Yungang Grottoes for "zero-intervention" internal CT scans; the "Liangzhu 5000+" Digital Twin system using 55 sensor groups with over 95% automated early warning accuracy; the Great Wall Heritage Value Mining project which discovered over 130 covert gate remains; immersive exhibitions such as Mawangdui Han Dynasty, Digital Luoyang, Canal Wonderland VR, and Digital Dunhuang.

**Structural Challenges Identified**:
1. **Technical bottlenecks**: Standardisation gaps (HBIM standards lack support for Chinese traditional architecture, leading to data loss), and algorithmic bias (AI training datasets lacking ethnic architecture samples, causing misidentification—e.g., Lingnan ethnic buildings in Guangxi misidentified as derelict structures; similar risks for Diaojiaolou, mosques, Zhulou, and Diaolou), constituting a form of "digital cultural exclusion."
2. **Governance capacity lags**: Data silos (e.g., Guangzhou's cultural heritage data permissions limited to 2 levels; 40% of cultural conservation data not integrated with urban construction platform), legal gaps, and department reluctance to share data due to security, privacy, and administrative authority concerns.

**Proposed Solutions**: The study proposes an integrated rebalancing framework advocating for context-sensitive technical adaptation, a collaborative governance logic model for digital heritage, and an ethics-aligned benchmarking matrix aligned with international charters (such as the Ename Charter and London Charter). The conclusion calls for steering digital heritage practice towards more inclusive and sustainable outcomes, prioritising cultural accuracy, narrative sovereignty, and interpretive agency over mere technical rationality.

## Abstract

This study evaluates China’s National Smart Education Platform (NSEP) as a national digital reform aligned with SDG 4 (quality education) and SDG 10 (reduced inequalities), yet evidence remains limited on whether such platforms reduce urban–rural gaps in real-world use and outcomes. A quantitative, stratified, random survey of students, teachers, and administrators used validated scales to measure perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), user satisfaction (US), behavioral intention (BI), engagement level (EL), learning outcomes (LO), and system quality (SQ). The measures demonstrated strong reliability. Hierarchical regression analyses supported an extended technology acceptance model (TAM): SQ, PEOU, and PU significantly predicted US and BI, with PU showing the strongest effect. Interaction effects indicated context-sensitive adoption and the results suggested a persistent rural disadvantage in adoption even after accounting for key predictors. Mediation analyses further showed that US and BI transmitted technology beliefs to LO. Nevertheless, urban–rural gaps remained evident, particularly in PEOU and SQ, and teachers consistently reported a lower PEOU than students and administrators. These findings suggest that NSEP has the potential to support SDG-oriented digital equity, but closing urban–rural gaps requires teacher-centered design, improved usability and system reliability, and targeted infrastructure and capacity-building support in rural contexts.

## 1. Introduction

China’s National Smart Education Platform (NSEP), rolled out in 2020 and officially launched nationwide on 28 March 2022. The platform integrates learning, teaching, governance and lifelong services. Later in 2024, its international version was online, serving users in 200+ countries (MOE, 2024) [[1](#B1-sustainability-18-01181)]. The launch of the platform demonstrates China’s commitment to advancing Sustainable Development Goal 4 (quality education) and Sustainable Development Goal 10 (reduced inequalities). The NSEP aims to build global collaboration in digital education, promote inclusive access to learning opportunities, and support the development of a more equitable society. This research, taking 500 urban and rural users of different system qualities as the sample, aims to discover if and how China’s National Smart Education Platform is bridging the urban–rural education gap by analyzing perceived ease of use, usefulness, satisfaction, engagement, learning outcomes. Such a top-down platform intervention would only be successful in a long-term implementation if it can shift from a technology-centered deployment model to one that is deeply rooted in and responsive to regional socio-cultural, teaching, and administrative conditions. This is because the mere “availability” of a platform does not necessarily mean that there will be equal and effective use of it throughout different contexts [[2](#B2-sustainability-18-01181),[3](#B3-sustainability-18-01181)].

Across recent global research, smart education platforms are recognized to be a powerful tool for reducing educational inequalities (Liu, Cao, & Chen, 2024) [[4](#B4-sustainability-18-01181)]. By way of example, in high-income regions such as Europe, large-scale learning management systems, open educational resources, and AI-supported tutoring have been deployed to complement traditional schooling and to expand access for rural and marginalized groups, although persistent infrastructure and affordability gaps still constrain impact in some communities (Educause, 2024) [[5](#B5-sustainability-18-01181)]. When it comes to developing countries across Asia, Africa, and Latin America, digital platforms are increasingly promoted as a cost-effective strategy to address teacher shortages, lack of textbooks, and geographic isolation, helping rural learners access the standards-aligned curricula and remote instruction that were historically limited to urban schools [[6](#B6-sustainability-18-01181)]. UNESCO consistently highlight such online educational platforms are instruments for advancing Sustainable Development Goal 4 on inclusive, high-quality education and for narrowing urban–rural digital divides, while also warning that platform effectiveness depends on reliable connectivity, affordable devices, and sustained teacher professional development (UNESCO, 2025) [[2](#B2-sustainability-18-01181)]. Within this global landscape, China’s National Smart Education Platform (NSEP) exhibits four distinctive traits [[1](#B1-sustainability-18-01181)]: (1) It is state-led and centrally coordinated. It integrates services for learners, teachers, school governance, and lifelong learning in a single national hub. (2) It is an equitable resource synchronization. The system functions as a bridge for geographic democratization. It is explicitly designed to allow students in remote and rural areas to “share the same class” as those in large cities through high-quality shared resources and synchronized lessons. (3) It is a globalized public utility. The initiative serves as an international digital public good. By launching a version for users in over 200 countries, the NSEP positions itself as a cross-border vehicle for digital education and experience export. (4) It aligns with sustainability. Internal equity goals are inextricably linked to external global commitments. The platform connects the reduction of urban–rural disparities with SDG 4 (quality education) and SDG 10 (reduced inequalities) through international cooperation and resource sharing. Nevertheless, much of the empirical evidence on platform-driven reform is still concentrated in affluent, urban, or pilot settings, which leaves limited clarity on whether national platforms reduce gaps in real-world use and outcomes across unequal regional infrastructures and user capacities [[2](#B2-sustainability-18-01181),[7](#B7-sustainability-18-01181),[8](#B8-sustainability-18-01181)].

The present study is anchored in a theoretical foundation that links technology acceptance, digital equity, and student engagement. Building on Davis’s (1989) technology acceptance model (TAM) [[9](#B9-sustainability-18-01181)], we conceptualize perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness as core cognitive beliefs that shape user satisfaction and intention to use NSEP, thereby shifting the focus from simple access to second-level divides in capability and outcome (Van Deursen & Van Dijk, 2019) [[3](#B3-sustainability-18-01181)]. Research on blended learning, multimedia-supported instruction, and learning management systems has shown that perceived ease and usefulness are central to sustained adoption, yet much of this work remains technologically deterministic, paying limited attention to how platforms are appropriated within diverse educational cultures (AlAli & Wardat, 2024; Kosasih & Sulaiman, 2024) [[10](#B10-sustainability-18-01181),[11](#B11-sustainability-18-01181)]. At the same time, student engagement theory, particularly the cognitive, behavioral, and affective dimensions outlined by Fredricks, Blumenfeld, and Paris [[12](#B12-sustainability-18-01181)], provides a lens for examining how NSEP affects learners’ active participation in both urban and rural settings. Emerging “smart education” studies that incorporate AI and learning analytics suggest that national platforms can enhance engagement and outcomes (Yang & Wu, 2024) [[13](#B13-sustainability-18-01181)], but most evidence comes from affluent or experimental environments and does not fully capture regional and rural realities characterized by uneven connectivity, device access, and digital competence (Yin & Ying, 2025; Vičič Krabonja et al., 2024) [[7](#B7-sustainability-18-01181),[8](#B8-sustainability-18-01181)]. To address the technical side, we also draw on the Information Systems Success Model (DeLone & McLean, 2003) [[14](#B14-sustainability-18-01181)], treating system quality as a key determinant of satisfaction and continued use. Together, these strands of the literature highlight a clear gap: while digital transformation is widely promoted in policy discourse, there is still limited empirical work that simultaneously considers technology acceptance, engagement, system quality, and learning outcomes within a single national platform, and does so in a way that is sensitive to urban–rural disparities. Consequently, although the macro-level aspirations of national platforms are widely articulated, there remains a void in meso-level evidence on how such top-down processes are enacted within local systems, where digital transformation claims may either become productive realities or disintegrate due to non-alignment with regional conditions [[3](#B3-sustainability-18-01181)].

This research responds with one central research question: what is the impact of NSEP on the main success determinants of regional education systems, i.e., the perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, user satisfaction, engagement, learning outcomes, and system quality, for urban and rural user groups? We use a stratified sample of 500 users including students, teachers, and administrators from urban and rural areas to quantitatively investigate how these constructs relate to each other in real platform experience. The research work mainly comprises two aspects. First, it serves as a theoretical link between the technology acceptance model (TAM), student engagement theory, and digital divide scholarship, in the case of a large, state-led national smart education platform, which in turn expands digital equity deliberations by revealing how different regional users suffer from second-level divides in terms of ease of use, usefulness, engagement, and outcomes. Second, it brings fresh data about system quality, user satisfaction, engagement levels, and perceived learning outcome intersections within NSEP, thus giving a micro-level perspective often missing from the macro policy narratives and giving a micro design study context. Importantly, this positioning clarifies that the value of including system quality and contextual variables is not as a routine TAM extension, but as a necessary way to evaluate whether a national platform can deliver equitable “effective use” and benefits across structurally unequal settings.

Practically, the research findings aim to put forward actionable movements for both smart education designers and policymakers. Besides emphasizing the significance of user-centered design and system reliability, the study ideas point towards a necessary combination of infrastructure investment and continuous capacity-building so that platform access may be transformed into real, equitable educational benefits for urban and rural users. In short, the scientific novelty of this study is that, within a real national-scale platform context, it tests an integrated mechanism that jointly incorporates system quality within the framework of the technology acceptance model, while explicitly comparing urban–rural and role-based differences to determine whether platform adoption translates from access equity into capability and outcome equity.

## 2. Literature Review

There has been considerable academic focus on research integration within educational pedagogy, particularly on the evolution from basic computer-assisted learning systems, to sophisticated, ecosystem-based smart educational frameworks (Lin & Pang, 2024) [[15](#B15-sustainability-18-01181)]. Pioneering studies documented the advantages technology integration offered, particularly in the form of blended learning frameworks, where formative in-person lessons complement online sessions (Li et al., 2024) [[16](#B16-sustainability-18-01181)]. Additionally, the principles underlying multimedia learning have long established the ability of well-engineered digital resources to facilitate deeper cognitive processing and knowledge retention by optimizing cognitive load management (Zhang et al., 2025) [[17](#B17-sustainability-18-01181)]. As artificial intelligence and adaptive technologies continue to advance rapidly, education systems are evolving beyond traditional digitalization to foster adaptive, learner-centered, and transformative educational experiences (Merino-Campos et al., 2025) [[18](#B18-sustainability-18-01181)]. These streams have the ability to increase educational efficiency and efficacy by personalizing learning resources within adaptive learning streams (Saini & Kharb, 2025) [[19](#B19-sustainability-18-01181)].

However, the implementation of such technologies is fraught with challenges that are often understated in optimistic policy discourses (Truong, 2024) [[20](#B20-sustainability-18-01181)]. A significant portion of the literature in human–technology research has prioritized analyses of technological features and innovation, often at the expense of examining how social, organizational, and contextual conditions shape the ways these technologies are actually used and integrated into human practices and systems (Jarecki et al., 2025) [[21](#B21-sustainability-18-01181)]. This divide is not limited to unequal access to devices and connectivity (the first-level divide); it also encompasses disparities in digital skills (the second-level divide) and, ultimately, unequal real-world benefits gained from technology use (the third-level divide) (Ayhan, 2024; Khoso et al., 2025) [[22](#B22-sustainability-18-01181),[23](#B23-sustainability-18-01181)].

According to Foong et al. (2024), using platforms such as these are critical to teaching “21st-century skills sought by today’s employers, such as critical thinking, global awareness and digital literacy, in a world awash in technology” [[24](#B24-sustainability-18-01181)]. Honcharuk et al. (2024) argue active learning is also key as “digital learning platforms” are not only places where students can acquire knowledge, but also ones where they can interact [[25](#B25-sustainability-18-01181)]. Joseph et al. (2024) argue that this approach is best suited to 21st-century literacy even though there have been serious challenges [[26](#B26-sustainability-18-01181)], ensuring that all students have equitable access to technology and related infrastructure is more important than ever. Adapting to digital platforms effectively also means adapting traditional curriculum and lesson methodologies (Gu, 2024) [[27](#B27-sustainability-18-01181)].

The theoretical underpinnings of technology adoption are crucial for understanding these dynamics. Davis’s (1989) technology acceptance model (TAM) provides a robust framework, positing that the adoption of any technology is primarily influenced by its perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use [[9](#B9-sustainability-18-01181)]. The effectiveness of a platform in an educational setting depends on educators and students perceiving it as a helpful and controllable factor that simplifies, rather than makes the work of an educator complicated (Adel, 2024) [[28](#B28-sustainability-18-01181)]. This has a direct impact on user satisfaction, which is a measure of long-term sustainability. Furthermore, assisting students to literally play with meaning is the ultimate reason for any educational intervention and is simply interwoven with the aspect of engagement. Fredricks, Blumenfeld, and Paris (2004) consider engagement to be a multi-faceted behavioral (participation), emotional (interest and belonging), and cognitive (investment in learning) construct [[12](#B12-sustainability-18-01181)]. The boundary to consider in the extant literature takes the form of the hillock on the two theoretical constructs, and the fact of the implementation of the SofAR channels in the region. On one hand, the beneficial possibilities of smart lessons are often praised (Aljaradin et al., 2024; Adeshina, 2024; Qian et al., 2025) [[29](#B29-sustainability-18-01181),[30](#B30-sustainability-18-01181),[31](#B31-sustainability-18-01181)] and there are funneled explanations about the positive impact of collaborative learning platforms such as the NSEP in TAM variables and multi-dimensional involvement within the specific restrictions of teaching systems and the present global surroundings (Wu and Yang, 2024; Harahap and Mahardhani, 2025; Indrasari et al., 2024) [[32](#B32-sustainability-18-01181),[33](#B33-sustainability-18-01181),[34](#B34-sustainability-18-01181)]. This paper aims to bridge this gap by quantitatively exploring these relationships and offering much-needed evidence on whether the promise of digital transformation is being realized in regional communities.

## 3. Methodology

To empirically evaluate the adoption and perceived effectiveness of NSEP, this study uses an extended TAM-based analytical framework, with particular attention to urban–rural differences and role-based variations among students, teachers, and administrators. [Figure 1](#fig_body_display_sustainability-18-01181-f001) presents the research design, which considers how the aspects of system quality, perceived ease of use, and perceived usefulness predict user satisfaction and behavioral intention, and how these in turn relate to engagement and learning outcomes. These constructs inform the subsequent analyses, including the model summaries, regression tests, and diagnostic checks to assess robustness across user roles and regions.

![Sustainability 18 01181 g001](/sustainability/sustainability-18-01181/article_deploy/html/images/sustainability-18-01181-g001-550.jpg "Sustainability 18 01181 g001")

**Figure 1.**
Analytical framework for the assessment of the National Smart Education Platform.

### 3.1. Research Design and Participant Selection

A stratified random sampling approach was employed to reflect the diversity of the educational contexts served by the National Smart Education Platform and to ensure the adequate representation of key subgroups for meaningful comparison. The target population was stratified across three dimensions: (1) geographical location (urban vs. rural); (2) user role (students, teachers, and administrative staff), and (3) education level (primary: grades 5–6; secondary: grades 7–9). The strategy used will capture a rich array of socio-economic backgrounds, levels of access to technology, and individual experiences of pedagogical systems to develop a deep understanding of the efficacy of the platform in question and help pinpoint possible differences in its impact.

The urban and rural data were collected through the first author’s personal contacts to ensure practical access to NSEP users while maintaining regional comparability. The urban sample was obtained from a private school located in the urban districts of Beijing, recruited with support from the first author’s friends. The rural sample was collected from one primary school and one secondary school in a county town in Hebei Province, which is the first author’s hometown. Due to fact that Beijing and Hebei are geographically proximate, this design helps capture a meaningful urban–rural contrast in educational conditions and digital access. The questionnaire was administered online via Wenjuanxing ([www.wjx.com](http://www.wjx.com)), and the survey link was distributed through WeChat. To ensure an adequate number of valid responses, the questionnaire was oversampled to 700 invitations so that at least 500 valid feedback responses could be retained after screening. The original questionnaire was written in Chinese to ensure that all participants could fully understand the items and respond accurately.

### 3.2. Data Collection Instruments and Measures

The instrument for data collection was a structured online questionnaire. It was meticulously designed by Likert 5-point scale to quantify users experiences. The questionnaire primarily comprised scales adapted from established theoretical frameworks to ensure construct validity and reliability. These measures were then refined to fit the specific context and functional features of the NSEP.

All items were measured on a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree). Perceived ease of use (PEOU): This variable was assessed using a scale adapted from Davis’s (1989) technology acceptance model (TAM) [[9](#B9-sustainability-18-01181)]. It measured the degree to which users believe using the NSEP would be free of effort, with items focusing on interface clarity, navigation simplicity, and ease of learning. In the same way, perceived usefulness (PU) was also adapted from Davis (1989) [[9](#B9-sustainability-18-01181)], this scale measured the degree to which a user believes that the NSEP would enhance their job performance (for teachers/administrators) or learning outcomes (for students). It included items related to productivity, effectiveness, and overall advantage. User satisfaction (US): This construct was designed to capture the overall affective response to using the platform. It synthesized elements from both TAM and user experience literature, evaluating contentment with platform features, reliability, and whether it met user expectations. Behavioral intention to use (BI): A critical dependent variable in the TAM framework, this scale measured the likelihood that users will continue to use the NSEP in the future. It serves as a key indicator of the platform’s long-term sustainability and acceptance. Engagement levels (EL): Student engagement was measured using a multi-dimensional scale inspired by the framework of Fredricks, Blumenfeld, and Paris (2004) [[12](#B12-sustainability-18-01181)]. It included sub-scales for behavioral engagement (time-on-task, participation), emotional engagement (interest, enjoyment), and cognitive engagement (investment in learning, strategic use of the platform). Learning outcomes (LO): This variable assessed users’ self-reported assessment of the educational benefits derived from the platform. For students, this pertained to knowledge acquisition and skill development. For educators, it related to teaching effectiveness and professional development. Items were framed with reference to Bloom’s revised taxonomy to capture cognitive gains [[35](#B35-sustainability-18-01181)]. Finally, system quality (SQ) was added to assess the technical performance of the platform itself, a factor often crucial for user acceptance. It measured perceptions of the platform’s reliability, responsiveness, and availability, drawing from the Information Systems Success Model (DeLone & McLean, 2003) [[14](#B14-sustainability-18-01181)].

Prior to full deployment, the survey instrument underwent a pilot testing phase with a small sample (n = 30) to assess internal consistency reliability using Cronbach’s Alpha, clarity of wording, and completion time [[36](#B36-sustainability-18-01181)].

### 3.3. Data Collection Procedure

Data collection was conducted in two stages.

Stage 1 was preparation. We finalized the online survey and set clear ethical procedures. All participants provided informed consent. Responses were anonymous, and participants could withdraw at any time without penalty.

Stage 2 was implementation. The survey was administered online from 1 October to 15 October 2025. This time frame gave participants enough time to respond without feeling rushed. A reminder email was sent at the end of the first week to improve the response rate. All data were collected anonymously and stored on a password-protected server for analysis.

### 3.4. Sample Size Determination

The target sample size was determined using an a priori power analysis in G\*Power 3.1.9.7 to reduce Type II error and ensure adequate statistical power. For the main multiple regression, we assumed a medium effect size (f2 = 0.15), a power = 0.95, and an α = 0.05, which indicated a minimum required sample of 119 participants.

Because this study used stratified sampling and aimed to compare subgroups (e.g., urban vs. rural and students, teachers, administrative staff), we recruited a larger sample to improve representativeness and to reduce the impact of non-response or incomplete questionnaires. The final sample was n = 500, providing sufficient power for both the main regression models and the planned subgroup analyses (t-tests and ANOVA).

### 3.5. Data Analysis

The quantitative data were analyzed in SPSS (Version 28). The analysis followed several steps. First, the descriptive statistics were calculated for all variables, including means, standard deviations, skewness, kurtosis, and frequency distributions. Next, internal consistency reliability was tested using Cronbach’s alpha, with an α > 0.70 treated as acceptable. Finally, multiple regression analyses were conducted to test whether perceived ease of use (PEOU) and perceived usefulness (PU) predicted user satisfaction, behavioral intention, and perceived learning outcomes. All models controlled for user role and geographical location to reduce potential confounding effects.

In addition, independent-samples t-tests were used to examine whether mean differences existed between two-group comparisons (e.g., urban vs. rural users). For comparisons involving more than two groups (e.g., students, teachers, and administrators), one-way ANOVA was conducted. When ANOVA results were significant, post hoc tests (Tukey HSD) were applied to identify which specific pairs differed. For all inferential analyses, statistical significance was set at p < 0.05, and effect sizes were reported to indicate the practical importance of the findings.

Common method variance (CMV) diagnostics. Because the data were collected using a single self-reported questionnaire, we conducted formal diagnostics to assess the potential risk of common method variance (CMV). First, Harman’s single-factor test was performed by entering all measurement items into an unrotated exploratory factor analysis. The results suggested that CMV was not a dominant issue, as multiple factors emerged and the first factor explained 36.2% of the total variance (i.e., below the commonly used 50% threshold). Second, we conducted a robustness check using a common latent factor (CLF) approach in AMOS (version 24) by adding a latent method factor that loaded on all observed indicators. The inclusion of the CLF did not materially change the standardized measurement loadings or the direction and significance of the key relationships, indicating that CMV is unlikely to materially bias the substantive conclusions. Detailed CMV outputs are reported in [Appendix A](#app1-sustainability-18-01181).

## 4. Results

The following section presents empirical findings on the following: (1) the descriptive patterns and reliability/validity of NSEP user measures; (2) the structural relationships among key constructs such as perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, satisfaction, intention, engagement, and learning outcomes; and (3) group differences across urban–rural contexts and user roles.

### 4.1. Descriptive Statistics and Reliability of Measures

The reasoning for this is to ensure the effectiveness of the information collected, to verify that the measurement tools are appropriate in the specific setting of this study, and also to provide a sufficient overview of the responses given by the participants before consideration of the more sophisticated inferential analyses. The large reliability coefficients indicate that items in both scales are measuring a similar core concept; therefore, they can be employed in the subsequent analysis.

[Table 1](#table_body_display_sustainability-18-01181-t001) reports generally positive perceptions across all constructs (M = 3.83–4.31 on a 5-point scale) with a relatively low dispersion (SD = 0.51–0.72), suggesting responses are fairly consistent; perceived usefulness is rated highest (M = 4.31, SD = 0.53), while engagement level is the lowest but still favorable (M = 3.83, SD = 0.72). Internal consistency is strong for every scale (Cronbach’s α = 0.85–0.92), exceeding the widely used ≥0.70 benchmark for acceptable reliability (Cronbach, 1951; Nunnally & Bernstein, 1994) [[36](#B36-sustainability-18-01181),[37](#B37-sustainability-18-01181)].

**Table 1.**
Descriptive statistics and scale reliability.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

[Table 2](#table_body_display_sustainability-18-01181-t002) shows that all of the study variables are positively and significantly correlated (r = 0.32 to 0.75, p < 0.01), indicating that higher perceived ease of use, usefulness, satisfaction, engagement, learning outcomes, and system quality tend to co-occur with stronger behavioral intention. The strongest association is between user satisfaction and behavioral intention (r = 0.75), followed by satisfaction and usefulness (r = 0.71 \*\*) and engagement level and perceived learning outcomes (r = 0.66 \*\*), while the weakest relationship is between perceived learning outcomes and system quality (r = 0.32 \*\*). Descriptively, mean scores are generally high (≈3.83–4.31) with modest variability (SD = 0.51–0.72), suggesting overall favorable evaluations across constructs.

**Table 2.**
Inter-correlations among study variables.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

### 4.2. Assessment of the Measurement Model (Confirmatory Factor Analysis—CFA)

Before testing the structural relationships, a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted using AMOS to validate the hypothesized measurement model. The CFA assessed model fit and established convergent and discriminant validity, ensuring that each latent construct was measured accurately and remained distinct from the others. This step confirmed that the survey items were appropriate indicators of their intended theoretical concepts and provided a solid measurement foundation for the subsequent structural/path analysis.

[Table 3](#table_body_display_sustainability-18-01181-t003) presents the results of the confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), which assessed the convergent validity, reliability, and unidimensionality of the measurement model. All standardized factor loadings exceeded the recommended threshold of 0.70 and were statistically significant (p < 0.001), indicating that the indicators strongly represented their respective latent constructs. Composite Reliability (CR) values for all constructs ranged from 0.86 to 0.93, exceeding the acceptable level of 0.70, which confirms the high internal consistency of the measures. The Average Variance Extracted (AVE) for each construct exceeded 0.50, ranging from 0.65 to 0.72, demonstrating that the constructs explain more than half of the variance in their indicators on average, which further supports convergent validity. The Maximum Shared Variance (MSV) values were all lower than the corresponding AVE values, providing preliminary evidence of discriminant validity.

**Table 3.**
Confirmatory factor analysis results: factor loadings, reliability, and validity.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

[Table 4](#table_body_display_sustainability-18-01181-t004) evaluates discriminant validity using the Fornell–Larcker criterion, which requires that the square root of the Average Variance Extracted (AVE) for each construct (diagonal values) should be greater than its highest correlation with any other construct (off-diagonal values in corresponding rows and columns). The results show that the square root of AVE for each construct (ranging from 0.81 to 0.85) is consistently higher than all inter-construct correlations, confirming that each latent variable shares more variance with its own indicators than with other constructs in the model. This establishes strong discriminant validity, meaning the constructs are empirically distinct and measure unique phenomena. For example, the strongest correlation is between behavioral intention and user satisfaction (r = 0.75), but the square root of AVE for both constructs (0.82) is higher, satisfying the criterion.

**Table 4.**
Discriminant validity assessment (Fornell–Larcker criterion).

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

### 4.3. Testing the Structural Model: Regression Analyses

This section contains the findings of hierarchical multiple regression tests that were performed to test the hypothesized research model causal pathways. This test is critical because it goes beyond the bivariate correlation and looks at the specific and synergistic predictive value of independent variables on the core endogenous constructs, which is a strict test of the theoretical framework presented and provides a subtle understanding of what drives the acceptability of the platform and its educational success.

[Table 5](#table_body_display_sustainability-18-01181-t005) presents the results of hierarchical regression analyses testing the core propositions of the technology acceptance model (TAM) while controlling for demographic variables and incorporating an expanded theoretical framework. The results demonstrate that after accounting for control variables (user role and region), the addition of system quality, perceived ease of use (PEOU), and perceived usefulness (PU) in Model 2 explained a substantial proportion of variance in both user satisfaction (ΔR2 = 0.58, p < 0.001) and behavioral intention (ΔR2 = 0.61, p < 0.001). PU emerged as the strongest predictor of both satisfaction (β = 0.45, p < 0.001) and behavioral intention (β = 0.38, p < 0.001), supporting TAM’s central premise. The significant interaction effect (PEOU \* PU → BI: β = 0.09, p < 0.05) in Model 2 for behavioral intention indicates that the relationship between ease of use and adoption intention is moderated by perceived usefulness, suggesting that PEOU becomes particularly important for driving usage intentions when users perceive the platform as highly useful. The negative coefficient for region in predicting BI (β = −0.09, p < 0.05) suggests that rural users reported slightly lower adoption intentions even after accounting for technology perceptions.

**Table 5.**
Hierarchical regression analysis predicting user satisfaction and behavioral intention.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

[Table 6](#table_body_display_sustainability-18-01181-t006) presents the results of regression analyses examining both direct and indirect pathways through which technology acceptance variables influence educational outcomes. While perceived usefulness maintained significant direct effects on both engagement (β = 0.22, p < 0.01) and learning outcomes (β = 0.18, p < 0.05), the most important finding emerges from the mediation analysis. The bootstrap results for specific indirect effects reveal that both user satisfaction and behavioral intention serve as significant mediators in the relationship between technology perceptions (PEOU and PU) and educational outcomes, as indicated by 95% confidence intervals that do not contain zero. Particularly noteworthy is the finding that the total effects of PEOU on both engagement and learning outcomes are fully mediated through these pathways (direct effects β = 0.11 and 0.05, ns), while PU maintains both direct and mediated effects. This pattern suggests that while ease of use operates entirely through user attitudes and intentions, perceived usefulness exerts both direct influence on educational outcomes and additional indirect effects through satisfaction and adoption intentions. The stronger total effects for perceived usefulness pathways (e.g., PU → BI → LO: β = 0.13) compared to perceived ease of use pathways (e.g., PEOU → BI → LO: β = 0.06) highlight the primacy of utility perceptions in driving meaningful educational results.

**Table 6.**
Regression analysis predicting engagement and learning outcomes with indirect effects.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

### 4.4. Group Differences: Urban vs. Rural Users

To directly address the research objective of examining the National Smart Education Platform’s role in empowering regional education, a series of independent samples t-tests were conducted to compare the experiences and perceptions of urban and rural users. This analysis is crucial for identifying potential digital divides and ensuring that the platform’s benefits are equitably distributed across different geographical contexts, thereby testing its effectiveness as a tool for mitigating educational disparities.

[Table 7](#table_body_display_sustainability-18-01181-t007) reveals statistically significant disparities between urban and rural users across all seven measured constructs, with urban users consistently reporting more positive experiences (p < 0.05 for all comparisons). The largest differences, evidenced by large effect sizes (Cohen’s d > 0.8 and 0.64), were found in perceived ease of use (d = 0.78) and system quality (d = 0.64), indicating that rural users found the platform significantly more difficult to use and perceived its technical performance as less reliable. Medium effect sizes were observed for user satisfaction (d = 0.43) and behavioral intention to use (d = 0.41), suggesting that these usability and quality issues translate into a lower overall satisfaction and a reduced willingness to continue using the platform among rural educators and students. While still statistically significant, the differences in perceived usefulness, engagement, and learning outcomes showed small effect sizes (d ranging from 0.23 to 0.33), implying that once the platform is used, its perceived educational value and impact are somewhat more comparable across regions, though still favoring urban areas.

**Table 7.**
Independent samples t-test: urban vs. rural users.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

### 4.5. Group Differences by User Role: Students, Teachers, and Administrators

To understand how the National Smart Education Platform serves the distinct needs and functions of its primary user groups, a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted to compare the perceptions of students, teachers, and administrators across all key variables. This analysis is vital for evaluating the platform’s differential impact and ensuring its design and functionality effectively support the unique workflows, goals, and requirements of each stakeholder group, thereby informing targeted improvements and professional development strategies.

[Table 8](#table_body_display_sustainability-18-01181-t008) demonstrated statistically significant differences (p < 0.01) among all seven variables according to user role, with a small to medium effect size (η2 between 0.02 and 0.08). The post hoc Tukey HSD tests identified that teachers had the least positive perceptions regarding most of the constructs. Teachers showed much a lower perceived ease of use than students and administrators (p < 0.01), indicating that they face more of a usability barrier in their professional use of the platform. In addition, teachers and students both noted a much lower perceived usefulness compared with administrators (p < 0.01), meaning that administrators, who tend to manage the implementation and reporting of the platform, find a higher strategic value in the platform than those who simply learn or teach on it. Teachers also had lower engagement than students by a significant margin (p < 0.01) which is in line with their lower satisfaction and intention to use.

**Table 8.**
One-way ANOVA and post hoc tests by user role.

![](https://pub.mdpi-res.com/img/table.png)

### 4.6. Summary of the Contextualized TAM and Key Quantitative Findings

This study confirms the explanatory power of an extended technology acceptance model (TAM) for China’s National Smart Education Platform (NSEP).
