Paris and the Paris region are home to many museums and monuments containing a **wealth of art and culture**: the [Louvre](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/culture/musee-du-louvre-p3489 "Musée du Louvre"), [Centre Pompidou](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/article/exhibition-at-the-centre-pompidou-a1006 "During the closure of the Centre Pompidou from 2025-2030, the cultural programme will be ongoing") (closed for work until 2030), [Musée du quai Branly - Jacques Chirac](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/culture/musee-du-quai-branly-jacques-chirac-p3480), [Musée d'Orsay](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/culture/musee-d-orsay-p3592 "Musée d'Orsay"), etc.

Several of these exceptional **cultural attractions open their doors free of charge on certain days and at certain times**. Another advantage is that some of Paris's museums offer **admission to their collections**. Finally, **some establishments are free for young people under the age of 26 and teachers, all year round**.

Below is a list of museums and monuments in Paris and the Paris region that open to the public free of charge, subject to various conditions.

## 🎯Discover museums and monuments free every day, all year round

### 📌Free admission to permanent collections: consult the list of museums

Entry is **free every day of the week to the permanent collections** of 11 Paris municipal museums such as the [musée de la Vie romantique](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/culture/musee-de-la-vie-romantique-p3580 "Musée de la Vie romantique") (reopening on 14 February 2026), [Musée Carnavalet - Histoire de Paris](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/culture/musee-carnavalet-histoire-de-paris-p3492 "Musée Carnavalet - Histoire de Paris"), [Petit Palais](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/culture/petit-palais-musee-des-beaux-arts-de-la-ville-de-paris-p3490 "Petit Palais") and the [Musée d'Art moderne de la Ville de Paris](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/culture/musee-d-art-moderne-de-paris-p3491).

N.B. Entry is free to the permanent collections of the [Maison de Balzac](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/culture/maison-de-balzac-p3501 "Maison de Balzac")**except when there is a temporary exhibition** whereas the permanent collections of the [Bourdelle](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/culture/musee-bourdelle-p3539 "Musée Bourdelle"), [Cognacq-Jay](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/culture/musee-cognacq-jay-le-gout-du-xviiie-p3509 "Musée Cognacq-Jay") and [Zadkine](https://parisjetaime.com/eng/culture/musee-zadkine-p3502 "Musée Zadkine") museums are **partially visible during temporary exhibitions**.

This webpage is from the official Paris je t'aime - Tourist Office website, specifically an article titled "Good ideas: free museums and monuments in Paris" (last updated 20 May 2026). It provides a comprehensive guide to free cultural attractions in Paris and the Paris region.

Key content covered:

1. **Museums free every day, all year round**: Entry is free to the permanent collections of 11 Paris municipal museums, including the Musée de la Vie romantique (reopening 14 February 2026), Musée Carnavalet - Histoire de Paris, Petit Palais, and Musée d'Art moderne de la Ville de Paris. Other permanently free museums include the Musée de la Légion d'honneur, La Maison Elysée, Musée du Parfum - Fragonard, and the Basilique du Sacré-Cœur de Montmartre (though access to its cupola is paid). Some free sites (like Notre-Dame de Paris) require online booking; the cathedral's treasure is paid, and its towers are only free on the 1st Sunday of each month from November to March.

2. **Free admission on the 1st Sunday of every month**: Various museums offer free entry on the first Sunday of each month, with some periods restricted to October-March or November-March.

3. **Other free options**: Free late-night openings once a month, free admission on 14 July (Bastille Day), and free admission for under-26s and teachers all year round at some establishments.

4. **Featured museums listed in detail** include: Musée d'Art Moderne de Paris, Maison de Balzac, Musée Bourdelle, Musée Carnavalet, Musée Cernuschi, Musée Cognacq-Jay, Musée de la Libération de Paris, Petit Palais, Musée de la Vie romantique, Maison de Victor Hugo, and Musée Zadkine.

5. **Important note**: The Centre Pompidou is closed for renovation work until 2030, though its cultural programme continues.

The page also serves as the main navigation hub for the Paris tourist office website, offering links to sections on Discover, Attractions, Events, Plan your stay, and Paris by district, plus ticketing services for attractions like the Eiffel Tower, Versailles, dinner cruises, and more.

In Paris, young people under the age of 26, as well as students and teachers, have the chance to enter many museums and monuments for free! Free on presentation of an identity card or student card, museums allow all young people to open up to the world, to art and to enjoy our exceptional heritage, without discrimination, discover what you are entitled to.

When you're young, you're often broke. But don't worry, Parisian **museums** still offer plenty to keep you entertained - **for free**! Whether you're going solo or with friends, there's always something to do. **[Culture](/arts-culture/exposition)** is something to be enjoyed without moderation, so make the most of it before you blow out your 26 candles! If you're **under 26** and a citizen of one of the 28 European countries, a student or an active teacher in the primary or secondary education system, you've come to the right place. You're welcome to visit Paris' museums and monuments free of charge all year round. See the list below.

args.summary:
This webpage from Sortiraparis.com is a comprehensive guide to museums and monuments in Paris and the Île-de-France region that offer free admission to young people under 26, students, and teachers. The key eligibility requirements are: being under 26 and a citizen of one of the 28 European countries, being a student, or being an active teacher in primary or secondary education. Entry is free upon presentation of an identity card or student card. The article was published/updated on April 24, 2024.

The guide lists numerous Paris museums offering free entry for under-26s, including:
- Musée de l'Armée (Hôtel des Invalides, 7th arrondissement) - military history
- Musée Bourdelle (15th arrondissement) - sculpture museum with café-restaurant
- Musée Guimet - Asian arts
- Musée du Quai Branly - Jacques Chirac - world cultures, near Eiffel Tower
- Musée d'Orsay - world's largest collection of Impressionist paintings
- Postal Museum (Montparnasse) - history of French postal service
- Musée Picasso
- Musée national de la Marine (Trocadéro)
- Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle (founded 1793, Jardin des Plantes)
- Institut du Monde Arabe (IMA)
- Musée de l'Homme (Trocadéro)
- Hôtel de la Marine (Place de la Concorde)
- Musée Gustave Moreau (9th arrondissement) - Symbolist artist's home/studio
- Cité de l'Architecture et du Patrimoine (Palais Chaillot, 22,000 m²)
- Musée de l'Orangerie - Monet's Water Lilies
- Musée Rodin (7th arrondissement)
- Musée de Cluny - Middle Ages museum, 13th-century building
- Musée des Arts et Métiers - technical inventions
- Musée de l'Ordre de la Libération (Invalides, founded 1970)
- Musée des Arts Décoratifs (Palais du Louvre)
- Maison de Balzac (16th arrondissement) - garden overlooking Eiffel Tower
- Cinémathèque française - "Jeudi Jeunes" free evenings on second Thursday each month for under-26s
- Musée des Plans-Reliefs (Invalides) - ~100 relief plans of fortified towns
- Musée de l'histoire de l'Immigration (Palais de la Porte Dorée) - 2,700 documents on Dreyfus affair
- Musée de Minéralogie (École des Mines) - minerals, gems, meteorites
- Musée des Égouts de Paris - sewer museum
- Galerie de Paléontologie et d'Anatomie Comparée (Jardin des Plantes)
- Grande Galerie de l'Évolution (Jardin des Plantes)
- Monnaie de Paris - coin minting history
- Musée Delacroix (6th arrondissement)
- Centre Pompidou - modern and contemporary art
- Louvre Museum
- Musée Nissim de Camondo (near Parc Monceau) - 17th-century decorative art
- Musée de la musique - Philharmonie de Paris (open daily 12pm-7pm, closed Mondays)
- Musée d'Art et d'Histoire du Judaïsme (open 11am-6pm, closed Mondays, reopens May 19)

Free museums in Île-de-France (outside central Paris):
- Musée de l'Air et de l'Espace at Le Bourget - aircraft and space history, climb aboard mythical aircraft
- Château d'Écouen - National Museum of the Renaissance, 20km from Paris
- MAC-VAL (Vitry-sur-Seine) - Val-de-Marne contemporary art museum
- Domaine National de Port-Royal des Champs (Yvelines, Magny-les-Hameaux) - Jansenism history
- Departmental museum of Seine-et-Marne (Saint-Cyr-sur-Morin) - housed in former riverside inn
- Paul Belmondo Museum (Boulogne-Billancourt) - works of sculptor Paul Belmondo, father of actor Jean-Paul Belmondo, open since 2010

# Free admission

Eligible Visitors and Required Documentation

©Camillegharbi / Camille Gharbi

Fermer

## Priority Access without Reservation

*   **Musée d'Orsay Carte blanche holders**

Valid membership card.

*   **Musée d'Orsay Carte blanche holders with a guest**

Valid “Duo” membership card.

## Free Admission (with priority access)

_Reservation available and recommended through_[_the museum’s official ticketing_](https://billetterie.musee-orsay.fr/index-css5-museeorsay-lgen-pg1.html)_service for visitors eligible for free admission._

*   **Persons with disabilities holding an official disability card or a "priority" card, with one companion**

Cards issued by an MDPH (Departmental Center for Persons with Disabilities) and CDAPH (Commission for the Rights and Autonomy of Persons with Disabilities) that are still valid, a COTOREP card with a DDASS stamp, an ONAC card, or an equivalent foreign certificate, accompanied by a photo ID, an RQTH certificate (Recognition of Disabled Worker Status), or a certificate of AAH benefits (Disabled Adult Allowance).

*   **Members of ICOM and ICOMOS**

Valid membership card for the current year.

*   **Benefactors, supporting members, and members of the Friends of the Musée d'Orsay or American Friends of the Musée d'Orsay**

Valid membership, supporter, or benefactor card for the current year.

*   **Barnes Foundation members with one guest**

Valid Member+1 card for the current year.

*   **Louvre Abu Dhabi members with one guest**

Valid "Membership for Everyone" card for the current year, plus one accompanying guest.

*   **Louvre Abu Dhabi members with four guests**

Valid "Patrons Circle" card for the current year, plus four accompanying guests.

*   **Students of the École du Louvre**

Valid student card for the current academic year.

*   **Auditors at the École du Louvre**

Valid enrollment card for the current academic year.

*   **Students at the École nationale du patrimoine, École des Chartes, IFROA, or university-level restoration programs**

Valid student card for the current academic year.

*   **Current or retired staff of the French Ministry of Culture, with one companion**

Valid Ministry of Culture ID card required.

*   **Museum professionals (curators and general inspectors) from French and foreign public museums**

Certificate of employment or valid professional ID for the current year.

*   **Staff members of the Institut National d’Histoire de l’Art (INHA)**

Valid INHA ID card required.

*   **Journalists and art critics (AICA)**

Valid press card or membership card from the Art Critics Association or the Artistic Press Syndicate.

*   **Professional artists (painters, sculptors, engravers)**

Valid proof of affiliation with the Maison des Artistes (with annual stamp), international artist identity card, or card from the Cité Internationale des Arts.

*   **Licensed Guides and Lecturers**

RMN (Réunion des Musées Nationaux) guides and national lecturers

National interpreters (including permanent auxiliaries)

Île-de-France regional interpreters (including permanent auxiliaries)

Certified guides from Cities and Lands of Art and History

Valid professional cards issued by the French Ministries of Culture and Tourism.

*   **Members of the French National Assembly, Senate, and European Parliament**

Official ID card from the relevant institution.

*   **Visitors on official state visits**

## Free Admission without Priority Access

*   **Visitors under 18 years of age**

Valid photo ID required.

*   **EU or EEA nationals aged 18–25**

Valid photo ID required.

*   **Non-EU nationals aged 18–25 with long-term residence in France or another EU country (visa of more than three months)**

Valid photo ID and student card or proof of residence required.

*   **Students (up to 30 years old) in public universities or art schools in the following fields:**Architecture, art history, archaeology, fine arts, graphic arts, industrial design, decorative arts, photography, cinema, audiovisual studies, fashion and design, museum studies, cultural heritage, and landscape studies. _Excludes evening class students and lifelong learning programs._

Valid student card specifying the artistic field for the current year required.

*   **Teachers in the above-mentioned fields at public universities or art schools**

Valid faculty card indicating the relevant artistic field.

*   **Job seekers**

Proof of status dated within the past six months or indicating validity period, along with valid photo ID.

*   **Recipients of social benefits, asylum seekers, and refugees**

RSA or equivalent certificate (CAF or city-issued), along with valid photo ID.

ATA (Temporary Waiting Allowance) or ADA (Asylum Seekers’ Allowance) recipients

Provisional residence permit for refugees from Ukraine.

*   **Recipients of minimum old-age pension**

Annual certificate confirming receipt of the supplementary allowance from the National Solidarity Fund.

Valid French Ministry of Education-issued Pass Éducation. **Important:**The only authorized issuance and distribution methods for the Pass Éducation are those defined by the Ministry. No company or association is authorized to issue it in any form. Any other version, such as an E-pass, is considered invalid by the Ministry of National Education and Youth.

Valid student card required.

*   **Staff members of the Institut National d’Histoire de l’Art**

Valid INHA ID card required.

Valid AMGC membership card.

args.summary:
This webpage from the official Musée d'Orsay website (musee-orsay.fr) details the museum's free admission policy, listing all eligible visitor categories and the required documentation for each. The page is organized into two main sections: visitors with "Priority Access without Reservation" and those with "Free Admission (with priority access)" where reservation is available and recommended through the museum's official ticketing service, and a third section for "Free Admission without Priority Access."

**Priority Access Categories (Free Admission):** The page lists numerous categories including Musée d'Orsay Carte blanche holders (and Duo card holders with a guest), persons with disabilities holding official cards (MDPH/CDAPH/COTOREP/ONAC or equivalent foreign certificates) with one companion, ICOM/ICOMOS members, benefactors and Friends of the Musée d'Orsay members, Barnes Foundation members (Member+1 card with one guest), Louvre Abu Dhabi members (Membership for Everyone card with one guest, or Patrons Circle card with four guests), École du Louvre students and auditors, students of heritage/restoration programs (École nationale du patrimoine, École des Chartes, IFROA), current/retired French Ministry of Culture staff with one companion, museum professionals (curators and general inspectors), INHA staff, journalists and art critics (AICA), professional artists (Maison des Artistes, international artist ID, Cité Internationale des Arts), licensed guides and lecturers (RMN, national and regional interpreters, certified guides), members of the French National Assembly/Senate/European Parliament, and visitors on official state visits.

**Free Admission without Priority Access:** This includes visitors under 18, EU/EEA nationals aged 18-25, non-EU nationals aged 18-25 with long-term EU residence, students (up to 30) in artistic/humanities fields at public universities, teachers in those same fields, job seekers, recipients of social benefits/asylum seekers/refugees, recipients of minimum old-age pension, Pass Éducation holders, ESPE students, INHA staff, and members of the Association of Friends of the Gustave Courbet Museum (AMGC). The page includes an important warning that the Pass Éducation is only valid if issued by the French Ministry of Education and that no other version (such as an E-pass) is considered valid.
args.key_excerpts: "Persons with disabilities holding an official disability card or a 'priority' card, with one companion" - eligible for free admission with priority access.

# The Future of Virtual Museum Tours: Immersive Art, Education, and Technology in 2026

May 19, 2026

![Professional minimalist workspace with person using VR headset to explore virtual museum exhibit.](/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/virtual-museum-tours-modern-workspace.webp)

![Sean McCue, CEO](/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/sean-about-v2.webp)

Virtual museum tours are interactive digital experiences that allow users to explore art, history, and culture through [immersive 3D environments](/vr-museums/) accessible via web browsers or VR headsets. They use technologies such as WebXR, OpenVR, and photogrammetry to recreate galleries and artifacts with high realism while adhering to accessibility standards like the W3C guidelines. Institutions including the Louvre, Smithsonian, and British Museum employ these tours to expand global access and preserve cultural heritage. By integrating AI-driven personalization, real-time collaboration, and metaverse connectivity, virtual museum tours are transforming education and cultural engagement worldwide.

## The Rise of Virtual Museum Tours in the Digital Age

Virtual museum tours are online experiences that allow users to explore galleries, artifacts, and exhibitions through interactive 3D environments. They matter because they democratize access to global culture, enabling anyone with an internet connection to engage with masterpieces and historical treasures once limited to physical visitors.

### From Static Websites to Immersive 3D Experiences

In the early 2000s, museums began posting static images of their collections online. While these digital archives were revolutionary, they lacked interactivity. The rise of **3D visualization**, **WebGL**, and **360° photography** changed that. Platforms like **Matterport** and **Sketchfab** allowed curators to build photorealistic walkthroughs, giving users the sense of walking through real galleries.

Today, virtual museum tours integrate **WebXR** and **OpenVR** technologies, enabling seamless transitions between desktop, mobile, and VR headsets. Museums now use **HTML5** and **glTF** standards to ensure compatibility across devices. This shift from static to immersive experiences mirrors the broader digital transformation across industries, where interactivity drives engagement and learning.

### How Cultural Institutions Embraced Digital Transformation

Cultural institutions such as the **Smithsonian Institution** ([si.edu](https://www.si.edu/)) and **The Louvre** ([louvre.fr/en/online-tours](https://www.louvre.fr/en/online-tours)) were early adopters of digital transformation. They recognized that virtual tours could expand their reach beyond physical boundaries. The **British Museum** and **Vatican Museums** followed suit, creating online collections that attract millions of virtual visitors annually.

These initiatives also align with global cultural preservation goals supported by **UNESCO’s digital heritage programs** ([unesco.org/en/digital-heritage](https://www.unesco.org/en/tags/digital-heritage)). By digitizing artifacts, institutions ensure long-term access to fragile or endangered cultural materials. This digital shift has also created new opportunities for collaboration between museums, developers, and educational organizations.

### The Role of Google Arts & Culture in Global Accessibility

One of the most influential platforms in this transformation is **Google Arts & Culture** ([artsandculture.google.com](https://artsandculture.google.com/)). Partnering with over 2,000 museums worldwide, Google has made art and history accessible to millions. Through high-resolution imagery, 3D scans, and immersive storytelling, users can explore the **Tate Modern**, **MoMA**, and **National Gallery of Art** from anywhere in the world.

Google’s use of **Street View** technology and **AI-driven curation** provides personalized recommendations, making virtual museum tours not only accessible but also deeply engaging. This democratization of culture has set a new standard for inclusivity and education in the digital age.

**Key takeaway:** Virtual museum tours have evolved from static web pages into immersive, interactive experiences that expand global access to art and culture.

## How Virtual Museum Tours Work: Technology Behind the Experience

Virtual museum tours operate through a combination of **3D modeling**, **photogrammetry**, and **immersive web technologies**. These tools recreate physical spaces digitally, enabling users to explore them interactively.

### Core Technologies Powering Online Exhibitions

The backbone of modern virtual museum tours lies in technologies such as **WebXR**, **OpenVR**, **HTML5**, and **WebGL** ([developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebXR\_Device\_API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebXR_Device_API)). These frameworks allow developers to create immersive environments that can run directly in web browsers without additional software.

Platforms like **Matterport** and **Sketchfab** provide the infrastructure for 3D scanning and hosting, while **Unreal Engine** ([unrealengine.com/en-US/](https://www.unrealengine.com/en-US/)) powers hyper-realistic rendering and lighting effects. Together, they enable museums to build digital twins of their galleries, complete with interactive hotspots, guided narration, and educational overlays.

### The Evolution of 3D Museum Walkthroughs and Interactive Art Tours

The transition from panoramic photography to **3D museum walkthroughs** has enhanced emotional engagement. Visitors can now zoom into brushstrokes, rotate sculptures, or listen to curatorial commentary. The **Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Met 360 Project** ([metmuseum.org/art/online-features/met-360-project](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/online-features/met-360-project)) exemplifies this evolution, offering breathtaking spherical views of iconic spaces.

Interactive art tours also integrate gamified learning—encouraging users to solve puzzles or complete quests related to exhibits. This interactivity increases **session duration** and **return visits**, key metrics for measuring engagement.

### Accessibility and Inclusivity Through W3C Accessibility Guidelines

Accessibility is central to the success of virtual museum tours. The **W3C Accessibility Guidelines** ([w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/)) ensure that digital exhibitions are inclusive for users with disabilities. Features such as text-to-speech, high-contrast modes, and keyboard navigation make virtual tours accessible to all.

Museums also use **AI-driven captioning** and **multilingual narration** to reach global audiences. These enhancements align with the mission of inclusive cultural access and broaden the educational impact of digital heritage.

**Key takeaway:** Advanced web technologies and accessibility standards make virtual museum tours immersive, inclusive, and universally accessible.

## Leading Examples of Virtual Museum Tours Worldwide

Virtual museum tours have become a global phenomenon, with leading institutions setting benchmarks for digital engagement and educational impact.

These institutions demonstrate how virtual tours can preserve history while engaging modern audiences through interactivity and storytelling.

### Comparing Visitor Engagement Across Platforms

Museums track performance through metrics such as **visitor engagement rate**, **session duration**, and **user satisfaction score**. For example:

* The Louvre’s online tours average a 12-minute session duration.
* The Smithsonian’s digital exhibits report a 70% return visit rate.
* The Getty’s open-access archives have increased educational downloads by 40%.

These metrics highlight that immersive, interactive experiences foster deeper engagement and repeat visitation.

**Key takeaway:** Leading museums use virtual tours to expand reach, enhance engagement, and preserve cultural heritage for future generations.

## Educational Impact: How Schools and Learners Use Virtual Museum Tours

Virtual museum tours are powerful educational tools that enrich learning through visual storytelling and interactive exploration.

### Enhancing Remote Art Education and Cultural Literacy

During the remote learning boom, educators turned to virtual museum tours to teach art, history, and science. Students can explore the **British Museum’s Rosetta Stone**, the **Louvre’s Mona Lisa**, or the **Smithsonian’s space exhibits** without leaving the classroom. These experiences enhance cultural literacy and foster curiosity.

### Integrating Virtual Tours into Classroom Curricula

Teachers now integrate virtual tours into lesson plans through platforms like **Zoom** and **YouTube 360**. They can host live discussions while navigating digital galleries, encouraging critical thinking and cross-disciplinary learning. Many museums offer educator toolkits, quizzes, and 3D printable models for hands-on engagement.

### Benefits for Students with Accessibility Needs

Students with physical or cognitive disabilities benefit immensely from virtual tours. Features guided by **W3C Accessibility Guidelines** ensure equal participation. Multisensory elements—such as audio guides and haptic feedback in VR—enhance understanding for diverse learners.

**Key takeaway:** Virtual museum tours empower educators to deliver inclusive, engaging, and globally connected learning experiences.

## Creating a Virtual Museum Experience: Tools, Platforms, and Best Practices

Creating a virtual museum tour involves selecting the right platform, designing for engagement, and measuring performance through actionable metrics.

### Choosing the Right Platform: Artsteps, Kunstmatrix, VeeR VR, YouTube 360, Zoom

Each platform offers unique capabilities:

| **Artsteps** | Easy drag-and-drop interface | Educational exhibitions |

| **VeeR VR** | VR headset compatibility | Immersive storytelling |
| **YouTube 360** | Broad accessibility | Public outreach |
| **Zoom** | Real-time guided tours | Classroom instruction |

Museums often combine these tools with **Unreal Engine** or **Unity** for advanced rendering and interactivity.

### Designing for Engagement and Interactivity

Effective virtual tours use **3D model design services** like [Frame Sixty’s](/3d-modeling-services/) to create realistic environments. Interactive hotspots, narrative audio, and gamified challenges increase **scroll depth** and **social shares**. The goal is to make the visitor feel like an active participant rather than a passive observer.

### Measuring Success: conversion rate, scroll depth, and social shares

Museums analyze data such as **conversion rate** (from visitor to donor), **scroll depth**, and **social shares** to assess performance. A high **visitor engagement rate** indicates that audiences find the experience compelling enough to explore multiple exhibits.

**Key takeaway:** Strategic design and data-driven optimization are essential for creating engaging, measurable virtual museum experiences.

## Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality in Museum Storytelling

Virtual and augmented reality technologies have revolutionized museum storytelling by merging physical and digital worlds.

### Immersive Art Experiences with ARCore and ARKit

Using **ARCore** and **ARKit**, developers can overlay digital content onto real-world environments. This allows visitors to view historical reconstructions or 3D artifacts through their smartphones. For example, a visitor could see an ancient sculpture restored to its original colors through AR visualization.

### Blending Physical and Digital Worlds Through Augmented Reality Exhibits

Museums now integrate AR into physical spaces, creating hybrid experiences. The **Frame Sixty** team explores this frontier through projects like [AI-Augmented Reality](/ai-augmented-reality/), blending artificial intelligence with spatial computing for interactive storytelling. These experiences deepen emotional connections and make learning more memorable.

3D walkthroughs, powered by [Frame Sixty’s](/3d-modeling-for-manufacturing-industrial-design/) modeling expertise, allow users to explore artifacts from multiple perspectives. This spatial immersion enhances empathy and understanding—key goals of museum education.

**Key takeaway:** AR and VR technologies transform museum storytelling into an emotionally resonant, interactive experience.

## Cultural Heritage Digitization and Preservation

Cultural heritage digitization ensures that art, artifacts, and historical records are preserved for future generations.

### The Role of High-Resolution Scanning and IIIF Standards

The **International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF)** ([iiif.io](https://iiif.io/)) standardizes how high-resolution images are shared and displayed. Museums use IIIF to provide scholars and the public with detailed, zoomable views of artworks. This open standard promotes collaboration and accessibility across institutions.

### Long-Term Benefits for Global Cultural Preservation

Digitization protects fragile artifacts from environmental damage and conflict. Initiatives supported by **The Getty** ([getty.edu/research/digital/](https://www.getty.edu/projects/digital-art-history/)) and **UNESCO** ensure that cultural treasures remain accessible even if physical sites are compromised. These efforts contribute to global cultural resilience.

### Case Studies in Digital Archiving and Open Access

Projects like **Google Arts & Culture’s Open Access** and **The Smithsonian’s 3D Digitization Program** demonstrate the power of digital archiving. By sharing collections openly, institutions foster research, innovation, and education worldwide.

**Key takeaway:** Digitization and open-access initiatives safeguard humanity’s cultural heritage while expanding global access to knowledge.

## The Future of Virtual Museum Tours: Trends Shaping 2026 and Beyond

The future of virtual museum tours lies in personalization, collaboration, and integration with the broader metaverse.

### AI-Powered Personalization and Guided Experiences

Artificial intelligence tailors virtual tours to individual interests. Systems analyze user behavior to recommend exhibits, similar to how streaming platforms suggest content. This personalization increases **user satisfaction scores** and encourages longer engagement.

### Real-Time Collaboration in Virtual Art Spaces

Emerging platforms enable multiple users to explore exhibits simultaneously. Teachers, students, and curators can meet in shared virtual spaces, discuss artworks, and annotate exhibits in real time. This social dimension transforms virtual museums into collaborative learning environments.

### The Convergence of Museums, Metaverse, and Education Platforms

As the metaverse matures, museums will integrate their collections into shared digital ecosystems. Partnerships between cultural institutions and technology companies will create persistent, interconnected worlds where art, history, and science coexist interactively.

## Abstract

**Introduction:**

Digital transformation is vital for preserving regional cultural assets, yet many projects lack a validated, systematic framework for implementation. This study addresses this gap by developing a framework for the Isan Local VR Museum.

**Methods:**

Employing a mixed-methods Research and Development (R&D) approach, the project utilized high-resolution 3D modeling and 360-degree panoramic imagery delivered via a responsive web platform. The system was validated through an expert quality review and a user satisfaction survey (n=157) using 5-point Likert scales.

**Results:**

Quantitative analysis showed high efficacy, with experts rating overall quality as “Very Good” ( = 4.63) and users reporting the “Highest” level of satisfaction ( = 4.51). Specifically, Simulated Map Navigation ( = 5.00) and immersive views ( = 4.62) were the highest-rated features.

**Discussion:**

While the results confirm the framework’s robustness for VR museum execution, findings suggest that Device Responsiveness ( = 4.37) remains an area for further technical refinement. This research establishes a crucial benchmark for the immersive digitalization and integration of regional cultural resources.

## 1 Introduction

The digital transformation of cultural heritage institutions represents a notable advancement in Information and Communication Technology (ICT), aimed at enhancing accessibility, preservation, and visitor engagement ([Del Soldato and Massari, 2024](#B5); [Lian and Xie, 2024](#B23); [Sallaku et al., 2025](#B33); [Tsoukala et al., 2024](#B41); [Uyar Oğuz and Aslan, 2026](#B42)). Virtual Reality (VR) museums have emerged as a compelling alternative that transcends the physical constraints of conventional exhibition spaces, providing immersive, interactive, and universally accessible experiences ([Shu, 2025](#B37); [Hutson and Hutson, 2024](#B14)). The shift to digital is permanent, driven by the objective of enhancing immersion and engagement while promoting active learning that transcends passive observation ([Kozinets, 2021](#B19); [Redd et al., 2025](#B32); [Karakuş Yılmaz et al., 2024](#B39)). Contemporary advanced VR platforms rely on significant sensory stimulation and robust human-computer interaction to maintain heightened visitor engagement and increased realism ([Lei et al., 2025](#B20); [Gong et al., 2024](#B9); [Sanfilippo et al., 2025](#B34)).

To achieve the necessary realism and fidelity, effective platforms must comprehend the digital documentation of heritage. Three-dimensional scanning techniques, such as LiDAR and photogrammetry, are essential for the high-precision, non-invasive digital preservation of artifacts ([Ertürk, 2020](#B8); [Kantaros et al., 2023](#B17); [Kartini et al., 2024](#B18); [Li et al., 2025](#B22)), whereas 360-degree photography represents the most cost-effective approach to capturing the entirety of an environment, which is vital for generating an authentic sense of presence ([Costa et al., 2024](#B2); [Shi et al., 2024](#B46); [Zhang et al., 2025](#B36)). The technical basis for next-generation immersive platforms is the synergistic integration of two methodologies: 3D models for intricate object analysis and 360-degree panoramas for extensive spatial context ([Zhang, 2024](#B44); [Rodríguez et al., 2025](#B31); [Singh et al., 2025](#B38)). Furthermore, visitor experience and satisfaction serve as essential metrics for evaluating such projects, with perceived ease of use and utility closely associated with favorable engagement ([Berta et al., 2025](#B3); [Pham et al., 2025](#B7); [Jung et al., 2025](#B16); [Liu et al., 2025](#B24); [Qureshi et al., 2025](#B30)). Technical quality evaluations are crucial to ensure platform usability, responsiveness, and accessibility ([Ai et al., 2025](#B1); [Bonino et al., 2025](#B4); [Drivas and Vraimaki, 2025](#B6); [Hassan et al., 2025](#B12); [López-del-Pino et al., 2026](#B26); [Mondo et al., 2026](#B28); [Tamim et al., 2025](#B40)).

Although the existing literature substantiates the significant potential of virtual reality and the applicability of 3D/360 technologies ([Hassan et al., 2025](#B12); [Joshi et al., 2025](#B15); [Li et al., 2024](#B21); [Mishra and Doria, 2025](#B27); [Vidyalakshmi G et al., 2025](#B43)), a notable methodological deficiency persists: the absence of validated, systematic development models that comprehensively document the integration of 3D/360 technologies into a singular, user-friendly web-based platform ([Hamash et al., 2025](#B10); [Mulush and Baik, 2025](#B29); [Scataglini et al., 2026](#B35); [Zhang et al., 2025](#B12)). Applied research clarifying the design, implementation, and effective adoption of sophisticated virtual reality systems in regional cultural institutions, particularly in Southeast Asia, exemplified by the Isan Local Museum, is inadequately represented ([Hassan et al., 2025](#B12); [Lopes et al., 2025](#B25); [Zhou and Wang, 2025](#B47)).

This study addresses this deficiency by demonstrating the design, implementation, and comprehensive validation of the Isan Local VR Museum platform. The primary objectives are to (1) establish a methodical framework for the platform’s development through the integration of 3D scanning and 360-degree photography; (2) employ expert assessment to evaluate technical quality and design; and (3) monitor visitor satisfaction and functionality among 157 users. This article delineates a robust, pragmatic, and replicable development methodology for the Immersive Digitalization of Cultural Heritage, essential for ensuring effective implementation across all regional cultural sites.

To systematically achieve these primary objectives through the sequential, two-phase Research and Development (R&D) process, the study was guided by the following specific inquiries:

* What is the comprehensive and cohesive framework required for the creation and implementation of a web-based Virtual Reality (VR) museum platform for the Isan Local Museum, utilizing 3D scanning and 360-degree imaging technologies? ## 3 Materials and methods

The study employed a sequential, two-phase Research and Development (R&D) design underpinned by a mixed-methods approach. This robust architecture was employed to methodically construct and rigorously evaluate a web-based Virtual Reality (VR) museum platform for the Isan Local Museum in Mahasarakham Province, Northeast Thailand. The institute serves as a pivotal hub for education and the dissemination of information. It supports the benefits of museums for society, such as providing educational resources that meet community needs, raising awareness about the importance of preserving traditional Northeastern Thai architecture, and giving the public a place for fun and interaction. The complete study procedure was conducted from January 1, 2024, to October 30, 2025.

### 3.1 Overall design structure: R&D with sequential mixed-methods

The R&D framework provides a definitive methodology for developing and evaluating a technological product prior to assessing its functionality. The study was executed in two distinct, sequential phases:

#### 3.1.1 Phase 1: development and engineering (qualitative/research and development)

This phase was qualitative and engineering-focused, centering on the intended design, construction, and technology execution of the operational VR platform. The most significant events that occurred were:

Design and Conceptualization: Determining the system’s architecture and user experience.

Content Integration: Combining 3D modeling with 360-degree virtual tour technologies.

Establishing the platform: configuring the web-based virtual reality museum for the Isan Local Museum.

#### 3.1.2 Phase 2: stringent validation (quantitative evaluation)

This phase transitioned to a quantitative, non-experimental methodology to comprehensively validate the established platform. The validation was conducted through two successive stages of data collection:

Stage 1: Expert Quality Assessment (System-Centered): This evaluated the platform’s adherence to established technical, pedagogical, and design criteria, including usability, interface design, and content accuracy.

Stage 2: End-User Acceptance Survey (User-Centered): Evaluated the extent to which the target audience accepted, was satisfied with, and perceived the platform’s functionality.

### 3.2 Phase 1: systematic platform development (R.Q. 1)

The development phase addressed [Research Question 1](#Research_Question_1) by employing a rigorous and replicable Research and Development (R&D) methodology. This systematic approach was essential to ensure the seamless and efficient integration of various 3D and 360-degree technologies into a unified, web-based platform accessible to all users. The final platform was constructed using responsive web architecture to ensure optimal functionality across many devices, including PCs, tablets, and smartphones.

#### 3.2.1 Data capture and hybrid digitalization

The data gathering for the Isan Local Museum employed a hybrid digitization process to optimize geographical context and artifact detail.

360-Degree Photography (Spatial Context):

A 3D Matterport camera captured high-resolution 360-degree panoramic images.

These images depicted both the interior and exterior of the museum, both of which were highly immersive. They established the overarching spatial framework and the important locations for the virtual tour’s navigation. 3D Photogrammetry (Artifact Detail):

A DSLR camera and an unmanned aerial vehicle (drone) were employed to capture aerial and close-up images of significant cultural artifacts and the primary structure (the Isan Thai House).

The data was transformed into meticulously detailed, metrically precise 3D models that enable visitors to virtually navigate and examine the historical pieces closely.

#### 3.2.2 Platform Assembly and integration

The data obtained was synthesized to create a user-friendly VR environment. This study employed the Navigational Plan ([Figure 2](#F2)) to ascertain the spatial relationships among the hybrid data points.

#### 3.2.3 VR environment creation and integration

The subsequent essential methods were implemented to integrate and incorporate the raw data into the final VR platform:

3D Modeling: The images were analyzed using Reality Capture photogrammetry software, resulting in intricate, textured 3D models (point cloud, mesh model, and texture mapping) of artifacts and structures. The models were subsequently exported.

Creating 360-Degree Views: 3D Matterport amalgamated unprocessed 360° photographs and rendered them to produce seamless, navigable spherical panoramas.

Integrating the platform and including interactive features: The 3D models and 360° panoramas were consolidated into a single web environment. The 3D Vista application was utilized to assemble the interactive 360-degree environment. [Sketchfab.com](http://Sketchfab.com) provided a platform for hosting exported 3D model files, enabling users to store and view them online. The interactive, functioning platform was built with a user interface (UI), navigational linkages, and crucial informational hotspots.

### 3.3 Phase 2: dual-level quantitative validation

Two quantitative validation methods were employed to rigorously assess the platform’s efficacy and ascertain its quality and user satisfaction.

#### 3.3.1 Expert quality evaluation

Participants and Selection Criteria: Three experts with experience in relevant fields (VR/media design, human-computer interaction, and digital heritage) were selected by purposive sampling. Selecting three experts ensures the minimum panel size required to achieve statistical consensus (the prevailing viewpoint) for reliability, while also providing a comprehensive perspective on technical, design, and cultural expertise.

Instrument: A 5-point Likert Scale Quality Evaluation Tool was utilized to assess the system’s quality. The rating ranged from 5 (best/excellent) to 1 (worst/destitute). The tool was developed based on three primary concepts: technical accuracy (including 3D model fidelity and data integrity), design criteria (encompassing visual fidelity, UI/navigation, and device responsiveness), and system stability (comprising link stability, loading speed, and bug rate).

Validity and Reliability: A comprehensive evaluation of the literature and insights from subject matter experts ensured the content’s validity. We statistically validated dependability using Cronbach’s Alpha (α), resulting in a high internal consistency score of 0.85.

Procedure: Experts independently explored the final web-based VR platform and utilized the quality tool, providing organized feedback according to established criteria.

#### 3.3.2 End-user satisfaction survey participants and sampling

A total of 157 target consumers participated. A non-probability sampling method was employed, incorporating elements of convenience and purposive selection.

Target Audience: Individuals interested in cultural heritage or digital tourism, typically from local communities or academic institutions.

Eligibility criteria for participation: willingness to engage, possession of a functional device, minimum age of 18 years, and proficiency in navigating the platform. A 5-point Likert Scale Satisfaction Survey Instrument was employed. The instrument was developed in accordance with established user acceptance frameworks, including the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), to assess attributes such as perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and overall satisfaction.

Procedure: Participants were granted access to the VR museum platform and instructed to complete the survey immediately following their experience.

### 3.4 Data analysis

This study utilized SPSS to analyze all the quantitative data we had acquired.

Descriptive Statistics: The mean () and standard deviation (S.D.) were calculated to summarize central tendencies and distribution for all evaluated criteria from both the Expert Quality Assessment and the End-User Satisfaction Survey.

Reliability Analysis: We employed Cronbach’s Alpha (α) to assess the internal consistency of both rating instruments. The instruments' reliability was confirmed by a high alpha value of 0.85.

Validity: Expert design ensured content validity, while associating the satisfaction survey with established models such as TAM enhanced construct validity.

### 3.5 Ethical compliance

Due to the inclusion of human subjects (experts and end-users), the Mahasarakham University Review Board evaluated and sanctioned the research methodology, tools, and consent forms. All participants provided informed consent, and all data was anonymized and handled in accordance with institutional regulations.

#### 4.1.4 Creation of the 360-degree views

The advancement of 360-degree perspectives is the foremost technological progression. This phase is the stage at which the previously captured raw pictures are processed and assembled to facilitate navigation and enhance immersion within the VR museum.

Stitching is a prevalent technique for creating 360-degree panoramas. The initial stage in this procedure is to align and amalgamate the photos. This is accomplished by downloading individual overlapping photographs from designated vantage points to specialized software. This software subsequently aligns these images automatically or manually, rectifying issues such as lens distortions and exposure discrepancies. The penultimate phase is spherical projection, which integrates the aligned images into a singular elongated panorama, typically in an equirectangular format. This final output is crucial for the VR environment since it enables the user to perceive in all directions (360° horizontally and 180° vertically) within the virtual realm ([Figure 6](#F6)).

### 4.2 Analysis of data on the quality assessment of the virtual reality museum design and development

This summary ([Table 1](#T1)) outlines the analysis of the quality assessment regarding the design and development of the virtual reality museum.

The expert quality assessment presented in [Table 1](#T1) determined that the integrated virtual reality museum platform possesses an overall quality rating of Very Good ( = 4.63, S.D. = 0.48). Experts unanimously concurred two critical factors that contributed to the product’s favorable rating: link stability and the utility of the simulated map. Both achieved a flawless score of  = 5.00 with zero standard deviation. Additionally, a significant proportion of the products (8 out of 13) received a rating of “Very Good” ( = 4.66), indicating their high quality in critical areas such as aesthetics, user-friendly navigation design, content accuracy, and the clarity of the 360-degree pictures. Three elements received a little lower but nevertheless commendable rating ( = 4.33), indicating minor areas for improvement: enhancing design consistency, augmenting the completeness and detail of the 3D model, and improving responsiveness across all screen sizes. In conclusion, the experts concurred that the integrated VR platform was highly useful and well-architected, with map integration and steady navigation identified as its most commendable attributes.

The expert evaluation in [Section 4.2](#s4-2) indicated that the VR platform was of superior quality and technically robust. The study indicates that it was effective from the perspective of the end-user. The prior examination confirmed the technical integrity and design superiority of the VR museum platform, as affirmed by subject matter experts (R.Q. 2). The emphasis now shifts to the experiential component to complete the two-step validation required for a successful R&D model. The subsequent section presents the results of the End-User Acceptance Survey, which inquired about visitors' satisfaction levels, perceived utility, and operational effectiveness from the perspective of the target audience (R.Q. 3).

Users expressed the highest satisfaction with the Map Utility ( = 4.68), which they deemed highly effective for visualizing the museum layout, and with Immersive Viewing ( = 4.62), which enables comprehensive exploration of the museum via 360-degree photographs. In conclusion, the data substantiates that the platform has effectively provided a very advantageous, beneficial, and user-friendly virtual learning experience.

This is a peer-reviewed original research article published in Frontiers in Virtual Reality (Volume 7, 2026, published April 23, 2026) under the "Technologies for VR" section. The study, titled "Immersive digitalization of cultural heritage: a validated virtual reality museum platform using integrated 3D and 360-degree technologies," was authored by Pongpipat Saithong (Faculty of Informatics, Mahasarakham University, Thailand) and Jiranai Yoddee (Faculty of Information Technology, Sripatum University, Khon Kaen Campus, Thailand).

**Purpose:** The research addresses a gap in validated, systematic frameworks for digitally preserving regional cultural assets, specifically developing the Isan Local VR Museum for the Isan Local Museum in Mahasarakham Province, Northeast Thailand. The study ran from January 1, 2024 to October 30, 2025.

**Methodology:** A sequential two-phase mixed-methods Research and Development (R&D) approach was employed:
- **Phase 1 (Development):** High-resolution 3D photogrammetry (using DSLR cameras and drones) and 360-degree panoramic imagery (using a 3D Matterport camera) were captured and integrated into a responsive web platform built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript (no specialized VR headset required). Reality Capture software was used for 3D modeling, 3D Vista for assembling the interactive 360° environment, and Sketchfab.com for hosting 3D models.
- **Phase 2 (Validation):** Two-stage quantitative evaluation — (1) expert quality assessment by 3 purposively selected experts (VR/media design, HCI, digital heritage) using a 5-point Likert scale, and (2) end-user satisfaction survey of 157 participants (age 18+, from local communities and academic institutions) using TAM-based instruments. Cronbach's Alpha reliability was 0.85. Data analyzed using SPSS.

**Key Results:**
- Expert quality rating: Overall "Very Good" (mean = 4.63, S.D. = 0.48). Link stability and simulated map navigation both scored perfect 5.00. Eight of 13 items scored 4.66. Three items (design consistency, 3D model completeness, device responsiveness) scored 4.33, indicating minor improvement areas.
- User satisfaction: Overall "Highest" level (mean = 4.51, S.D. = 0.50) from 157 users. Top-rated features included Map Utility (4.68) and Immersive Viewing via 360° photos (4.62). Lowest scores (4.37) were for Device Adaptability and Interactive System usability, identifying device responsiveness as the primary area for technical refinement.

**Key Platform Features:** Digital museum map with navigation markers, 360-degree views, interactive information hotspots, and access to detailed 3D models of the Isan Thai House (a traditional stilt house). The platform was built to work across PCs, tablets, and smartphones.

**Conclusions:** The study establishes a benchmark for immersive digitalization of regional cultural heritage and provides a replicable development framework. It confirms that integrating 3D modeling with 360-degree panoramic technology creates an effective, validated VR museum platform, while noting that device responsiveness remains the key area for future technical optimization.

# Trends in Museum Education: Technology

Published

August 19, 2019

[![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/68fbbd5d74950e8e0d593510/68fd7bfa09ed7a4457726967_copy-Link.svg)

Copy Article](#)

While some museums have looked at technology with a skeptical and weary eye, others are embracing the shift and are creating unique experiences that encourage a young and emerging generation of museum-goers. For those institutions more open and willing to experiment with the role of technology at their venues, technology can present a myriad of new opportunities for curators to create unique, never-before seen experiences in museums. Regardless of opinion, it’s clear that technology in museums are not only here to stay but will be the future for many exhibits. Here are some of the most current and engaging technology trends in museum education today.

## **Self-guided Tour Trends in Museum Education**

While self-guided audio tours have been around for quite some time, the emergence of several interactive apps that can be accessed via phone or tablet are changing the ways that people learn about exhibits. Apps can provide both video and audio tours of an exhibit and highlight certain features of the museum that visitors couldn’t get without a guide. Detailed information and educational materials can be found through the digital interfaces, thus providing visitors with pages of pictures, text, historical background and videos that you simply couldn’t fit into a small information plaque usually found beside an exhibit item.

## **Augmented Reality Trends in Museum Education**

Beyond self-guided tours, app developers have found more fun and technologically creative ways to engage visitors in museums. Augmented reality trends are changing the ways visitors interact with the exhibits and the people around them. Apps like [Actionbound](https://en.actionbound.com/) allow users to create their own personalized tours, scavenger hunts, missions, and other educational games that can be shared with friends in museums. Teachers can create games prior to taking their classes to museums, provide each student with a device that hosts the app, and let their class off to race for all the items in a museum. Here some exciting ways that augmented reality trends are enhancing museum education:

* **QR code scanning to learn about exhibit items and objects**

* Motion/gesture technology to interact with parts of an exhibit

* Fun and educational quizzes that can accompany a tour

* Apps that utilize photo-taking to engage visitors with exhibits and galleries
* Augmented reality screens that bring visitors into the action and fun

## **Virtual Reality Trends in Museum Education**

Unlike Augmented reality trends that rely on enhancing experiences in the real world, virtual reality looks to complete transform guests’ surroundings and take them on adventures never thought possible before.VR trends are blowing up in nearly every industry, but the museum world has a unique opportunity to capitalize on a technology that compliments much of the industry’s subject matter. As a supplement to educating visitors on how the dinosaurs lived, museums can give their guests the unique opportunity of actually visiting the Mesozoic Era and seeing, first-hand, how these creatures interacted with each other.What better way is there to follow up a school lesson on the predators of the prehistoric world than to introduce students to those very creatures in the virtual world?Guests can meet canonized historic figures, stroll through ancient cities, embark on thrilling adventures through the arctic, and endure some of the most inhabited regions of the earth, all from the comfortable setting of your museum. From science and history to art and geography, virtual reality is creating new and exciting ways for students to learn, live, and remember the experiences they share with technology.

## **3D Printing Trends in Museum Education**

3D printers and scanners are allowing museums to bring back artifacts that have been lost to the test of time. Replicas of ancient artifacts, tools, and antiquated items of history are now making their way into museums across the world. Scanners are also allowing visitors to view digital replicas of artifacts that would be otherwise too fragile or worn down for exposure. Additionally, museums can create unique experiences like the digital unravelling of real mummies to showcase to their guests.Having the most current and up-to-date technology trends in museum education can play a huge role in revitalizing your museum, increasing memberships, and galvanizing a new wave of creativity in your curating team. *   •AR/VR is increasingly used to support learning in science, art and history museums. 
*   •AR/VR is more often used to superimpose digital materials onto physical exhibits. 
*   •AR/VR is used to visualize complex phenomena or abstract concepts. 
*   •AR/VR is used to simulate virtual exhibition and [narrative](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/narrative) scenarios. 
*   •AR/VR in museum learning has positive effects on academic achievement and perception. 

## Abstract

Virtual reality (VR) and [augmented reality](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/augmented-reality) (AR) have been increasingly used to support museum learning by creating engaging and appealing [learning experiences](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/learning-experience). However, there is a lack of meta-analytic reviews of empirical studies in this field. This study reviewed 51 relevant studies to investigate (a) the situations in which AR and VR have been applied in museum learning (RQ1) and (b) how AR and VR are incorporated in museum learning (RQ2), and conducted a meta-analysis of 17 studies to examine the effects of these technologies on learning achievement (RQ3). The results reveal that AR and VR have been mostly used in science, arts, and history museums to support the learning of science and art with a focus on conceptual knowledge. Second, they were often used to superimpose supplementary materials onto physical exhibits, dynamically visualize complex phenomena or concepts, and simulate virtual exhibition and [narrative](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/social-sciences/narrative) scenarios. Mobile devices were more commonly used than head-mounted displays (HMDs) and others. Third, AR and VR have significant positive effects on academic achievement (ES=0.45) and perceptions (ES=0.59) in museum learning. A number of suggestions for future research arose from this review.

## Introduction

Since the 19th century, educators have begun to see museums as important informal learning environments that provide the general public (from children to adults) with visual, accessible and even tangible objects and exhibits to explore disciplinary content knowledge about art, history, culture, and science in depth, as well as to develop children's interest and career aspirations related to these subjects (De Rijcke & Beaulieu, 2011; Kisiel, 2006; Lewalter et al., 2021). Museums may house exhibits, collections or experiences that are often designed explicitly to meet educational goals targeting school-aged children (Crowley et al., 2014). However, museum educators often face the challenge of creating engaging activities for learners (Watson & Werb, 2013). In particular, guided school field trips to museums are mostly based on a whole-class lecture model that constrains the group's movements to exhibits and displays preselected objects. These trips generally focus more on meeting formal educational goals valued in schools, but fail to foster lifelong learning and social skills valued in museums, such as inquiry, observation, and conversational elaboration on topical issues in science, art, and history (Kisiel, 2003).

Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) technologies are among the new technologies that are increasingly integrated into museum educational activities and aim to create more engaging and appealing learning experiences (Crowley et al., 2014). VR is a computer-generated completely virtual and simulation environment that provides a sensory illusion of being present in another environment (Makransky & Lilleholt, 2018; Renganayagalu et al., 2021; Smith, 2015). Users experience deep immersion, presence, and interactivity through specific VR technology devices like helmets or glasses on which the scene is represented. VR has been broadly utilized in education and has shown promising effects on learners’ cognition (Akçayır & Akçayır, 2017; Morélot et al., 2021), behavioral skills (Çakiroğlu & Gökoğlu, 2019), and positive emotions such as enjoyment (Alfadil, 2020; Innocenti et al., 2019). In particular, VR technologies have been used to enrich learning experiences in museums. For example, VR can be used to reconstruct virtual historical settlements where visitors are totally surrounded by the scenes of ancient society and thus foster a holistic understanding of ancient society, which is difficult to conceive using only the artifacts and annotations shown in museums (Puig et al., 2020).

Unlike VR, which immerses users in a totally virtual and simulation environment, AR is a combination of virtual space and physical scenes (Carmigniani et al., 2011; Garzón et al., 2019), i.e., overlaying real-world objects or their digital representations with extra text, audio, video, or other virtual elements or information which are known as “digital augmentations” (Azuma, 1997; Sommerauer & Müller, 2014). This superimposing digital augmentation effect often occurs through a camera view with mobile platforms or a see-through display such as smart glasses (Pellas et al., 2019; Scavarelli et al., 2021). For example, a mobile device camera captures and recognizes a real-world object and then overlaps this object or its digital representation with extra text, audio, videos or other virtual elements (Calle-Bustos et al., 2017). In the study Yoon et al. (2017), when a physical ball is floating in the front of a Bernoulli blower, an AR device presents a digital image of the moving air around a digital ball that has been generated by the AR device as a digital representation of the physical ball; that is, visitors can see both the physical ball and the digital ball with a superimposed image of moving air. In other situations, AR devices directly project digital virtual objects in the physical space, e.g., displaying a virtual volcano in the classroom. Therefore, in museum learning, AR can provide learners easy access to unobservable phenomena or digital information on exhibits and promote their understanding of the real world (Danaei et al., 2020; Ibanez & Delgado-Kloos, 2018).

The theoretical foundation of incorporating VR and AR in museum learning is grounded in experiential learning (Behrendt & Franklin, 2014; Kolb, 2014), situated learning (Falk & Dierking, 2000; Johnson, 2002), active learning (Prince, 2004), and the multimedia learning theory (Mayer, 2014; Mayer & Estrella, 2014). Experiential learning typically involves four interactive learning processes: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, and active experimentation (Kolb, 2014). Learners gain deeper understanding of the learning contents through these learning processes in authentic and first-hand context (Behrendt & Franklin, 2014; Kolb, 2014). Similar to experiential learning, situated learning involves learning within the context in which knowledge is situated and it might be used and applied (Choi & Ahn, 2021; Johnson, 2002). Active learning refers to learners' active engagement in meaningful learning activities and their reflection on learning (Chiang et al., 2021; Prince, 2004). Multimedia learning theory emphasizes the presentation of text and relevant graphical illustrations to promote learners’ cognitive processing. Recently, researchers have expanded multimedia learning theory by incorporating emotional designs that can motivate learners to exert more mental effort to make sense of the presented material (Mayer, 2020; Mayer & Estrella, 2014). There is no doubt that VR and AR technologies are able to combine multiple media contents (such as texts, audio, video), provide an interactive, engaging educational context to support experiential and situated learning in museums, and induce learners to search more information for meaning-making and understanding, thus promoting active learning (e.g., inspecting historical settlements of ancient society) (Huang et al., 2016; Sultan et al., 2019).

According to the International Council of Museums (ICOM), museums are institutions open to the public that acquire, conserve, research, communicate and exhibit the tangible and intangible heritage of humanity and its environment for the purposes of education, study and enjoyment (ICOM, 2007). They involve various objects, exhibits and programs related to the subjects of science, history, archaeology and the arts (Andre et al., 2017). Learning in museums (also called museum learning) enables visitors to understand the value of historical artifacts, learn about science, history and the arts and respect different cultures (Guzin et al., 2017; Xanthoudaki, 1998). Moreover, museum learning has shown great promise in increasing interest and cognitive skills (Yoon et al., 2012).

However, museums are currently suffering from reduced interest and lower attendance among the younger generations (Crowley et al., 2014). Thus, it is important to improve visitors' interest by designing engaging learning experiences (Hassan & Ramkissoon, 2016). Existing review studies on museum learning have focused on the adoption of technology in museums. Wang et al. (2017) reviewed the studies on ubiquitous language learning using location-based systems in museums from the perspective of system usefulness, activity usefulness and activity playfulness; they found that ubiquitous location-based systems using mobile devices helped to promote students’ collaboration in group learning activities. Lin et al. (2021) investigated the trends in research on museum-based mobile learning in terms of research methods, learning domains, location-based technologies, learning strategies, and research topics. Xu et al. (2021) conducted a meta-analysis analyzing 42 experimental or quasi-experimental studies on technology applications in museum learning published during 2011–2021 and showed that technology application has a moderate or high effect on museum learning. In recent years, AR and VR are increasingly used to create engaging activities for learners (Falomo Bernarduzzi et al., 2021; Scavarelli et al., 2021).

Many empirical studies have explored the use of AR and VR in museum learning across different domains, such as science, art, archaeology, medicine and the military. For example, Oh et al. (2018) designed a multiuser participatory simulation called ARfract, where visitors can learn about complex concepts such as the refraction of light through full-body immersion using optical see-through AR glasses, projection-based AR, and gesture technology. Yoon et al. (2017) used an AR device to help students develop a more accurate understanding of fluid dynamics, a challenging concept of Bernoulli's principle in a science museum by visualizing air flow. Likewise, in art museums, history museums or archaeology museums, AR and VR have been widely exploited to provide augmentation or simulation of artworks and relics to create a more vivid and immersive learning environment. For example, in Chang et al. (2014), a mobile AR guide system presented paintings in a more instinctive way, aiming to foster college students' appreciation for painting. Moreover, AR has also been used in medical museums to display virtual labels, images and natural interfaces to advance students' understanding of medical specimens (Sugiura et al., 2019).

The learning outcomes measured in existing studies vary and generally include knowledge achievement, thinking skills, individuals' affections, etc. For example, Yoon et al. (2017) found that even when given only a short period for investigation in a science museum, students using AR demonstrated significantly greater knowledge gains than those who did not. Some studies have reported that AR/VR-assisted museum learning promotes learners' higher-order thinking skills, such as creative thinking (Guazzaroni, 2013; Hammady et al., 2020), inquiry (Hsiao et al., 2016), and critical thinking skills (Poce et al., 2019). Some studies have investigated learners' motivation and emotions. For example, Dieck et al. (2018) and Puig et al. (2020) revealed that these technologies enhance visitors’ satisfaction and enjoyment and that wearable equipment helps to personalize their learning experience. Additionally, Nechita and Rezeanu (2019) reports that a multisensory augmented museum space can enhance empathy by allowing learners to experience various historical circumstances from a first-hand perspective.

However, other studies found negative effects of AR/VR-assisted museum learning. For example, Savela et al. (2020) found that AR games in a science center did not necessarily improve learning performance or social interaction when compared to the traditional pen-and-paper learning method. Additionally, learners claimed that using VR devices made them feel nauseous and dizzy (Rhee, 2019), and some devices such as HMDs also physically inconvenienced visitors (Oh et al., 2018; Sugiura et al., 2019). Therefore, whether and to what extent AR and VR applications could benefit visitors in museum learning are questions that still need to be synthesized and clarified.

AR and VR have become a focus in educational studies in recent years, most of which concentrate on formal learning environments. Akçayır and Akçayır (2017) presented a systematic review on AR application in both K-12 and higher education and explored the advantages and challenges of using AR, concluding that AR can potentially support learning and teaching. Bacca et al. (2014) reviewed the usage, advantages, limitations, effectiveness, challenges, and features of AR in educational settings and found that it has been most commonly used in science, humanities and arts learning. Radianti et al. (2020) reviewed the application of VR in higher education by focusing on three key aspects: the learning contents, the design elements, and learning theories. Saltan and Arslan (2017) provided a comprehensive overview of the emergence of AR research on pedagogical and educational outcomes, specifically in formal education, and illustrated the evidence of improved academic achievements and perceptions. Goff et al. (2018) reviewed AR in exhibit-based informal science education settings and reported the STEM-focused topics covered by AR applications, various devices, and positive learning outcomes.

The abovementioned reviews provide syntheses of the trends, advantages and challenges of using AR and/or VR in educational settings, mostly in formal settings. Thus, there is as yet no meta-analytic review of empirical studies on the use of AR and VR in museum settings. Specifically, it is unclear in which contexts these technologies have been applied in museum learning and how the learning activities incorporating AR and VR are designed (i.e., the design elements). Moreover, the effects of AR and VR on museum learning are ambiguous as some reported positive effects while others reported negative effects.

Thus, the present study aims to provide a comprehensive meta-analytic review of AR/VR-assisted museum learning. First, education researchers and museum practitioners may be interested in the contexts in which AR and/or VR have been used, such as the learning domains and learning contents. Second, it is important for them to gain a deeper understanding of AR and VR affordances and their corresponding design elements. Third, there is a great need to know the overall effects of AR and VR on museum learning. Therefore, our research questions are as follows:

Research Question 1 (RQ1): In which contexts or situations have AR and VR technologies been applied to support museum learning?

Research Question 2 (RQ2): What are the design elements (the technology affordances, in particular) of AR and VR for museum learning?

Research Question 3 (RQ3): What are the effects of AR/VR-assisted museum learning versus non-AR/VR-assisted museum learning on students’ academic achievement and perceptions?

To answer RQ1, we analyzed museum types, learner types, learning domains, and learning contents. To address RQ2, we explored the design elements of existing empirical studies, the technology affordances, and how the design elements used therein were implemented in technology devices. Finally, we conducted a meta-analysis to investigate the impact of AR and VR on museum learning (RQ3).

Sixty-five papers met the inclusion criteria and were classified depending on the study’s purpose: education, entertainment, edutainment, touristic guidance systems, accessibility, visitor profiling, and management. Immersive cultural heritage systems allow visitors to feel completely immersed and present in the virtual environment, providing a stimulating and educational cultural experience that can improve the quality and learning purposes of cultural visits. Nonetheless, the analyzed studies revealed some limitations that must be faced to give a further impulse to the adoption of these technologies in the cultural heritage domain.

Despite the differences in the results between the two applications, the items generally scored high, which supports earlier studies that found that AR produced greater immersion and UX than the average immersion obtained when AR was not employed [20,24], suggesting that AR technology creates an overall positive UX in cultural experiences. This is consistent with earlier findings [85]. On top of that, through the data analysis of the pilot experiment, the study supported that AR is a worth promoting as an effective immersive storytelling tool in cultural metaverse.  Show abstract Enthusiasm for the metaverse is intensifying in academia and industries. The metaverse is a complex concept, combining many technologies to create many different types of user experiences (UX), depending on the intended use. The cultural metaverse was first introduced in this study. This study is an initial attempt to fill the gaps in the practical research and storytelling research in the metaverse. Augmented reality (AR) technology is an applicative tool in cultural experience, which displays computer – generated virtual information on a real-world scene. AR displays digital information realistically, making it appear to be part of the actual environment, deepening or expanding the user's understanding of “reality”. This study constructed a cultural metaverse using the innovative AR storytelling. The cultural metaverse is a new cultural ecology in which advanced information technologies are deeply integrated with cultural spaces and exhibits. It combines digital technologies and cultural industries, mixing virtual space and physical space to facilitate the UX in cultural experiences. In this study, the existing AR e-book and the innovative AR version were compared while measuring multiple aspects of UX, including presence, flow, enjoyment, education, and engagement. By analyzing questionnaire data from two groups with a total of 368 participants, the results indicated that the innovative AR storytelling produced a better UX across all variables compared to the AR e-book application. Overall, innovative AR storytelling allows visitors to transition between real and virtual spaces, enriches their interactive experience, and improves user engagement with the metaverse exhibition of cultural experience. Therefore, practitioners can construct a primary cultural metaverse through innovative AR storytelling.
