# We Need More Than Empathy: A Call for Social-Emotional Learning in Museums

Written By [Andrea Jones](/blog?author=57d603f46b8f5b7fd8041888)

Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) is arguably one of the hottest topics in formal education in the last couple of years. Education policy is shifting rapidly. Yet the term is almost non-existent in the museum field.

![what+is+SEL.jpg](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562642493414-QMSJ2DO1ZBTS7J97GTGC/what%2Bis%2BSEL.jpg)

Why all the buzz about SEL in formal education? Although we can’t say for certain, it may be the recent increase in political divisions, the way that technology sequesters us, or the surge in bullying and discrimination. There is a lot of palpable anger out there. And although the movement towards SEL began more than two decades ago, we are now more urgently grasping for ways to address this maelstrom of confusing feelings.

The museum field is concerned with the same societal issues, but very few of us are using SEL’s more holistic approach. We seem to have rallied around our mental health crisis in a sort of piecemeal fashion. We talk of “well-being” and “self-care.” We clamor for ways to accept each other through diversity and inclusivity efforts. And perhaps most often, we talk explicitly about the need for “empathy.”

[![aam_trendswatch_2017_cover.png](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562606430852-CDBKUJVMAYXA7Z1BU9YV/aam_trendswatch_2017_cover.png)](https://www.aam-us.org/programs/center-for-the-future-of-museums/trendswatch-2017/)

Empathy is everywhere in our field. In its [2017 Trendswatch Report](https://www.aam-us.org/programs/center-for-the-future-of-museums/trendswatch-2017/), the Center for the Future of Museums named “empathy” as one of five major future trends. At every conference I attend, sessions on empathy are packed with standing room only crowds.

## My Deep Dive with Empathy

In the last year, I’ve been to several major “convenings” that have focused solely on discussing the best ways to foster empathy and compassion in museum visitors – including one epic journey to India with [Elif Gokcigdem](http://elifgokcigdem.com/fostering-empathy-through-museums/) and others to meet with the Dalai Lama. [See my blog post here.](http://www.peakexperiencelab.com/blog/2019/1/30/how-meeting-the-dalai-lama-changed-my-museum-practice) His Holiness spoke eloquently of the need to teach secular ethics and of learning to manage one’s emotions. I learned later that the Dalai Lama’s team worked with Emory University to create their own version SEL called SEE - [Social Emotional and Ethical Learning](https://seelearning.emory.edu/) (See framework below). I love the emphasis on ethics and on recognizing our common humanity. SEE, from what I can tell, has a much more globally oriented world-view.

![_DSC9764.jpg](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562606820273-8BJM6QZ2D67EW7BN24WG/_DSC9764.jpg)

I’ve also had really interesting discussions with Gretchen Jennings and others in the [Empathetic Museum](http://empatheticmuseum.weebly.com/) group. This group’s focus is distinctive from other empathy initiatives I’ve seen in that it does not concentrate on fostering empathy in visitors, but rather improving the museum’s organizational culture so that it is more inclusive of different perspectives.

![The photo above was taken at an lively and inspiring two-day “Empathy Lab” mini-conference I attended earlier this year (Me - second row).  It was hosted by the Minneapolis Institute of Art’s Center for Empathy and Visual Arts. Our efforts focused o…](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562607360355-5W4LA4NV2Y5ZU5NBA1U3/Empathy+Lab+March+2019%281%29.png)

*The photo above was taken at an lively and inspiring two-day “Empathy Lab” mini-conference I attended earlier this year (Me - second row).   
It was hosted by the Minneapolis Institute of Art’s Center for Empathy and Visual Arts. Our efforts focused on finding ways to foster empathy through Mia’s collections and programs. What a great group of empathy enthusiasts!*

In short, I’ve been in deep with the empathy crowd. One of my biggest take-aways from all of these discussions is that, yes, many of us in the museum field have the desire to address the very real empathy deficit in society ([a 40% decline since 1970!](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1088868310377395)). But we seem to be fumbling towards best practices for how to do that. What kind of empathy are we trying to foster? Some kinds of empathy frame stories in a way that can leave visitors with more of a “selective empathy” - reserved for people just like them. What if we ignite empathy in visitors that opens up strong emotions - strong emotions that museum staff are not prepared to deal with? Do we need to change organizational culture first?

There is no shortage of ideas, but we have little agreement about what we are really trying to do with empathy and how we should best do it. Don’t get me wrong, I don’t think it’s necessary for us all to agree. Experimentation is vital. But wouldn’t it be nice if we didn’t have to reinvent the wheel completely?

That’s why I was elated to find out that there is already a very well-thought-out set of frameworks (SEL and SEE) being used in school systems across the country. And they are much more comprehensive than aiming to foster empathy alone.

[The SEL framework](https://casel.org/core-competencies/), devised by [CASEL](https://casel.org/) has 5 “competencies” for students. It is the most widely used. The newly unveiled [SEE framework (Social Emotional and Ethical Learning)](https://seelearning.emory.edu/) created by the Dalai Lama and Emory University is newer and less pervasive, but very seems (to me) a bit more adaptable to use with adults.

### SEL Competencies Framework by CASEL

![SEL framework.jpg](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562612018364-PH1OR9XJ7AH30FX2W7PZ/SEL+framework.jpg)

### SEE Competencies Framework from The Dalai Lama

![SEE framework.png](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562612047010-2MUQWU7NVASY1KJF5Z1Z/SEE+framework.png)

## SEL is More Than Empathy

In looking at these competencies, try to envision what these skills would look like in practice. Isn’t this really everything we want for people in a good functional society? I’m not just talking about children learning to stand nicely in line at the water fountain. I’m talking about adults whose decisions affect all of our lives.

To underscore the dire need for an emotionally healthy and ethically aware human race just peruse the news. Almost every conflict or disturbing trend involves a deficit of these skills:

* Mass shootings
* Inhumane treatment of undocumented immigrants
* Climate change denials
* Public internet shaming
* Fake news and dishonest public figures
* Pervasive racism, classism, sexism, ableism, and all the isms

![Illustration: Golden Cosmos](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562638258143-VR8913S4DM00BC380GVD/Golden+Cosmos+School+Shootin.jpg)

Illustration: Golden Cosmos

[Research tells us](https://www.theatlantic.com/science/archive/2016/09/the-best-headspace-for-making-decisions/500423/) that human beings make decisions in their lives based mostly on emotion. Then they use rational thought to justify their emotional response. Thus far museums and schools have focused mostly on building skills in only rational thought. Do we think we are going to help people reason their way out of racism? We’re missing half of the equation. SEL and SEE employ the use of critical thinking in a new way - to examine the roots of our emotions, values, ethics, and relationships. All of these together can give empathy a nice, well-supported environment to live in.

![emotional-learning plato.jpg](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562638434159-I1QGDHQXXTVEN38PJJDV/emotional-learning+plato.jpg)

Is empathy important? Absolutely! Not only is it important, it is perhaps at the root of all of social and emotional skills. But it’s not all we need. We need to be able to understand and identify emotions –in ourselves and others. We need to figure out our purpose and our values. We need to delve into our own beliefs and design our own moral compass. These are all things we may feel innately as we grow up, but we have to *learn* to make choices about them and to use them purposefully. Where are you supposed to learn this? At home? Ok maybe, if you’re lucky enough to have an emotionally healthy family. How about church? Well, that may not be an option since [half of Americans don’t go to church anymore](https://news.gallup.com/poll/248837/church-membership-down-sharply-past-two-decades.aspx). And besides we need a new kind of character education, one that’s less prescriptive.

Are museums willing to fill in some of those gaps? One thing is for certain, the purpose of museums is changing. We can all feel that. What I’m proposing here, is one possible path for reinvention – a path that museums seem well-suited for. [FYI: For an excellent deep-dive into the paradigm shift museums find themselves in, PLEASE listen to [this episode](https://soundcloud.com/museopunks/episode-34-paradigm-lost-and-found) of the MuseoPunks podcast]

## SEL Is Not Just for Children

In the early days, school systems put all their SEL eggs in one or two baskets – pre-school and kindergarten. As a parent of a two-year-old I can verify the prevalence of these lessons from teachers and parents alike. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve heard parents teach lessons to toddlers on the playground about kindness or taking turns – lessons that our politicians and business leaders have forgotten. And it seems logical that they’ve forgotten. Do we really expect kids to get a one-stop-shop character education when they’re three years-old and then be set for life?

![Teaching and learning about sharing has traditionally been reserved for pre-school and kindergarten. Photo: Ellen. Buikema](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562639468050-RE57598TK2WNCKKNAMEH/Screen+Shot+2019-07-08+at+10.30.29+PM.png)

*Teaching and learning about sharing has traditionally been reserved for pre-school and kindergarten. Photo: Ellen. Buikema*

![Adults have trouble sharing too. For decades, Alabama, Georgia, and Florida have been in a heated legal battle due to their inability to equitably share water from two river basins that sustain economic growth for their states.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562639546931-PHJ946ZOBASSWGE4ZTSA/tri_state_water_wars.jpg)

*Adults have trouble sharing too. For decades, Alabama, Georgia, and Florida have been in a heated legal battle due to their inability to equitably share water from two river basins that sustain economic growth for their states.*

That’s why school systems have taken massive steps towards prioritizing SEL in ALL grades. In 2009, only one state (Illinois) had state SEL standards post pre-k. Now, at last count, there are 14 states with SEL learning goals or standards. And city school districts are joining the movement in droves. Chicago, Austin, Atlanta, Baltimore, Minneapolis, Oakland, and countless others. To find out about the momentum of the movement where you live, check out state and district pages on the [CASEL](https://casel.org/) website (Collaborative for Academic Social and Emotional Learning). Changing educational policy to include SEL is one of this organization’s biggest initiatives. Personally, I have never been a fan of state standards. They make any subject too, well, standard. And their existence invites testing. But this is a good movement to keep tabs on because it can tell you how to position your museum to be a support for teachers.

![Screen Shot 2019-07-08 at 10.39.42 PM.png](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562640018681-ZSSF1XX0VB6447QB8WDX/Screen+Shot+2019-07-08+at+10.39.42+PM.png)

## Teachers will Need the Support of Museums to Meet New SEL Standards

All of this policy change is happening very quickly. And teachers will probably be caught in the cross-hairs, as they always are. Many will be responsible for helping students learn SEL skills without adequate training to do so. Museums can play a vital role by supporting teachers with professional development and innovative SEL programming. Of course, that means museum staff will need to learn a bit about another discipline - psychology. But if we are already obsessed with empathy, this is definitely within our reach. And trust me, museum staff (as busy as we are) have lots more time to delve into psychology than teachers do.

## SEL is Backed by Tons of Research

Another advantage of adapting SEL frameworks for museums is that effects of SEL on student success, mental health, and wellness is well documented. For the two decades, researchers have been connecting the dots between SEL and academic/personal success. [CASEL](https://casel.org/research/) has a wealth of this research on their website so that schools can arm themselves with data for our evidence-obsessed era. And so that districts and states can justify policy changes. Granted, this is not research done in museums, but it’s still relevant enough to be cited in a museum grant.

## Not Just for the Museum’s Education Department

Just because the SEL movement originated in schools doesn’t mean the torch should be passed to museum education departments alone. To be good at SEL, we have to work at making our organizations more emotionally healthy overall. We have to learn how to identify toxic workplace dynamics, be mindful of our emotions, and identify our values in ethical decision making. In fact, this is one of the things I like best about the SEL movement in schools. There is a real emphasis on creating an SEL-literate workplace for staff. The school has to exude a healthy feeling if the SEL lessons are going to seem authentic.

![Screen Shot 2019-07-05 at 10.19.51 PM.png](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/57d68f2d03596e4e5bf47c9e/1562640682874-X8Q8D3025ZFZPLW9OG2Q/Screen+Shot+2019-07-05+at+10.19.51+PM.png)

Translated to museums this would mean SEL literate workplaces, exhibits, social media, adult programming, field trips, visitor services, community partnerships, and mission statements. The transformation would affect every department.  I don’t know about you, but this sounds like my dream workplace.

## But what does an SEL museum really look like?

Because I understand the power of real case studies, I’ve started the process of gathering examples from museums across the country. Some are doing this work on purpose, some are doing it NOT on purpose. Please send all examples my way and I promise to write about them.

In the meantime, I’ll leave you with the idea of “sub specie aeternitatis” – a beautiful phrase from the Enlightenment Era. Translated from Latin, it means “in the light of eternity.” When it is all over, what is it all for? What can we do to create some good in the world?

***Andrea Jones*** *is an independent consultant and experience designer working with museums to reinvent storytelling and interpretive methods in the service of greater relevancy for audiences.  
 She is located Washington DC.*[***Join Peak Experience Lab on Facebook!***](https://www.facebook.com/peakexperiencelab/)

Key arguments and points:

- The author's deep involvement with empathy initiatives includes a trip to India with Elif Gokcigdem to meet the Dalai Lama (who discussed secular ethics and emotional management), work with the Empathetic Museum group (focused on organizational culture rather than visitor empathy), and attendance at an "Empathy Lab" mini-conference hosted by the Minneapolis Institute of Art's Center for Empathy and Visual Arts.
- Two existing SEL frameworks are highlighted: CASEL's 5-competency SEL framework (most widely used) and the newer SEE (Social Emotional and Ethical Learning) framework created by the Dalai Lama and Emory University, which the author finds more adaptable for adults.
- SEL is more comprehensive than empathy alone, covering understanding/identifying emotions, purpose, values, and moral compass development. - SEL is backed by two decades of research connecting it to academic/personal success, useful for museum grant applications.

# Empowering Kids Through Art

**The  Power of Social Emotional Learning Through Art**

At The New Children’s Museum, we believe in the transformative power of art to inspire growth, foster understanding, and create meaningful connections. That’s why we’re committed to integrating Social Emotional Learning (SEL) into our educational programming—equipping children with essential skills to manage emotions, build empathy, and form strong relationships.

This innovative program is a collaborative effort with San Diego Unified School District’s Visual and Performing Arts Department, an Art Therapist, a project evaluator, and 11 passionate teachers from 7 Title 1 schools. Together, we’ve developed a dynamic curriculum that empowers teachers to use visual arts as a tool to cultivate SEL in their students.

[SUPPORT THIS PROGRAM](https://thinkplaycreate.ticketapp.org/portal/product/10)

![]()

Video

### Social Emotional Learning: Empowering Students Through Art

Learn about The New Children’s Museum’s Social Emotional Learning (SEL) Program. Discover how it continues to change the lives of children across San Diego.

### What is Social Emotional Learning?

Social Emotional Learning is the process through which individuals acquire and apply the skills to manage emotions, develop healthy identities, build supportive relationships, and make responsible decisions. Our program taps into the creative power of the arts to bring SEL to life in classrooms, helping children express themselves and connect with others in meaningful ways.

### 专题（七）智慧博物馆

 发布时间： 2025.12.22

**报告一**李华飙（中国国家博物馆）

**报告题目：**数智时代智慧博物馆建设研究与实践

**报告摘要：**智慧博物馆是利用大数据、人工智能等最新技术，提供“人、物、数字空间”三者之间的双向多元信息交互通道，实现透彻感知、泛在互联、智慧融合，并具有自主学习、迭代演进能力的博物馆新业态。但是智慧博物馆建设面临如下四个方面的挑战：藏品数字化效率低，信息失真损失较大；数据构成分散割裂，烟囱孤岛广泛存在；展示手段单向为主，系统集成程度较低；理论研究基础薄弱，缺乏统一标准规范。中国国家博物馆通过承担国家重点研发计划项目、构建智慧博物馆体系并开展“智慧国博”应用实践，加快推进文物数据采集工作，基于大模型建设高价值人工智能应用场景，取得了良好成效，为文博同行提供了可循的建设思路。

**讲者简介：**李华飙，中国国家博物馆数据管理与分析中心主任、正高级工程师。担任馆藏资源活化技术文化和旅游部重点实验室主任、中国电子学会文化遗产数字化标准化专业委员会主任、全国博物馆学名词编写委员会委员。主要负责智慧国博建设，承担了10余项国家级、省部级科研项目，包括国家重点研发计划“文物数字资源管理与利用标准体系研究”等。承担标准研制10余项，获得多项授权专利、软件著作权；主持完成的项目成果获得国家级、省部级奖励。

**报告二**夏晓飞（国家自然博物馆）

**报告题目：**国家自然博物馆在数智化方面的初步尝试

**报告摘要：**博物馆在数智化的过程中，通过引入人工智能和知识图谱等方式做出了一系列尝试和应用。在展览展示、导览导航、数据分析等领域取得了可喜成果。然而，自然类博物馆在藏品特点、观众组成等方面有着与文博类博物馆不同的属性或区别，这使得自然类博物馆在该方面的研究和应用还面临比较大的挑战。报告将以国家自然博物馆新馆建设中的具体案例尝试分析，并提出一些初步思考。

**讲者简介：**夏晓飞，国家自然博物馆信息技术部主任、研究员。曾主持、参与国家林业局、国家自然科学基金、北京市自然科学基金、北京市组织部优秀人才项目、北京市科学技术研究院等多项国家和省部级科研、科普项目；发表核心及以上论文40余篇，专利14项。主要研究方向为：博物馆数字底座建设、博物馆信息化场景应用、博物馆信息专项规划设计、数字藏品保护与管理等。负责的信息化项目获2024年北京市文旅局“十大优秀案例”、文化和旅游部“十大优秀案例”，入选中国博物馆协会《智慧博物馆蓝皮书2024》。

**报告三**龚玉武（上海博物馆）

**报告题目**：以藏品为核心的数字化业务体系构想与实践

**报告摘要**：报告立足博物馆数字化转型背景，针对当前普遍存在的“信息孤岛”问题，提出构建以藏品为核心、贯通全业务流程的一体化数字体系。该体系通过统一数据标准与规范，实现藏品从保护、管理、研究到展示、教育、文创等多业务数据的互联互通与动态归集，推动数据在系统间有序流动与共享，支撑智慧博物馆的“一网统管”与“一网通办”。报告强调体系建设需统筹标准规范、系统融合与数据治理，旨在提升管理效率、深化研究能力、拓展公共服务，最终推动文物“活”起来，助力中华优秀传统文化的传承与创新。

**讲者简介**：龚玉武，上海博物馆信息中心主任，中国博物馆协会博物馆数智化专业委员会副秘书长，研究馆员。参与科技部国家重点研发计划项目、国家文物局课题、国家社科基金重大项目、上海市科委课题、上海市经信委人工智能专项等10余项，主持开展上海市人工智能创新发展专项项目。打造的“上海博物馆智慧场馆”场景在2023年获国家工信部颁发的“国家人工智能创新应用先导区‘智赋百景’人工智能典型应用场景”荣誉；牵头开展的“AR辅助文物修复应用”获国家工信部、文旅部等五部委颁发的“2023年度虚拟现实先锋应用案例”荣誉；参与实施的数字展“山水江南”项目入选《世界互联网大会文化遗产数字化案例集（2025）》展示利用方向优秀案例。参与编制国家标准1项、文物保护行业标准1项，获国家实用新型专利1项，发表论文20余篇。

**报告四**庄颖（故宫博物院）

**报告题目：**故宫博物院可移动文物知识图谱建设的实践与思考

**报告摘要：**2021 年，故宫博物院启动"中国古代可移动文物知识图谱"建设项目，旨在通过对藏品信息的系统化标注与知识组织，构建面向文化遗产领域的知识图谱，并在此基础上提供知识探索与智能检索服务，推动文物研究的智能化转型。基于故宫博物院在相关领域的建设实践，结合当前面临的机遇与挑战，探讨文化遗产信息资源建设的未来路径，包括：构建领域本体与知识表示体系、发展面向文化遗产的AI技术方法、建立人机协同的知识构建机制、推动跨机构知识资源的互联互通等，以期为文化遗产领域的语料建设与公共文化服务探索潜在解决方案。

**讲者简介：**庄颖，故宫博物院数字与信息部大数据管理组组长、副研究馆员。主要研究方向涵盖博物馆数字化转型、数据管理与利用、文化资源智能服务等领域。自2008年起从事博物馆线上服务运营、数字产品研发与实施、数据管理与服务体系构建等方面的实施及管理工作。主持或参与“应用于人工智能搜索的可移动文物概念参考模型研究”、国家重点研发计划“大型综合性博物馆数字孪生关键技术研究与服务示范”等项目。

**报告五**库尔班·吾布力（新疆大学）

**报告题目：**《从图像到知识：克孜尔石窟壁画智能检索与问答系统的构建与应用》

**报告摘要：**本报告围绕克孜尔石窟壁画数字化资源的知识挖掘与交互应用，探讨图像检索与智能问答技术协同实现的路径。面对自然风化与人为破坏，壁画保护与数字化研究已刻不容缓。龟兹艺术整体风格较为统一、类间差异较小，而修复痕迹与损坏状况又造成类内差异显著；同时，壁画元素复杂、多目标共存，传统全局特征难以妥善刻画局部差异，破损与污渍易被突出，背景干扰强，进而削弱有效语义区域的表达等挑战。针对上述问题，我们设计了一套集成视觉特征提取、语义关联分析与自然语言理解的技术框架。该系统支持用户以图像或文字形式发起查询，实现壁画主题、风格、故事内容等多维度检索；同时，通过结合知识图谱与深度学习模型，系统能够回答用户关于壁画历史背景、艺术特征等更深层次问题。报告将重点阐述壁画领域知识的表示方法、跨模态语义融合机制，以及系统在克孜尔石窟数字化项目中的实践案例。该研究推动文化遗产从“数字化存档”向“智能化释读”的跨越，为公众教育、学术研究与文化创意应用提供新的技术支撑。

**讲者简介：**库尔班·吾布力，工学博士，教授，博士生导师。中国计算机学会(CCF)常务理事，中国图象图形学学会(CSIG)理事，CCF乌鲁木齐主席，新疆维吾尔自治区天山英才科技创新领军人才，自治区青少年科普专家。中国自动化学会模式识别与机器智能专业委员会(CAA-PRMI)副秘书长，CCF/CSIG杰出会员，IEEE,IAPR,IAENG会员，新疆大学计算机科学与技术学院场景认知计算和智能系统研究中心主任。研究领域：数字图像处理，模式识别，生物特征识别，计算机视觉，计自然语言处理。主持国家重点研发课题1项，国家自然科学基金4项，省部级和其他项目10余项，在国内外期刊和会议上发表论文400余篇，出版学术专著3部，专利10余项，计算机软件著作权60余项，获得中国图象图形学科技进步二等奖，自治区自然科学优秀论文二等奖等省部级以上奖项20余项。

args.summary:
This webpage announces and details the content of "专题（七）智慧博物馆" (Special Session 7: Smart Museums) from the CCF First Conference on Humanities and Intelligence (第一届人文智能大会), published on 2025.12.22. The session features five presentations from leading Chinese museum and academic institutions:

1. **Li Huabiao (中国国家博物馆/Counternational Museum of China)** - Report on "Research and Practice of Smart Museum Construction in the Digital Intelligence Era." Addresses four key challenges in smart museum development: low digitization efficiency of collections with information loss, fragmented data silos, one-way display methods with low system integration, and weak theoretical foundations lacking unified standards. The museum has implemented a "Smart National Museum" initiative through national key R&D programs and AI-based application scenarios.

2. **Xia Xiaofei (国家自然博物馆/National Natural History Museum)** - Report on "Preliminary Attempts at Digital Intelligence in the National Natural History Museum." Discusses AI and knowledge graph applications in exhibitions, navigation, and data analysis. Notes that natural history museums face different challenges than cultural heritage museums due to differences in collection characteristics and audience composition, using the new museum construction as a case study.

3. **Gong Yuwu (上海博物馆/Shanghai Museum)** - Report on "Conception and Practice of a Collection-Centric Digital Business System." Proposes an integrated digital system centered on collections that connects the entire business process (protection, management, research, display, education, cultural products), solving "information silo" problems through unified data standards, supporting "one-network management" and "one-network service" for smart museums.

4. **Zhuang Ying (故宫博物院/The Palace Museum)** - Report on "Practice and Reflection on Building a Knowledge Graph for Movable Cultural Relics at the Palace Museum." Covers the 2021-initiated project on "Ancient Chinese Movable Cultural Relics Knowledge Graph," discussing domain ontology construction, AI methods for cultural heritage, human-machine collaborative knowledge building, and cross-institution knowledge resource interconnection.

5. **Kuerban Wubuli (新疆大学/Xinjiang University)** - Report on "From Images to Knowledge: Construction and Application of Intelligent Retrieval and Q&A System for Kizil Grottoes Murals." Details a technical framework integrating visual feature extraction, semantic association analysis, and natural language understanding for mural retrieval and question-answering, addressing challenges of weathering damage, high intra-class variation, and complex multi-object elements. Supports multi-dimensional retrieval by theme, style, and story content, advancing cultural heritage from "digital archiving" to "intelligent interpretation."

The page also includes the conference navigation structure (registration, agenda, forums, keynote speeches, courses, posters, papers, datasets, volunteer recruitment) and is hosted by CCF (China Computer Federation).

# 近十年我国年增200多家博物馆

2025-04-15 18:17:33  来源：新华网

新华社杭州4月15日电（记者冯源、郑可意）记者从15日在浙江杭州举办的博物馆管理能力建设和提升国际培训班开幕式上获悉，我国已进入博物馆快速发展期。近十年来，中国博物馆数量以平均每年200多家的速度持续增长。

　　当日，在西子湖畔的中国丝绸博物馆，中国国家文物局、国际文化财产保护与修复研究中心(ICCROM)及亚洲文化遗产保护联盟合作举办的博物馆管理能力建设与提升国际培训班启幕，共有来自20个国家和中国港澳地区的37名从事博物馆领域工作的学员参加。

　　国家文物局副局长罗文利在主旨讲话中提到，截至2023年底，中国博物馆总数达到6833家。2024年底的统计结果有望超过7000家，在总数上超过德国，仅次于美国，居于世界第二位。其中国家一、二、三级博物馆总数达1662家。这些博物馆覆盖国内300多个地市，平均每20.63万人就拥有一座博物馆。

　　罗文利说，中国博物馆事业坚持以人为本的发展理念，具有普惠均等的发展特征。目前，除文物建筑及遗址类博物馆外，全国免费开放博物馆数达6248家，占博物馆总数91%以上，累计优惠观众100余亿人次，是世界上享受博物馆免费开放服务人口最多的国家。

　　此外，中国坚持专业研究，注重科技应用。全国博物馆一年实现科研项目3547个，修复文物藏品9.86万件（套），有效改善了文物健康状况。国家文物局大力推进智慧博物馆建设和文物资源数据库建设，1.08亿件（套）国有可移动文物信息实现数字化，数据资源总量超过140TB。

　　罗文利表示，接下来，中国将完善高质量制度体系、优化高质量布局体系、强化高质量供给体系、拓展高质量服务体系，更好满足人民群众精神文化需求，为推动人类进步和世界和平发展作出积极贡献。

　　中国是历史悠久的文明国度，拥有不可移动文物76.7万余处，国有可移动文物1.08亿件（套），重点文物保护单位5058处，世界遗产总数59项。

This Xinhua News article (published April 15, 2025) reports that China has entered a period of rapid museum development, with the number of museums growing by an average of over 200 per year over the past decade. The announcement was made at the opening ceremony of an international training program on museum management capacity building and enhancement held in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, at the China National Silk Museum.

Key facts from the article:
- As of the end of 2023, China had a total of 6,833 museums. By the end of 2024, the number was expected to exceed 7,000, surpassing Germany to rank second in the world, behind only the United States.
- China has 1,662 national-level museums (Grade 1, 2, and 3). These museums cover over 300 cities across the country, with approximately one museum per 20.63 people.
- Excluding heritage buildings and site museums, 6,248 museums (over 91% of the total) are free to the public, having served over 10 billion visitors cumulatively — making China the country with the largest population enjoying free museum access in the world.
- In one year, Chinese museums completed 3,547 research projects and restored 98,600 cultural relics (sets), effectively improving relic preservation. The National Cultural Heritage Administration has advanced smart museum construction and relic resource databases, with 108 million (sets of) state-owned movable cultural relics digitized, totaling over 140 TB of data resources.
- Luo Wenli, Deputy Director of the National Cultural Heritage Administration, stated China will improve its high-quality institutional systems, optimize layout systems, strengthen supply systems, and expand service systems to better meet the public's cultural needs.
- China has over 767,000 immovable cultural relics, 108 million (sets of) state-owned movable cultural relics, 5,058 key cultural relic protection units, and 59 World Heritage sites total.
- The training program was co-organized by China's National Cultural Heritage Administration, ICCROM (International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property), and the Asian Cultural Heritage Protection Alliance, with 37 participants from 20 countries and China's Hong Kong and Macao regions.

  专稿  

博物馆经济贡献力评估研究——以湖南博物院为例

段晓明 吴镝 魏彬 陈茜 程嘉洋

博物馆不仅是人类文化的坚实守护者，也是社会经济发展的重要推动者。当今进行博物馆经济贡献力评估是值得深入探讨的学术问题，也具有较强的现实意义。目前围绕这方面开展的相关研究与评估多不全面、不充分。湖南博物院采用经济影响分析法理论，构建投入产出模型，从直接经济贡献和间接经济贡献两个方面，全面估算湖南博物院在产出、就业、税收等方面对湖南省经济发展所做的贡献，并针对博物馆自身和决策部门层面提出提升博物馆经济贡献力的策略和路径。

  实践  

中国博物馆国际交流展览体验式设计路径探讨

管晓锐 刘薇 

 中国博物馆举办国际展览的展示形式，已从较为单一的文物本体展示，转向更加多元的“文物+辅助展项”综合展示。推动这一变化的原因主要来自国际展览复杂性、博物馆学界新兴议题和办展目的更加多元等挑战与机遇。在文明交流互鉴视角下，中国博物馆试图形成中华传统文化符号化语言并构建阐释逻辑体系，形成具有可视化、交互式和光影艺术化设计特征的体验式设计，为博物馆遵循“体验经济”市场规律，满足观众体验消费需求，创新对外国际展览阐释设计，提供理论支撑和实践路径。

This study uses economic impact analysis theory and input-output models to estimate Hunan Museum's direct and indirect economic contributions to Hunan Province's economy in terms of output, employment, and taxation, offering strategies to enhance museum economic contribution.
2. **Practice Section**: "Exploring Experience-Based Design Paths for Chinese Museums' International Exchange Exhibitions" by Guan Xiaorui and Liu Wei. The article discusses how Chinese international exhibitions have shifted from single artifact displays to more comprehensive "artifact + auxiliary exhibits" formats, driven by international exhibition complexity, emerging museum academic topics, and diverse exhibition goals. It explores symbolic language for Chinese traditional culture and experience-based design with visualization, interactivity, and light-art features within the "experience economy" framework.
3. **Practice Section**: "Reshaping Museum Time-Space Boundaries: Development and Construction of Mobile Museums" by Fu Wanlu.

观点

# 中国：散落世界各地的青铜器，在数字博物馆重聚

20 October 2020

Last update:21 October 2020

![ ](/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/article/courier/photos/cou_03_20_wide_angle_chine_web_0.jpg.webp?itok=_bSs61Gd)

中国铜陵数字铜博物馆的虚拟展厅。

**中国铜陵市的一家新型博物馆通过虚拟方式，展出了汉代以来的中国古代铜器和青铜器，其中包括多件由国外博物馆收藏的文物。这预示着未来数字博物馆的发展方向——成为能够实现资源共享的机构，并且以前所未有的观展方式将馆藏珍品呈现在全球观众面前。**

**唐际根**  
  
*深圳[南方科技大学](https://www.sustech.edu.cn/)讲座教授，专攻中国青铜时代考古学*

许多文物曾被卷入历史的漩涡，流落异国他乡，从此不得回归故里。这种被盗走的遗产通常是不会归还的，至少在短期内不会。有些文物流落海外数年，乃至数百年，其来源国的民众如何才能看到这些文化瑰宝呢？

中国东部的安徽省铜陵市建起了一家数字博物馆，一举解决了如何欣赏到流落海外文物珍品的问题。铜陵市只有160万人口，却是著名的铜都，早在公元前17世纪末，这里的铜矿开采和青铜铸造活动就已经初具规模。到了汉代（公元前202至公元220年），铸造铜币的大部分原料都来自长江边的这处内河港口。

2016年，铜陵市政府在专家的帮助下，决定建造一座铜和青铜专题博物馆。中国数字铜博物馆（DMCB）的目标是在全球范围内在线共享中国古代铜器和青铜器文化资源，特别是那些流失海外的文物。

一只特别的犀牛

在中国数字铜博物馆的网站上（预计2020年底开通），参观者可以看到“青铜文物精华百品”在线展览。这是经由考古学家投票选出的一百件青铜器，部分由海外博物馆收藏。另一个展览“青铜文物故事百则”详细讲述了这些青铜器是如何流落海外，至今不能回归的。

在那之中，就有关于小臣艅犀尊的故事。这是一尊有着3000年历史、形似犀牛的商代（公元前1600－前1046年）青铜礼器，其独特之处在于以动物为形制。犀尊通过艺术品经销商卢芹斋（C. T. Loo）之手辗转来到巴黎，后被美国体育行业管理者、国际奥林匹克委员会（IOC）前任主席艾弗里·布伦戴奇（Avery Brundage）购得，最终捐赠给了旧金山[亚洲艺术博物馆](http://searchcollection.asianart.org/view/objects/asitem/18907/5?t:state:flow=5f0d38c6-bf87-4596-a689-d4162e7777ab)，是馆内吸引参观人数最多的展品，甚至成为这家博物馆的镇馆之宝。

在线共享文化资源，并不是新的创意。在国际博物馆理事会（([ICOM](https://icom.museum/en/)）成员当中，已有多家博物馆开设了网站。中国数字铜博物馆之所以与众不同，是因为它整合并展现了散落在不同国家的文化资源。几百年来，中国文化遗产蒙受了巨大的损失。估计有数百万件文物因各种缘由流失海外。

不只是网站

本文作者在2016年开展了一项调查，结果显示超过90%的受访者都希望流失海外的中国文物有朝一日能够回归家园。通过中国数字铜博物馆在线共享海外中华文物，或许有助于缓和中国与这些文物当前所在国家之间长久以来的矛盾。

中国数字铜博物馆带来了创新理念，但它仅限于在线共享一种特定类型的文物——中国青铜器。未来，不同国家的多个博物馆将联手建立数字博物馆，整合丰富的资源，展现琳琅满目的各类艺术品。这些新型数字博物馆可以称为“数字博物馆网络”或“云博物馆”。

云博物馆不是仅仅展示某一博物馆藏品的网站，也不是若干博物馆网站的叠加，而是世界各地多家博物馆通力合作的成果。这种未来派数字博物馆已有先例，比如英国剑桥大学[考古和人类学博物馆](https://maa.cam.ac.uk/)以及[大英博物馆](https://www.britishmuseum.org/)的在线展览。

大数据存储和传输技术的迅猛发展将推动云博物馆的问世。一些学者预测，云博物馆的诞生可能会改变博物馆的现状，甚至可能从整体上改变文化。

无限的可能性

未来的数字博物馆可以围绕多个主题选择不同类型的文物，在策展时可以通过分享海量数据，让展出达到前所未有的规模。数字博物馆还可以利用全球文化资源，对同一件文物进行多方位的解读和展示。来自不同国家的学者可以围绕展品相互交流，或是与公众开展对话。

在3000年前的商代——中国历史上有记录可考的最早的朝代，青铜工匠们铸造出了至少两件目前已知的虎食人铜卣。由于历史的原因，这两件文物目前分别收藏在巴黎吉美博物馆和日本京都泉屋博古馆。假如这两个博物馆的收藏和专门研究商代历史的中国考古学家有朝一日能够同时出现在一家云博物馆里，向全世界的观众讲述这些卣的知识和故事，那该多好啊！

### 拓展阅读：

在社交网络上关注联合国教科文组织《信使》：[微博](https://www.weibo.com/unesco)、微信公众号“联合国教科文信使”、[Twitter](https://twitter.com/UNESCO_chinese)、[Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/unescocourier/)、[Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/unescocourier/?hl=en)。

**By Tang Jigen**

Caught in the turmoil of history, many cultural objects were taken away from their countries of origin, and remain overseas. Often, it is unlikely that this stolen heritage is returned – at least in the short term. When the objects are not restituted for years, sometimes centuries, how do people in their countries of origin get to see these cultural treasures?

In the city of Tongling in the Anhui province of eastern China, the question of how to enjoy these objects that have remained overseas has been resolved by establishing a digital museum. A city of only 1.6 million, Tongling is famous for the production of copper – copper mining and bronze casting were established there in the late seventeenth century BC. During the Han Dynasty (202 BC–220 AD), this river port along the Yangtze river supplied most of the raw material for the casting of copper coins.

In 2016, the city’s local government, with the help of experts, decided to construct a museum dedicated to copper and bronze. The goal of the Digital Museum of Copper and Bronzes (DMCB) is to share globally, the cultural resources of ancient Chinese copper and bronze objects online – especially those that remain abroad.

## A very special rhino

Some of the treasures that visitors to the DMCB website (expected to go online by end 2020) will have access to, are: *100 Highlights of Chinese Bronze Objects*, an online exhibition of a hundred bronzes selected by archaeologists through a voting process. It includes some Chinese bronzes from museum collections overseas. Another exhibition, *100 stories about Bronze Objects*, recounts details of how these bronzes left China and still remain abroad.

One of these stories tells of how the *Xiao Chen Yu zun* – a 3,000-year old ritual bronze vessel shaped like a  rhinoceros, from the Shang Dynasty (1600-1046 BC) – made its way to Paris through C. T. Loo, an art dealer, and was bought by Avery Brundage, an American sports administrator and former president of the International Olympic Committee (IOC). This Bronze Age Chinese ritual vessel, unique because it was made in the shape of an animal, was finally donated to the [Asian Art Museum](http://searchcollection.asianart.org/view/objects/asitem/18907/5?t:state:flow=5f0d38c6-bf87-4596-a689-d4162e7777ab) of San Francisco – where it remains one of the museum’s most visited pieces, and even serves as its mascot.

The idea of sharing cultural resources online is not new. Many museums which are part of  the International Council of Museums ([ICOM](https://icom.museum/en/)) network have their own websites. What makes the DMCB unique is that it integrates and shows cultural resources spread across different countries. China has experienced great losses of its cultural heritage over centuries. Millions of cultural objects are estimated to have left the country through different means.

## More than just a website

A survey conducted by this author in 2016 concluded that over ninety per cent of respondents hoped that the cultural objects which had left China would one day be returned to their country of origin. The fact that these cultural objects can now be shared online through the DMCB, may serve to relieve the long-lasting tension between China  and the countries that currently house them.

Though the DMCB is an innovative idea, it is limited to sharing only a specific type of object online – Chinese bronzes. In future, digital museums will be built and run by several museums collaborating across different countries, integrating a wealth of resources to exhibit a wide range of art objects. These new digital museums could be called “digital museum networks” or “cloud museums”.

The cloud museums are neither simply websites that display a specific museum’s collections, nor the combination of the websites of different museums. Instead, they are the result of collaborations of various museums across the world. These futuristic digital museums already exist – the online exhibition by the [Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology](https://maa.cam.ac.uk/) at the University of Cambridge and the [British Museum](https://www.britishmuseum.org/), both in the United Kingdom, is one such example.

The rapid and dramatic strides in big data storage and transfer technologies will facilitate the birth of cloud museums. Some scholars have predicted that the advent of these museums could change the current state of these institutions, and even culture in general.

## Limitless possibilities

The digital museums of the future will be able to select different types of objects on a range of themes, to design exhibitions on an unprecedented scale by sharing huge amounts of data. They may also be able to interpret and display an object in a variety of ways, drawing on cultural resources from across the globe. Scholars from different countries would be able to engage in a conversation with each other, and with the public, about the objects on display.

Three thousand years ago, during the Shang Dynasty – the earliest archaeologically recorded dynasty in Chinese history – bronze craftsmen created at least two known bronze you objects, depicting a tiger eating a human. Because of historical reasons, these two objects are now in the collections of the [Musée Guimet](https://www.guimet.fr/) in Paris and the [Sen-Oku Hakukokan Museum](https://www.sen-oku.or.jp/tokyo/english.html) in Kyoto, Japan. If these two museums and the Chinese archaeologists specializing in the Shang period all featured on a cloud museum one day to share their knowledge and stories about these you objects with a worldwide audience, how wonderful it would be.

**Tang Jigen**   
  
*Chair Professor at the Southern University of Science and Technology (**[SUSTech](https://www.sustech.edu.cn/en/)**) in Shenzhen, with an expertise in Chinese Bronze Age archaeology.*

Please follow these guidelines to create your summary:

1. Identify and preserve the main topic or purpose of the webpage.
2. Retain key facts, statistics, and data points that are central to the content's message.
3. Keep important quotes from credible sources or experts.
4. Maintain the chronological order of events if the content is time-sensitive or historical.
5. Preserve any lists or step-by-step instructions if present.
6. Include relevant dates, names, and locations that are crucial to understanding the content.
7. Summarize lengthy explanations while keeping the core message intact.

When handling different types of content:

- For news articles: Focus on the who, what, when, where, why, and how.
- For scientific content: Preserve methodology, results, and conclusions.
- For opinion pieces: Maintain the main arguments and supporting points.
- For product pages: Keep key features, specifications, and unique selling points.

Your summary should be significantly shorter than the original content but comprehensive enough to stand alone as a source of information. Aim for about 25-30 percent of the original length, unless the content is already concise.

Present your summary in the following format:


This article from UNESCO Courier (published October 20, 2020) discusses the Digital Museum of Copper and Bronzes (DMCB) in Tongling, Anhui Province, China — a digital museum designed to virtually display ancient Chinese bronze artifacts, including those held by foreign museums. Written by Tang Jigen, Chair Professor at the Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech) in Shenzhen specializing in Chinese Bronze Age archaeology.

Key points:
- Tongling is a city of 1.6 million people, famous for copper production dating back to the late 17th century BC, and supplied most raw material for copper coin casting during the Han Dynasty (202 BC–220 AD).
- In 2016, the local government decided to build a museum dedicated to copper and bronze. The DMCB's goal is to globally share ancient Chinese copper and bronze cultural resources online, especially those remaining abroad.
- The DMCB website (expected online by end of 2020) features two exhibitions: "100 Highlights of Chinese Bronze Objects" (bronzes selected by archaeologists via voting, including overseas pieces) and "100 Stories about Bronze Objects" (detailing how these bronzes left China).
- A featured artifact is the Xiao Chen Yu zun, a 3,000-year-old Shang Dynasty (1600–1046 BC) bronze ritual vessel shaped like a rhinoceros. It passed through art dealer C. T. Loo to Paris, was bought by Avery Brundage (former IOC president), and was donated to the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco, where it remains a mascot and most-visited piece.
- A 2016 survey by the author found over 90% of respondents hoped lost Chinese artifacts would one day return home. The DMCB may help ease tensions between China and countries currently housing these artifacts.
- The DMCB is limited to Chinese bronzes, but the author envisions future "cloud museums" or "digital museum networks" — collaborative efforts of multiple museums across countries to integrate resources and exhibit diverse art objects. Precedents include online exhibitions by Cambridge's Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology and the British Museum.
- The author notes that advances in big data storage and transfer technologies will facilitate cloud museums, which some scholars predict could transform museums and culture.
- Example: Two known Shang Dynasty bronze "you" vessels depicting a tiger eating a human are housed respectively at the Musée Guimet in Paris and the Sen-Oku Hakukokan Museum in Kyoto, Japan — the author hopes a cloud museum could someday bring these together with Chinese archaeologists for global audiences.

--- SOURCE 2: ICOM Webinar | Stimulating Employment in the Museum Sector ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0dhnF5KgMvY

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This ICOM (International Council of Museums) webinar, posted February 15, 2021, addresses "Recover and Recreate: Stimulating Employment in the Museum Sector" following the COVID-19 pandemic. Sponsored by the French Ministry of Culture and moderated by Dr. Mathew Trinca (Director of the National Museum of Australia and Chair of ICOM Australia), the webinar explores rebuilding the museum sector not just through recovery but through innovation and change. Four main sub-themes are discussed: policy responses to stimulate museum employment, impact on young professionals, emerging professions and new skills for the post-COVID era, and new business models for museums.

**Key data from ICOM surveys (April and September 2020):**
- In spring, almost all museums worldwide were closed (95% for two or more months); by September half were open, but many closed again, with some regions (like Latin America) closed all summer
- One third of museums expected to lose more than half of their income, especially in Asia, Africa, and the Arab region
- Two-thirds of survey respondents expected their museum to reduce programs; 14% of staff were furloughed or had contracts not renewed (highest in North America at 20%)
- In spring, 13% expected their museum to close permanently; by September this dropped to 6% (highest at 22% in the Arab region)
- Half of museums worldwide increased their social media and online activities, accelerating digital transformation

**Speakers and key points:**

1. **Peter Keller** (ICOM Director General) presented survey results showing the sector's profound disruption and the need for museums to generate income from digital activities.

2. **Ekaterina Travkina** (OECD Centre for Entrepreneurship) emphasized that the crisis revealed the fragility of the freelance/creative ecosystem around museums. She advocated for adapting self-employment support schemes to creative jobs, including nonprofits in small business support programs, tax incentives for donations, investing in cultural production during recovery, and addressing the digital divide. She stressed that museums should be part of recovery strategies at city, regional, and national levels, and highlighted the OECD-ICOM Guide for Local Governments, Communities and Museums.

3. **Angelita Teo** (Director, Olympic Foundation for Culture and Heritage) discussed the "phygital" (physical + digital) blending of museum experiences. She described the foundation's restructuring to create a "Development and Innovation Unit" with skills in project management, content creation, digital and international marketing. She noted receiving 200+ applicants for positions (unprecedented), reflecting widespread job losses in the sector. She cited World Economic Forum data predicting 85 million jobs displaced and 97 million new roles by 2025, with half of workers needing reskilling. She emphasized that organizations must create learning environments where staff can reskill, not just individual responsibility.

4. **María Mercedes González** (Director, Museum of Modern Art of Medellin, MAMM) discussed how the pandemic made digital transformation essential. Her team (mostly digital natives) learned quickly, but she stressed the future need for new skills like audiovisual production, digital communication, and re-skilled education teams, as these competencies are now essential rather than outsourced.

5. **Daniel Ronan** (Resilient Heritage consultancy, Chicago) presented the "Prairie State Museums Project," which employed 16 freelancers from 14 news outlets across Illinois (9 journalists of color, 6 women of color) to amplify stories of how museums face the pandemic. He cited the American Alliance of Museums' finding that one in three U.S. museums could close permanently. He noted that the U.S. lacks universal healthcare, and that younger professionals should develop adaptable skill sets and broader definitions of museum work (his own background is public policy/planning, not museum studies).

**Panel discussion highlights:**
- Travkina argued that national policymakers lack an "ecosystem view" of the cultural labor market and that museums should be part of recovery task forces (which they often are excluded from)
- Teo noted Singapore's museums are largely publicly funded ("iron rice bowl") and face visitor-confidence challenges rather than job security issues, while parts of Southeast Asia relying on private funding and foreign partnerships were harder hit; Europe has seen unprecedented job applications reflecting sector-wide displacement
- González emphasized the need for in-house audiovisual and digital skills to avoid expensive outsourcing
- Ronan highlighted the precariousness of freelance/casualized work for younger professionals and the importance of diversifying skill sets and understanding diverse revenue streams (government, nonprofit, for-profit models)
</summary>

"One third of the museums expect to lose more than half of their income... 14 percent of the staff has been furloughed or had their contract not renewed with the highest rate in North America at 20 percent." - Peter Keller, ICOM

--- SOURCE 3: A Shared Enmity: Germany, Japan, and the Creation of the Tripartite Pact | The National WWII Museum | New Orleans ---
URL: https://www.nationalww2museum.org/war/articles/germany-japan-tripartite-pact

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National WWII Museum article by Jason Dawsey, PhD, examines the creation of the Tripartite Pact between Nazi Germany, Imperial Japan, and Fascist Italy, signed on September 27, 1940, in Berlin. The article argues that shared enmity toward Franklin D. Roosevelt's United States was the primary force that brought Germany and Japan together, rather than the anti-communism that had underpinned their earlier 1936 Anti-Comintern Pact.

The article traces the fitful course of German-Japanese relations. Two 1939 events fundamentally transformed their relationship: (1) Japan's devastating defeat at the Nomonhan/Khalkhin-Gol Incident against the Red Army, where Japan suffered more than 8,600 killed and more than 9,000 wounded under General Georgi Zhukov's leadership, and (2) the August 1939 Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact, which rendered the Anti-Comintern Pact useless and shocked Tokyo. These twin blows led to the fall of Prime Minister Kiichirō Hiranuma's government on August 30, 1939, and his replacement by General Nobuyuki Abe, under whom Japan pursued diplomacy with Stalin and avoided war with the Red Army—a lesson that held into 1945.

German conquests in Scandinavia and Western Europe in 1940, combined with Japanese moves into northern Indochina, raised the specter of war with the United States. American countermeasures—including the Two Ocean Navy Act (July 1940), the relocation of the Pacific Fleet from San Diego to Pearl Harbor, the one-year draft, and the Destroyers-for-Bases arrangement with Britain—convinced Berlin and Tokyo that Roosevelt was preparing for intervention. The Tripartite Pact was a 10-year defensive alliance calling for military, political, and economic assistance if any signatory was attacked by "a Power at present not involved in the European or in the Sino-Japanese Conflict"—clearly referring to the still-neutral United States. The article concludes that by the end of 1940, conflict between the United States and the Tripartite Pact appeared increasingly inevitable.

Recommended reading includes Richard B. Frank's Tower of Skulls, Richard Overy's Russia's War, and Gerhard Weinberg's A World at Arms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"What eventually brought them together again in the early fall of 1940 to certify a new agreement was shared enmity toward Franklin D. Roosevelt's United States of America."

--- SOURCE 5: The future of French museums in 2030 - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7576371

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, "The future of French museums in 2030" (Technological Forecasting and Social Change, 2020, doi: 10.1016/j.techfore.2020.120384), presents a Delphi-based foresight study on the future of French museums up to 2030. Authored by Bertrand Pauget (Karlstad University, Sweden), Jean-Michel Tobelem (University of Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne), and Jean-Philippe Bootz (EM Strasbourg Business School), the study was conducted between late 2017 and early 2018 with 99 French-speaking experts.

**Background/Context:** France is a major museum player, hosting three of the world's ten most visited art museums (Louvre with ~10 million visitors/year, Pompidou Center, and Musée d'Orsay). Museum attendance in France rose from 40 million (2005) to 62 million (2017) but stagnated since 2010, concentrated in large establishments. France invests 2.6% of GDP in culture (vs. 2.3% elsewhere), and the sector represents 88 billion € in annual turnover. Smaller museums (under 20,000 visitors/year) face economic pressure, and public funding is stagnating or declining. Major challenges include the Covid-19 crisis, technological disruption (Google virtual visits, robots), and internationalization (Louvre Abu Dhabi, Pompidou partnerships).

**Methodology:** A two-round Delphi study was used (a method developed in the 1950s by Dalkey and Helmer for expert consensus-building). Round 1 (fall 2017): 99 experts responded (38.8% return rate from 255 initially contacted). Round 2 (January-February 2018): 79 experts responded (79.8% of round 1 respondents). The questionnaire contained 44 variables across 7 themes (demography, tourism, technology, governance, strategy and management, law and regulation) using Likert scales plus open-ended questions. Cohen's Kappa showed strong inter-author agreement (0.70 round 1, 0.85 round 2). Experts included museum directors (39%), curators (12%), administrative staff (11%), supervisory authority representatives (19%), academics, journalists, consultants, and fundraising professionals. The sample included major Parisian institutions (Louvre, Orsay, Versailles, Picasso, Pompidou) and museums in Bordeaux, Lyon, Lille, Nancy, Rouen, and Strasbourg, plus smaller local museums. The average expert age was over 50.

**Key Results:** The most important missions for museums by 2030 per experts were educational issues and democratization of culture (round 2 mean: 4.63, SD: 0.53). Experts agreed on collaboration with institutions but were reluctant on audience participation in exhibitions. They predicted decreased funding and demanded more transparency, efficiency, and cost control. Technology played a minor role—only one variable (online publication of digitized collections) was validated. Demographics variables did not achieve consensus.

**Three Scenarios for 2030:**
1. Museums centered around youth and democratization of culture.
2. Museums responding to decreased public funding (economic future focus).
3. A breakdown scenario where museums undergo evolutions, characterized by direct participation of nearby stakeholders (unlike the other two scenarios).

The paper argues this is the first academically rigorous foresight study on French museums, contrasting with prior professional association reports (USA's Center for the Future of Museums, UK's Museums 2020, Dutch Agenda 2026, Swiss reports, and a 2017 French Ministry report) that lacked scientific methodology, peer review, or Delphi-type methods.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The purpose of this article is to describe the possible futures of French museums up to 2030. To do this we rely on a Delphi study that took place between late 2017 and early 2018 with 99 experts from the field. We propose three scenarios."
</key_excerpts>

It also provides training programs for museum professionals in collections care, museum management, and education.
- **Family and Continuing Education**: Weekend programming at all museums, summer evening events at international art museums, the annual Smithsonian Folklife Festival on the National Mall, and The Smithsonian Associates programming (120+ programs monthly in D.C., plus Scholar in the School, Smithsonian Voices of Discovery, and Study Tour programs organizing 300+ trips annually worldwide).

The project brings museum objects to primary schools, giving students access to ancient treasures normally kept behind glass. In late 2022, Billingham South Community Primary (Stockton) and St Joseph's Catholic Primary (Middlesbrough) collaborated to select a 3,500-year-old canopic jar, which became the centrepiece of exhibitions at both schools and was linked to the show "Ancient Egyptians: secrets of the afterlife" at the Dorman Museum in Middlesbrough.

The British Museum's learning department comprises approximately 20 staff supported by a team of 70 artists, educators and museum teachers, plus around 500 volunteers. Head of learning and programmes Shani Crawford notes that most of the museum's school offer targets Key Stage Two (KS2) students (ages 7-11). On-site activities include "tablet tours" using augmented reality, interactive presentations in the museum lecture theatre, and smaller workshops for around 35 students (e.g., exploring what it meant to be an Athenian citizen in fifth-century BC Greece).

Digital learning is highly important, with Virtual Visits (live interactive workshops linking classrooms to museum experts), a "peek into prehistory" programme aligned with the UK national history curriculum, and trials of livestreamed lessons where experts cannot see students. The department also offers provision for neurodiverse students and students with additional learning needs, including whiteboard presentations posted online to help prepare for visits. The museum has also used schools resources designed by artists and educators of African Caribbean heritage to address issues linked to empire and slavery.

For young people, the "Where We Are..." national programme targets underserved groups aged 16 to 24, with partners such as Wakefield Museums and Castles (2023-2024). National outreach manager Hanouf Al-Alawi told UK Museums Journal that the programme helped create a Youth Forum in Wakefield and made a huge difference to young people, noting "the onus of that disengagement is on the museums themselves."

Looking ahead, the museum's masterplan (described by director Nicholas Cullinan as "the biggest transformation of any museum in the world") presents an opportunity to review the learning programme, with new discussions around "object-based learning" and the possibility of getting closer to—and even touching—objects as they come off display. Through workshops, students observed their surroundings, reimagined objects and urban spaces, and worked alongside the artist to envision their dream city. The webpage presents their ideas across several themed sections:

- **The Play Crossing**: Children propose more colorful zebra crossings and invent games to make street crossing fun (e.g., a "maze zebra crossing" with sequences of turn, jump, slide).
- **Buildings in Colour**: Children want more colorful buildings rather than the typical black or white, treating buildings as works of art with imaginary shapes.
- **The Bench**: Ideas for benches where you can sit standing up, lie down and read, nap while waiting for the bus (with music to wake sleepers), and meet people.
- **The Apple Tree of Possibilities**: Dreams of fruit trees, "wishing trees" (wishes written on letters come true after five years, with help from squirrel, owl, or fox), and trees that dispense games, vegetables, clothes, or treats.
- **The Extraordinary Garden**: Requests for bigger parks, bees and honey, chocolate fountains, perfumed bins, and dream huts (in trees, underwater, flower-shaped, or with ziplines).
- **Rain is Life!**: Water butts to collect rainwater for plants and reduce tap water use and pollution.
- **Wind over the Roofs**: Wind turbines on rooftops (where wind is stronger) and children's desire to walk on roofs to see Paris from above and count stars.

The page includes audio excerpts of children's voices and the artist's introduction. Credits list interviews by Alice Maxia and Laura Samoilovich, recording/editing/mixing by Bastien Pigeon, production by Fanny Cerizier, and the voices of 22 participating children plus Sara de.Gouy.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"I am Sara de.Gouy, architect, designer and artist. I like to think about my projects in collaboration with those they are destined for. I imagined this workshop-exhibition for Centre Pompidou with students from a primary school in Paris."

--- SOURCE 19: Visiting the Pompidou Kids Studio ---
URL: https://www.tours-in-paris.com/post/visiting-the-pompidou-kids-studio

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Flora, a professional tour guide at Tours-in-Paris.com, discusses visiting the Centre Pompidou's Kids Studio (Atelier des enfants) with children. The author shares her expertise in making art museums engaging for young visitors, drawing on over a decade of experience as a tour guide and her background growing up with a mother who was also an art museum guide.

Key points covered:
- The Centre Pompidou is Europe's largest modern art museum, housing France's National Museum of Modern Art, a public library, and a music/acoustic research center. The building itself is a work of art in a high-tech architectural style resembling a ship or an inside-out building.
- The Pompidou creates special programming that "translates" touring exhibits for children, and offers exhibits made entirely for teens and children, including the Kids Studio (Atelier des enfants) where children can make art, including drawing on walls.
- Studio 13/16 provides programming specifically for teenagers.
- The Pompidou's children's guided tour lasts about an hour and follows a specific structure: yoga stretches to calm children, a meditation exercise where kids close their eyes and imagine colors and lines, a fun activity of walking on a black line on the floor (similar to "floor is lava") to teach museum etiquette, views of Paris landmarks (Notre Dame, Sacre-Coeur), and discussions of artworks by artists including Marc Chagall, Henri Matisse, Piet Mondrian, Joan Miro (including his Blue I from 1961), and a Yaacov Agam installation.
- The tour teaches children to draw their own conclusions about art, keeps a slow pace suitable for 3-4 year olds, and builds children's confidence by encouraging them to share their thoughts.
- The Pompidou's children's programming is only in French, but the author can translate and offers English-speaking kids tours, including a "Treasure Hunt in the Louvre."
- The author also references other Paris children's art education institutions she has learned from, including the Musée en Herbe (a museum dedicated entirely to children, operating since the mid-70s) and the Cité des Enfants at the City of Science and Industry.
- Her advice for parents: engage children directly with art rather than lecturing about art history, and keep visits short so kids leave excited rather than tired.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It aims to teach children not only about art but how to draw your own conclusions about art. To help this along, they keep things calm and orderly while still allowing the kids to express their excitement, joy, and insights."

--- SOURCE 1: English ---
URL: https://www.museumspaedagogik.org/english

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The German Association for Museum Education (BVMP) is the federal organization representing over 1,000 museum educators across Germany. Formed in 1991 through the merger of six regional associations, the BVMP promotes professional exchange, networking, cooperation, publications, and projects that advance education and communication in museums in a qualitative and forward-looking manner.

The association works primarily through the following formats:
- **Conferences, Training Courses, and Network Meetings**: Annual major (inter)national conferences combining practical work with theoretical aspects, plus regional training and network meetings.
- **Specialist Groups**: Nationwide networks addressing topics such as children and young people in museums, inclusion and diversity, digitality, the 60-plus generation, and education for sustainable development.
- **Magazine "Standbein Spielbein"**: The only specialist magazine for museum education in Germany, covering national and international developments, research, and projects.
- **Guidelines & Position Papers**: Concise guidance on inclusion, accessibility, school-museum cooperation, and museum education organization. Published in cooperation with the German Museums Association and NEMO (Network of European Museum Organisations), including the guidelines "Developing Education and Public Engagement in Museums."
- **International Networking**: BVMP is a member of the German Cultural Council and the Federal Association for Cultural Education for Children and Young People (BKJ), and works with various international partners.

Contact: info@museumspaedagogik.org
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Museums in Germany | Projects for children and young adults ---
URL: https://www.deutschland.de/en/topic/culture/museums-in-germany-projects-for-children-and-young-adults

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from deutschland.de (published January 29, 2022, by Alexander Wenzel) covers "Museum macht stark" (Museums make you strong), a German project run by the German Museums Association aimed at introducing children and young adults aged 5-18 to museums, particularly those who would otherwise have little opportunity to experience them. The Federal Ministry of Education and Research is funding the project with 6.4 million euros. Currently, 69 museums participate, offering 97 projects, with over 17,000 young people having taken part so far. Participating institutions include the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, the German Port Museum in Hamburg, and the Bach Museum in Leipzig.

The article highlights two specific projects: "Hier sind wir!" (Here we are!) by the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, which targets children and young adults whose social environment offers limited contact with museums, featuring discovery tours of Berlin's Museum Island (a UNESCO World Heritage site) including the Pergamon Museum with its reconstructions of the Pergamon Altar and the Processional Way of Babylon. The second project, at Leipzig's Bach Museum, involves the temporary exhibition "Bach & Triegel. Im Dialog," where works by painter Michael Triegel dialogue with the music of Johann Sebastian Bach, and children use experimental drawing techniques, conduct interviews, and work on still lifes. German Museums Association president Eckart Köhne emphasized that collaborations show "how much children and young adults profit long-term from their experiences at museums and how they make museums into 'their own spaces'."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The programme is targeted primarily at five to 18-year-olds in Germany who would otherwise have little chance to experience museums. The Federal Ministry of Education and Research is providing a total of 6.4 million euros to support the project., As Eckart Köhne, the president of the German Museums Association, explains, the collaborations show "just how much children and young adults profit long-term from their experiences at museums and how they make museums into 'their own spaces'", Currently 69 museums are taking part, including the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, the German Port Museum in Hamburg and the Bach Museum in Leipzig. A total of 97 projects are being offered by the museums at present, and more than 17,000 young people have so far taken part in the "Museum macht stark" programme.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: Schools - Deutsches Museum ---
URL: https://www.deutsches-museum.de/en/museum-island/programme/educational-offers/schools

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the "School and Museum" page of the Deutsches Museum (German Museum) in Munich, Germany, designed for teachers and school classes planning educational visits. The page outlines the museum's offerings for schools, including bookable programmes and guided tours, downloadable supplementary materials for preparing and following up on lessons, and a Hands-on Exhibition called "Kid's Kingdom" for children aged 3 to 8 years. Key practical information includes reduced admission for schools and a School Membership option that allows pupils to visit all Munich locations of the Deutsches Museum at very favourable conditions. The page also provides contact details for the museum's education department (Abteilung Bildung), located at Museumsinsel 1, 80538 München, with an email address of museumspaedagogik@deutsches-museum.de, which handles educational programmes for schools, daycare centres (Kitas), and families in Munich.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Taking the school class to the museum: bookable programmes and guided tours, material for discovering on your own or digital offers for free use - everything teachers and classes need."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Museums in the 21 Century Pioneers o f Education ---
URL: https://junges-museum-frankfurt.de/sites/default/files/upload/pdf/21st-children3-guidecho.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is "Museums in the 21st Century: Pioneers of Education Part 3 — Practical Guidebook" by Sarai Lenzberger (2022), published by Hands On! International Association of Children in Museums. It serves as a capacity-building tool for starting, running, or enhancing organizations dedicated to children-focused museum work.

**Core Vision and Generational Model:**
The guide presents a three-generation model (inspired by Gail Dexter Lord) for children-focused museums:
- **First Generation (1899–1980s):** Focus on interactivity/play (Hands-on), tailored to the industrial economy, teaching compliant learning.
- **Second Generation (circa 1970):** Added knowledge/critical thinking (Minds-on), reflecting the shift to the post-industrial knowledge economy. The children's museum boom in the 1990s coincided with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
- **Third Generation (today):** Added soft power/change agents (Hearts-on), addressing societal demands for museums to become "Homes of 21st Century Education," empowering children and testing new means of informal education. This became especially relevant during the Covid-19 pandemic.

**Target Groups:**
Babies/toddlers (0–3), non-readers (3–6), primary school children (7–10), pre-teens (10–12), teenagers (noted as the most neglected age group), and adults (who organize visits). Distinctions are made between frequent, occasional, and potential visitors.

**Key Definitions:**
- **Children's museum:** Defined by ACM as "a non-profit educational and cultural institution committed to serving the needs and interests of children by providing exhibits and programs that stimulate curiosity and motivate learning." Children are valued citizens; play is learning; family/culture/environment are critical; equity and inclusion are best practices.
- **Children-focused museum work:** Encompasses children's museums, museums, science centres, galleries, and similar organizations emphasizing permanent heritage-based and interactive children's programming.
- **Children-friendly museum:** Welcoming infrastructure including baby changing facilities, stroller parking, family tickets, highchairs, child-friendly staff, and family tours.

**Legal Types, Funding & Partners:**
Two superordinate categories: autonomous organizations (NGO/NPO: clubs, foundations, LLCs) and parts of overarching entities (public entities, traditional museums, corporate brands). Funding sources include public budgets, sales (tickets, shops, cafés, events), grants (EU programs like Creative Europe, Erasmus Plus, Horizon Europe, New European Bauhaus), and sponsoring. Key partners include individuals, cultural organizations, public governance departments, formal education institutions, and research institutions.

**Forms of Children-Focused Museum Work:**
Ten generic types (often used as hybrids): universal children's museum, topic-focused children's museum, inhouse children's museum, children-only museum, mobile/pop-up museum, family museum, children's exhibitions (hosting), children's exhibitions (development), children-focused programmes (inhouse and external), children-curated spaces, and children-themed museums.

**Educational Approach — "Hands-on, Minds-on, Hearts-on":**
Play-based approach combining tactile-cognitive experiences with emotional experiences. Historical roots: children's museums were significant at ICOM's founding in 1946 (with a Children's Museums Committee chaired by a woman). Michael Spock of Boston Children's Museum revolutionized museum education in the 1960s by removing display cabinets. "Minds-on" was added in the 1990s; "Hearts-on" emphasizes emotional connection and empathic resonance.

**Progressive Education Theorists Covered:**
A non-exhaustive list including Comenius, Rousseau, Basedow, Salzmann, Pestalozzi, Fröbel, Parker, Robin, Dewey (learning by doing), Reddie, Steiner (Waldorf), Montessori, Neill (Summerhill), Parkhurst (Dalton Plan), Hengstenberg, Vygotsky, Freinet, Piaget, Pikler, Bruner (spiral curriculum), Malaguzzi (Reggio), Gardner (multiple intelligences), and Falk & Dierking (free-choice learning).

**Techniques for Children-Focused Museum Work (alphabetical):**
Aesthetic practices, case studies/scenarios (dilemma-based), co-creation, digital learning, enquiry-based learning, gamification, media-based learning, nature play/outdoor play, object-based learning, open-ended play/loose parts play, peer/intergenerational learning, phenomenon-based learning, role play, storytelling, take-over (day), and tinkering & making (originated at Exploratorium, San Francisco).

**Additional Elements:** The guide includes a "Directory: Homes of 21st Century Education" criteria section, certification guidance, and resources/further reading. It emphasizes that children-focused museum work has lacked comprehensive international working standards and that expertise has historically been lost when key individuals left the field.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Unlock your superpower: be a change agent, empower children, and test new means of informal education! We encourage and dare museums, galleries, and science centres to take on the role of change agents, by meeting the immediate learning needs of children and thereby future-proofing next generations." — Sarai Lenzberger, "A children's museum is defined as a non-profit educational and cultural institution committed to serving the needs and interests of children by providing exhibits and programs that stimulate curiosity and motivate learning." — ACM definition, "The idea of children requiring other learning settings than adults developed in the 19th century along with the perception of childhood as an independent stage of life, separate from adulthood." — page 22, "It is an important but little-known fact that when ICOM - the International Council of Museums was founded in 1946, they had a Children's Museums Committee - notably with a female chair and mostly female members - proving the early significance and influence of children-focused museum work." — page 22, "Hands-on, Minds-on, Hearts-on exhibitions and formats aim to enable learning by functioning as mediators between an actuality and the child and are therefore closely associated with reform pedagogical approaches." — page 23
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: Museum education ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_education

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Museum education is a specialized field devoted to developing and strengthening the education role of informal education spaces and institutions such as museums. This Wikipedia article covers the field's definition, history, theory and practice, publications, and professional organizations.

**Definition & Core Concepts:** Museum education falls under informal education—organized educational activity outside the formal system—which expands learning spaces to include homes, national parks, zoos, and museums. The 1992 American Association of Museums report *Excellence and Equity* identified the educational role of museums as core to their public service.

**Historical Development:**
- In 1906, J. Randolph Coolidge Jr. experimented with a gallery guiding system at the Boston Museum of Fine Arts.
- The term "docent" first appeared in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston's June 1906 bulletin.
- After WWII, museums increased focus on education, with field trips and volunteerism (docents) gaining importance. By 1946, leaders like Otto Wittmann (Toledo Museum of Art) advocated for volunteer use and museum educator training.
- Philip H. Coombs, first Assistant Secretary of State for Education and Culture (1968), emphasized informal education's importance as a complement to formal education, especially for developing countries.
- A 2019 study found art museum educators are predominantly White, heterosexual, cisgender women aged 26-40, reflecting low pay and unpaid internship prerequisites that create barriers to entry.
- Graduate programs in museum education exist at Ohio State University, Bank Street College of Education, and Tufts University.

**COVID-19 Impact:** During the pandemic, ~95% of museums worldwide closed for part of 2020. A survey found Education positions were the second-most affected by layoffs/furloughs (40%), after Guest Services/Admissions (68%). Museums shifted to virtual programming including Zoom events, social media channels, take-home art activities, and virtual tours.

**Theory & Practice:** Museum pedagogy is influenced by constructivism, postmodernism, and critical multiculturalism. Teaching strategies include Visual Thinking Strategies (VTS), the dialogical model of art interpretation, Feldman's Model of Art Criticism, aesthetic scanning, and the FTC (Form+Theme+Context) Palette.

**Publications:** Key publications include *Excellence in Practice: Museum Education Principles and Standards*, *The Journal of Museum Education* (from the Museum Education Roundtable), *The Museum Education Monitor* (ended 2015), *Art Museum Teaching*, *Viewfinder*, *Studies in Art Education*, and the *Journal of Cultural Research in Art Education*.

**Professional Organizations:** The NAEA Museum Education Division (620+ members), the Museum Education Roundtable, the American Alliance of Museums (AAM), and the International Council of Museums (ICOM), which maintain codes of ethics for museum professionals.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It has been proposed to the Trustees to consider the permanent appointment of one or more persons of intelligence and education who could act as intermediaries between Curators and the many who would be glad to avail themselves of trained instruction in our galleries. Through these docents, as it has been proposed to call them, the heads of departments could instruct many more persons than it would be possible for them to accompany through the galleries..." (June 1906 bulletin, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston), "She is a married woman, thirty to thirty-five years old, with one or two children in school, and a husband in an executive position. She has attended exhibitions quite regularly for several years and has for some time brought her children to your classes and special events. She has some years of college education but is not always a graduate... Most important — she has a curiosity, imagination, and enthusiasm, and she believes in the importance of your organization to the community" (Otto Wittmann, 1946, on the ideal museum volunteer educator), Unpaid internships have become prerequisites to securing future employment in the field, creating a "cruel paradox" in which paid employment is restricted to those with economic resources to contribute unpaid labor.
</key_excerpts>
