## II. UNITED KINGDOM

### 1. Museum Education System and Institutional Organization

**The British Museum — Learning Department:**
- The British Museum's learning department comprises approximately 20 staff supported by a team of 70 artists, educators and museum teachers, plus around 500 volunteers. Head of learning and programmes: Shani Crawford. Most of the museum's school offer targets Key Stage Two (KS2) students (ages 7-11). [12-ArtNewspaper]
- On-site activities include "tablet tours" using augmented reality, interactive presentations in the museum lecture theatre, and smaller workshops for around 35 students (e.g., exploring what it meant to be an Athenian citizen in fifth-century BC Greece). [12-ArtNewspaper]
- The "British Museum in your Classroom" initiative (part of the National Programmes partner organisation programme) brings museum objects to primary schools. In late 2022, Billingham South Community Primary (Stockton) and St Joseph's Catholic Primary (Middlesbrough) collaborated to select a 3,500-year-old canopic jar, which became the centrepiece of exhibitions at both schools, linked to the show "Ancient Egyptians: secrets of the afterlife" at the Dorman Museum in Middlesbrough. "The children were bouncing off the walls; we had children coming up to read the hieroglyphs," says Loretta Kilroe, the British Museum's curator for Sudan and Nubia. [12-ArtNewspaper]
- **Digital learning:** Virtual Visits (live interactive workshops linking classrooms to museum experts), a "peek into prehistory" programme aligned with the UK national history curriculum, and trials of livestreamed lessons where experts cannot see students. The department also offers provision for neurodiverse students and students with additional learning needs, including whiteboard presentations posted online to help prepare for visits. The museum has also used school resources designed by artists and educators of African Caribbean heritage to address issues linked to empire and slavery. [12-ArtNewspaper]
- **Young people — "Where We Are..." national programme:** Targets underserved groups aged 16 to 24, with partners such as Wakefield Museums and Castles (2023-2024). National outreach manager Hanouf Al-Alawi told UK Museums Journal the programme helped create a Youth Forum in Wakefield and made a huge difference to young people, noting "the onus of that disengagement is on the museums themselves." [12-ArtNewspaper]
- **Masterplan transformation:** The museum's masterplan (described by director Nicholas Cullinan as "the biggest transformation of any museum in the world") presents an opportunity to review the learning programme, with new discussions around "object-based learning" and the possibility of getting closer to—and even touching—objects as they come off display. Crawford's priorities include making the learning programme curriculum-led and inclusive of what schools want, reaching schools that don't come to the museum, and ensuring diversity in adult programmes: "It sounds trite but the British Museum is for everyone." [12-ArtNewspaper]
- **Home Educators offer (2026/27):** The British Museum welcomes UK Home Educators. Due to Masterplan infrastructure changes, some public programmes are reduced. Programmes continuing in 2026/27 include KS2 presentations (BP Lecture Theatre), KS2 taught workshops (Clore Centre for Education), creative workshops for ages 9–14, KS3 presentations, and KS4 gallery-based talks. Pricing examples: Home Education Days (ages 7–11) £9.00 per child (accompanying adults free); KS2 presentations £2.50 per child; KS2 taught workshops £3.00 per child (60-minute sessions in the Clore Centre for Education, topics including Prehistory, A question for the people, Excavation in Egypt, How to find out about Greek life); KS3 presentations £2.50 per child; KS4 gallery-based talks £3.00 per child (the Parthenon talk supports the Classical Civilisations GCSE component Myth and Religion J199/11). Free downloadable activity sheets and resources are organized by age group: Ages 3–7 (EYFS/KS1), Ages 7–11 (KS2), Ages 11–14 (KS3), and Ages 14–16 (KS4). Family activities include Museum Explorer Trails, Museum Missions (free phone/tablet-based activities), YouTube videos for young learners, and the Young Friends membership programme. [14-BM]
- Note: The British Museum's "Schools" page (britishmuseum.org/learn/schools) as captured was a cookie/privacy page and did not yield substantive program content. [13-BM]

**Tate — Learning Programmes:**
- Tate's Learning department draws inspiration from Tate's collection and exhibitions, creating activities and resources for London galleries and online: large-scale events, festivals, workshops, talks, tours, film screenings, and paper/digital resources. "Our programme is free and often requires no ticket. We do not presume any art knowledge or experience – all are welcome!" Five main programme areas: (1) Early Years and Families — dedicated gallery spaces where families can make, play, read, and imagine together, including UNIQLO Tate Play events; (2) Schools and Teachers — supports young people and teachers to learn about themselves and others through art, including students with special educational needs or disabilities; (3) Young People's Programmes — including the Tate Collective Producers group (15–25-year-olds who co-create events and resources for peers); (4) Public Programmes — workshops, talks, film screenings, live music, and gatherings; (5) Learning Research — research and evaluation inform all programming, with specific projects on creative learning, arts education, and the cultural sector. Tate works with artists and partner organizations across youth, cultural, education, and community sectors. [11-Tate]
- **Tate Schools digital platform (2023–2025):** Developed through collaboration between Tate's Learning and Digital teams, presented by Effie Coe, Curator of Digital Content in the schools and teachers team, at the Museum Digital Summit 2026. Key elements: (1) a teacher friends group drawn from educators across the UK (from the Shetland Islands, Newcastle, Birmingham, London, St. Ives, and Margate) who helped identify gaps and priorities from the start; (2) an SEND-first design philosophy (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities) — resources designed to work for the most complex and diverse learners first, developed through one-to-one conversations with six SEND practitioners; (3) two notable commissions — Lightbox (an interactive digital resource for sensory and SEND learners developed with creative studio The Workers) and All The Feelings (the first commission in a new Immersion series, a video artwork by artist India Harvey created with students in a special school setting; the Immersion series will feature a new artist commission every two years); (4) Tate Schools now offers over 80 resources spanning key stages one to five, featuring more than 300 collection artists; 75% of content foregrounds underrepresented artists (global majority, disabled, LGBTQ+, working class, and women artists); over 40% of resource series were co-produced with artists, teachers, students, or sector peers. The representation focus responds to the Visual Eyes Report, which found teachers want to diversify their curriculum but need better resources. Formats include Discover Art, Art Makes, Artist Stories, and Meet The Artist, searchable by key stage, art form, or SEND accessibility. [15-Tate]
- "When Tate set out to build a new digital learning platform for schools, the team began with a deliberately uncomfortable question: why would teachers want to engage with art through digital spaces at all?" "The measure of success, as Coe put it, is ultimately the classroom itself." [15-Tate]

**National Maritime Museum (Greenwich) — inclusive school collaboration:**
- A museum-school collaboration with Willow Dene Special School (serving children aged 2-19 with a wide range of disabilities including autism and profound and multiple learning difficulties, PMLD) centered on "sea creatures real and imagined." The project unfolded in three stages: (1) sensory sea sessions at the museum; (2) a "power day" at school involving sensory storytelling and hands-on art with paint, clay, and collage; (3) collaboration with artist Shermaine Slocombe, who layered photographs, textures, and original artwork into a large-scale banner displayed at the museum. Insights from Willow Dene staff and parents informed the development of an accessible playground at the museum called "The Cove," featuring wooden shapes inspired by the students' sea creature designs, now a permanent museum fixture. The success set a benchmark, leading to a new partnership with Phoenix Primary and Secondary School (an autism-specialist school), for which the museum adapted its approach by bringing projects directly to the school. Key figures: Ruth Boley (Senior Manager for Learning), Lisa Parascandolo (cultural capital lead at Willow Dene), and Hollie Witton (Learning Partnerships and Projects Producer). "There's no one right or wrong way to be creative," Ruth noted. [7-NMM]

### 2. Policies, Laws, and Regulations

- **National curriculum alignment:** British Museum school programs are aligned with the UK national curriculum — e.g., the "peek into prehistory" programme aligns with the UK national history curriculum, and the KS4 Parthenon talk supports the Classical Civilisations GCSE component Myth and Religion (J199/11). [12-ArtNewspaper][14-BM]
- **Charity law framework:** Free admission is a policy, not a legal obligation — it has never been a statutory requirement, so it could theoretically be changed without primary legislation. National museums are exempt charities (regulated by DCMS, not the Charity Commission) but are still charities, so their purposes must be exclusively charitable and for public benefit. The Charity Commission's guidance (RR10) states "access is fundamental to charitable status"; where access is restricted, it must only be to the extent necessary to better achieve the charity's objects. Charges must be "reasonable, appropriate to the overall purposes of the organisation and set at a rate which balances the current and future activities of the organisation and are not set at a level which excludes a substantial proportion of the public." Restricting access risks breaching the spirit of trusts under which many works were given (Acceptance in Lieu scheme, Cultural Gifts Scheme, traditional philanthropy), requiring an object-by-object review of trust conditions. [6-StoneKing]
- **Arts Council England:** Reaffirmed that access and public benefit remain central to its statutory purpose. Darren Henley, chief executive of Arts Council England, said the organisation had "absolutely heard" it needed to become "simpler and easier to deal with" and would streamline processes over the next six months. [6-StoneKing][9-Guardian]
- **Hodge review of Arts Council England:** Baroness Margaret Hodge's December 2025 review urged ministers to protect arts funding from politicisation and remove red tape. The government agreed the Arts Council should be "strong, politically impartial and independent," earmarked £8m to simplify application processes, cited a £2m investment in regional arts scenes, and announced the reintroduction of regional arts boards. Hodge advocated a cautious approach to charging international visitors, contingent on a universal identification system to avoid discrimination risk. [6-StoneKing][9-Guardian]

### 3. Operating and Funding Models

- **Universal free admission policy:** Charging for museum entry has been contentious since the 1960s. The 1997 Labour government committed to reinstating free entry; charges were dropped in stages — for children in 1999, over-60s in 2000, and all visitors from 1 December 2001. The policy was made feasible when Chancellor Gordon Brown changed VAT regulations in the 2001 budget to allow free museums to reclaim VAT. Museums dropped charges in exchange for extra government funding (via DCMS) to compensate for lost ticket income, though they continue to charge for special exhibitions. Scotland and Wales also introduced free entry at national museums in April 2001. [7-CPI]
- **Impact of free admission:** Museums dropping charges saw average visitor increases of 70%. The V&A's figures rose 111% in the first year (1.1M to 2.3M visitors). By 2009, visits to previously charging museums had more than doubled from 7.2M to 16M annually. Eight of the top ten UK visitor attractions in 2010 were free national museums, with 40 million visits in 2011/12. However, the visitor profile changed little — free admission did not substantially achieve social inclusion goals; barriers remained including lack of art knowledge and feelings of intimidation. Foreign visitors make up about 40% of museum visits. [7-CPI]
- **Historical context:** In the 1980s, Conservative governments pressured national museums to charge; about half did so, while the British Museum, National Gallery, and Tate resisted. Over 15 years, free museums saw spectacular visitor growth while charging museums declined — the V&A's £5 charge in 1997 halved its visitor numbers. [7-CPI]
- **Debate over ending free admission (2025–2026):** The free-entry policy celebrated its 25th anniversary in December 2026, amid a funding crisis. On 26 March 2026, DCMS and Arts Council England published responses to the Hodge review; the government confirmed it will "explore the potential opportunities that charging international visitors at national museums could bring," with an update promised before end of 2026. The Treasury had previously considered ending free entry in the November 2025 budget, but plans were scrapped after pushback from culture ministers including Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy. Art Fund research showed 72% of the public supported a tourist levy subsidising free entry to national museums. Alison Cole, director of the Cultural Policy Unit thinktank, called charging international tourists a "very bad idea," advocating instead for a hotel levy. [6-StoneKing][9-Guardian][10-MA]
- **Museum leaders' positions on charging:** Nick Merriman (former leader of Horniman Museum & Gardens and English Heritage) changed his view, noting "the statistics show that, actually, for the national museums, not charging has increased numbers vastly, but it hasn't done much in terms of widening the audience. So you just get more middle class people going." Roy Clare (former head of Royal Museums Greenwich) called for a "more sophisticated approach," saying entry doesn't have to be free "24/7 or 365." Mark Jones (former V&A director, recently interim director of the British Museum) called universal free entry "regressive and inequitable," noting lower-income taxpayers subsidise tourists, and said charging could reduce overcrowding. [10-MA]
- **Museums Association position:** Director Sharon Heal called free entry "a major cultural policy success" delivering cultural, learning and economic benefits, warning charging could create access barriers, impact visitor numbers, cause ID-related issues for UK residents, and damage UK tourism reputation. [10-MA]
- **NAO financial assessment (March 2026):** DCMS-sponsored museums face sustained financial pressure despite significant increases in self-generated income since the pandemic. The NAO does NOT recommend ending free admission; it warns continued reliance on commercial income and cost containment risks eroding public benefits and calls for stronger DCMS oversight and improved early-warning mechanisms. [6-StoneKing]
- **The VAT refund scheme** for national museums (a Treasury mechanism, not law) would likely need reform if charging were reintroduced. [6-StoneKing]
- **Local/civic museum funding:** In UK cities, some local government-funded museums are free (Manchester, Newcastle, Glasgow, Derby) while others charge (Norwich, Nottingham). Tony Butler, director of Derby Museums Trust (2014-16), described public funding: 30% from Arts Council England (general taxation), 58% from Derby City Council, with about 35% of council income from council tax; during austerity public sector income (87% of turnover) dropped by nearly 30%. Alistair Brown (Museums Journal): "Our local authority museums are vital parts of the civic sphere. They support happy, peaceful communities. They educate and entertain. They care for collections that preserve collective memory and information about the local, national and international. And they should be accessible to all, not just a privileged few." [8-Butler]

### 4. Featured Programs and Classic Case Studies

- **British Museum "tablet tours"** using augmented reality; **Virtual Visits** live interactive workshops; **"peek into prehistory"** curriculum-aligned programme; **"Where We Are..."** national programme for 16–24-year-olds in underserved groups; **Home Education Days**; **KS2 taught workshops in the Clore Centre for Education**; **Museum Missions** phone/tablet-based family activities. [12-ArtNewspaper][14-BM]
- **Tate Collective Producers** (15–25-year-olds co-creating events and resources for peers); **UNIQLO Tate Play** family events; **Tate Schools** digital platform with over 80 resources; **Lightbox** SEND resource; **All The Feelings** Immersion series commission. [11-Tate][15-Tate]
- **National Maritime Museum + Willow Dene Special School:** inclusive museum-school collaboration producing "The Cove" accessible playground. [7-NMM]

### 5. Distinctive Characteristics and Digital Technology Trends

- The UK is characterized by its landmark free-admission policy (now under review), strong curriculum alignment between museum programming and national curriculum/GCSEs, a robust school-partnership culture, and leadership in SEND-first digital learning design (Tate Schools). [11-Tate][15-Tate][7-CPI]
- **Digital technology:** The British Museum uses augmented reality tablet tours, livestreamed lessons, and Virtual Visits; Tate built the Tate Schools platform with an SEND-first design philosophy; the UK is among the markets served by Google Arts & Culture (2,000+ partner museums worldwide). [12-ArtNewspaper][15-Tate][16-FrameSixty]

## III. FRANCE

### 1. Museum Education System and Institutional Organization

**The Louvre Museum — Education Services:**
- The Louvre offers in-person workshops and educational programs for students of all ages covering art history and cultural education; online resources including virtual tours and digital content designed for remote learning; and the "Louvre Kids" interactive platform featuring engaging narratives and stories about the museum's masterpieces targeted at young audiences. [16-HomeTrail]
- The Louvre offers free admission on the first Friday of the month after 6 PM (except in summer), and family-friendly programming including workshops, storytelling tours, shows, youth films, and the "Petit Louvre" digital extension with videos, comics, coloring pages, and puzzles. [17-France][18-FTC]
- Note: The Louvre's education page is linked at louvre.fr/en/education. [16-HomeTrail]

**Centre Pompidou — Children's Workshops and Mediation for Young Audiences:**
- Centre Pompidou is France's national modern and contemporary art center, home to one of the world's two largest collections in modern and contemporary art (over 120,000 works), with 40 years of expertise and innovation in cultural partnerships with museums, art centers, public administrations, and private companies. [20-Pompidou]
- **Mediation for Young Audiences:** Dedicated spaces — the Children's Workshop (Atelier des enfants), Galerie des Enfants, and Studio 13/16 — plus travelling exhibitions/workshops for children of all ages. Featured works/creators include Marion Barraud (Dans la forêt, ages 0-24 months), Jean-Charles de Castelbajac (Le peuple de demain, ages 2-16), Françoise Pétrovitch (Passer à travers, ages 3-12), Laterna Magica (ages 3-12), matali crasset (Saule et les Hooppies, ages 5-12), La Fabrique mobile (ages 6-11), and Studio 13/16 au collège (ages 13-16). [16-Pompidou]
- **Kids Studio (Atelier des enfants):** Where children can make art, including drawing on walls. Studio 13/16 provides programming specifically for teenagers. The children's guided tour lasts about an hour and follows a specific structure: yoga stretches to calm children; a meditation exercise where kids close their eyes and imagine colors and lines; a fun activity of walking on a black line on the floor (similar to "floor is lava") to teach museum etiquette; views of Paris landmarks; and discussions of artworks by artists including Marc Chagall, Henri Matisse, Piet Mondrian, Joan Miro (including his Blue I from 1961), and a Yaacov Agam installation. "It aims to teach children not only about art but how to draw your own conclusions about art." [19-Tours]
- **"Il était une ville" (Once Upon a Time, a City):** Exhibition-workshop by space designer, architect, and visual artist Sara de.Gouy at the Galerie des enfants, 13 February to 30 June 2025, inviting visitors to imagine a more joyful, poetic, and sustainable city designed with children. Developed in collaboration with two second-grade classes from a Parisian elementary school in spring 2024; children observed their surroundings, reimagined objects and urban spaces, and worked alongside the artist to envision their dream city. Themes: The Play Crossing, Buildings in Colour, The Bench, The Apple Tree of Possibilities, The Extraordinary Garden, Rain is Life!, and Wind over the Roofs. The page credits interviews by Alice Maxia and Laura Samoilovich and the voices of 22 participating children. [18-Pompidou]
- **Centre Pompidou-Metz:** France's most visited modern & contemporary art centre outside Paris. Features projects for school-goers, rural audiences, partnerships with activist organizations and Metz hospital, blending live performance and exhibitions. [16-Pompidou]
- **Centre Pompidou Francilien:** A new 30,000m² conservation and creation centre being built in Massy (Ile-de-France), opening spring 2027. Since 2019, a pre-opening programme has circulated works, educational tools, and forged partnerships with academic and community stakeholders. [16-Pompidou]
- **"mille formes" network:** Art initiation centres for children aged 0–6. mille formes Clermont-Ferrand (inaugurated 2019, welcomed over 35,000 visitors, hosted 150 artistic offerings; designed by Laure Jaffuel with architect Sharmily Guyot); mille formes Montpellier (1,000 m² space inaugurated 6 February 2026, designed by artist-architect Sarah de.Gouy, featuring two exhibition galleries, studio, performing arts room, reading room, and parenting support area). [16-Pompidou]
- **Travelling Museums:** Centre Pompidou mobile (2011–2013), a demountable pavilion by architect Patrick Bouchain that brought masterpieces to regions with limited cultural access (Aubagne, Boulogne-sur-Mer, Cambrai, Chaumont, Libourne); MuMo (Mobile Museum, founded 2011 by Ingrid Brochard), partnered with Centre Pompidou in 2022 with support from the Art Explora Foundation and French Ministry of Culture, touring thematic exhibitions in a travelling museum truck for 40 weeks per year across France. [16-Pompidou]
- **International offers:** Centre Pompidou co-created spaces in Metz (2010), Málaga (2015), Louvre Abu Dhabi (2017), Brussels (2018, Kanal-Centre Pompidou), and Shanghai (2019, Centre Pompidou x West Bund Museum Project). Centre Pompidou-Málaga welcomed over 500,000 visitors in two and a half years in a city of 600,000 inhabitants; Kanal-Centre Pompidou welcomed over 60,000 visitors in its first month. It offers international partners: travelling exhibitions based on the collection (e.g., "Elles: Women Artists in the Collection" at CCBB Rio de Janeiro with 250,000 visitors; "Vassily Kandinsky: A Retrospective" at Palazzo Reale Milan with 215,000 visitors; "Masterpieces from Centre Pompidou" at Metropolitan Art Museum Tokyo with 200,000 visitors); expertise in cultural fields; tailor-made educational projects and travelling exhibitions for young audiences; and services including venue development and staff training. [20-Pompidou]
- **Loans and Deposits:** Centre Pompidou is the world's leading lender of artworks. In 2023, over 2,200 works were loaned within France, and approximately 5,350 works are currently on deposit in various institutions in Paris and across the regions. [16-Pompidou]
- **Professional Training:** Tailored training programmes for local authorities to strengthen skills of decision-makers and teams in support of community cultural policy development. [16-Pompidou]

**École du Louvre (The Louvre School):**
- A public institution run by the French Ministry of Culture, founded in 1882, located in the Palais du Louvre in Paris, specializing in art history, archaeology, epigraphy, anthropology, and museology. Its mission is to educate students for careers in museums, monuments, heritage sites, schools, universities, and other art-related professions. [18-Sorbonne]
- Offers an undergraduate diploma (licence/B.A.) covering the history of art and artefacts from prehistory to the present; a graduate diploma (master/M.A.) in museology with specializations in Art history and museum studies research, Mediation, Collection conservation, Art Market or Provenance, and Sensitive objects and international contexts; and post-master's and post-graduate (PhD) diplomas with a Research Centre organized around six themes (Global Art History, Object Biographies, Museology(ies) and Heritage, Methods and Historiography, Provenance, and Gender Studies). It also offers continuing education for auditors (extramural students) of any age or qualification. [18-Sorbonne]
- Enrolls nearly 1,800 students from undergraduate to doctoral levels; every year some 200 students (13% of the total student body) of around forty nationalities are selected. Since 2006 it has partnered with the Fondation Culture & Diversité to support students from underprivileged backgrounds. Nearly 30% of students receive scholarships (up from 10% in 2000), including 38% of first-year students. The Endowment Fund provides living support grants of €5,000 annually, housing assistance grants of approximately €400, emergency aid of around €350, and the Maison des Élèves (opened 2021 in Paris's Odéon district, providing affordable housing for 50 non-Parisian first-year students). [20-EDL]
- A Joint Master's program with Sorbonne Université (taught in English) trains museum professionals for Abu Dhabi — the only professional museum training program in the Gulf States. [19-EDL]

**"Le musée fait école" (The Museum as Educator):**
- A cooperation project launched January 28, 2020, supported by the Canada-France Agreement and France's Ministry of Culture, in cooperation with France's Department of Public Policy of the Directorate General of Heritage. It brings together the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts (MMFA) with partners including the Georges Pompidou National Centre for Art and Culture, the Louvre Museum, the Royal Ontario Museum, and the Art Gallery of Ontario to redefine new models for 21st-century museums. Through tours, workshops, and residencies, teams from Canadian and French institutions share innovative practices in education and cultural mediation. It followed the earlier "Musées du XXIe siècle" (Museums of the 21st Century) mission. Key participants included Nathalie Bondil (Director General and Chief Curator, MMFA), Thomas Bastien (Director of Education and Wellness, MMFA), and representatives from the Centre Pompidou, the Louvre, and France's Ministry of Culture. [17-MMFA]

### 2. Policies, Laws, and Regulations

- **Free admission policies:** EU residents under 26 (including international students with a long-stay visa) get free admission to national museums (Musée d'Orsay, Centre Pompidou) and national monuments (Arc de Triomphe, Panthéon); most national museums are free for everyone on the first Sunday of each month; the Louvre offers free admission on the first Friday of the month after 6 PM (except in summer); some establishments are free for young people under 26 and teachers all year round; free late-night openings once a month; free admission on 14 July (Bastille Day). Entry is free to the permanent collections of 11 Paris municipal museums (including the Musée Carnavalet - Histoire de Paris, Petit Palais, and Musée d'Art moderne de la Ville de Paris, Maison de Balzac, Musée Bourdelle, Musée Cernuschi, Musée Cognacq-Jay, Musée de la Libération de Paris, Musée de la Vie romantique, Maison de Victor Hugo, and Musée Zadkine). [12-Paris][13-Sortiraparis][11-FTC]
- **Musée d'Orsay free admission categories:** Visitors under 18; EU/EEA nationals aged 18-25; non-EU nationals aged 18-25 with long-term EU residence; students (up to 30) in artistic/humanities fields at public universities; teachers in those same fields; job seekers; recipients of social benefits/asylum seekers/refugees; recipients of minimum old-age pension; Pass Éducation holders (only valid if issued by the French Ministry of Education); ICOM/ICOMOS members; persons with disabilities holding official cards with one companion; École du Louvre students and auditors; and others. [14-Orsay]
- **The French museum context and state support:** France is a major museum player, hosting three of the world's ten most visited art museums (Louvre with ~10 million visitors/year, Pompidou Center, and Musée d'Orsay). Museum attendance in France rose from 40 million (2005) to 62 million (2017) but stagnated since 2010, concentrated in large establishments. France invests 2.6% of GDP in culture (vs. 2.3% elsewhere), and the sector represents 88 billion € in annual turnover. Smaller museums (under 20,000 visitors/year) face economic pressure, and public funding is stagnating or declining. [5-Pauget]
- **Delphi study on French museums to 2030:** A Delphi-based foresight study (Technological Forecasting and Social Change, 2020, doi: 10.1016/j.techfore.2020.120384) by Bertrand Pauget, Jean-Michel Tobelem, and Jean-Philippe Bootz, conducted 2017–2018 with 99 French-speaking experts. The most important missions for museums by 2030 per experts were educational issues and democratization of culture (round 2 mean: 4.63, SD: 0.53). Experts agreed on collaboration with institutions but were reluctant on audience participation in exhibitions. Technology played a minor role — only one variable (online publication of digitized collections) was validated. Three scenarios for 2030: (1) Museums centered around youth and democratization of culture; (2) Museums responding to decreased public funding; (3) A breakdown scenario with direct participation of nearby stakeholders. [5-Pauget]
- **Cultural policy philosophy:** André Malraux's aphorism — "Culture is not inherited, it is conquered" — is widely invoked in French museum-education discourse. [17-France]

### 3. Operating and Funding Models

- **State funding and national ownership:** The École du Louvre is a public institution run by the French Ministry of Culture. [18-Sorbonne]
- **Public funding stagnation:** France invests 2.6% of GDP in culture; public funding for museums is stagnating or declining; smaller museums face economic pressure. [5-Pauget]
- **Admission fee policies:** Free for under-26 EU residents at national museums/monuments; free first Sundays; free permanent collections at Paris municipal museums; free for teachers; free for ICOM members. [11-FTC][12-Paris][13-Sortiraparis][14-Orsay]
- **Philanthropy and endowment:** The École du Louvre Endowment Fund supports students in financial distress; U.S. donors can make tax-deductible donations through Friends of Fondation de France. [20-EDL]
- **International partnerships as revenue/outreach:** Centre Pompidou's international partnerships (Metz, Málaga, Brussels, Shanghai, Louvre Abu Dhabi) and its status as the world's leading lender of artworks (2,200 works loaned within France in 2023; ~5,350 works on deposit) represent a distinctive French operating model. [16-Pompidou][20-Pompidou]
- **Centre Pompidou closure:** The Centre Pompidou is closed for renovation work until 2030, though its cultural programme continues. [12-Paris]

### 4. Featured Programs and Classic Case Studies

- **Louvre:** Workshops, storytelling tours, shows, youth films, "Petit Louvre" digital extension, "Louvre Kids" platform, free Friday-evening admission, under-26 free entry. [17-France][16-HomeTrail]
- **Musée d'Orsay:** Impressionist workshops where children aged 6-8 and 8-12 paint in the style of Van Gogh, Renoir, or Pissarro. [17-France]
- **Centre Pompidou:** Atelier des enfants (Kids Studio), Galerie des Enfants, Studio 13/16, "Il était une ville" exhibition-workshop, mille formes network, Centre Pompidou mobile, MuMo travelling museum, and international educational projects. [16-Pompidou][18-Pompidou][19-Tours]
- **Other notable French children's museums/programs:** Musée en Herbe (a museum dedicated entirely to children, operating since the mid-70s); Cité des Enfants at the City of Science and Industry; Louvre-Lens's "The 10 Rights of the Little Visitor" charter (sensory experiences, mini-tours, painting, engraving, and drawing activities); Cité de l'Espace in Toulouse ("Little Astronauts' City" for children as young as 4); Musée des Confluences in Lyon ("Secrets of the Earth" exhibition with sensory workshops on precious stones and minerals); Palais Fesch in Ajaccio (children from age 6 create plastic works; older kids 11+ design exhibitions; theatrical tours); Mucem in Marseille; and Cité du Vin in Bordeaux (customized wine-themed tour for children 7+ with grape juice tasting). [17-France][19-Tours]
- **Foresight research:** The Delphi study established the first academically rigorous foresight study on French museums. [5-Pauget]

### 5. Distinctive Characteristics and Digital Technology Trends

- France's museum education is distinguished by: a strong national/state role (Ministry of Culture); universal free-admission policies for young people (under 26) and teachers; the professionalization of mediation through the École du Louvre; the concept of "la médiation culturelle" (cultural mediation); dedicated children's spaces at major museums; regional outreach via mobile museums and the mille formes network; and international museum partnerships exporting French educational expertise. [5-Pauget][16-Pompidou][17-MMFA][18-Sorbonne]
- **Digital technology:** The Louvre offers virtual tours and digital content for remote learning and the "Petit Louvre" digital extension; Google Arts & Culture partners with the Louvre. The Delphi study found experts gave technology a minor role in museums' future, validating only online publication of digitized collections. Virtual museum tour metrics include the Louvre's 12-minute average session duration. [16-HomeTrail][16-FrameSixty][5-Pauget]

## IV. GERMANY

### 1. Museum Education System and Institutional Organization

**German Association for Museum Education (BVMP — Bundesverband Museumspädagogik):**
- The BVMP is the federal organization representing, bundling and coordinating the expertise of over 1,000 museum educators across Germany. Formed in 1991 through the merger of six regional associations, it promotes professional exchange, networking, cooperation, publications, and projects that advance education and communication in museums "in a qualitative and forward-looking manner." [1-BVMP][12-BVMP]
- Working formats: (1) Conferences, Training Courses, and Network Meetings — annual major (inter)national conferences combining practical work with theoretical aspects, plus regional training and network meetings; (2) Specialist Groups — nationwide networks addressing topics such as children and young people in museums, inclusion and diversity, digitality, the 60-plus generation, and education for sustainable development; (3) Magazine "Standbein Spielbein" — the only specialist magazine for museum education in Germany, covering national and international developments, research, and projects; (4) Guidelines & Position Papers — concise guidance on inclusion, accessibility, school-museum cooperation, and museum education organization, published in cooperation with the German Museums Association and NEMO (Network of European Museum Organisations), including the guidelines "Developing Education and Public Engagement in Museums"; (5) International Networking — BVMP is a member of the German Cultural Council and the Federal Association for Cultural Education for Children and Young People (BKJ). [1-BVMP][12-BVMP]

**Jugend im Museum e.V. (Berlin):**
- Jugend im Museum e.V. is a partner organization supporting museum education in Berlin. It designed and runs the Atelier Bunter Jakob at the Berlinische Galerie, a studio where children and teenagers can experiment with paints, techniques, materials, photography, drawing, printing, cartoon film, and sculpture. [1-BG]
- Jugend im Museum e.V. also developed project days in the Waldraum (forest room) at the Brücke-Museum Berlin: 3-hour artistic-practical workshops (€140, €100 reduced, for up to 15 participants). [5-Brücke]

**Berlinische Galerie (Berlin):**
- Its education programme is designed to make art accessible to a wide range of visitors: Berliners and travellers, adults and teenagers, children and families, pre-school groups and secondary students, and people with disabilities. The programme is supported by two partner organizations: Jugend im Museum e.V. and Kulturprojekte Berlin GmbH. Activities are offered both on-site and through long-term community projects. The museum has a 207 m² space within the exhibition area dedicated to workshops, collaborative projects and artistic activities for children, families, schools and neighbourhood groups. Contact: Christine van Haaren (Head of Education and Outreach) and Katrin-Marie Kaptain (Education). [1-BG]

**Deutsches Museum (Munich):**
- The "School and Museum" page outlines offerings for schools, including bookable programmes and guided tours, downloadable supplementary materials for preparing and following up on lessons, and a Hands-on Exhibition called "Kid's Kingdom" for children aged 3 to 8 years. Reduced admission for schools and a School Membership option allow pupils to visit all Munich locations at very favourable conditions. The education department (Abteilung Bildung), email museumspaedagogik@deutsches-museum.de, handles educational programmes for schools, daycare centres (Kitas), and families in Munich. [3-DM]

**Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (National Museums in Berlin):**
- The Education, Outreach, and Visitor Services Department serves as the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin's central educational institution, designing and implementing special events across all 15 collections, targeting children, families, young people, adults, schools, universities, and other educational institutions. Heike Kropff is Head of the Department of Education/Communication. [4-SMB]
- On 9 July 2018, the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin launched "HERE WE ARE!" (Hier sind wir!), a large-scale education and outreach project on the Museumsinsel Berlin, part of the Federal Ministry of Education and Research's initiative "Kultur macht stark: Bündnisse für Bildung" (With Culture Comes Strength: Educational Alliances) and funded by the Deutsches Museum's activity programme "Von uns für uns! Die Museen unserer Stadt entdeckt." The funding enabled implementation of 20 education and outreach programmes focused on the Museumsinsel over two years. Children and teenagers explore the Bode-Museum, Neues Museum, Pergamonmuseum, Alte Nationalgalerie, and Altes Museum in groups, deciding which perspectives to apply to collections and architecture, with specially designed didactic materials such as a "tool box" and support from art education staff and social workers. Partners include Internationaler Bund, IB Berlin-Brandenburg GmbH, Landesjugendwerk im AWO Landesverband Berlin e.V., Moabiter Ratschlag e.V., Mädchen-Kultur-Treff Dünja, Pestalozzi-Fröbel-Haus, Stiftung SPI, and Haus der Jugend. HERE WE ARE! carries on from CRACK THE CODE! (2014–2017), which likewise targeted children and young people whose social milieu offered few points of connection with the museum. [4-SMB]

**Brücke-Museum Berlin:**
- The Education & Outreach programme is directed by Daniela Bystron (Curator of Outreach) with a team of art mediators. Offerings include public and private guided tours, gallery talks, project days in the Waldraum (developed with Jugend im Museum e.V.), the Brücke-Box (free lending box of materials for playful art engagement, recommended age 5+), family workshops (for children from 5 years), "Re-sighting" series (expert tours), and digital talks. School collaborations include "Naturally Art!" garden redesign with two Berlin schools, "Sometimes Unanswerable" student-centred research with Kurt-Tucholsky-Schule, and "Voices on the exhibition" with Dreilinden-Gymnasium. University collaborations include Freie Universität Berlin, Kunsthochschule Weißensee, University of Applied Sciences Berlin, and Berlin University of the Arts. The programme addresses colonial contexts (e.g., Karl Schmidt-Rottluff's collection of ~100 ritual and everyday objects) and fosters dialogical, participatory, and discrimination-sensitive art mediation. [5-Brücke]

**ANOHA — The Children's World of the Jewish Museum Berlin:**
- ANOHA is a children's museum for ages 3–12, opened on 27 June 2021 at the W. M. Blumenthal Academy in a former wholesale flower market. The story of Noah's Ark from the Torah is the central theme; more than 150 animal sculptures populate a gigantic round wooden ark designed by the Seattle-based firm Olson Kundig Architecture and Design. Animals were created by selected artists using recycled materials and can be explored as monkey bars, hammocks, snuggle caves; some make noises or contain treasures. Featured animals include the naked mole rat (representing respect, openness, and tolerance of the unfamiliar) and extinct/endangered animals such as the mammoth and polar bears, drawing attention to environmental issues. ANOHA follows the "Early Excellence" approach, building on children's individual abilities and talents. A dedicated Children's Advisory Council of 8–11-year-olds actively shaped the museum's development, contributing ideas for spaces and programming. Funded by the German Federal Government Commissioner for Culture and the Media, based on a resolution by the German Bundestag. [3-ANOHA]

**European children's museum context (German examples):**
- The first European children's museums were the Juniormuseum of the Ethnological Museum in Berlin (1970, now closed) and the Junges Museum Frankfurt (1972). The Junges Museum Frankfurt (CMA-Nominee 2018), opened 1972, combines original objects with hands-on displays and family trails. [13-HandsOn-Part1]

### 2. Policies, Laws, and Regulations

- **"Museum macht stark" (Museums make you strong):** A German project run by the German Museums Association aimed at introducing children and young adults aged 5-18 to museums, particularly those who would otherwise have little opportunity to experience them. The Federal Ministry of Education and Research is funding the project with 6.4 million euros. Currently 69 museums participate, offering 97 projects, with over 17,000 young people having taken part so far. Participating institutions include the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, the German Port Museum in Hamburg, and the Bach Museum in Leipzig. German Museums Association president Eckart Köhne: the collaborations show "just how much children and young adults profit long-term from their experiences at museums and how they make museums into 'their own spaces'." [2-deutschland.de][11-deutschland.de]
- **"Kultur macht stark: Bündnisse für Bildung" (With Culture Comes Strength: Educational Alliances):** The Federal Ministry of Education and Research initiative funding museum education/outreach projects such as HERE WE ARE! [4-SMB]
- **Federal government funding:** ANOHA was funded by the German Federal Government Commissioner for Culture and the Media, based on a resolution by the German Bundestag. [3-ANOHA]

### 3. Operating and Funding Models

- Germany's museum education is funded through a mix of federal government programs (Federal Ministry of Education and Research funding "Museum macht stark" at €6.4 million; the "Kultur macht stark" initiative), state-level funding, and the federal government's Culture and Media Commissioner. [2-deutschland.de][4-SMB][3-ANOHA]
- **BVMP guidelines** address museum education organization in cooperation with the German Museums Association and NEMO. [1-BVMP]
- German children-focused museum work reflects state-funded educational systems and is less commercial than the US model. [13-HandsOn-Part1]
- There is no universal free-admission policy at German national museums comparable to the UK/France; the sources gathered did not detail German admission-fee policies.

### 4. Featured Programs and Classic Case Studies

- **"Hier sind wir!" (Here we are!) by the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin:** Targets children and young adults whose social environment offers limited contact with museums, featuring discovery tours of Berlin's Museum Island (a UNESCO World Heritage site) including the Pergamon Museum with its reconstructions of the Pergamon Altar and the Processional Way of Babylon. [2-deutschland.de]
- **Leipzig's Bach Museum project:** The temporary exhibition "Bach & Triegel. Im Dialog" — works by painter Michael Triegel dialogue with the music of Johann Sebastian Bach; children use experimental drawing techniques, conduct interviews, and work on still lifes. [2-deutschland.de]
- **ANOHA Children's World (Jewish Museum Berlin):** Noah's Ark-themed children's museum with 150+ recycled-material animal sculptures and a Children's Advisory Council. [3-ANOHA]
- **Atelier Bunter Jakob (Berlinische Galerie):** Studio for children and teenagers designed and run by Jugend im Museum on behalf of the museum. [1-BG]
- **Deutsches Museum "Kid's Kingdom":** Hands-on exhibition for children aged 3 to 8. [3-DM]
- **Jugend im Museum e.V.:** The Berlin-based association (a classic case study in German museum education) partners with museums across Berlin (Berlinische Galerie, Brücke-Museum) to run children's and youth workshops and project days. [1-BG][5-Brücke]

### 5. Distinctive Characteristics and Digital Technology Trends

- Germany is characterized by: a strong professional association infrastructure (BVMP with 1,000+ museum educators); the federalist structure (regional associations merged into a federal body); the German term "Museumspädagogik" (museum pedagogy) as a recognized profession; a dedicated specialist magazine ("Standbein Spielbein"); strong federal government funding for outreach to underserved youth ("Museum macht stark," "Kultur macht stark"); and influential children's museums (Junges Museum Frankfurt, ANOHA). [1-BVMP][2-deutschland.de][3-ANOHA]
- **Digitality:** The BVMP has a specialist group on digitality (Digitale Vermittlung). [1-BVMP]
- **Children's museum theory (Hands-on, Minds-on, Hearts-on):** A three-generation model (inspired by Gail Dexter Lord): First Generation (1899–1980s) focused on interactivity/play (Hands-on); Second Generation (circa 1970) added knowledge/critical thinking (Minds-on); Third Generation (today) adds soft power/change agents (Hearts-on), addressing societal demands for museums to become "Homes of 21st Century Education." Michael Spock of Boston Children's Museum revolutionized museum education in the 1960s by removing display cabinets. "Hands-on, Minds-on, Hearts-on exhibitions and formats aim to enable learning by functioning as mediators between an actuality and the child and are therefore closely associated with reform pedagogical approaches." Progressive education theorists covered in the Hands On! guide include Comenius, Rousseau, Basedow, Salzmann, Pestalozzi, Fröbel, Parker, Robin, Dewey (learning by doing), Reddie, Steiner (Waldorf), Montessori, Neill (Summerhill), Parkhurst (Dalton Plan), Hengstenberg, Vygotsky, Freinet, Piaget, Pikler, Bruner (spiral curriculum), Malaguzzi (Reggio), Gardner (multiple intelligences), and Falk & Dierking (free-choice learning). Techniques include aesthetic practices, co-creation, digital learning, enquiry-based learning, gamification, media-based learning, nature play, object-based learning, open-ended play, peer/intergenerational learning, phenomenon-based learning, role play, storytelling, take-over (day), and tinkering & making (originated at Exploratorium, San Francisco). [4-Part3]
- **The 8 Quality Characteristics of a "Home of 21st Century Education"** (Hands On! International Association of Children in Museums certificate framework): Door to Culture (public, barrier-free, accessible places connecting children to cultural heritage; no entrance fees ideally); Learning Through Play; With All the Senses! (Holistic learning: Hands-On! Mind-On! Heart-On!); A Better World (children as equal partners in society, co-creators and agents of change; learning "at eye level"); Bridging the Gap; Be Heard!; Digitally Aware & Active; Constantly Changing. The Children in Museums Award (CMA), established in 2011 by Hands On! International and the European Museum Academy, was renamed in 2014 from "Children's Museum Award." Jury criteria include Innovation, Creating immersive learning environments, Embracing the Digital Revolution, Creative ways to use collections, Addressing contemporary issues, Achieving social impact, and Participation. [13-HandsOn-Part1]
- **ICOM context:** ICOM was founded in 1946 with a Children's Museums Committee — notably with a female chair and mostly female members — proving the early significance of children-focused museum work. [4-Part3]

## V. JAPAN

### 1. Museum Education System and Institutional Organization

**The Museum Act (博物館法, Hakubutsukan Hō) and the institutional system:**
- Enacted December 1, 1951 as Law No. 285 during the Allied occupation, the Museum Act is Japan's primary legislation governing museum establishment, registration, operation, and standards. It entered into force March 1, 1952, builds on the Social Education Law of 1949, and was later aligned to the Basic Act on Culture and the Arts (2001). The most comprehensive revision came with Law No. 24 of April 15, 2022 (effective April 1, 2023) — the first standalone amendment in 67 years — expanding eligibility to NPOs and corporations, mandating digital archiving, and introducing flexible registration. [1-Grokipedia][2-Wiki]
- The Act defines museums as facilities "collecting and preserving (including nurturing) materials related to history, the arts, folk customs, industry, natural science, etc., exhibiting them, providing them for use by the general public on the basis of educational considerations, conducting necessary work in order to contribute to education, research, recreation, etc., and in addition undertaking surveys and research relating to these materials." This includes botanical gardens, zoos, aquaria, and planetaria. [1-Grokipedia][2-Wiki][3-Bunka]
- Museums are classified into three legal categories: registered museums (登録博物館), museum-equivalent facilities (博物館相当施設), and museum-like facilities (博物館類似施設). As of October 2018, there were 5,738 museums in Japan: 914 registered museums, 372 museum-equivalent facilities, and 4,452 museum-like facilities. (FY2005 figures: 865 registered, 331 museum-equivalent, 4,418 museum-like.) Registered museums require prefectural board of education accreditation, a stable economic foundation, qualified staff (director plus certified curators with bachelor's-level education), adequate facilities, and at least 150 annual public opening days (100 days for museum-equivalent facilities). [2-Wiki][3-Bunka]
- Registered museums receive tax benefits (real estate acquisition tax, fixed asset tax) and easier donation incentives; public museums can receive subsidies. [3-Bunka]
- Article 12 of the Basic Act on Education (Act No. 120 of December 22, 2006) promotes community-based education (social education) through libraries, museums, community halls, and other facilities; Article 13 requires schools, families, and local residents to cooperate in education. [5-MEXT]
- **Curators:** A curator is a "staff member with specialized knowledge" handling collection, storage, exhibition, and research. Curator qualifications can be obtained through university coursework (accounting for ~99% of qualifications, with ~10,000 students per year), qualification examinations, certification without examination (master's/doctor's degrees or teaching experience), or MEXT training courses. As of FY2005, there were only 6,225 curators at museums (out of 44,619 total museum staff, about 14%) — "The ratio of the actual number of curators to the number of persons with curator qualifications is extremely low, showing that the opening is very narrow indeed." [3-Bunka]
- By founder (FY2005 Social Education Survey): 129 national, 68 by independent administrative institutions, 4,023 by local governments, 603 by general incorporated associations/foundations, and 791 by private entities. Total 5,614 museums: 3,200 history museums (highest), 1,087 art museums, and 474 science museums. Since 2003, public museums can use a designated management system allowing consignment to private enterprises. Major national museums are managed by Independent Administrative Institutions (e.g., the National Institute for Cultural Heritage manages the Tokyo, Kyoto, Nara, and Kyushu National Museums). [3-Bunka]

**Miraikan (National Museum of Emerging Science and Innovation, Tokyo):**
- Established by Japan's Science and Technology Agency, famous for its Geo-Cosmos spherical exhibit (a 3D rendition of Earth with a resolution exceeding 10 million pixels, displaying daily satellite data). Located at 2-3-6 Aomi, Koto City, Tokyo (Odaiba). [1-MuseumNext][4-Gotokyo]
- Two permanent exhibitions, "Quantum Computer Disco" and "The Universe: Unread Messages," launched in April 2025, allow visitors to experience cutting-edge R&D. The Future Lab lets visitors experience cutting-edge research, development, and field trials, including the Miraikan Accessibility Lab (developing technologies to support people with visual impairments in collaboration with external organizations). The Dome Theater features 3D videos; the planetarium offers "Birthday - What Links the Universe and Me." Admission: General 630 yen; closed Tuesdays, New Year holidays, and from Oct. 1, 2026 to mid-April 2027 (refurbishment). Multilingual support in Japanese, English, Chinese (simplified), and Korean. [4-Gotokyo][5-Miraikan]
- **Sustainability as education (Green Museum Summit 2023):** Miraikan formed a sustainability promotion project team "contributing to the realization of a sustainable society," focusing on energy, water, food, and materials. Electricity accounts for 2,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions annually (the museum's largest source); district heating/cooling adds another 1,000 tonnes. Miraikan contracted Zero Watt Power (wind-power renewable energy supplier) to reduce electricity emissions to near zero. The museum's restaurant offers soy-based meat alternatives; vending machines eliminating plastic bottles were installed with free water dispensers. Yasushi Ikebe, Principal Investigator for Science Communication at Miraikan (PhD in astrophysics, 1995; at Miraikan since 2004), presented at the Green Museum Summit 2023. The museum's three prioritized areas: making business operations more sustainable, ensuring transparency in sustainability efforts as a public model, and engaging the community in dialogue about sustainability. [1-MuseumNext]

**National Museum of Nature and Science (Tokyo, kahaku.go.jp):**
- The Museum promotes "communication between science and society in general for the purpose of cultivating the kind of 'scientific literacy' that lends itself to scientific thinking, and rational judgment and behavior." It creates exhibitions and educational programs in collaboration with universities, academic societies, other museums, enterprises, and organizations both in Japan and overseas. [2-Kahaku]
- **Exhibitions:** Ueno exhibition theme is "Human Beings in Coexistence with Nature" — Japan Gallery ("The Environment of the Japanese Archipelago") and Global Gallery ("The History of Life on Earth"); Tsukuba Botanical Garden (approximately 3,000 plant species; Tropical Rainforest and Savanna Greenhouses); Institute for Nature Study (a cultural property designated as a natural monument and historic site; offers Nature Walks on Sundays, Natural History Seminars, Nature Classes for Children, and teacher trainings). [2-Kahaku]
- **Educational Programs:** Programs for children and adults drawing on the Museum's expertise, collection, and research results; partnerships with schools to develop study programs and promote teachers' understanding of museums; a University Partnership Program to improve students' science literacy and science communication skills; personnel training programs for science communicators to bridge science, technology, and society; and a volunteer system operating in all three districts. The Ueno district introduced its "Kahaku Volunteers" system in 1986, who serve as exhibition guides and participate in educational programs such as the "Touch and Talk Wagon." "Botanical Garden Volunteers" (Tsukuba) and "Shizen-en Volunteers" (Shirokanedai, established 2019) serve as garden guides and support educational programs. [2-Kahaku]

**Museum-School Collaboration (general):**
- The Museum Act's Article 3 lists twelve types of services museums engage in, including cooperating with schools and other facilities. [4-JLT]
- Japan's April 2002 education reform encouraged hands-on learning, with Japanese museums looking to U.S. counterparts as models. [6-STANFORD]
- Museum education in Japan is "primarily concerned with meaningful interaction with objects, activities, and knowledgeable people. There is nothing like seeing an original work of art with your own eyes, touching an artifact with your own hands, or engaging in activities with people of another culture to bring meaning to an otherwise dry set of facts." [6-STANFORD]

### 2. Policies, Laws, and Regulations

- **The Museum Act (1951, amended 2008, 2022):** Governs museum registration (accreditation by prefectural boards of education), standards, curator qualifications, public/private museum regulation, and the museum-equivalent facilities designation (Article 31). The 2022 amendment (effective April 1, 2023) expanded eligibility to NPOs and corporations (excluding national entities), mandated digital archiving, and introduced flexible registration. [1-Grokipedia][4-JLT]
- **Basic Act on Education (2006):** Article 12 promotes social education through museums; Article 13 mandates partnership among schools, families, and local residents. [5-MEXT]
- **Social Education Law (1949):** The foundation on which the Museum Act builds. [1-Grokipedia]
- **Basic Act on Culture and the Arts (2001):** Later alignment of the Museum Act. [1-Grokipedia]
- **Tax incentives:** Registered museums receive preferential treatment with regard to real estate acquisition tax and fixed asset tax; donors to registered museums are granted preferential treatment in the tax system. [3-Bunka]
- **Japan's Science Council 2023 advisory opinion** highlighted unresolved deficiencies: inconsistent entity classifications, inadequate curator qualifications, and digitization challenges for natural history specimen collections; proposed reforms include a unified registration system encompassing national museums, nationwide criteria tailored to museum types, third-party advisory organizations, and distinguishing "specialized curators" from "comprehensive curators." [1-Grokipedia]

### 3. Operating and Funding Models

- Museums in Japan are predominantly publicly funded: of 5,614 museums (FY2005), 4,023 were established by local governments, 129 national, 68 by independent administrative institutions, 603 by general incorporated associations/foundations, and 791 by private entities. [3-Bunka]
- Since 2003, public museums can use a designated management system that allows consignment to private enterprises. [3-Bunka]
- Public museums may not collect admission fees or compensation for using museum materials, "except in unavoidable circumstances for maintenance"; the national government may subsidize part of facility/equipment costs for local governments establishing museums; subsidies may be suspended or returned if accreditation is revoked, the museum closes, grant conditions are violated, or subsidies were obtained fraudulently. [4-JLT]
- Registered museums receive tax benefits and easier donation incentives. [3-Bunka]
- Miraikan admission: 630 yen general admission. [4-Gotokyo]

### 4. Featured Programs and Classic Case Studies

- **Miraikan (Tokyo):** Geo-Cosmos, Future Lab, Dome Theater, sustainability initiatives, and the Miraikan Accessibility Lab. [1-MuseumNext][4-Gotokyo][5-Miraikan]
- **National Museum of Nature and Science:** "Touch and Talk Wagon" (Kahaku Volunteers, since 1986), Nature Classes for Children, teacher trainings, science communicator training programs, and the University Partnership Program. [2-Kahaku]
- **School-museum partnerships:** The Museum Act explicitly lists cooperation with schools among museums' services; Japanese museums partner with schools to develop study programs and promote teachers' understanding of museums. [2-Kahaku][4-JLT]
- **Japanese science museums:** Japan has over 300 planetariums (second most in the world); the Japanese Council of Science Museums has 235 members and is located in the National Museum of Nature and Science; the Japan Science Museum Association has 184 members. [3-Bunka]

### 5. Distinctive Characteristics and Digital Technology Trends

- Japan's museum education is distinctive for: a statutory framework (Museum Act) that formally embeds museums in the social education system; the curator qualification system; the classification into registered/museum-equivalent/museum-like facilities; strong science-museum culture (Miraikan, National Museum of Nature and Science, 300+ planetariums); school-museum cooperation mandated and supported by law; and a "museum boom" in the 1980s–1990s integrating museums into regional cultural tourism. [1-Grokipedia][2-Wiki][3-Bunka]
- **Digital technology:** The 2022 Museum Act amendment mandates digital archiving. The Science Council noted digitization challenges for natural history specimen collections. Japan's Society 5.0 initiative is cited as a driver of Asia-Pacific growth in the virtual museums market (Asia Pacific is the fastest-growing region at 16.9% CAGR). [1-Grokipedia][18-Dataintelo]
- **Community-based museum education:** Museums are integrated into regional cultural tourism and community education through the social education framework. [1-Grokipedia][3-Bunka]

## VI. THE NETHERLANDS (Optional Representative Country)

### 1. Museum Education System and Institutional Organization

**NEMO Science Museum (Amsterdam):**
- NEMO is the largest science museum in the Netherlands, housed in a striking green building shaped like the bow of a giant ship (designed by Renzo Piano), located just east of Amsterdam Central Station. "The biggest difference with most museums is simple: children are encouraged to touch everything. They can build, test, push buttons and carry out experiments instead of quietly looking at objects behind glass." [6-Family][10-Rembrandts]
- Best suited for children aged 6-14; the "sweet spot" for a first visit is around ages 6-8. Ticket price in 2026 starts at €22 (one source says adults ~€17-18); children under four enter free. Families are allowed to bring their own lunch with designated picnic areas. At least four hours is recommended. [6-Family][10-Rembrandts]
- **Vision of learning:** NEMO views learning as a lifelong journey that "begins even before we're born and continues every day. It's not just about gaining knowledge, but about building skills, developing insight, sparking curiosity and nurturing the drive to explore." NEMO designs activities to spark curiosity, fuel imagination, and bring people together through diverse themes and hands-on experiences. [9-NEMO]
- **Endowed chair:** Maartje Raijmakers, endowed professor at the University of Amsterdam, is affiliated with NEMO through the chair of Cognitive Developmental Psychology, researching how people of all ages learn science in informal settings. [9-NEMO]
- **Visitor experience taxonomy:** NEMO uses a taxonomy of visitor experiences as a foundation for designing exhibitions and programs — visitors engage with science in six ways: gaining knowledge and insight; independently exploring and designing; reflecting on scientific ideas; feeling inspired by curiosity and experiencing motivation; identifying with scientific roles; and joining real research. [9-NEMO]

**Rijksmuseum (Amsterdam):**
- The Rijksmuseum and NEMO Science Museum jointly invite children and their families to investigate real works of art at "Mission Masterpiece" — becoming real-life science investigators. [7-Rijks]
- The Rijksmuseum Fellowship Programme offers researchers the opportunity to conduct part of their academic research at the museum, with fellowships including the Johan Huizinga Fellowship, the Migelien Gerritzen Fellowship (conservation and scientific research), and the Conrad Whelan 42 Fellowship. Funded by the Migelien Gerritzen Fund/Rijksmuseum Fund, Johan Huizinga Fund/Rijksmuseum Fund, Annenberg Foundation/Rijksmuseum Fund, Conrad Whelan 42 Fund/Rijksmuseum Fund, Dr. Anton C.R. Dreesmann Fund/Rijksmuseum Fund, and Pruikenburg Fund. Partners include the J.S. Lee Memorial Fellowship Programme, The Museum of National History at Frederiksborg, and Bard Graduate Center, plus a cross-fellowship/post-doctoral researcher hosting programme with the Musée du Louvre. [8-Rijks]
- The Rijksmuseum offers digital family games and the Teken-school education center with three studios. [13-HandsOn-Part1]

**Tropenmuseum Junior (Amsterdam):**
- The first European children's museums included Tropenmuseum Junior Amsterdam (1975); Tropenmuseum Junior is a CMA-Winner 2012 + Nominee 2021, featuring exhibitions like "Sabi Suriname" using sand animation and interactive music. [13-HandsOn-Part1]

### 2. Policies, Laws, and Regulations

- The Netherlands' museum education operates within the Dutch "Agenda 2026" framework mentioned in the French Delphi study context (a Dutch professional association report on the future of museums). [5-Pauget]
- The Children in Museums Award (CMA), established in 2011 by Hands On! International (based partly in the Netherlands) and the European Museum Academy, uses jury criteria including Innovation, Creating immersive learning environments, Embracing the Digital Revolution, Creative ways to use collections, Addressing contemporary issues, Achieving social impact, and Participation. [13-HandsOn-Part1]

### 3. Operating and Funding Models

- NEMO's ticket price starts at €22 (2026); children under four free. The museum is family-friendly, allowing visitors to bring their own lunch. [6-Family]
- The Rijksmuseum fellowship programme is funded by multiple named funds (Rijksmuseum Fund, Annenberg Foundation, Dr. Anton C.R. Dreesmann Fund, Pruikenburg Fund, etc.), illustrating Dutch museum reliance on private funds and foundations. [8-Rijks]

### 4. Featured Programs and Classic Case Studies

- **"Mission Masterpiece"** (Rijksmuseum + NEMO): invites children and families to investigate real works of art as real-life science investigators. [7-Rijks]
- **NEMO's "Humania" exhibition** (CMA-Nominee 2016 + 2021) covers complex topics for young learners. [13-HandsOn-Part1]
- **Rijksmuseum digital family games and Teken-school education center** with three studios. [13-HandsOn-Part1]

### 5. Distinctive Characteristics and Digital Technology Trends

- The Netherlands is notable for its science-museum pedagogy (NEMO's research-based visitor experience taxonomy and endowed university chair), children's museums (Tropenmuseum Junior), and strong family-oriented digital learning (Rijksmuseum digital games). The Rijksmuseum is cited among the European anchors of the virtual museums market (Europe held ~29.1% share in 2025, growing at 13.8% CAGR, anchored by the Louvre, British Museum, Uffizi, Hermitage, and Rijksmuseum, plus EU Horizon Europe and Creative Europe (EUR 2.4 billion) funding). ## VIII. CROSS-CUTTING AND INTERNATIONAL CONTEXT

**ICOM (International Council of Museums):**
- ICOM was founded in 1946 with a Children's Museums Committee (with a female chair and mostly female members), proving the early significance of children-focused museum work. [4-Part3]
- ICOM's 2022 museum definition was discussed in German museum digital talks (Brücke-Museum "Table Discussions"). [5-Brücke]
- **ICOM webinar "Recover and Recreate" (February 15, 2021):** Sponsored by the French Ministry of Culture, moderated by Dr. Mathew Trinca (National Museum of Australia). Speakers included Peter Keller (ICOM Director General), Ekaterina Travkina (OECD), Angelita Teo (Olympic Foundation for Culture and Heritage), María Mercedes González (Museum of Modern Art of Medellin), and Daniel Ronan (Resilient Heritage consultancy). Key data: in spring 2020, almost all museums worldwide were closed (95% for two or more months); one third of museums expected to lose more than half of their income; two-thirds of survey respondents expected their museum to reduce programs; 14% of staff were furloughed or had contracts not renewed (highest in North America at 20%); in spring, 13% expected their museum to close permanently, dropping to 6% by September (highest at 22% in the Arab region); half of museums worldwide increased their social media and online activities. World Economic Forum data predicted 85 million jobs displaced and 97 million new roles by 2025, with half of workers needing reskilling. Travkina argued museums should be part of recovery strategies at city, regional, and national levels and highlighted the OECD-ICOM Guide for Local Governments, Communities and Museums. [2-ICOM]

**UNESCO:**
- UNESCO published "Museums and children" by Ulla Keding Olofsson (1979), a 195-page book in the "Monographs on education" series (volume 12, ISBN 92-3-101692-X), available in English and French. [15-UNESCO]
- UNESCO's digital heritage programs support cultural preservation goals; UNESCO partnered with Google, Microsoft, and Matterport for all 1,199 World Heritage Sites. [16-FrameSixty][18-Dataintelo]

**Museum education as a field (Wikipedia overview):**
- Museum education falls under informal education — organized educational activity outside the formal system. The 1992 American Association of Museums report *Excellence and Equity* identified the educational role of museums as core to their public service. Museum pedagogy is influenced by constructivism, postmodernism, and critical multiculturalism. Teaching strategies include Visual Thinking Strategies (VTS), the dialogical model of art interpretation, Feldman's Model of Art Criticism, aesthetic scanning, and the FTC (Form+Theme+Context) Palette. [5-Wiki]
- **COVID-19 impact on the profession:** During the pandemic, ~95% of museums worldwide closed for part of 2020. A survey found Education positions were the second-most affected by layoffs/furloughs (40%), after Guest Services/Admissions (68%). Museums shifted to virtual programming including Zoom events, social media channels, take-home art activities, and virtual tours. [5-Wiki]

**Digital technology trends (international):**
- **Virtual museum tours:** Interactive digital experiences using immersive 3D environments via web browsers or VR headsets, evolving from static web images in the early 2000s to today's experiences powered by WebXR, OpenVR, HTML5, WebGL, and glTF standards, with platforms like Matterport and Sketchfab. Institutions highlighted include the Smithsonian (70% return visit rate), Louvre (12-minute average session duration), British Museum, Vatican Museums, Metropolitan Museum of Art (Met 360 Project), Getty (40% increase in educational downloads), and Tate Modern. Google Arts & Culture has partnered with over 2,000 museums worldwide. [16-FrameSixty]
- **Market data:** Global virtual museums market valued at $3.8 billion in 2025, projected to reach $12.6 billion by 2034 (CAGR 14.2%). North America led with 38.4% share (~$1.46 billion) in 2025; Europe second at ~29.1% (13.8% CAGR); Asia Pacific fastest-growing at 16.9% CAGR. Key drivers: immersive technology adoption (standalone VR headset shipments surpassed 12.8 million units in 2025; Meta Quest 3 and Apple Vision Pro installed base exceeded 28 million devices); government-backed digitization (EU Creative Europe allocated EUR 2.4 billion for 2021-2027; US disbursed $340+ million in digitization grants 2022-2025); AI integration (AI-powered guides respond in 50+ languages; institutions using AI personalization report session duration increases of 34-47%); educational integration (over 14,000 US school districts incorporated virtual museum field trips by 2025; global EdTech sector projected to exceed $400 billion by 2028). Key players: Google Arts and Culture (3,000+ institutional partners across 80 countries); Smithsonian (2.8-million-item Open Access collection, 200+ digital staff); British Museum, Louvre, Met, Rijksmuseum, Getty, Tate Modern, Vatican Museums, MoMA; technology vendors Matterport, Artsteps, Sketchfab, Kunstmatrix, Exhibbit. [18-Dataintelo]
- **Technology trends in museum education (ACME Ticketing, 2019):** Self-guided tour apps replacing traditional audio tours; Augmented Reality apps like Actionbound for personalized tours, scavenger hunts, missions, and educational games; Virtual Reality recreations of historical periods; 3D printing to recreate artifacts and create replicas. [19-ACME]
- **Academic meta-analysis (Zhou, Chen & Wang, 2022):** AR and VR have significant positive effects on academic achievement (ES=0.45) and perceptions (ES=0.59) in museum learning; museums have been recognized since the 19th century as important informal learning environments; theoretical foundations include experiential learning (Kolb), situated learning, active learning, and multimedia learning theory. [20-Zhou]
- **Peer-reviewed VR museum platform validation (Frontiers in Virtual Reality, 2026):** A Thai study (Saithong & Yoddee) developed the Isan Local VR Museum using high-resolution 3D photogrammetry (DSLR cameras and drones) and 360-degree panoramic imagery (3D Matterport camera), built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Expert quality rating: "Very Good" (mean = 4.63); end-user satisfaction: "Highest" (mean = 4.51) from 157 users. [17-Frontiers]
- **"Museum thinking" (Big Think, Oct 2025):** Kristen Alford (The Ubuntu Lab) described three aspects — objects as portals for storytelling and critical questioning; immersive physical spaces; and the participatory/communal nature of museums. Michael Radke noted museums "are among the more mature formal environments" regarding pedagogy and practice; informal learning has transformed STEM education over the past 40 years. Over the last 20 years (citing Nina Simon's "The Participatory Museum"), museums have moved from visitors contributing (sticky notes, voting) to communities having actual ownership of content (e.g., Māori communities at Te Papa in Wellington). The Ubuntu Lab is building the world's first globally distributed museum focused on "a public understanding of humanity," planning ~100 retail-sized spaces (like Apple stores) around the world over the next 10 years. [10-BigThink]

**OECD-ICOM Guide for Local Governments, Communities and Museums:** Highlighted by Ekaterina Travkina as a key resource for integrating museums into recovery strategies. [2-ICOM]

**Children-focused museum work — legal types, funding & partners (Hands On! guide):**
- Two superordinate categories: autonomous organizations (NGO/NPO: clubs, foundations, LLCs) and parts of overarching entities (public entities, traditional museums, corporate brands). Funding sources include public budgets, sales (tickets, shops, cafés, events), grants (EU programs like Creative Europe, Erasmus Plus, Horizon Europe, New European Bauhaus), and sponsoring. Key partners include individuals, cultural organizations, public governance departments, formal education institutions, and research institutions. Ten generic types of children-focused museum work: universal children's museum, topic-focused children's museum, inhouse children's museum, children-only museum, mobile/pop-up museum, family museum, children's exhibitions (hosting), children's exhibitions (development), children-focused programmes (inhouse and external), children-curated spaces, and children-themed museums. [4-Part3]

**International collaboration in museum education:**
- The MMFA-Louvre-Centre Pompidou "Le musée fait école" project exemplifies cross-national collaboration in museum education. [17-MMFA]
- The Rijksmuseum has a cross-fellowship/post-doctoral researcher hosting programme with the Musée du Louvre. [8-Rijks]
- An academic study (International Journal of Education & the Arts, 2025) examined tripartite collaboration among artists, museum educators, and schoolteachers at two large publicly funded contemporary art museums in New Zealand, finding that increased collaboration with artists facilitates a gradual shift for schoolteachers and museum educators from routine teaching practices to more flexible teaching pedagogies. [15-IJEA]
